Saudi Arabia dropped from World Rally Championship
- Published
The final round of the 2026 World Rally Championship (WRC) will be held in Italy instead of Saudi Arabia because of the ongoing unrest in the Middle East.
Saudi Arabia had been set to host the 14th and final rally of the season from 11-14 November.
The championship has now been shortened to 13 rounds and will conclude with the Rally Italia in Sardinia from 1-4 October.
Rally Saudi Arabia in Jeddah, which joined the WRC calendar in 2025, will still take place on the planned dates but as part of the Middle East Rally Championship.
The FIA, the global governing body for motor sports, said Saudi Arabia "remained ready to host the event safely" but the decision was due to "ongoing uncertainty in the region and its effect on logistical arrangements".

In a statement, FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem said: "We have worked closely with our partners to explore every possible route that would allow Rally Saudi Arabia to take place as planned.
"These are never easy decisions, particularly after the significant work undertaken by everyone involved in preparing for the event.
"While the WRC element of the event will not take place this year, our confidence in the organisers and in the long-term future of the rally remains unchanged."
Great Britain's Elfyn Evans sits at the top of the WRC standings before the final round, 17 points clear of Finland's Sami Pajari, and is the favourite to take the title with a maximum of 35 points up for grabs across the final round.
The Welshman has finished runner-up in the championship five times, and is looking to join former British winners Colin McRae and Richard Burns in winning the title.
Numerous conflicts are ongoing in the Middle East, including the Israel-Gaza war, with Israel and the United States at war with Iran and Saudi Arabia battling Houthi rebels in Yemen.
The WRC is not the first sporting event to avoid the region, with the FIA cancelling Formula One Grand Prix races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia in April.
The Bahrain race has since been relocated to Malaysia - to be staged in early October - with races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi later in the season are scheduled to go ahead as planned.
In February, tennis players, staff and media were left stranded in Dubai following missile strikes on the United Arab Emirates while in March, an ATP Challenger event in the country was disrupted by drone strikes. The sport's governing bodies are reportedly considering replacement hosts for events in the region for the 2027 season.
On Wednesday, English golfer Matt Fitzpatrick said he is not "100% comfortable" with prospect of travelling to Dubai for his DP World Tour Championship title defence in November.

Thailand’s Muslim separatists vow to fight for independence ‘until the end of time’
Since 2004, over 7,000 militants, security forces and civilians have been killed in the region, once part of a Malay-Muslim sultanate
“This struggle will continue until the end of time,” Nikmatullah Seri, the spokesman for the Barisan Revolusi Nasional (BRN) peace negotiation delegation, said in a rare interview. “As long as our objectives remain unachieved, we will continue to fight.”
Militants from BRN have fought for an independent Islamic nation in Thailand’s Muslim-majority south since the 1960s, although the current unrest began in 2004.
Thailand has been negotiating with the BRN under Malaysian mediation since 2013, the most recent high-level talks taking place in December. But the process has repeatedly stalled, and Bangkok suspended dialogue in July following an attack that killed five soldiers.

From -17 to dream European start for Bournemouth
- Published
'From -17 to Europe', read a flag in the away end at at the Anoeta Stadium.
As Bournemouth embarked on the first European campaign in the club's 127-year history, it served as a reminder of just how far they have come.
But a 2-1 victory at Real Sociedad in their Europa League opener shows they are not ready to stop there.
It is now 11 years since the Cherries were first promoted to the Premier League, meaning there is now a generation of supporters who will view top-flight football as the norm.
From that perspective then, qualifying and playing in Europe might simply appear the next logical step for a well-run and ambitious club.
"It's a brilliant win in our first European game. It's brilliant for the club and the 2,000 fans from Bournemouth," manager Marco Rose told TNT Sports.
Yet for the vast majority of fans celebrating a famous victory on Thursday, the whole thing still seems surreal.
Just 18 years ago, the club was on the brink. A 10-point deduction for entering administration resulted in their relegation to League Two.
To even stay in the Football League for the 2008-09 season, they had to accept a 17-point deduction and agree not to appeal against the decision after it was ruled that, as they had been unable to agree a Company Voluntary Arrangement, they had not met their terms for exiting administration.
Thoughts of a £100m-rated midfielder picking out a Brazil winger to head Bournemouth to victory in Europe was the stuff of fantasy as the Dorset club battled for survival.
But that now is Bournemouth's reality with Alex Scott swaggering around San Sebastian, showing why there is such a clammer for his signature among top Premier League clubs, and Rayan providing another example of why the Cherries will demand every penny of a reported £130m release clause to let him go.
Bournemouth have nothing to compare it to but this was a proper European away performance.
Up against a Real Sociedad side led by a World Cup-winning forward in Mikel Oyarzabal and who beat Atletico Madrid to win the Copa del Rey last season, they were dominant for 45 minutes.
They suffocated Sociedad with their relentlessness off the ball, winning the ball back high up the pitch time and again and showing the quality on the ball to create chances - even when the defence was set.
But there is an edge to the Basque side and, poor as they had been, that they came out fighting after the break was no surprise.
The adrenaline-fueled exuberance of Rose's side in the first half appeared to catch up with them in the second, but their desire to compete never wavered.
Bournemouth are not known for their defensive resilience and, as Sociedad ramped up the pressure as the game wore on, thoughts might have turned to leads surrendered in each of their first four Premier League games.
But the Cherries, aided by the sharp reflexes of Djordje Petrovic in goal, held on to secure a famous win.
"It was very intense and tough," Rose told TNT Sports.
"Brilliant first half in everything. The way we won balls and the possession high up. In the second half, we needed to suffer because we were not so sharp."
Speaking on BBC Radio Solent, former Cherries full-back Charlie Daniels added: "It is a big occasion. A big moment for the club, and they should be applauded for it."
Special moment for captain Smith
Bournemouth's incredible rise can be traced back to the appointment of Eddie Howe in January 2009.
The former boss guided the Cherries to safety, finishing nine points clear of the relegation zone despite that 17-point deduction.
A mere six and a half years later, Howe - back for his second spell as manager - had taken a transformed Bournemouth to the Premier League.
It was fitting then, that on this latest milestone night for the club, the team was led out by a man involved during Howe's first stint.
Adam Smith joined Bournemouth on loan during the 2010-11 campaign, returned on a permanent deal in 2014 and has been at the club ever since, with approaching 400 league appearances to his name.
"Adam has been with the club for so long," Daniels said. "Dedicated himself to the club, and it's such a proud moment, not only for him, but for his family, his team-mates and old team-mates to see how he's grown - not only as a player but as a man as well.
"To lead out the Cherries on this historical night is fantastic."
Smith also made history of his own, becoming, at 35 years and 141 days, the oldest English outfielder to make their debut in major European competition since Ipswich's Reginald Pickett in 1962.
The club captain will appreciate more than most what a special night this was for Bournemouth.
Things have been far from straightforward for the club, even in recent years, with relegation in 2020 and, since re-establishing themselves in the top-flight, the seemingly annual battle to replace players picked off by Europe's top clubs.
Even qualifying for Europe was not enough to keep hold of manager Andoni Iraola, who returns to the Vitality Stadium with his new club Liverpool on Sunday.
That pattern is unlikely to stop anytime soon but, while there is the prospect of more nights like this one, Bournemouth supporters won't be complaining.
They've seen enough to know that these are the good times.

Apple is working on an AI server that would use Apple’s high-performance M-series Ultra chips found in Mac desktops. The potential product’s expected release in 2029 would mark the first Apple server to hit the market in nearly two decades—and could capitalize on the surging popularity of Apple hardware among AI developers.
The enterprise server would come in two configurations that include either two or four of Apple’s future M8 Ultra chips, according to The Information. The project reportedly received support from new Apple CEO John Ternus when it began a year ago, back when Ternus led Apple’s hardware engineering efforts.
This revelation coincides with booming sales for Apple’s Mac mini and Mac Studio as AI developers and companies snap up the Mac computers to run AI workloads. The popularity of such computing devices that rely on Apple’s M-series Ultra chips has undoubtedly encouraged Apple’s pursuit of an enterprise server using the same chips.
The Information reported that AI companies such as OpenAI have bought “tens of thousands” of Mac minis and Mac Studios to train AI agents through trial-and-error reinforcement learning, while Anthropic has also rented Mac minis from Amazon Web Services.

FA chair demands Infantino release World Cup sell-off documents
- Published
Fifa president Gianni Infantino has been told to release all documents relating to his controversial plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup in a letter sent by Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt.
Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, said that the Fifa Council should also receive a written explanation for the cancelled suspension of United States forward Folarin Balogun at the World Cup.
Infantino should make all documents available before the next Fifa Council meeting, which is on 15 October.
The letter, also sent to Fifa secretary general Mattias Grafstrom, makes accusations of failures in governance and a breakdown in culture within the world football governing body.
Infantino has come under increasing pressure over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal.
FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all competitions, including World Cups, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.
The proposal was scrapped following widespread opposition from national associations.
Hewitt's letter adds that there should be an independent review of how FFE was conceived, by whom, and how the private investment was put to tender.
Last month, Uefa began preparing criminal legal proceedings against Infantino at three US courts over the FFE plan, demanded the release of all documents.
Fifa hit back and accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership" in a challenge to the litigation.
Infantino, 56, will stand for election for a fourth time in March, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate.
Balogun incident placed doubts in FA's mind
The Football Association was troubled by the Balogun situation from the outset, and had requested the release of the documents relating to his overturned ban during the World Cup.
Forward Balogun, 25, was allowed to play against Belgium in the last 16 when he would have expected to be serving a one-match suspension.
The striker had been shown a straight red card for a foul on defender Tarik Muharemovic in the 2-0 win over Bosnia-Herzegovina in the last 32.
Fifa then said the automatic one-match ban would be suspended for a year. No reasoning behind the move was provided, beyond citing a rule which allows punishments to be suspended.
The FA, which had sent a letter of support for Infantino's re-election before the Balogun incident, had deep concerns about political intervention.
US President Donald Trump later confirmed he called Infantino asking for Balogun's ban to be reviewed.
Then the FFE proposal, revealed through the media just days after the World Cup final, fractured the game.
Fifa and Infantino were accused of breaking trust "through deception" in an open letter issued by Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation last month.
Many national associations, including those of England, Wales and Scotland, have withdrawn letters of support for Infantino's re-election.
But Infantino still holds a great deal of support around the globe, with the confederations of Africa, South America and Oceania reiterating their backing.
After FFE was cancelled, Infantino called a meeting of the Fifa management board in Rabat, Morocco.
But as yet there has been no contact with the Fifa Council to explain the controversial plan.
That is set to change next month when Infantino must face Hewitt and the other 35 Fifa Council members.

For years, Microsoft and OpenAI have fought to keep certain information out of the public eye in their fight with news organizations that have accused the AI firms of teaming up to violate copyright laws by stealing tons of news content to train AI.
However, now the details that should never have been marked confidential are starting to leak. In a motion for summary judgment that was unsealed Thursday from news plaintiffs led by The New York Times, internal documents are exposed that news groups alleged show exactly how Microsoft and OpenAI viewed the threat to news before unleashing new AI products like ChatGPT and Copilot.
Perhaps most explosively, Microsoft Director of Applied Science Brent Hecht repeatedly warned in documents that scraping news for AI training was “an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions,” calling it perhaps the “largest theft of labor in human history,” news orgs said. In another document, Hecht contradicted Microsoft and OpenAI’s argument that training AI on news content is fair use, suggesting that the plan to widely scrape news made “a complete mockery of the idea of ‘fair use.’”
Over at OpenAI, ChatGPT head Nick Turley wrote in an internal message that publishers would face an “existential threat” from commercial products trained on news content that can be used to substitute news providers. One Microsoft document even described a “doom loop,” news orgs said, “that will hurt the performance of our models and the entire web at the same time.”
“It is highly unusual that an end-product threatens the economic foundations of its essential suppliers, but that is the situation we have created for our LLM business with respect to its ‘content supply chain,’” that document said.
Data from both firms shows that this prediction was accurate. Microsoft recorded 83–93 percent drops in click-through rates for some news plaintiffs, and 51–94 percent drops for others. Add to that reporting on low click-through rates from ChatGPT search results and news organizations’ own reporting on traffic declines. Suddenly, it becomes easier to see how declining news revenue could ultimately rob chatbots of the abundant streams of reliable information that supposedly makes them such groundbreaking tools.
Meanwhile, “almost no one intended for content they created to be used in this fashion, nor are they compensated for its use,” Hecht acknowledged in a Microsoft document.
News organizations say they’re ready to go to trial because there’s so much “compelling evidence of substitution.” If they can prove that chatbots are replacing them in their own markets, while serving to spit out excerpts of articles verbatim, they think that one-two punch may eviscerate Microsoft and OpenAI’s fair use arguments.
“The future not just of journalism but of responsible AI too depends on preserving incentives for humans to produce the creative works on which a healthy society depends,” news groups argued.
Chatbots are “largely substitutive, period”
Under oath, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella testified that AI companies shouldn’t be violating news sites’ terms of use by dodging paywalls. But over at OpenAI, internal messages showed that when a staffer, Nick Ryder, informed President Greg Brockman that “a hack” was found for OpenAI crawlers “to get around” the NYT paywall, Brockman replied, “Ah, nice.”
Nadella also acknowledged that chatbots have served as substitutes for news platforms, describing the chatbot as stealing clicks from news sites by “giving you the information right there on the website on the AI platform versus needing to go to the underlying source.”
There’s consensus on that at OpenAI, where a software engineer said in an internal message that “no matter how prominently we show the links, users won’t click.”
OpenAI’s Turley agreed that there is “no good reason to click” when the chatbot provides information, the motion said. He also seemingly suggested that the doom loop was already in motion, describing chatbots as “largely substitutive, period” and predicting that they “will get more and more substitutive as they get better.”
News groups argued that insiders’ own statements should be damning.
“With respect to outputs that are substantially similar to training or grounding sources, courts have rejected claims that copying news articles to provide a product that substitutes for demand for news is fair use,” news groups argued.
Microsoft disclaims exec’s comments
News groups tried many different tactics to test if Microsoft and OpenAI products would output their news articles verbatim. Their motion shows they went further than early strategies where they would ask chatbots to provide access to entire news stories by repeatedly asking “what’s the next line?”
In some cases, news organizations found that chatbots would generate long excerpts of articles when users requested summaries of articles. Other flagged outputs were generated by asking for key bullet points of articles. Particularly successful were prompts requesting that chatbots “rate the bias” of news articles. Chatbots also reproduced portions of articles if users asked them to pick any article off a certain site’s homepage.
In their motion, news plaintiffs have only asked the court to rule on infringed articles where outputs “demonstrate extensive verbatim overlap,” because they’re confident that the “substitutive purposes of defendants’ copying weigh against fair use.” Legal concerns with other articles will be raised at trial, they said.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to Ars’ request to comment.
However, a Microsoft spokesperson defended Microsoft’s AI products as a transformative fair use that don’t substitute for news sites. The spokesperson said that Nadella’s testimony touched on “broad principles and changes underway in how people find and consume information,” which were merely “observations” that “should not be confused with conclusions about copyright questions before the Court, which Microsoft addresses in its filings.”
Regarding Hecht’s comments, the spokesperson claimed that those documents only “reflect one employee’s individual perspective, are not a legal analysis, and do not represent the company’s views.”
Steven Lieberman, counsel for the New York Daily News and seven of its sister papers, disagrees. He told Ars that “the evidence revealed here for the first time shows that OpenAI and Microsoft knew that what they were doing was wrong.”
“Throughout this case Defendants insisted that these documents be treated as confidential so that the public could not see them,” Lieberman said. “Well, now the cat is out of the bag. Finally, the world can see what OpenAI and Microsoft thought all along about the fairness of their own behavior.”
Microsoft exec described “accidental cover up”
News plaintiffs have argued that regardless of the individual expressing the views, the internal documents make clear that firms anticipated that verbatim outputs would harm news sites. Further, they alleged that instead of preventing the outputs, the firms tried to make it harder for news groups to test chatbots by creating a filter that Hecht suggested could be perceived as an “accidental cover up” because it would result in “people who have a right over the content having less visibility into what was used for training.”
News groups are also upset that instead of listening to insiders warning that scraping news was theft, Microsoft and OpenAI never chose to license content, allegedly usurping them in another market in ways they couldn’t anticipate.
Specifically, their motion accused Microsoft of violating “industry norms” by selling a dataset purchased for Bing as training data for OpenAI, allegedly doing so without consulting news groups that would not have approved of that repurposing of their consent to basic search engine crawling. Further, OpenAI allegedly “acted improperly” by obtaining a NYT dataset with 1.8 million articles from a third party that was bound to an agreement that the data wouldn’t be used for commercial purposes. OpenAI’s employees knew it “would not be appropriate” to use that data “to train a model,” but they did it anyway, news groups alleged.
For news groups, the problem isn’t just Microsoft and OpenAI, but all the AI firms that are following their lead in “free-riding” on their content, the motion said. Most notably, after ChatGPT’s launch, Google’s AI Overviews was quickly introduced and started absorbing even more traffic that previously went to news sites.
If courts don’t clarify that AI firms must license news content, both news publishers and AI firms could be doomed, news plaintiffs argued. One Microsoft internal document agreed that “there is a ‘real risk’ that GenAI could ‘significantly disrupt’” the “employment of the very people who generated the data on which the foundation model was trained,” they noted. Microsoft even included a cartoon illustrating the problem of LLMs destroying their own supply chains, they said:
“AI companies remain powerless to break out of this ‘doom loop,’ because, while the industry as a whole would benefit if every company paid to sustain the continued production of the creative works their technology depends on, each individual company is better off taking content for free while others pay,” news groups argued.
As evidence of this blind greed, their motion emphasized that Brockman wrote that he was “deeply motivated by the gazillions” that could be gained by commercializing OpenAI’s technology.
“Finding that copying news for AI is not fair use would solve this prisoners’ dilemma by putting all AI companies, OpenAI and Microsoft included, on an even footing,” news organizations said.
This story was updated with a quote from New York Daily News counsel Steven Lieberman.
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

Imagine walking into a neighbourhood medical store with a prescription in hand. The pharmacist checks the medicine, packs it and hands it over. But what happens when there is no prescription? According to a nationwide survey, for a large number of consumers, the answer is that the medicine may still be sold. The finding comes as the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has proposed installing CCTV cameras at medical stores to make prescription-medicine sales traceable.
The survey, conducted by LocalCircles, saw about 1.06 lakh responses from consumers across 327 districts of India. Of the total respondents, 63% were men and 37% women. Besides, 52% of them were from tier-1 districts, 29% from tier-2 districts and 29% from tier-3, 4 and 5 districts.
The survey found that 64% of consumers said their chemist never or rarely asked for a doctor’s prescription before selling medicines in the past 12 months. Only 15% said their chemist mostly or always refused to sell medicines without a prescription. The survey also found that only 31% of consumers were able to get assistance from a qualified pharmacist most of the time or always, while 13% said they were assisted by someone who was not a qualified pharmacist.
The findings come as the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has floated a draft notification proposing mandatory CCTV surveillance at every medical store that dispenses drugs sold on a doctor’s prescription. Under the proposal, the supply, other than by wholesale, of any drug sold on the prescription of a Registered Medical Practitioner would have to take place under a CCTV surveillance system installed and maintained at the premises.
The proposal also comes against the backdrop of intensified enforcement in multiple States against chemists selling prescription medicines without valid prescriptions, operating without registered pharmacists and failing to provide proper bills.
Neighbourhood chemist remains the main source
The survey found that the neighbourhood chemist remains the primary source of medicines for most consumers. The question on how respondents had primarily purchased medicines in the previous 12 months received 16,822 responses. This revealed that 86% of the respondents primarily depended on local chemists, followed by 14% on ePharmacy apps.
Who is actually behind the counter?
The survey then looked at whether consumers were receiving assistance from qualified pharmacists when they needed help with medicine or disease-related queries. The question received 19,409 responses. 31% of the consumers said they were able to get assistance from a qualified pharmacist most of the time or always. 27% of them said they never or very rarely received such assistance.
Home delivery is not free of the prescription gap
The survey also examined prescription checks when medicines were delivered to consumers’ homes. The question received 15,473 responses. 41% of consumers surveyed said a prescription was never or rarely asked for during home delivery.
A missing bill can mean a missing trail
Consumers were also asked whether they received proper bills when buying medicines from local chemists. Of the 20,573 respondents, 26% said they were not provided a GST bill. “A bill is not merely a tax document. It carries the batch number, expiry date and identity of the seller and provides a record if a medicine turns out to be expired, defective or counterfeit,” it said.
The survey also sought to establish whether consumers had purchased medicines that later turned out to be counterfeit or ineffective. The question received 18,457 responses. 15% of consumers said they had bought medicines that were later found to be fake or counterfeit.

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, has said he will not deploy the military to the Middle East in a way that could draw the country into conflict, resisting calls from Donald Trump to support his war in Iran.
“There won’t be deployment that would involve or enter war. I can tell you that very clearly,” Lee said at a news conference on Friday. “We won’t deploy military assets in any form to that end.”
However, Lee added that he was reviewing whether to play a greater role in safeguarding navigation in the region. South Korea maintains a naval presence off the coast of Somalia as part of an anti-piracy mission.
“[It] is also clear that we must do the minimum as other countries do to protect our commercial shipping and crude shipments, and also the safety of our people,” he said.
Trump has criticised Seoul for what he called insufficient support for the Iran war and scaled back major joint military drills by the two countries’ armed forces this summer, a move that unsettled the US ally.
South Korea’s government has been reviewing a possible military deployment to the Strait of Hormuz, although the idea is proving unpopular domestically.
Asked about progress in reaching an agreement with the US on Seoul’s US investment commitments under its trade deal with Washington, Lee said concern over the commercial viability of the package was the main sticking point.
Lee said there were elements that were difficult for Seoul to accept, but that the two sides were nearing an agreement.
South Korea committed last year to invest $350bn in US manufacturing in return for Washington lowering tariffs on Korean imports to 15%.
Seoul this week postponed a parliamentary briefing on the investment plans, which is expected to take place next week instead.
The South Korean president also said it was possible that a meeting could take place in the coming months between Trump and the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, but many factors needed to align for that to happen.
“What’s clear is that President Trump wants talks, and I want him to as well, and we’re continuing coordination to make dialogue between the North and the US possible,” he said.
North Korean state media has so far remained largely silent on the repeated calls from Trump for such a meeting. Trump has been pushing aides for a meeting with Kim as soon as the autumn, the Wall Street Journal has reported.

EU announces plan to restrict social media access for under-15s
- Published
The EU has announced plans to restrict social media access for under-15s across its member states, in a bid to increase wellbeing and tackle online safety.
Under the plans, there would be a gradual approach to children using social media which would include banning under 13s from accessing platforms.
Those aged 13 to 15 would only be able to access platforms for an hour per day via "mini accounts" set up through their parent or guardian's social media account.
The European Commission said social media companies would need to prove their platforms were safe by design, while EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the move would "put parents back in the driving seat".
She added the legislation - called the EU Kids Act - would give parents "the tools to help their children navigate a safer world".
"Too many children are being exposed too early to an online world they are not ready to navigate - an environment where bullying can follow you home, where every mistake can be recorded forever," von der Leyen said.
Under the act, only children aged 15 and over would be able to set up their own social media accounts.
But von der Leyen told the EU Parliament on Thursday that "an age limit does not mean letting tech companies off the hook for the content on the platform".
She added that under the legislation - if it is approved - companies would be required to submit detailed child safety plans.
"For every person under 18, the platforms must follow the principal of safety by design, no toxic or addictive features, no traps, etc," she said.
The proposal sets out that age would be verified using the EU's preexisting age verification app.
Von der Leyen had previously proposed a social media "delay" for children in Europe, saying in May that "the discussion about a minimum age for social media can no longer be ignored".
The policy, formally outlined on Thursday, was also trailed in the EU chief's annual address on Wednesday.
Some individual EU countries have already announced their own separate plans to restrict social media for children, including France and Spain.
Any potential EU-wide legislation would supersede those, but it would be possible for individual EU members to then go further than the bloc's action.
It is not clear which platforms the proposed bloc-wide measures would apply to, but von der Leyen said the Commission had "looked at Australia" when putting together the proposal.
Platforms like Instagram, Snapchat and TikTok were banned for under-16s in Australia in December last year.
The ban has been difficult for the country to enforce, with its Communications Minister Anika Wells admitting earlier this month that so far no tech firm had been fined despite research showing many under-16s were still on platforms.
A similar ban for under-16s is set to come into force in the UK in spring next year.

Tailgate parties, marching bands... and Ted Lasso? Wembley hosts US college game
- Published
The NFL has been playing in London since 2007 but now a different kind of American football is coming to the capital of England.
American college football games were being played abroad long before the NFL headed overseas, in countries as diverse as Cuba, Japan and Tanzania.
But this Saturday the UK will host just its second college football game, and it will be a far bigger event than the first at Crystal Palace in 1988.
About 2,500 fans were there that day, whereas 60,000 will be at Wembley to watch the Kansas Jayhawks face the Arizona State Sun Devils (17:00 BST).
The inaugural Union Jack Classic (UJC) will feature marching bands, spirit squads and tailgate parties outside the stadium - and Ted Lasso actor Jason Sudeikis might be there too.
Why bring a college game to London?
The UJC chief executive is entrepreneur Brian Dubiski. He and a business partner both played college football, with the latter then working with the NFL in London.
And while chatting over a few beers, they asked themselves why no-one had taken college football back to England, especially since Wembley's first NFL game in 2007.
After mulling the idea over for a few years, they decided to do it themselves and managed to book a date at English football's national stadium.
Then they had to find the teams. Brett Yormark, commissioner of the Big 12 Conference, is "bullish" about building its global appeal and was keen to be involved.
So two Big 12 teams committed to the trip. Founded in 1890, the University of Kansas (KU) has one of the oldest college teams and wants to expand its brand, while the game coincides with Arizona State (ASU) opening a London campus this month.
Before this trip, most of their players did not own a passport so both teams also wanted to give them a cultural experience they will never forget.
- What is the Union Jack Classic and who is in it? 
  - Published16 hours ago
What makes college football different?
Virtually all NFL players come via the US college system, and in many parts of America, college football is more popular than the NFL.
College games often have bigger crowds - eight of the world's 10 biggest stadiums are for college football, all holding more than 100,000.
The fans are also more passionate as support is often passed down from one generation to another, and multiple generations attend the same school. Kansas player Calvin Clements, for example, is a fifth-generation Jayhawk.
Actor Paul Rudd is also a Jayhawk, while lifelong fan Jason Sudeikis grew up in Kansas and frequently weaves KU references into his work.
"They're very spirited, and you get the tribalism, so it's the closest thing we have to European football fanbases," Dubiski told BBC Sport.
Both the NFL and college football have tailgate parties, where fans gather in the car park and eat and drink for hours before the game.
But college football fans chant during games, which feature marching bands and spirit squads - made up of cheerleaders, dancers and mascots.
"We want the game to showcase what we think is one of the greatest sports in America," said Yormark.
"There's something special about college football - the pageantry, the traditions, the fandom. It's dynamic - there's a lot of energy and passion. It truly is an experience."
Who has bought tickets?
According to the NFL, 14 million people in the UK identify as fans of America's biggest sports league.
UJC organisers have tried to tap into that fanbase and the UK infrastructure the NFL has built, but also appeal to younger fans.
It formed partnerships with the British American Football Association (Bafa), British Universities and Colleges Sport (BUCS), and the Jacksonville Jaguars, who host an annual NFL game at Wembley.
About 60,000 tickets have been sold and 15,000 fans are travelling from the US, with student sections to help create the typical college gameday atmosphere.
"We're really pleased with that in year one," said Dubiski. "We never expected to sell the stadium out, and 60,000 is higher than the average Big 12 attendance."
Dubiski agreed an exclusive multi-year deal with Wembley and is already working on games in the next three years. He might expand to other European cities and bring basketball games too.
Why college football could rival NFL
Yormark believes a positive experience for fans and players would constitute success, plus an exciting game.
Former NFL quarterback Robert Griffin III, now a college football analyst with Fox Sports, agrees that "we've got to bring excitement".
"The way to encourage fandom is to create moments, so I'm happy the two teams coming over know how to score points - and score them in bunches," he said.
Griffin also believes college football could ultimately be more successful overseas than the NFL.
"The fandom around college football is better, it just is," he added. "It's more similar to world football so there's a better opportunity to connect, also because there's more teams. In the NFL there's 32, but in college football there's 400 you can fall in love with.
"And if you want to be a real NFL fan, you have to be a college football fan because that's the feeder system into the league and you get to watch these guys develop."
What's happening on gameday?
Griffin will be at Wembley as part of Fox's team for their flagship pre-game show, which has gone overseas for the first time, with coverage starting two hours before kick-off.
"They'll be set up right outside Wembley," said Dubiski. "They get the crowd worked up into a frenzy, so it's loud, it's boisterous and a lot of fun.
"We've focused on picking up the tailgating experience and Americana of a college gameday in the States and planting it in London."
The main tailgate party begins at 10:00 - seven hours before kick-off - serving authentic Kansas barbecue food, and there will be cheerleaders and marching bands on Wembley Way.
Inside the stadium, there is a pre-game music line-up and half-time show, and organsiers hope Sudeikis is among the crowd. He and some British actors have been invited, although it is not confirmed who will attend.

Fin Smith sets England autumn ultimatum to hit form
- Published
England fly-half Fin Smith says an under-par autumn should trigger fundamental questions about the team's direction.
The 24-year-old was asked by Rugby Union Weekly about the state of the team after a miserable Six Nations and a summer campaign that featured a 45-21 defeat by world champions South Africa, a 73-8 thrashing of Fiji and a narrow 31-24 win over Argentina.
"It is so hard to say," replied Smith.
"I am not going to sit here and say 'we are building' because that is what you will get every time.
"We will honestly find out in the autumn. If we have a pretty ropey autumn, on the back of building some momentum over the summer, I think we will need to have a pretty hard look at ourselves."
England will play Australia, Japan and New Zealand on successive weekends in November, before a play-off against a southern hemisphere opponent in the finale of the new Nations Championship competition.
"Playing New Zealand at Allianz Stadium will be a great way to test ourselves," said Smith.
"I think on our day, in front of a big crowd and when we are up for it, we can beat anyone. The last time New Zealand came we had a great result."
England beat the All Blacks 33-19 last November in arguably the high point of head coach Steve Borthwick's near four-year spell in charge.
However the team's form has tailed off in 2026, with only three wins in eight Tests. A chastening 42-21 defeat at home by Ireland and a first-ever loss to Italy were among the low points.
Smith, who has started the past five Tests to establish himself as first-choice stand-off ahead of George Ford and Marcus Smith, says he is getting aligned with the demands of Test rugby and Borthwick's gameplan.
"I have been given a fair bit of licence to put my footprint on the attack and lead a lot of meetings about how I want us to play," he said.
"England are probably set up in a slightly different way. Northampton would probably be slightly more attacking and set up with maybe a slightly lighter-weight forward pack that might be suited to the style of play there.
"England is a little bit more set-piece and arm wrestle and tactical, so I have to adapt my game to suit that as well.
"But most of the time I am just going out there to just play what I see."
Dowson admits ambition to step up to Test role
Smith's Northampton boss Phil Dowson has said he has aspirations to eventually coach internationally, having racked up four impressive seasons in charge at Franklin's Gardens.
As director of rugby, the 44-year-old has led Saints to two Prem titles and the 2025 Champions Cup final.
That success has shown in England's selections. Northampton provided six players – more than any other club - to England's Nations Championship squad this summer.
"Fundamentally, we are having a great time at Northampton," Dowson said of himself and head coach Sam Vesty.
"From a personal point of view, at some point, we'd like to coach international rugby because it is different.
"There's no timeline on that. That's not just England. It is just the opportunity to go and do something different to test ourselves - either as a team or individually - under different pressure and to have new experiences."
Dowson said there has been no contact from the Rugby Football Union about preparing him for such an opportunity with England.
He prepared a developmental England XV's forwards, external for a fixture against the Barbarians in May 2019, but has not been brought into the fold since.
Vesty, meanwhile, was seconded to be the attack coach for England A's 91-5 rout of Portugal in February 2024. Back in 2017, he also stepped in as skills coach under Eddie Jones for England's summer tour to Argentina.
Both men signed new contract extensions with Northampton in December.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Kang "Kay" Soo-il, a 39-year-old South Korean national who quit his job and traveled, before returning home to run a farm. It has been edited for length and clarity.
Eight years ago, at 31, I was living in a Korean city south of Seoul, and working as a software developer and designer for Samsung Electronics. Burned out, I texted my friends, "I'm quitting my job to travel the world!"
Lily, then my childhood friend, who's now my wife, replied: "I'm also quitting my job." At the time, she was working as a flight attendant. The timing was a complete coincidence. We'd known each other since middle school, and got back in touch.
We both grew up in Yesan, a rural town that's about a two-and-a-half-hour drive from Seoul. She grew up on her family's farm where they grew deodeok, or bonnet bellflower. It's a mountain root vegetable commonly used in Korean cooking. I lived a 10-minute walk away.
We started dating in January and were married by May. A month after our wedding, we started traveling the world together.
Newlyweds traveling the world
We started in Russia, cut through Europe, and traveled through North and South America for about two years from 2018 to 2020. We funded our travels with the savings from our work. We spent extra time in Calgary, Canada, because I'd loved it there as a study abroad student. During that year in Calgary, we noticed how proud the local farmers were of their work.
In South Korea, that kind of atmosphere doesn't exist. Farming can often be viewed with a sense of shame. But since my wife's father is a farmer, she's always taken pride in her roots.
Traveling abroad, Lily noticed that deodeok was impossible to find abroad. It's not an ingredient that's widely exported, and when it is, it's rarely cooked the same way outside Korea.
Returning to the countryside
During our travels, we also came to realize that we preferred the calm countryside towns over big capitals like Paris. In 2020, we decided to return home and take over my wife's family's farm. It wasn't difficult to get permission from her parents. They were OK with it from the start.
Back then, it was called Ssabdari Deodeok. It's a third-generation family-run farm started by Lily's grandmother nearly 45 years ago. At the end of 2022, we launched it as Deodeokmong, or Dream of Deodeok.
Other than helping out my parents when I was young, who grew food on their weekend plot, I'd never really raised a crop from start to finish. We trailed her father at first to learn the basics of farming.
During our first two years, we operated the farm as usual, but I noticed that we threw out almost 50% of our produce because it wasn't attractive enough for the market. We couldn't afford to sustain the business by selling only half our harvest. We decided to pivot by using these in popular products like butter cookies, lattes, and scones studded with deodeok.
In 2022, we also secured a local government small-business support program grant for about 100 million South Korean won, or about $70,000, bought new equipment, and hired a design studio to help with the rebrand and renovation. It took nearly a year, and we're still developing the business, but the program grant changed everything.
Soon, local resorts reached out to feature our products in their lobbies. The Hyundai Department Store invited us to host pop-up markets in Seoul.
Older customers have told me that they love that young farmers are keeping traditional crops alive. The younger city buyers are probably attracted to our packaging; it's not the usual old-fashioned, medicinal stuff you find elsewhere.
My wife focuses on branding, marketing, and product development. I focus on planting, farming, accounting, and making the products.
Running a farm while raising a family
We have a five-year-old daughter and we're expecting our second child soon. Honestly, I haven't found the right balance between parenthood and work yet. I wake up around 6 a.m., send our daughter to kindergarten by 9 a.m., work, and when she comes home at 4 or 5 p.m., I focus on her.
My candid advice to anyone dreaming of quitting their corporate job to farm? Don't do it!
Farming is so difficult that it often feels like a futile endeavor. But if you've deeply considered your options and won't give up, test-drive the lifestyle first.
Try living in the countryside for at least three months. If you still enjoy the lifestyle, then go ahead. And read widely — not just technical farming guides, but business and branding books. Building a modern farm isn't just about growing crops; it's as complex as sales and marketing.

The Delhi High Court on Wednesday (September 16, 2026) asked the Centre to respond on whether it was contemplating formulating a policy to regulate addiction-causing design features on social media platforms like infinite scroll and autoplay.
A bench of Justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre and Justice Amit Sharma said it would hear a PIL seeking the constitution of an expert committee to examine engagement-maximising and addiction-causing design features on social media platforms after three weeks. It asked Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma to take instructions on the issue.
Mr. Sharma said that it would be in the domain of the policymakers to consider some of the issues raised in the plea and suggested that the petitioner could submit a representation to the government.
The counsel for the Centre and certain social media platforms also took objection to the maintainability of the petition in view of some orders from the Supreme Court and high courts which refused to entertain petitions on a similar issue.
Addictive architecture
Petitioner Vikas Kathuria, a professor of law, said the fulcrum of the issue is not what content social media platforms carry, but how such platforms are architecturally designed to cause addiction through infinite scroll, autoplay, algorithmically curated and personalised feeds, notification systems, and variable-reward engagement metrics, such as “likes”, to capture, retain and repeatedly re-stimulate the attention of the user.
The plea said the concern assumes significance in the Indian context as statistics reveal that Indian youths aged 18-24 spend more than an average of 120 minutes daily on social media.
It has been clinically proven that long hours on social media are linked to suicide and depression among adolescents, the petition said.
The plea sought the court’s direction to the Central Government and the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights to restrict, prohibit, or regulate the use of these features.

Around this time of year, new products launch left and right. I wrote similar words just yesterday ahead of Boox launching its latest devices. And now, Dyson, one of the big names in vacuum cleaners, just launched three innovative products.
Dyson already announced several new products earlier in September, from vacuums to an electric toothbrush with a built-in camera. Some of those vacuums are now available to buy, specifically the three robot vacuums in the new Dyson Nurovi line: the Dyson R1 Nurovi Dry ($550), the Dyson R2 Nurovi Wash + Dry ($700), and the Dyson R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV ($1,200).
This robot vacuum line has a new look, but the technology has changed too. All three Nurovi models share a light gray color scheme that makes the base station and vacuum easy to distinguish from the Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai, but the base stations keep the canister-style compartments that make these vacuums look and feel distinctly Dyson. They also feature lidar laser-precision navigation—Dyson's last robot vacuum relied on an HD camera—and the most expensive model now uses a UV light to help find stains on your floors. Finally, they have what Dyson calls a Twin-Capture System to pick up dust and debris on both hard floors and carpets. The cheapest R1 model is a vacuum only, while the R2 and R3 are both vacuum-mop hybrids. But the R2 will only be available at Costco, while the R1 and R3 will be available on Dyson's website (and presumably at other retailers).
Here's a look at the three new robot vacuums. I'll be testing these soon to see how they measure up against similar vacuums, but a few features already intrigue me.
Dyson’s Nurovi Robot Vacuum Lineup
The Nurovi R1 is a vacuum-only robot, but like its siblings, it uses lidar to navigate and features the Twin-Capture tech. It promises a much better experience than what we had with the Dyson Vis Nav from a few years ago. It's an interesting option if you have mostly carpet and soft flooring that doesn't need a mop job, but I'm curious to see how it compares, since you can find other vacuums for this price that do both.
Dyson R2 Nurovi Wash+Dry for $700
This is the vacuum I'm most intrigued about. It's a great price point—nearly half the price of the Spot+Scrub model—but has lidar navigation and the new Twin-Capture technology. It has triangle-style pads for mopping, which is unique and something I hope works as well as I imagine, as someone who loves to corner-test a robot vacuum. It promises 21,000 Pa of suction, which is a nice amount of power. The only downside is that you need a Costco membership to purchase one, as it's a Costco exclusive.
Dyson R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV for $1,200
This is the new top-of-the-line model of Dyson's robot vacuums. I wasn't super impressed by the previous Spot+Scrub Ai, since it didn't really seem to find stains. My favorite robot vacuum uses UV successfully to spot stains on floors, so I'm curious whether this Dyson model will deliver a similarly great experience. This vacuum still incorporates AI, which Dyson says can identify up to 200 types of household substances and clean them until they're gone. Why the Bomb Is Bad for Democracy
A famous documentarian’s new book suggests that secrecy is a major impediment to sensible nuclear policy.
“In August of 1945, the city of Hiroshima was destroyed in about nine seconds by a single atomic bomb.” So begins the 1981 documentary The Day After Trinity, in a voice-over against a black background. “The man responsible for building the bomb was a gentle and eloquent physicist named J. Robert Oppenheimer.”
Directed by a young filmmaker named Jon Else and financed by a public-television station in San Jose, The Day After Trinity quickly became a hit across the United States. One of its innovations was to pair the story of the bomb with that of Oppenheimer, foregrounding the contradiction of this “gentle” pacifist giving the nation its greatest weapon of war. As the historian David K. Hecht has argued, Else’s film helped transform Oppenheimer from a Cold War political figure into a symbol of the profound moral dilemmas inherent in the nuclear age.
In the years since the documentary premiered, Americans have continued to view Oppenheimer (and, by extension, his bomb) through Else’s lens. American Prometheus, the Pulitzer Prize–winning biography written by Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin, repeatedly cites Else’s interview transcripts and largely replicates his approach. Oppenheimer, Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster 2023 film adaption of the book, does much the same.
Now Else, at 82, has revisited the bomb, this time in a nonfiction book he’s been working on for 20 years. Yet Frenchman Flat: The Rise and Fall of Atomic Bombs is not another story of the doomed Oppenheimer; Else relies on his own remarkable interviews from almost half a century ago but doesn’t focus on the scientist, and he declines to “relitigate the decision to drop the bomb” on Japan.
Neither is Frenchman Flat quite what its publisher is promoting, the “story of a single nuclear bomb” (a 37-kiloton nuke called Priscilla that exploded over Frenchman Flat, a dry lake bed in Nevada, in 1957). That story, though compellingly told, disappears for whole swaths of the text. Instead, much to its credit, the book unspools an unhurried, capacious story of human society’s collective journey to the brink of annihilation, and of the individuals and movements that have, so far, held us back from the edge. It is a major work, highlighting the heroism and the absurdity of our atomic present and this Strangelovian, Lovecraftian thing we call “nuclear policy.”
Today, the famous Doomsday Clock, which measures the risk of nuclear cataclysm, is at just 85 seconds from midnight, the closest it’s been to Armageddon since the clock’s creation in 1947. After decades of disarmament, Russia, China, France, and several other nuclear powers are rapidly expanding their arsenals, while Germany, South Korea, Japan, and others are considering developing their own programs. The agreements that long ago halted U.S. and Russian testing recently expired. Donald Trump has been expressing an alarming interest in the use of nuclear weapons for decades.
Among Else’s most important accomplishments is recognizing how crucial secrecy has been to the maintenance of nuclear stockpiles. Since the bomb was first developed, the U.S. government has denied the public basic facts about atomic weapons. “The extreme secrecy surrounding almost everything concerning nuclear weapons impeded effective democratic debate for decades,” one report quoted by Else concluded. The bomb, in other words, is bad for democracy, just as democracy is bad for the bomb.
The tight grip on information goes back to the beginning—to the Manhattan Project, which brought hundreds of scientists and their families to the New Mexico desert to build an unprecedented weapon. At the height of World War II, the U.S. military concluded that the decision to develop a bomb could not be subject to public debate. Even among members of the U.S. Congress, the historian Alex Hellerstein has calculated, only about 1 percent were brought into the loop. In 1943, the wartime Office of Censorship banned media references to “war experiments,” and officials issued false or misleading responses to press inquiries. Thus, when a bomb exploded onto Hiroshima and “instantly broiled the skin of every person in the open within half a mile,” in Else’s appropriately gruesome phrasing, almost everyone on the planet was genuinely shocked.
But that was wartime—and the cessation of hostilities generated new complexities. Could this degree of unaccountability really persist in a time of peace? Else’s interview subjects felt that it shouldn’t. Within weeks of Japan’s surrender, hundreds of Manhattan Project scientists put out a statement calling for “free and enlightened public discussion” of atomic power. Oppenheimer and liberal members of Harry S. Truman’s administration quickly proposed a plan to place control of all nuclear materials and weapons in the hands of the United Nations.
As the historian Daniel Immerwahr has noted, much of the scientific community went so far as to seek a “global government” to regulate the bomb. Today this idea might seem unthinkable, but in the ’40s, the notion enjoyed the support of such wild-eyed radicals as Winston Churchill, Richard Nixon, John F. Kennedy, and Ronald Reagan. The postwar constitutions of France and Italy explicitly countenanced a future global body that would trump their own sovereignty. Else cites polls suggesting that about two-thirds of Americans supported some version of this concept.
It did not come to pass. U.S. leaders waffled on the idea, and eventually the U.S.S.R., hastily developing a bomb of its own, rejected it. What, then, to do with America’s swelling nuclear arsenal? Many elected officials feared that some “dashing lieutenant colonel” might go rogue with a nuke or three, and so in 1946, Congress passed the Atomic Energy Act, taking control of the bomb away from the military and placing it solely in the hands of the president.
Given the trigger-happy proposals floated by many within the military brass in the years to follow, this structure may well have saved countless lives, but it hardly provided for democratic accountability, much less actual arms control. The historian Garry Wills has powerfully argued that the postwar nuclear chain of command altered the United States “down to its deepest constitutional roots,” giving the president exclusive and unfettered power far beyond the comprehension of our country’s founders. Kennedy, for one, considered the presidential nuclear prerogative “insane.”
Much of Frenchman Flat is devoted to documenting the insanity that resulted from a nuclear-powered state (and, soon, states) freed from checks and balances and uninterested in public debate. There was no public hearing concerning the U.S. decision to start exploding nuclear bombs in Nevada in 1951; the state’s governor heard about it only a week before the first bomb fell. For years thereafter, the government insisted that nuclear fallout was safe, even as kids across the desert West started receiving leukemia diagnoses. Decades later, studies estimated that as many as 212,000 cases of cancer resulted from U.S. nuclear testing.
Meanwhile, behind closed doors, the global superpowers were accelerating the arms race. Both the Americans and the Soviets seriously considered nuclear testing on the moon. The first U.S. test of a hydrogen bomb (hundreds to thousands of times stronger than an atom bomb) was in 1952, and the first Soviet H-bomb test followed in 1953. When a government committee chaired by Oppenheimer recommended strongly against the development of the H-bomb, the Atomic Energy Commission buried the report by classifying it as secret. The H-bomb’s existence became public only after a congressman inadvertently disclosed it on live television. Even Truman hadn’t learned of the “super bomb” until years after its development began.
Over the course of the 1950s, as information leaked, public opposition to nuclear testing spread. Impelled by increasing discontent, the Americans and Soviets tentatively entered arms-control discussions. In 1963, they agreed to halt aboveground nuclear testing (underground testing would cease 30 years later). Dozens of countries suspended in-progress nuclear programs. “We are alive to discuss these things thanks in large measure to the grand patchwork of treaties, agreements, and unilateral actions,” Else writes.
Yet the nuclear peace has always been a fragile one. At least twice, full-scale nuclear war has likely been averted only because a single individual—Vasily Arkhipov in 1962 and Stanislav Petrov in 1983—decided to stand in the way. The U.S. and Russia still have about 5,000 bombs apiece, more than enough to end human civilization. Only voluntary forbearance precludes renewed testing or development or, for that matter, the deployment of intercontinental ballistic missiles and B-2 stealth bombers that are always at the ready. The oceans still teem with nuclear submarines, Else notes, “each boat packing more firepower than what was spent in all the wars in history.” The “nuclear club,” according to an essay in this magazine, is on track to double.
Remarkably, Else concludes Frenchman Flat on a note of ambivalence about this unstable status quo. “I have come to appreciate deterrence and understand that until we learn differently our bombs may save us from their bombs,” Else writes. Global abolition, the goal of generations of peace activists, including Martin Luther King Jr. and Pope Leo XIV, is, he adds, “unrealistic.” He shares this perspective with several of his interview subjects, who are international negotiators—members in good standing of what Else labels the “diplomatic bomb squad.” At the same time, he recognizes the absurdity of the nuclear buildup. “Why are you so concerned with saving lives?” he quotes one U.S. general as having said in 1963. “Look, at the end of the war, if there are two Americans and one Russian, we win.”
Ultimately, Else does not recommend a path out of the nuclear quagmire (which in fairness was not the task he set for himself). In any event, our international institutions are presently far too weak to provide the supranational control envisioned by mid-century luminaries, and a good number of our current world leaders are almost uniquely ill-suited to steer political bodies that are armed to the teeth.
Yet Frenchman Flat does provide some directional cues toward a safer future. Integral to an awareness of nuclear dangers is an end to the regime of secrecy—or at least substantial reform. Democratic oversight of this greatest weapon of war is impossible if the people are deprived of basic information. Of course, democracy is not a sufficient condition for disarmament, much less abolition. The H-bomb was popular with the American public at moments of peak anti-Soviet fervor, just as 70 percent of South Koreans, facing a nuclear regime to the north, want the bomb today. Nonetheless, popular discontent, often driven by leaked information, has historically curbed the nuclear ambitions of many of the most martial leaders. It is reasonable to imagine that even more awareness would spur even more opposition.
Sunlight alone will not solve the problem of nuclear proliferation. The aim of the abolitionists, realistic or not, has always been not just to eliminate the bombs but also to alter the conditions that might lead countries to use them. The prospect of a future free of mushroom clouds, they believe, is inseparable from a global order built on cooperation and democracy.
