The Artist Who Ripped Up the Rules of Drawing
Willem de Kooning was the best draftsman of his generation of postwar American artists. He had to unlearn everything he knew.
Most retrospectives unfold like a stately procession. You buy your ticket and proceed through a choreographed sequence of galleries, scrutinizing first the juvenilia, then the promising early work. Next come the triumphal years, and finally (if the artist was lucky) a poignant late phase. An idea of timelessness prevails, enhanced by an enveloping atmosphere of climate control, security, and massive insurance coverage. The lighting is good; the frames are tasteful. Everything looks marvelous.
There’s not a whiff of the urgency of the studio, no hint of the emotional or psychological state in which these objects were made. Lost is any suggestion of that feeling, deep inside the creator, of an improvised, inner necessity.
“Willem de Kooning Drawing,” at the Art Institute of Chicago, is a classic retrospective—a decorous, deeply researched exhibition about a much-lauded artist at a major museum. In another, more robust sense, however, the show is a giant debauch. It’s frankly (and thrillingly) unseemly. I’ve never been to an art show that takes you so far inside the creative process. You start to wonder if you should even be permitted to get so close.
“Art never seems to make me peaceful or pure,” De Kooning once said. “I always seem to be wrapped in the melodrama of vulgarity.” This show, more than any other De Kooning exhibit I’ve seen, delivers on the spirit of that oft-quoted statement. De Kooning, arguably the most widely revered of America’s 20th-century avant-garde artists, took the language of drawing, ripped it up, and rearranged it. Put that way, what he did sounds rebellious. It sounds punk. The exhibition, which will travel to the Rijksmuseum, in Amsterdam, in early October, embraces that spirit. But it has a more conservative purpose, which is to demonstrate that you can’t rip up art’s language effectively—or interestingly—without first really knowing it.
De Kooning knew, from long study, how to draw contours. He knew how to create volume using gradations in tone or marks that move in certain ways, how to apply ink or paint with varying degrees of pressure and velocity, and how to employ color relations to suggest depth. Before you can throw all that technique up in the air and have it land again, you need to have the tools.
De Kooning was both the best draftsman and the most lavishly gifted painter of the generation of postwar artists (among them Jackson Pollock, Lee Krasner, Mark Rothko, and Helen Frankenthaler) who helped move the art world’s center of gravity from Paris to New York. Born in the Netherlands in 1904, he trained, from the age of 13, as a commercial artist at the Rotterdam Academy of Visual Arts and Technical Sciences while apprenticing with a design firm.
The show kicks off with a large drawing, Dish With Jugs, that De Kooning made at the academy. Working in charcoal and conté crayon two days a week for an entire year—600 hours—the young student achieved a remarkable level of photographic verisimilitude in the still life. As one of the exhibit’s curators, Kevin Salatino, writes of De Kooning’s trajectory in an introductory essay for the show’s catalog, the drawing became “the archetype of what he would forcibly reject while retaining the learned skills the work so brilliantly exemplifies, only now putting them to radically different purposes.”
That De Kooning could draw like Ingres (or like Picasso during his Ingres-inspired period, from roughly 1917 to 1925) is amply demonstrated by other early works in the show, such as his adoring, fastidiously controlled pencil portrait of Elaine Fried, a fellow artist and his future wife. But, like a libertine desiring undiscovered pleasures, his appetite for new sensations only seemed to grow with time.
Drawing has long been regarded as an intellectual activity, something generated, above all, by the mind, with its capacity for conceiving, imagining, and mandating. (You draw to design buildings and invent machines; you “draw up” battle plans and national borders.) “Drawing, as a way of thinking,” Salatino notes of De Kooning, “lay at the core of his practice, the root of everything.”
But is it thought, as such, that we’re seeing in De Kooning’s drawings? The critic Peter Schjeldahl, who knew the artist, described him as “a hand with a man attached.” If you can attribute thought to a hand—and I’m willing to admit that you can, but it surely isn’t rational—then this show is indeed a record of thinking. But it may be better described as the record of some more mysterious melting of mind into body.
De Kooning came to America as a stowaway in 1926. Residing first in Hoboken, New Jersey, for less than a year before settling in New York City, he remained without legal status for the next 35 years. During an extended period of hard graft as a house-and-sign painter, a window dresser, a show-card letterer, and an advertising-layout man, he encountered various avant-garde artists, including Arshile Gorky, who became a close friend. Under the Armenian American painter’s influence, he gradually shifted his focus from commercial art to modernist fine art, experimenting with different styles derived from Picasso, Miró, and Matisse.
Even when ostensibly abstract, De Kooning’s work was populated by bobbling fragments of body parts. He conveyed these with his characteristic wobbling contours and flesh-textured paint. “Content is a glimpse of something, an encounter like a flash,” he once said. “It’s very tiny—very tiny, content.” He proceeded in the studio intuitively, precipitously, as if wanting to catch his subjects unawares.
De Kooning had his first solo show in 1948. He broke through to widespread acclaim in 1950 with Excavation, a painting he labored over for many weeks, using a process of patient buildup and repeated erasure. At almost seven feet high and more than eight feet wide, Excavation was the largest canvas he’d ever worked on. (The following year, it was awarded a prize by the Art Institute of Chicago, which subsequently acquired it.) The work was initially inspired by scenes from an Italian movie, Bitter Rice, an art-house hit in Greenwich Village that year, showing young peasant women working in water-soaked fields. But over time, the bodies dissolved into their surroundings and the pictorial space flattened out into a scrim of fleetingly seen forms with hooked and curving contours that push forward from the surface or twist back into shallow space.
If, in its genesis, the work recalled Picasso’s proto-cubist breakthrough, Les Demoiselles d’Avignon—the Spaniard’s 1907 painting of five naked women in a brothel—it also pointed the way to what would become a more explicit, and enduring, obsession for De Kooning: depictions of women, wobbly-edged, many of them leering or aggressive, disintegrating before our eyes into a welter of ambient marks. Inspired by prehistoric figurines of such powerful female divinities as the Venus of Willendorf, and by depictions of women by Rubens and Picasso—and riffing, too, on female figures in contemporary cartoons, movies, and magazine advertisements—De Kooning’s women take up a hefty portion of the show.
The critic Harold Rosenberg, an early champion of his work, admired the classical balance of Excavation, likening it to “a formula wrung out of testing explosives.” Observing De Kooning drawing, another critic, Thomas Hess, noted that the artist “made a few strokes, then almost instinctively, it seemed to me, turned the pencil around and began to go over the graphite marks with the eraser. Not to rub out the lines but to move them, push them across the paper.” De Kooning’s line, he concluded, “is always under attack.”
This ethos of creative destruction remained a guiding principle for De Kooning. The artist’s methods, however, continued to change. His drawings appear to be in a state of constant becoming. Shapes swell and fall away. They coalesce and unravel. De Kooning’s reversals of figure and ground aren’t binary or static, as in classic cubism; they’re in flux, like water moving in water.
The show’s emphasis on the muck and mess of the studio may explain why artists in the Chicago area have flocked to the exhibit—and keep on returning, according to Mel Becker Solomon (who organized the show with Salatino, Margaret Holben Ellis, and Charlotte Healy). Solomon recounted to me that she walked through the exhibition with an artist, who told her, “This is what students are missing in their current practice: the tenacity and rigor to keep pushing, experimenting, and searching for what comes next.”
What the show demonstrates, in ways that aren’t always obvious with his paintings, is that De Kooning never lost touch with the vocational skills he acquired as a young man. As Rosenberg wrote in 1962, “There was not a trick of the painter’s trade that de Kooning did not have up his sleeve.” Ellis, a paper conservator at the Art Institute of Chicago, lists those “tricks” in the catalog and explains how De Kooning adapted them to purposes for which they were never intended. She describes, for instance, his use of carbon-transfer paper and translucent vellum to copy motifs from one drawing to another. Such processes were typically used to duplicate technical drawings. But De Kooning would apply fragments of the reproductions to new compositions, often in different orientations.
He also used frottage, or rubbing—another technique favored by commercial artists—to activate his lines. He would apply charcoal to thin vellum placed over corrugated cardboard or other textured surfaces to give the marks a stuttering look. “Frottage transformed stillness into speed,” Ellis writes of Reclining Nude, a 1963 drawing. This observation approaches the core of De Kooning’s art: More than any other artist I can think of, he gave painted marks and lines different velocities and trajectories. Co-existing in the same composition, those visible shifts in speed, thickness, and direction carved out three-dimensional spaces of ravishing complexity and urgency.
Salatino suggests, in his catalog essay, that the artist’s use of frottage “functions, inescapably, as a metaphor for the masturbatory—making and meaning converging in an act dependent upon the probing, rubbing, exploring hand.” Salatino is a first-rate curator, but this sort of writing, to which his introduction is rather too prone, gives art writing a bad name. De Kooning didn’t traffic in metaphors. He wasn’t interested in meanings. There’s a reason Susan Sontag quoted him at the beginning of her essay “Against Interpretation.”
Other techniques that De Kooning learned as a commercial artist included cutting out parts of images he found in magazines and inserting them into his compositions, or using masking tape and paper overlays to give his own marks abrupt, crisp boundaries.
When drawing, De Kooning loved to use liner and sword brushes, which are favored by sign painters. Both have short handles and extended, bushy bristles. Loaded with ink and applied with control, they allow artists to make long, even lines. De Kooning had mastered their use as a younger man. (Ellis reports that the illustrator Gus Falk, who was taught by De Kooning at Black Mountain College, remembered him applying a perfectly even line to a spinning bicycle wheel by holding the brush steady. “He was in control,” Falk said. “He was interested in exactitude.”) But in his own drawing, De Kooning let rip with liner brushes, swishing them about all over the paper, achieving undulant lines that contract and expand like living creatures.
Perhaps the most remarkable of De Kooning’s maladapted techniques was his use of fixatives. The word itself suggests De Kooning’s perversity. Fixatives are sprayed onto vulnerable media, such as charcoal and crayon, to stabilize drawn marks. But instead of spraying a fine, even mist from an appropriate distance, De Kooning aimed the fixative straight at his drawings from close range, creating puddles and rivulets that turned the paper gray, creating strange, smudgy marks and chemical textures.
Later in his career, De Kooning tried drawing with his eyes closed or with both hands at once. Long plagued by alcoholism, he was often inebriated. “I’m in my element when I am a little bit out of this world,” he once said. “When I’m falling, I’m doing all right; when I’m slipping, I say, Hey, this is interesting!” The words could sound somewhat pathetic, like a drunk man’s sad, self-soothing rationalization. But the relationship between De Kooning’s virtuosity and the lengths to which he went just to get in his own way is intriguing to consider.
Clement Greenberg, the most influential critic of the postwar period, framed the problem in a review of De Kooning’s first solo show. The artist’s “really great facility,” Greenberg argued, risked getting in the way of his ability to express authentic emotion with real originality. “Facility,” Greenberg argued, “has a stubbornness of its own and is loath to abandon easy satisfactions.”
For Greenberg, “easy satisfactions” were always close to kitsch. But his assessment was reductive. De Kooning was an immigrant from Europe. His extensive training and virtuosic way with line connected him to an evolving tradition of European drawing that led from Tintoretto, Rubens, Delacroix, and Ingres to, in the modern era, Picasso and Matisse. He would never disown that tradition.
But he was in America now. It was the 20th century. Young women were screaming in front of the Beatles. Crowds crammed into theaters to see Marilyn Monroe magnified on the screen. Betty Boop and Minnie Mouse bounced from frame to frame in the cartoons. De Kooning—neither calm nor pure and “wrapped,” as he had put it, “in the melodrama of vulgarity”—longed to incorporate all this impudent American energy into the authority of his European inheritance, and especially into his drawings and paintings of female figures.
His efforts to interfere with his own facility were an expression both of his dividedness and of his deep hunger for freedom. Anyone who stands in front of De Kooning’s urgent, sensuously greedy drawings, with their writhing contours, cacophonous colors, and perverse processes, can feel the force of that craving.

RFK Jr.’s Bold Reassurance to Anti-Vaxxers
“You have friends in the White House,” he said at a conference hosted by the anti-vaccine organization he founded.
Since becoming Health and Human Services secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has repeatedly denied that he opposes vaccines and has toned down some of his more extreme rhetoric on the subject. But in a keynote speech today at a conference for Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine organization he founded, the old Kennedy was back. He complained about safety studies, floated disproven theories about a link between vaccines and autism, and all but declared himself an anti-vaxxer. “You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House,” he told the crowd.
His choice to take the stage at the conference signaled a shift. Since becoming HHS secretary, Kennedy had distanced himself from Children’s Health Defense as he worked to convince the Senate that he held mainstream-enough views on vaccines. Children’s Health Defense, meanwhile, attempts to convince parents that vaccines are a threat to their children’s well-being. In just the past few days, CHD has used its X account to warn parents against trusting babies with health-care providers who might give them vaccines, claimed that childhood vaccines kill more children than do the diseases they prevent, and alleged that COVID vaccines were designed to cause infertility. The speakers at its conference were a who’s who of the anti-vaccine movement.
Nearly everything the organization promotes runs counter to guidance from the CDC, an agency that Kennedy leads as head of the Department of Health and Human Services. But much of Kennedy’s speech was consistent with CHD’s brand of scaremongering. He suggested that vaccines contribute to chronic disease and disorders such as autism. He bemoaned the fact that more vaccines are recommended for American children now than when he was a child. And he falsely claimed that nothing is known about their safety. “We have no idea what the risk profile is for these products,” he told the crowd.
In one of the more bizarre moments of his address, Kennedy read from the manufacturer’s list of possible adverse events for the vaccine against hepatitis B, a disease that can lead to liver failure. Among those he mentioned was anaphylaxis, an allergic reaction that occurs roughly once for every 1 million doses administered. He ignored the benefits of the vaccine, which has drastically reduced infections and is projected to have prevented millions of deaths. Instead, he implied that the vaccine was merely part of an industry “gold rush.”
The speakers surrounding Kennedy are publicly hostile to vaccination. He was introduced by Mary Holland, the CEO of Children’s Health Defense, who took over the organization after Kennedy’s departure and praised him for taking on “the corrupt medical pharmaceutical complex.” Mark Gorton, the president of a pro-Kennedy think tank called the MAHA Institute, had earlier told the crowd that vaccines are a “public-health nightmare” and that eliminating them would make the country healthier. And then there was Andrew Wakefield, known for his discredited 1998 Lancet paper that alleged a connection between autism and the MMR vaccine. Anti-vaccine activists have spent decades citing Wakefield’s faulty research in an effort to fuel fear of immunizations.
Now is a terrible time for Kennedy to return to public anti-vaccine advocacy. Pennsylvania is in the midst of a deadly measles outbreak. The official count in the state is 731 cases since April and 117 in just the past week; the real number of infections is almost certainly much higher. Four people, two of them infants, have died since mid-August. Much of the suffering has been concentrated among the state’s Amish community, where immunization rates are low, about 25 percent in Lancaster County. Before becoming HHS secretary, Kennedy praised the Amish for declining to get vaccinated, telling a crowd at an Amish country fair in 2021 that, when it comes to vaccines, “it’s so important for us to think more like the Amish think.”
Rather than speaking publicly about how low vaccination rates are the reason that measles is sickening and killing Americans, Kennedy has spent the past month squabbling with Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, over how to define measles-associated deaths. Under Kennedy’s leadership, the CDC has so far declined to list any deaths from Pennsylvania’s ongoing outbreak; this afternoon, while he was onstage, HHS’s official X account called the state government’s demands that the CDC do so “political blackmail.” In his speech at the conference, Kennedy’s only mention of measles was part of a complaint that deaths from the disease “get headlines” while the alleged dangers of vaccines are ignored. (An HHS spokesperson didn’t respond to a question about why Kennedy was appearing at an anti-vaccine conference during a measles outbreak.)
Kennedy reassured the crowd that research into vaccine safety was going on behind the scenes at HHS. “As I said, you have friends in the White House,” he said, “and we are doing this one day at a time.” He claimed that HHS had failed to study vaccine risks and told the audience that he was remedying that. He mentioned making use of the Vaccine Safety Datalink, a collection of Americans’ electronic health records. That database has long been a topic of fascination for Kennedy and other anti-vaccine activists who believe that it might contain hidden evidence that vaccines are harmful.
Kennedy built his reputation on being the country’s most prominent anti-vaccine activist. As HHS secretary, he has often emphasized less controversial issues, such as ultraprocessed foods and artificial dyes. Today, he took to the stage with a message for his longtime allies: He is still one of them.

Pakistan says time has come to implement Mecca defence pact
18 September 2026 04:23 BST
  
  Pakistan’s defence minister has said the time has come to implement the Mecca defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey as Houthi attacks on the kingdom intensify.
Speaking to Geo News on Wednesday, Khawaja Asif said Pakistan remained committed to defending Saudi Arabia and the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, adding that Islamabad had a duty to protect them even without the agreement.
“Makkah Agreement applies to us, and we will fulfil our duty,” said Asif without elaborating on what Pakistan may do.
Houthi officials have denied targeting the holy city.

Champion Van Gerwen loses in first round to Gurney
- Published
Defending champion Michael van Gerwen fell to a 6-5 defeat by Daryl Gurney in the opening round of the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam.
Northern Ireland's Gurney raced into a 3-0 lead before the Dutch top seed reeled off five consecutive legs to put himself on the brink of victory.
However, Gurney, who was drafted in as a late replacement when Lourence Ilagan withdrew from the 32-man field, responded by taking the ninth leg.
And when Van Gerwen missed six match darts, he was able to level the match at 5-5 and win the decider with the throw.
Gurney will now take on England's Ross Smith in the last 16 on Saturday after he advanced past Kevin Doets 6-3.
World number one Luke Littler will get under way on Friday against former UK Open champion Danny Noppert, having recently whitewashed the Dutchman 6-0 on his way to winning the Czech Darts Open.
World number two Luke Humphries also emerged victorious in another England versus Netherlands encounter, progressing 6-4 against Jermaine Wattimena.
Dutch number one Gian van Veen gained a measure of revenge for the home fans with a 6-2 triumph over Chris Dobey.
Dirk van Duijvenbode fought back from 4-1 down to defeat Sweden's Viktor Tingstrom 6-4, while Ryan Searle threw four 180s as he dispatched former world champion Rob Cross 6-2.
Searle goes on to play Josh Rock, who won the last three legs to edge out Stephen Bunting 6-5.
Karel Sedlacek marked his debut at the tournament with a 6-4 win over New Zealander Ben Robb and will take on Van Veen next.

In September 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that U.S. President Donald Trump helped a farmer's widow clear her debts to keep her farm in Georgia after her husband died by suicide.
A long text about the alleged act of kindness circulated on Facebook. It began:
On a February morning in 1986, a Georgia farmer named Leonard Hill walked out of his house twenty minutes before the bank was set to auction off his land. He never came back inside.
He took his own life that morning, believing his life insurance policy would cover the debts that had buried his family. It did not come close.
Leonard left behind a widow.
Annabel Hill was 66 years old, and the farm her husband died trying to save had been in her family for five generations.
Years of drought had wiped out the crops and the income that came with them. By the time Leonard died, the family owed the bank more than $300,000. His death did nothing to change that number.
The auction was still coming, and Annabel was now facing it alone.
That fall, an Atlanta businessman named Frank Argenbright heard what had happened to the Hills. He did not know the family. He simply decided that a widow in her sixties should not lose five generations of land because it stopped raining. So he started making phone calls, looking for anyone with the money and the will to step in.
Those calls eventually reached a New York developer whose name the Hill family had never heard. Donald Trump was 40 years old and building his reputation in Manhattan real estate.
The same text and claim also circulated elsewhere on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived) and X (archived). Snopes readers contacted us asking whether Trump really saved a Georgia farm.
The claim was true. According to reports at the time in reputable news outlets such as The Associated Press, Trump helped fundraise for Annabel Hill, a farmer's widow whose husband, Leonard Dozier Hill III, died by suicide in 1986 trying to save his fifth-generation farm through his life insurance payments.
Some details, like exactly how much money the Hill family owed, the exact size of the farm and how much money the fundraiser collected varied between reports, but what appeared consistent was that Trump and a Texas farmer named Tom McKamy contributed a vital final portion of the fundraiser, allowing most of the land to stay with Hill's family.
None of the parties to the story have publicly refuted the reported account of Trump helping to save the Hill farm. Trump and Hill's daughter, Betsy Sharp, shared the story during a campaign rally in 2016.
Snopes attempted to reach the McKamy family and Sharp to confirm the unclear details of the story and await replies to our queries.
Trump, Texas farmer provided vital funding
News outlets including The Associated Press and Time magazine reported in September 1986 that the Hill family farm was due to be sold at auction on Feb. 4, 1986. However, 20 minutes before the auction was scheduled to start, Leonard Hill fatally shot himself, hoping his life insurance payment would be enough to cover the farm's $300,000 debt and keep it in the family's ownership. The payments were not enough, and the bank collecting Hill's debt scheduled another auction for Sept. 2.
However, the AP reported that Trump spokesperson Norma Foerderer told the outlet that Trump stopped that second auction by offering Hill $20,000 up front and pledged to help fundraise the remaining $173,000 needed for the family to keep the 705-acre farm.
By mid-September 1986, Time reported that Trump, working with Frank Argenbright Jr., a Georgia businessman who helped Hill bring her cause to the public, had raised about $77,000 and hoped to raise about $100,000 more.
The AP reported in December 1986, that the fundraiser ultimately reached $187,000. The news agency United Press International reported, citing a Trump spokesperson, that Trump had contributed $39,000, which was half of the $78,000 in missing funding after public donations, and McKamy had contributed the other half.
The New York Times reported a year later, citing Hill and Foerderer, that the auction had ultimately saved 715 acres of farmland. According to that article, the fundraiser reached $180,000 with an additional $5,000 raised in legal fees. Trump reportedly contributed $46,000.
Snopes contacted the White House Press Office and the Trump Organization to confirm the correct fundraising figures and await replies to our queries.
Trump's own account
Trump included his account of helping save Hill's farm in his memoir/business advice book "The Art of the Deal," published in 1987. Trump wrote that he had seen Hill's story on the news and "was moved." He said he contacted the bank that held Hill's mortgage which told him it was "too late" to save the farm. Trump wrote (pages 4-5):
That really got me going. I said to the guy, "You listen to me. If you do foreclose, I'll personally bring a lawsuit for murder against you and your bank, on the grounds that you harassed Mrs. Hill's husband to his death." All of a sudden the bank officer sounded very nervous and said he'd get right back to me.
Sometimes it pays to be a little wild. An hour later I got a call back from the banker, and he said, "Don't worry, we're going to work it out, Mr. Trump." Mrs. Hill and Frank Argenbright told the media, and the next thing I knew, it was the lead story on the network news.
By the end of the week, we'd raised $40,000. [Radio personality Don] Imus alone raised almost $20,000 by appealing to his listeners. As a Christmas present to Mrs. Hill and her family, we've scheduled a mortgage-burning ceremony for Christmas Eve in the atrium of Trump Tower. By then, I'm confident, we'll have raised all the money. I've promised Mrs. Hill that if we haven't, I'll make up any difference.
Trump made good on his promise to carry out a "mortgage-burning ceremony" by Christmas 1986. AP photographer Richard Drew captured Trump and Hill holding a burning piece of paper aloft in front of a Christmas tree on Dec. 23, 1986.
Trump showed another photo from the 1986 "mortgage-burning ceremony" to attendees at a campaign rally in Augusta, South Carolina, on Feb. 16, 2016, before bringing Hill's daughter Betsy Sharp on stage. Sharp praised Trump's generosity, who described (at 16:15) his fundraising as: "I paid off her mortgage, big deal, right."
The Atlanta Journal-Constitution's political columnist Jim Galloway wrote in 2015 that Hill's son, Leonard Dozier Hill IV, "still lives on the farm that Donald Trump saved." Snopes asked Sharp whether anyone from the family still lived on or worked the farm at the time of this writing and await a reply to our query.
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated a number of acts of kindness that Trump reportedly carried out.

The traditional Indian workplace is being reimagined. Whether it is a year-old startup or a decades-old enterprise, companies now want their offices to be more than just functional spaces. They want them to feel personalised, vibrant, contemporary, and aligned with global office trends. This is precisely why the demand for flexible workspaces is on the rise. Numbers support this thesis well. The flexible workspace market has grown more than 8.4X in the last decade, with transaction volumes climbing to 18.6 Mn sq ft in 2025 from a mere 2.2 Mn sq ft in 2017. But the opportunity is not just about leasing space. Management contracts, where workspace operators manage and run office spaces on behalf of property owners, are also emerging as another way for operators to expand their footprint. For businesses, this can offer greater flexibility in creating tailor-made workplaces, while for operators, it opens up another route to scale without relying entirely on venture capital to achieve growth. Dextrus is a key example. Founded in 2018 by Robin Chhabra, the startup operates premium coworking and managed office spaces in Mumbai for startups, enterprises, remote professionals and growing teams looking for ready-to-use workspaces. The company engages with businesses seeking tailor-made workspace solutions, capturing their identity and culture. Today, Dextrus operates at four key spots in Mumbai: BKC Crescenzo, Lower Parel Peninsula Corporate Park, ONE BKC & Mint in Andheri. Its core proposition and offering span fixed and flexible desks, membership plans, and daily and virtual plans, catering to professionals and teams at varying scales and tenures. Against this backdrop, Inc42 spoke with Chhabra to understand how he sees the Indian market adapting to the needs of the flexible workspace. What value proposition does Dextrus bring to a market already dominated by the likes of Awfis, WeWork India, and Indiqube? What does it take to build a sustainable workspace business without chasing scale at any cost? Can a well-thought-out workspace truly add to workforce productivity? An engaging chinwag with Chhabra revealed a lot about the changing dynamics of the contemporary workspace in the country and the way enterprises are becoming increasingly selective, if not picky, about how and where they sit. Here are the edited excerpts from our tête-à-tête with Chhabra... Inc42: What pulled you towards the workspace business? Was it real estate, a user pain point, or a broader view on how work itself is changing? Robin Chhabra: I'm a trained architect, so the way I look at spaces and cities has always been a little different. What led me to start Dextrus was the glaring infrastructural gap in Indian metros, and the office space was the worst offender. Sterile corporate floors on one side, high-density coworking on the other, almost nothing designed around the person sitting there for ten hours. Over the years, the office has tremendously evolved. Organisations today want flexibility in tenure, in scale, and in how much operational burden they can carry. This called for design thinking to be applied to offices. We understood this early on, leading to the inception of Dextrus in 2018. Inc42: How has your definition of a ‘good workspace’ evolved since you started Dextrus? What are the non-negotiables when designing a new workspace? Robin Chhabra: A good workspace is one that truly understands the depth of what people need from it. Not just a desk and a table, but the full range of how work actually happens. It has to be designed with a wide lens, built to last, and adaptable enough to evolve with the people using it. The amount of light, building design and grade are some of the other crucial factors that impact design. Inc42: In a business that sits at the intersection of design, real estate and operations, where do you personally spend most of your thinking time today? Robin Chhabra: Honestly, most of my thinking today goes into how we can improve our product and service quality, which in turn can expand on what Dextrus can offer to its clients. That's where enterprise solutions came from. It focusses on creating customised and premium workspaces for companies, designed around their specific operational, branding and employee needs. We’ve built workspaces for companies like Welspun One, Rabobank, Harvard Business School and others, keeping their requirements at the centre of our design. The intersection of design, real estate and operations is where we live, and enterprise solutions are pushing us deeper into that space. Inc42: How different is India’s workspace demand from that of our global counterparts? Where are we structurally unique? Robin Chhabra: India’s workspace demand is ever increasing into global capability centers and managed office spaces. Globally, it's a different picture. We are leading the way in creating managed offices in the world, which has not materialised in the West as much. India is seeing true value in office space as a cost on their P&L rather than on their balance sheet. Inc42: Is Dextrus’ core business model more real estate or services-led? Robin Chhabra: We are a real estate company, but that is not how I would define ourselves. Dextrus is customer-first, which means service and experience are at the forefront of everything we do. We see ourselves as partners in our clients’ business journey. Real estate is the foundation, but what we're actually selling is far more than just office space. We're selling a managed solution. And once you recognise the product is a capability rather than a lease, a lot of other things become possible. Inc42: How do you manage your business priorities among long-term enterprise clients and more flexible short-term customers? Robin Chhabra: We decided very early on that tailoring the product to a client's need will be where the market will see value. Long-term enterprise clients want a workspace built around their operations, their brand and their people, which means design autonomy and separate access inside their own footprint, while still drawing on shared infrastructure. That's the flexibility of a managed space with the ownership feel of a private office. We do run short-term and daily offerings, but due to its nature, it requires higher costs to manage and hence is difficult to build durably on that demand. Inc42: You did not raise external capital to date. What’s your rationale behind this decision, and does it cap your growth? Robin Chhabra: It would, if we were planning to expand the way the industry has. The conventional route is to sign long leases, fund the buildout yourself, and carry that for a decade. And while this works, it ties your growth to the size of your balance sheet. For us, following the same route would mean making every new market a 10-year bet placed on day one. And we all know that real estate is cyclical, which means whatever is soaring today will eventually come down. We feel that our future at Dextrus lies in the other direction, where the landowner becomes our business partner. In our model, we structure a management contract as a profit share. The developer brings the building and funds the buildout, while we bring the design standard, the brand, the operating system and the team that runs it. In fact, I would say that bootstrapping qualifies us for growth. We spent eight years running centres, and they had to be profitable at the unit level because there wasn’t anyone to bail us out of a bad decision. In a regular lease, a property owner might expect a 6-7% return. Under our model, they can target 10-12%, which is a 50-70% uplift on the same asset. Inc42: Why would a developer hand you their asset rather than run it themselves or lease it to a larger operator? Robin Chhabra: Running it themselves sounds simple until you try. Workspace is an operating business, and it requires design and build, service, hospitality, community and daily problem-solving. Most developers are excellent at building and have no wish to become a hospitality company. The hard part isn't the fit-out. It's the two thousand decisions that come after it. Leasing to a large operator gets them a covenant, but their building becomes indistinguishable from that operator's building anywhere else in the country, and the upside is capped at the rent. We offer a third thing, and the yield is what they respond to fastest. We can generate materially more revenue per square foot, on the same floor plate, at comparable density, because the product commands a higher rate. Plus, they participate in that upside rather than receiving a fixed rent, and the asset is worth more when they come to value it. Inc42: But doesn't this eventually dilute you? Most of the boutique brand that scales stops being boutique. Robin Chhabra: That's the right question, and it's why the model has to be asset-light rather than leased. The two are connected in a way that isn't obvious. A leased portfolio forces volume on you. Rent is a fixed obligation, so you need occupancy, which means you take the building that's available and the client who'll sign. Scale becomes something that happens to you. Under a management contract, growth is a choice made one building at a time, and the cost of saying no is close to zero. We are able to look at each asset and its natural advantages, whether that's location, size or something else, and then think through the programme mix and design to unlock the right revenue potential for the building and, in turn, improve returns. So asset-light isn't the threat to the boutique positioning. It's what protects it. Boutique is a yield strategy. Fewer, better centres generate more revenue per square foot, longer tenures and lower churn than a larger footprint of ordinary ones. The premium end is where the economics are best. The management contract helps us make every asset unique and ultimately enhance returns for the landlord. Inc42: What does growth look like for Dextrus over the next three to five years? Also, what are some of the things that you would be most cautious about as you scale? Robin Chhabra: Growth for us over the next three to five years is about disciplined expansion in micro-markets. We are four centres now, all in Mumbai. Growth means deepening in Mumbai and entering New Delhi and Bangalore, around 15-20 centres in total across the three cities. We intend to be in the right building in each micro-market rather than present in all of them. What I am most cautious about as we scale is the geographical and operational complexity of entering new markets. Every market has its own dynamics, and getting that understanding wrong is an expensive mistake. The focus has to stay on identifying the right opportunities, not just the available ones, to keep the essence of the brand intact and deliver the best offices to our clients.

Judge asked to prevent Trump from carving his name on yet another historic Washington building
Most Americans oppose Trump naming buildings after himself while still in office
A federal judge has been asked to prevent President Donald Trump from carving his name on yet another historic building in Washington, D.C.
During his second term, Trump has tried to literally make his mark on Washington, slapping his name on several D.C. landmarks, most notably the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.
Last December, the State Department announced that it had renamed the U.S. Institute of Peace “to reflect the greatest dealmaker in our nation's history” shortly before Trump hosted a signing ceremony for a peace deal between the presidents of Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
“Welcome to the Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace. The best is yet to come,” the department’s X post read. Trump’s name is tacked onto the building while the “Institute of Peace” is permanently etched in.
But now, ousted board members of the Institute of Peace asked the court in an emergency motion Thursday to stop any “plans to carve President Trump’s name into the facade of the iconic USIP headquarters building.” The motion was first reported on X by Kyle Cheney, a senior legal affairs reporter for Politico.
“The building — which was largely funded by private donations to USIP as a tax exempt nonprofit corporation — is a work of expressive architecture designed to be ‘symbolic of USIP’s’ independent ‘mission,’” the emergency motion said, according to a subsequent Politico article. “Alteration of the design to impose a different message would cause irreparable harm.”
Despite Secretary of State Marco Rubio calling Trump the “president of peace” when the building was renamed, the leader of the free world was the one who gutted the think tank created to resolve global conflict.
Trump called for the dismantling of the Institute of Peace in a February 2025 executive order as part of his and tech billionaire Elon Musk’s effort to reduce what they saw as government waste.
The executive order led to mass firings at the agency, which are still being challenged in court.
Most Americans oppose Trump naming government buildings after himself while in office.
Only 9 percent of Americans said it would be acceptable for Trump to name government buildings after himself while serving as president, according to a Pew Research Center poll released in May.
Around 70 percent said it would not be acceptable or would only be acceptable after he's no longer leading the country.
Last December, the Trump-appointed Kennedy Center board voted to put the president’s name on the building, prompting a wave of artists to refuse to perform at the arts center.
In May, U.S. District Court Judge Christopher Cooper ordered Trump’s name to be removed from the Kennedy Center, stating, “Congress gave the Kennedy Center its name, and only Congress can change it.” Weeks later, construction crews were seen taking Trump’s name off the building.

In a series win as emphatic as India’s 3-0 sweep over Afghanistan, there tend to be many bright spots to revel in. But if there was a fresh takeaway from the T20I series, it was arguably Nitish Kumar’s enhanced contribution with the ball. Back from a quadriceps injury, the 23-year-old seam-bowling all-rounder started the series shakily with figures of 2-0-30-0 in his first outing, but bounced back with three scalps each in the next two games.
More than the wickets, which can come arbitrarily in a format where batters are obliged to attack from the outset, the fact that Nitish bowled at brisk pace in different phases was heartening. Particularly in light of the prolonged absence of Hardik Pandya, who has been sidelined with injury since the conclusion of the Indian Premier League. The 32-year-old is expected to return to action when India-A plays three One-Dayers against Australia-A in Puducherry from October 6 to 11.
With India’s next big priority being the 2027 ODI World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia, coach Gautam Gambhir understandably wants both all-rounders to be fit and firing.
“We know how important seam bowling all-rounders will be in a year’s time when we go to South Africa. The more the merrier. And once Hardik comes back, obviously it is going to be good. Sometimes we could even go on to play both of them in the XI,” Gambhir told reporters on Thursday. “At the moment, Hardik cannot bowl 10 overs. He hasn’t played cricket since the IPL. So, we don’t want to push him into international cricket because it can be extremely tough on your body.
“If Hardik plays in the India-A series, obviously he will get some game time. That was the clear message to him. In the meantime, Nitish will get more game time because he hasn’t played enough cricket since the IPL either. The more he bowls, the better he becomes. When you can have a couple of seam-bowling all-rounders, it will be handy in a year’s time,” the 44-year-old added.
Gambhir conceded that the recent tendency of India’s players to have injury breakdowns wasn’t ideal. He was echoing the views of Test and ODI skipper Shubman Gill, who had expressed his concerns after India’s tour of England in July.
During the just-concluded series against Afghanistan, spinner Varun Chakaravarthy, who had only recently recovered from a hamstring injury at the Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru, suffered a side strain in the first game. He was subsequently ruled out of the Asian Games and next month’s T20I series against the West Indies.
“If I can give you an honest answer, then yes (it is a problem), especially in Tests and ODIs. You want your best players to play as many Tests and ODIs. The next World Cup is in the 50-over format. It’s not fair on a young captain as well if he doesn’t get the best team playing regularly. As a coach, I can take all the criticism, but I think it is important for Shubman to get the best playing XI as many times as he can in Tests and ODIs,” Gambhir stated.
The former India opener also explained the decision to bring back Sanju Samson into the playing XI at the expense of 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi. Samson, who had been dropped in England, justified his recall with two half-centuries against Afghanistan. Gambhir labelled the call to omit Samson, who was Player-of-the-Tournament in India’s victorious T20 World Cup campaign in March, as “probably the toughest” of his coaching tenure.
“Samson doesn’t need to give me any credit. His talent is enough for him to be in the dressing room. In this series, we were always very clear. From my point of view, I was very clear that we want to go back to the combination that we had during the World Cup. If a team has gone unbeaten from one World Cup to another and defended the title, I’m sure it’s a gun team. These guys do not become bad players after two or three failures,” said Gambhir.
It means that Sooryavanshi, despite smashing two half-centuries in Zimbabwe, will have to bide his time.
“From Vaibhav’s point of view, it was again a very clear conversation that he will have to wait for his opportunity. We know what he can do,” Gambhir elaborated. “But again, someone who has done extremely well over a period of two years will always be ahead of someone who is just part of the team. Whenever Vaibhav gets in, he will get a longer run as well. And that is what Indian cricket is all about. Whether you’re 15 or 30, you have to wait for your opportunity.”

Six-time Grand Slam champion Salisbury retires
- Published
Former world number one doubles player and six-time Grand Slam doubles champion Joe Salisbury has retired from professional tennis.
Londoner Salisbury chose this month's US Open as his final event and reached the semi-finals with his long-time partner Rajeev Ram, who had also decided to retire.
The venue was fitting, as in 2023 Salisbury and Ram became the first pair in history to win three consecutive US Open men's doubles titles.
Salisbury is Britain's most successful men's doubles player of the Open era. He also won the 2020 Australian Open with Ram, and two mixed doubles titles with Desirae Krawczyk.
The 34-year-old says he has been thinking about his future for a while, and is now "very happy with the decision".
"Tennis has been my life for as long as I can remember and I have been incredibly fortunate to have had all the opportunities, experiences and success that I have," he posted on Instagram.
"To be able to travel the world and call playing tennis my job has been a dream come true and I never believed I could have lived the life and had the career that I have.
"I gave it my all and know I can be proud and look back with no regrets."
Salisbury took a three-month break at the start of this year, having told BBC Sport about the anxiety which had been affecting him on tour.
While he did not think it affected his tennis very much, he said it left him with a "feeling of dread" which made life on the road far less enjoyable.
Salisbury finishes his career with 17 tour level titles, including the season-ending ATP Finals of 2022 and 2023.

Silliness, in general, is not hard for me to come by: I have a toddler who is, as she declares often, a “silly person.” Still, the very pleasure I take in being silly with my child and her friends reveals to me its rarity in adult public life. Few social situations encourage or even allow unadulterated loopiness. In general, art made for adults tends to abide by this taboo. We get satire, scatological jokes, imitations, and absurdity, but rarely do we get silliness.
A new play, Bocking, reminds us that this is a mistake. A wild, sometimes surreal, and ultimately tenderhearted farce that premiered last month at Baltimore Center Stage, Bocking does not suggest at the outset that it will be silly.
It does, however, seem interested in provocation. It begins with a pair of glamorously behatted ladies moving through the crowd, thanking theatergoers for “coming to church.” When the show’s action begins, some of it is, indeed, a church service—but as a pastor delivers at the center of the stage a sermon that turns more and more homophobic, two other characters, a cisgender man and his trans wife, begin to have raucous sex at stage right. It’s a good bit, and it drew uproarious laughs the night I saw the play. In most regards, the scene sets up the show’s concerns well, if rather transparently: Bocking’s author, the young playwright Preston Crowder, wants to teach his religious characters some lessons about acceptance and sex positivity.
The show’s comedy tends to cater to a crowd that already agrees with its message. But Bocking has one scene that I found fairly transcendent—one that was not just dirty or gasp-inducing but was also silly to its very core. It’s also the best scene in the play.
The moment builds on Bocking’s oddest plotline: One of the characters, an anxious school guidance counselor named Erickson, suffered an unusual childhood trauma. When he was 8, he and his mother caught his stepfather having sex with—stick with me here—a hen. (Animal-rights activists may object to the levity with which this is portrayed; other people may be reminded of the Swedish Chef.) Erickson’s grief-stricken mother then attempted to turn into a hen herself, an event that the play shows as a descent into madness rather than a true transformation. Still, years after her death, the adult Erickson communes with her by “bocking”—that is, speaking in chicken.
For much of the play, he does so in private, which registers to the audience as an inexplicable subplot. But when the pastor’s wife, Tiana, visits him to express her marital woes, she winds up extracting the secret of his chicken talk from him—and then demands to give it a try. At first, Erickson is reluctant, but soon, the two begin bocking together. As dialogue, the exchange that follows is incomprehensible. As a moment of human connection, it’s undeniable. And as sheer silliness—not spectacle or satire like the rest of the play—it beats almost any recent piece of art I’ve heard, read, or seen.
Crowder understands, clearly, that silliness is a vehicle for catharsis. By behaving ridiculously with each other, Tiana and Erickson get respite from their isolation and their troubles. In watching them behave ridiculously, the audience gets a break from the show’s moralizing and can, instead, connect directly to the characters’ emotions. As a result, the scene deepens the rest of the show.
Sketch comedy is typically the most frequent source of silliness in art and culture: Saturday Night Live is often silly, and in my view no one has ever been sillier on camera than the comedians of the legendary British sketch group Monty Python. Plenty of the Pythons’ work is satirical—consider their send-ups of English sexual repression—but what sets their comedy apart for me is their willingness to be purely silly. In the beginning of their sketch “The Ministry of Silly Walks,” a bowler-hatted, briefcase-carrying John Cleese, his back beautifully straight, gavottes down a London street. Viewers don’t know why he’s moving so ludicrously; it doesn’t matter. His silly walk undermines not only his dignified wardrobe but also the very idea of a professional persona. Just by changing his gait to something ridiculous, Cleese gives his audience a moment of release from the entire world of work.
But sketch comedy, even when it has recurring characters, cannot develop those characters in the way a full-length work can. Its silliness, therefore, cannot have the emotional impact of the chicken-talk scene in Bocking, or the hot-dogs-as-fingers segment in the movie Everything Everywhere All at Once. One of that film’s many interwoven strands involves an alternate universe in which the characters played by Michelle Yeoh and Jamie Lee Curtis move through their days, experiencing life and love, with frankfurters for fingers. It’s a ridiculous conceit, pointless except to force a visceral sense of frustration, followed by acceptance, into their scenes together—which it does quite well, just as Tiana and Erickson’s bocking creates a visceral sense of relief. Silliness, in both cases, circumvents cerebral experience.
No other means of getting a laugh goes so directly to the heart. Real silliness—serious silliness, if you will—lands in a sweet spot between the intellectualism of satire and the visual heft of spectacle. It strips away layers of adult logic, convention, and pretense, delivering grown-ups to the instinctive knowledge that toddlers possess: Work clothes are just costumes. Maneuvering a body through the world is both annoying and a cosmic joke. And communication, as Bocking so well demonstrates, often isn’t really about what gets said. Reasonably, this is tough for many writers, verbal creatures that we are, to admit, but in times of real emotional duress, words are rarely what counts. What matters are the feelings that lie underneath.

'Unacceptable at any cost': Delhi HC raps student unions on violence, vandalism amid DUSU poll campaign
The court directed the University of Delhi and the Delhi Police to file reports detailing the action taken in connection with the alleged incidents.
The Delhi high court on Thursday reprimanded authorities and student unions over allegations of violence and vandalism during campaigns for the upcoming Delhi University Student Union elections.
In its hearing, the high court observed that allowing student union elections to take on such a colour, as reflected in the material placed before the court, is “unacceptable at any cost.”
The court directed the University of Delhi and the Delhi Police to file reports detailing the action taken in connection with the alleged incidents by Friday.
Deep Dive
While the court did not stay the DUSU polls scheduled for Friday, September 18, it warned that if it is not satisfied with the reports, the court may pass stringent orders, including stopping the counting of votes and postponing the declaration of results.
DUSU polls set for tight contest
The Delhi University student unions polls are scheduled for Friday. Major student organisations such as the RSS-affiliated Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP), Congress-backed National Students' Union of India (NSUI) and the Left alliance of the All India Students' Association (AISA) and Students' Federation of India (SFI), are expected to be engaged in an intense battle in one of the most closely watched contests in student politics.
Ahead of the elections, the university has restricted vehicular movement on key stretches, including Chhatra Marg, Probyn Road and University Road, while student organisations are taking their campaigns to classrooms, college campuses and social media.
Traffic restrictions will also remain in place on both Friday and Saturday, till the declaration of results. The counting of votes will be held on Saturday from 8 am at the Multipurpose Hall of the University Sports Stadium in North Campus.

Earlier this year, Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) which affects one in eight women worldwide, was renamed Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS) by the Endocrine Society.
A global consensus article published in the Lancet in May, led by Professor Helena J. Teede, argued that the name reduced a long-term hormonal and endocrine disorder to focus on ovaries and cysts, leading to inadequate treatment, or fewer people getting diagnosed with the condition.
Professor Terhi Piltonen, president of International Androgen Excess and Polycystic Ovary Syndrome Society (AE-PCOS Society), and also one of the co-leads of the Lancet publication, from Oulu University Hospital, Finland, in conversation with The Hindu speaks about the name change, and its implications on patients, treatment plans, and research.
Excerpts from the interview:
Can you tell me about the process of renaming the syndrome from PCOS to PMOS?
It was sustained work over 14 years that eventually led to the name change. Earlier, there were some individual opinion papers. There were fifty-six societies were invited to be part of the whole process. And about one hundred persons represented these organisations, the patient organisations, and healthcare professionals.
We had meetings where we narrowed down on the different opinions, and we had to take into consideration many different aspects; cultural aspects, acceptability, and adaptability to understand how is it that we want it to change the life of these women. It's been a long process, but the last bit of the process took around two years.
How would the name change impact existing treatment protocol?
We are now thinking about it in a more holistic way; not only looking at the ovary, but also looking at how it affects the mood, the psychological profile, the metabolic profile and also the menstrual cycles. And I think I'm hoping that with the new name, we will now understand that this is a whole-body syndrome.
We know how to manage it, but the name change emphasises how we need to listen to the patients and take a more holistic view and invite other disciplines to play their part.
The women need the opportunity to be asked about their mental health issues, weight management, their skin, their quality of life, how they manage at work, and when they would like to conceive so that we can anticipate how they can have overall good health.
Does the name change impact the research that is being conducted?
There is a three-year overlap period where we are going to put in the codes for PCOS and PMOS while researching and eventually we will transition to using PMOS.
But of course, I am hoping that we'll see more diverse studies, for example my colleague who is an endocrinologist or in internal medicine, or a dermatologist, might take an interest in researching certain parts of the condition. So far, it was only OB-GYNs who were diagnosing it. But I think that others might acknowledge their work in seeing PMOS.
Is it also monetarily challenging to conduct research in an area that impacts women, and not men?
Yes, it is. This is only a fraction of the money that goes into erectile problems or diabetes. , In terms of funding, I think it is not proportional to the prevalence. I'm hoping that there will be more grants and that the industry would get involved as they now know that it is a condition that needs a lot of different approaches.
PMOS is often seen as a ‘modern’ condition. How true or untrue would you say that is?
When we think about nutrition, our bodies haven't been developed to be capable of dealing with very high energy foods. In our evolution, there has been a problem of not having enough food, and we had been moving around and collecting things, and having low-calorie food for thousands and millions of years. And now in a very short time, we have entered a period where food is available, that too, food with high-energy content. So, I think it kind of became a disadvantage for this type of genotype that women have.
And in society now, we have lots of pressure with hectic work lives, and with social media, and other stress factors. This sort of environment does not really serve any of the people who are sensitive to stress. And women are especially sensitive to stress altogether. I think it is linked to modern society in one way, but it does not mean that it's not relevant or that it is not meaningful.

Fast-casual burrito chain Chipotle is working with the data infrastructure giant Palantir.
The company is working on a “food safety risk platform” hosted on Palantir’s flagship software platform Foundry, according to screenshots viewed by WIRED. The platform appears to analyze factors like a store’s health department scores, pest incidents, and employee illnesses to assign a food safety score—basically, the store’s risk level.
Chipotle spokesperson Erin Wolford confirmed the initiative, but declined to comment further. Palantir did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
It's not known exactly when the partnership started or how widely the platform has been deployed, but it comes amid a particularly disastrous period for food safety. The Food and Drug Administration identified more than 12,800 illnesses tied to foodborne outbreaks so far this year, most from a massive cyclospora outbreak connected to iceberg lettuce.

|---|
| Are you a current or former Chipotle or Palantir employee who wants to talk about what’s happening? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at khtaylor.24. | 
Chipotle was not directly impacted by the turbo diarrhea outbreak or the related recall, since it doesn’t serve iceberg lettuce. In July, however, it proactively stopped serving jalapenos from a particular supplier that was linked to a salmonella outbreak that went on to sicken more than 430 people.
Palantir has substantial offerings aimed at food-and-beverage companies, with contracts with poultry and beef supplier Tyson, cereal giant General Mills, and the independent purchasing co-op for the fast-food chain Wendy’s. Companies can use Foundry to manage inventory, automate ordering and delivery, and track their supply chains. At Wendy’s, for example, Palantir’s software is used to spot potential ingredient shortages before they occur.
Palantir’s work with corporate America now accounts for nearly half of its US business. In August, the company reported US commercial revenue reached $764 million in the most recent quarter, a 149 percent year-over-year increase.
The company has also done significant work with government entities focused on supply chains and food safety, including a $22 million contract with the FDA in 2022.
But Palantir remains best known for its other government contracts, including its work with Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security. Last year, ICE awarded Palantir a $30 million contract to build a surveillance platform that provided visibility on people self-deporting.
Palantir’s work with ICE has the potential to be particularly controversial in the restaurant industry, where immigrants make up roughly a fifth of the workforce. In 2010 and 2011, Chipotle fired hundreds of workers who were ineligible to work in the US, following an ICE audit.
In 2025, Chipotle CEO Scott Boatwright said it would be “naive” to believe that Chipotle employees would not be impacted by the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, “whether that’s directly or psychologically.”
“I think it’s a really important moment for us to connect with all individuals in our organization, as a mental check in, to say, hey, how are you doing, how are you feeling, is there anything we can do to help or support?” Boatright told NBC News at the time.

Furniture and appliance rental startup RentoMojo made a strong stock market debut, with its shares listing at a premium of nearly 19% over the IPO issue price. The stock listed at ₹482.45 on the NSE, a premium of 19.42% over its issue price of ₹404. On the BSE, RentoMojo opened at ₹480, up 18.81% from the issue price. The shares gained further following the listing and touched a high of ₹500 on the BSE. At 10:10 IST, the stock was trading at ₹500, up 23.76% over the issue price and 4.15% from its BSE opening price. The company’s market capitalisation stood at ₹5,205.74 Cr ($543 Mn). This was about 30% higher than the valuation of approximately ₹4,006 Cr sought by the startup at the upper end of its IPO price band of ₹384-₹404. The strong listing followed robust demand for RentoMojo’s ₹1,256 Cr IPO, which closed with an overall subscription of 72.88X. Ahead of the public issue, RentoMojo raised ₹376.1 Cr from 41 anchor investors by allotting 93.1 Lakh shares at ₹404 apiece. RentoMojo’s public issue comprised a fresh issue worth ₹150 Cr and an OFS of up to 2.74 Cr shares worth ₹1,105.6 Cr. The OFS delivered sizeable cash-outs for RentoMojo’s early investors. Accel India pocketed around ₹317 Cr by selling 78.47 Lakh shares, clocking an 8.6X gross return. Cofounder and CEO Geetansh Bamania received ₹34.31 Cr from selling 8.49 Lakh shares. Australian athlete apologizes for racing with diarrhea, forfeits the Beijing competition she won
Hyrox updates its competition rules after Joanna Wietrzyk left feces on shared equipment
The Hyrox athlete who started a global uproar after soiling herself and leaking feces at the popular indoor fitness competition has apologized for continuing to race, and forfeited her win.
"I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the Hyrox organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing," Australian Joanna Wietrzyk wrote in a statement posted to Instagram Thursday morning.
"Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice."
Wietrzyk explained she felt "completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness." She added that, "on reflection," she decided to retroactively forfeit her win and the points she earned.
"I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected."
The graphic images of world record holder Wietrzyk competing with feces running down her legs at Saturday's Hyrox in Beijing have sparked debate about the health and safety of competitors versus the mentality that a win is a win, no matter the cost.
Footage showed Wietrzyk continue to push through her events using communal equipment such as ropes, sandbags, rowing machines and medicine balls, and doing burpees and lunges on a shared indoor track. She was the pro women's champion with a time of 1:01:23, beating the U.S.'s Alyssa McElheny by about 45 seconds.
"Go hard or go home … a win is a win," Wietrzyk posted — then later deleted — on Instagram after the event along with a selfie in what appeared to be a hospital bed, according to multiple news outlets.
McElheny has not yet made a public comment about the incident at the competition. She called Beijing "incredible" and thanked the crowd on Instagram Sunday. She also discussed the race — with no mention of feces — in an interview with Hybrid Fitness Media the same day. CBC News has reached out to her press team.
Meanwhile, multiple media outlets report that Wietrzyk's major sponsor, Puma, is distancing itself from the athlete by quietly removing "Joanna Wietrzyk x PUMA" clothing items from its website.
But a spokesperson for Puma says there's "no change" to their partnership with Wietrzyk, telling CBC News in a statement Thursday that some landing pages were "unintentionally taken offline."
On social media, people have flooded the brand's comments with plays on "Puma," such as "Pooma," "Poopma" and "Poo Ma Pants."
Hyrox refunding affected participants
As the incident went viral, online commenters were quick to point out the health risks for other competitors, with many people saying Wietrzyk should have quit or Hyrox should have disqualified her. Others are calling on Hyrox to refund the other competitors or offer them compensation.
On Wednesday, Hyrox China announced it was refunding the entry costs to more than 1,000 participants affected by the incident, according to the South China Morning Post. A spectator at the event told the outlet that feces was visible on the track about 30 minutes after Wietrzyk started her race, causing several runners to slip.
Other athletes who competed in the same race described having to use equipment smeared with feces.
On Monday, Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste wrote in an Instagram statement that the organization has since changed its rules to prevent similar situations from happening again.
Its official rulebook already lists penalties for other bodily fluids, noting that spitting or clearing of nostrils onto the floor is strictly prohibited. Until this week, there was no mention of penalties for feces contaminating the race course.
"I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away," Wietrzyk wrote in her apology.
She added that she will be taking some time to "recover, reflect and look after myself and my family away from the noise."

A lot of X posts, prose, and proselytizing have been spilled on the internet recently about the impending AI apocalypse and whether we've passed the point of no return.
Here's another one eloquently put by the acclaimed theoretical computer scientist Scott Aaronson, whose research has helped us understand the limits of quantum computing. Oh, and he had a stint at OpenAI working on the theoretical foundations of AI safety and alignment:
"AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA," he wrote. That's 113 letters A.
In a blog post published Tuesday, Aaronson made the case for why he, a self-proclaimed skeptic of the AI singularity, "updated" his position on its arrival.
The singularity is a hypothetical concept in which AI's progress surpasses human intelligence and can improve on its own — a process known as recursive self-improvement.
Aaronson wrote that, 20 years ago, he had a "conservative, skeptical position" on self-improving AI. He and other colleagues in computer science largely dismissed the idea as the stuff of science fiction.
Recent developments have led him to change his tune, he wrote, namely, reports of AI agents breaking out of containment and an apparent AI-assisted mathematical breakthrough on the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem, a long-standing question about the math of fluid dynamics.
"I thought that building AIs able to solve millennium problems, hack the servers they're running on, play leading roles in their own improvement, etc etc might for all I knew take hundreds of years," Aaronson said in an email to Business Insider. "But here we are in 2026 and all those things have happened, so I said so."
In his blog, Aaronson also briefly chimed in on the latest AI boom-or-doom debate that has split the tech industry.
"I feel like it would be healthy for everyone to stop grinding their ideological axes, their sentiments about Dario Amodei or Sam Altman, for long enough simply to acknowledge that the wonders and terrors are here," he wrote. "They couldn't be here more clearly if the sky had turned reddish-orange like in the Matrix movies."
Aaronson said in the email that humanity is "certainly at risk" but he doesn't agree with the premise that doom is the "'default' outcome."
"I think there's a huge range of possible outcomes, and a lot depends on what we do now, whether we treat what's being created with the awe and humility and caution that it deserves, or simply as another consumer product to rush to market or a geopolitical weapon (or something that will go away if we pretend it's not real and a marketing stunt)," he said.
In his view, as AI's transformative phase begins, Aaronson wrote in the blog that human theorem-provers like himself may be becoming obsolete. The last gap could now be between intelligence and the physical world.
"Yes, I still unload the dishwasher and clip my toenails," he wrote. "On the other hand, in whatever years I have left, I don't expect that I'll ever again prove a theorem because I'm actually needed to prove it. If I do, it will only be for my or others' enjoyment or edification."

On 15 September 2026, an Indian Navy vessel and a Pakistani naval vessel came into contact in the North Arabian Sea. India said the Pakistani vessel approached at high speed and manoeuvred unsafely while the Indian vessel was on a routine surveillance mission, and summoned Pakistan’s Chargé d’Affaires on 16 September to protest. Pakistan gave a different account, saying the incident occurred during its SEASPARK-26 naval exercise and alleging that the Indian vessel carried out aggressive manoeuvres near the Pakistani ship.
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here) with the claim that it shows the collision between a Pakistani naval vessel and an Indian Navy warship on 15 September 2026. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows the collision between a Pakistani naval vessel and an Indian Navy warship on 15 September 2026.
Fact: The video does not show the collision between an Indian Navy warship and a Pakistani naval vessel on 15 September 2026. It shows a 2011 incident involving PNS Babur and INS Godavari during an escort mission for the merchant vessel MV Suez. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to the same clip (archived) uploaded on a YouTube channel named “mix” on 16 October 2014. The video was titled “Pakistan Navy Ship BABUR VS Indian Navy Ship”, and its description stated that it showed a Pakistan Navy ship and an Indian Navy ship in the Gulf of Aden during the rescue of the merchant vessel MV Suez. This confirms that the video predates the recent collision by over a decade.
Using these clues, we searched for relevant keywords and found a 2011 NDTV report showing similar footage from another angle. According to the report, the collision occurred on 16 June 2011 when the Pakistani warship PNS Babur rammed into the rear of the Indian frigate INS Godavari while attempting to overtake it during an escort mission for the merchant vessel MV Suez. The report stated that PNS Babur, caught in INS Godavari’s wake in heavy sea conditions, scraped against the frigate and damaged its helicopter deck. It also showed footage recorded from the deck of PNS Babur, capturing crew members celebrating after the collision.
A press release issued by India’s Ministry of External Affairs on 18 June 2011 confirmed that India had formally protested Pakistan’s conduct, stating that PNS Babur’s risky manoeuvres jeopardised the safety of INS Godavari and its crew and violated international maritime safety regulations and the 1991 India-Pakistan agreement on advance notice of military exercises.
To sum up, this viral video shows a 2011 Pakistan-India naval collision, not the September 2026 incident.

A clinical trial by doctors at a private medical college hospital in Chickballapur near Bengaluru has found that a dual stellate ganglion block (SGB) procedure may help reduce anxiety symptoms in patients who do not respond to standard treatment.
The study, published in the July-August 2026 issue of Pain Physician, an open-access journal, involved 63 patients with moderate to severe treatment-resistant anxiety. The researchers found that those who underwent the procedure had a significantly greater reduction in anxiety symptoms than those who received a sham procedure.
What the study involved
Led by G. Niraj, senior consultant, anaesthesiology, and a multidisciplinary team of pain medicine physicians, psychiatrists, and clinical psychologists at the Sri Madhusudan Sai Institute of Medical Sciences and Research (SMSIMSR) in Chickballapur, the randomised controlled trial evaluated dual SGB specifically for treatment-resistant anxiety.
The study focused on patients whose anxiety had persisted despite standard treatment. Treatment-resistant anxiety was defined as failure to respond to at least one first-line medication and one first-line psychotherapy, each given for at least eight weeks. Most patients in the study had tried several medications. Forty-six of the 63 participants had tried at least two medications.
The study involved 63 patients, of whom 42 received the dual SGB procedure and 21 received the sham treatment. The patients were followed for 12 weeks.
What is the procedure?
A stellate ganglion block involves injecting a local anaesthetic and steroid mixture into a group of nerves in the neck under ultrasound guidance. These nerves are part of the sympathetic nervous system, which controls the body’s ‘fight-or-flight’ response.
The procedure was performed on both sides of the neck, with the second block given between 24 hours and seven days after the first. The researchers said that reducing excessive activity in the sympathetic nervous system may help ease some symptoms of anxiety.
“Persistent anxiety is not just in the head. The body’s stress alarm can remain stuck in the ‘on’ position. Our research helps to reset this stress response, offering hope to people whose anxiety has not responded to standard treatments,” Dr. Niraj said.
He stressed that SGB was not intended to replace psychological therapy or medication. “It provides another valuable option for patients with poorly controlled anxiety,” he said.
The procedure was generally well tolerated by the patients in the study. None of the adverse events reported in the SGB group was serious. Temporary hoarseness lasting one to three hours was reported by 14 patients, while one patient experienced numbness in an upper limb that resolved within six hours.
Future potential
Dr. Niraj and his colleagues said the findings could have implications for mental healthcare in both rural and urban areas, particularly where access to long-term psychological therapy is limited. The researchers said a clinic-based intervention, when used appropriately alongside existing mental health treatment, could provide a valuable option for patients with difficult-to-treat anxiety.
The researchers cautioned that the findings need to be confirmed through larger studies. The trial was conducted at a single centre and followed patients for only 12 weeks. Further research is needed to determine how long the benefits last and to better understand the mechanism through which SGB may help reduce anxiety.
