Tens of thousands flee as Iran-backed rebels draw Yemen into the wider war
The lightning advance of the Iran-backed Houthi rebels has forced tens of thousands of people to flee their homes in Yemen
CAIRO -- As Houthi rebels closed in, Eshraq Abdel Gelil and her husband fled their home, walking through the mountains before catching a ride to a nearby city. Four months pregnant, she feared another miscarriage.
They are among more than 125,000 people who have fled as the Iran-backed rebels have advanced down the Red Sea coast to a key maritime chokepoint. The offensive, linked to the wider Iran war, has threatened Saudi oil exports, pushed up global fuel prices and rattled markets.
The cost has been far greater for Yemenis caught in the crossfire. Many have fled their homes with only what they could carry. The Arab world’s poorest country was pushed to the brink of famine in an earlier phase of the civil war, which killed an estimated 150,000 people.
A Saudi-led blockade, along with the Houthis’ repressive rule and detention of U.N. and aid workers, has made life miserable in the now-expanding territory under rebel control. Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, weak and fragmented, has struggled to push them back.
Abdel Gelil is now sheltering with family in the southwestern city of Taiz, while others are sleeping in the streets or erecting makeshift tents out of plastic.
Her husband, Mohamed Thabet, said the latest fighting was “extremely fierce” and more intense than a battle in 2017 that had also forced him to flee. “There was shelling and shrapnel near the house,” he said.
They walked for 5 kilometers (3 miles) before taking a vehicle for around 60 kilometers (37 miles) on mountain roads.
When they arrived in Taiz, a doctor told them that the baby had moved lower in the womb. Abdel Gelil miscarried at the same point in a previous pregnancy.
“My wife cried from the shock and was very fearful,” Thabet said.
Now they are packed into a home with extended family. They can only afford to eat twice a day, and they worry that Abdel Gelil is not getting enough nutrients for her and the baby.
Thabet also worries about his sister, who hasn't been able to afford her diabetes medication for over a month. She and her two daughters, 8 and 13, have a blood condition that makes them susceptible to anemia, he said.
The civil war dates back to 2014, when the Houthis seized much of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa. Saudi Arabia intervened the following year in support of Yemen's internationally recognized government. A 2022 ceasefire largely halted the fighting.
Hostilities erupted again in July, when the Houthis renewed attacks on Saudi Arabia in what the rebels said was an attempt to lift the blockade. The attacks on Saudi Arabia's oil industry came as the U.S. was having some success in reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
The fighting in Yemen has killed eight civilians and wounded another 32, according to the U.N. humanitarian office, which says an estimated 125,000 people have fled their homes. The U.N. children's agency, known as UNICEF, says the displaced include more than 57,000 children.
“This is one of the most fast-moving and volatile displacement waves Yemen has seen in years,” said Obia Achieng, a UNICEF representative in Yemen. “Families are fleeing with little or no warning, often at night, carrying only what they can grab.”
“The situation is particularly concerning because it comes on top of an already severe humanitarian crisis,” Achieng added.
Before the latest fighting, the U.N. had warned that around 5 million Yemenis were experiencing “crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity.”
Milena Murr, of Prosper Global, a humanitarian group previously known as Mercy Corps, said some people arriving in Taiz had walked for over 16 hours, arriving at displacement camps exhausted, dehydrated and with some of the children appearing malnourished.
Iman Abdullahi, country director for CARE, another aid group, said there's an urgent need for food, maternal and newborn healthcare, hygiene supplies, private latrines and mental health support.
“One woman had to wash her only clothes and remain inside her tent until they dried because she had nothing else to wear. Another was forced to flee just two weeks after giving birth,” he said.
Nashwan Ahmed Said was stitching together a tent from plastic wheat sacks. He said this is the third time he's been displaced since the start of the war.
“We are in such a state! We have no home, no toilet, no food and nothing to drink,” he said.
Arwa Ahmed, who was displaced with her five children, said she and her family ate nothing but rice for days.
“We need everything. We need tents, we need food and all the essentials, because we were displaced and took nothing with us,” she said.

Celtic were punished again for their defensive errors as they followed up their Old Firm loss with a 3-1 home defeat to Ferencvaros in their Europa League opener.
Martin O'Neill vowed his team would get things right after their League Cup collapse against Rangers, but it was more of the same after a promising start against the Hungarians.
They had plenty of early possession, but were soon a goal down when Liam Scales turned Bamidele Yusuf's shot into his own net after Kieran Tierney had failed to deal with a cross.
With half-time approaching, Mika Baur slammed the ball into the net to pull Celtic level only for the visitors to quickly restore their lead.
Yusuf beat Tierney and Callum McGregor was too slow to clear the ball, leaving Kristoffer Zachariassen to flick the ball past the returning Viljami Sinisalo.
The mistakes continued in the second half. Colby Donovan, handed his first Scotland call-up this week, was caught out and Australian winger Daniel Arzani smashed the ball into the top corner.
Celtic did have a flurry of late chances, but they could not salvage anything from the game as the fans who stayed until the full-time whistle made their frustrations clear.
It is back-to-back defeats for O'Neill's side ahead of Sunday's Premiership clash with Rangers, live on Sky Sports.
The key moments from Celtic Park:
8: CHANCE! James Forrest crosses the ball into Camilo Duran. He takes a double touch and it's past the post.
20: GOAL FERENCVAROS! Tierney fails to deal with a cross and it falls to Yusuf. His shot takes a final touch off Scales before it hits the back of the net.

More questions than answers
Sky Sports' Alison Conroy:
Celtic started well, and Forrest appeared to be rolling back the years as he caused problems for Ferencvaros down the left.
But their defensive frailties soon proved costly, again. The goals were self-inflicted.
How to solve the problems at the back is the big question, but there is no obvious answer.
O'Neill made four changes from Sunday's defeat to Rangers but they did not appear to make any difference.
Celtic's big summer signings like Duran and Hogh have yet to step up in the big games this season and, for a frustrated Hoops support, that is a real worry.
O'Neill admits he is still trying to work out his best starting XI, but he does not have too much time to figure that out.
No matter what happens on Sunday, they will be top of the Premiership heading into the international break. But they need a win - two Old Firm defeats and a Europa League loss in eight days would not be accepted by the fans.
Just months after snatching a league and cup double, is the pressure now on O'Neill?
O'Neill: We'll get ourselves together
Celtic manager Martin O'Neill:
"We're naturally disappointed getting beaten.
"It's not the start we wanted. We have seven games in which to try and get some points on the board. Really need to concentrate now on Sunday [against Rangers].
"Tonight was a European lesson for us in many aspects. We'll get ourselves together. We need to re-energise ourselves as much as anything else.
"When we have decent possession of the ball, just don't give it away. But also I think taking a few risks as well too - risks in the proper areas of the field."

I've recently introduced a few friends to the power of a great robot vacuum. One of my friends calls hers a marriage saver, while the other was both thrilled and horrified by how many stains the vacuum’s AI found on her floors. Personally, my robot vacuums keep me from wanting to set the litter box on fire, since my cat is on a mission to create his own navigational trail of litter through my home.
The best robot vacuums these days aren’t just vacuuming your floors, nor are they blindly bumping around your house like they used to. These gadgets are mopping, scrubbing away stains, lifting themselves off obstacles, and even reminding you to clean the dirtier areas in your home more frequently. A good robot vacuum can cost a pretty penny, but it doesn’t have to, depending on what you’re looking for. Curious about what’s the best model for you? I’ve been testing every new robot vacuum I can in my three-story home filled with three adults, a preschooler, and a cat who’s on a mission to get litter all over the house.

What’s a Robot Vacuum?
A robot vacuum is an automated vacuum, usually shaped like a round disc, that moves around your house to vacuum (and mop, as many models these days include mopping) on your behalf. You might’ve heard some refer to these devices as “Roombas,” which is the brand that made the concept popular, but today just about every cleaning brand—from high-end Dyson to affordable Bissell—makes some kind of robot vacuum. They come with either a charging station or a larger docking station that can self-empty.
What Your Robot Vacuum Will Need
There are a few things most robot vacuums will need to work properly:
- Space around the base station. Many robot vacuum manuals recommend at least a foot of clearance on three of the four sides of the vacuum’s base station to ensure it has room to return home.
- A good Wi-Fi signal. If your robot vacuum connects to Wi-Fi, as many do these days for app control and software updates, it’ll need a strong connection wherever it’s placed. Most of them can only connect to the 2.4-GHz wireless band, so make sure you have that (and choose only that band when you’re setting up if your Wi-Fi shows those bands separately). Confused? Check out our guide to setting up your smart home.
- Regular maintenance. It might be a robot, but it can’t take care of itself. See below for my tips for basic robot vacuum maintenance, and make sure to read your vacuum’s manual to know what your specific model requires.
Are Robot Vacuums Going to Get Banned?
The Federal Communications Commission announced in late July that foreign-produced advanced robotic devices will now be included on the FCC’s Covered List. That list includes communications equipment and services that are deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States, and as of this week, that includes robot vacuums (and similar devices like robotic pool cleaners and lawn mowers). While it won’t ban any models already on the market that have FCC approval, we’ll likely see a huge decline in available new models after this year. Models made in the US will be fine, but future vacuums from popular brands like Dreame, Eufy, Roborock, and more could be affected. For now, you'll still see vacuums launching from these brands, though, since FCC approval is given months ahead of product launches.
This decision comes from an interagency body in the White House executive branch called the National Security Determination, which has deemed automated robotic devices a security risk due to the data they collect, which could be used for surveillance and be remotely commandeered by “malign actors.” While the initial documentation describes humanoid robots and a recent case of a humanoid robot’s cybersecurity vulnerability to be remotely taken over, the official description of these robot devices will include robot vacuums and any devices meeting the following criteria:
- Autonomous mobile robots that are capable of locomotion, obstacle avoidance, navigation, or movement on the ground
- Operates at a distance from a human operator or supervisor
- Combined weight of the device and docking station is over 4.4 pounds
- Contains a sensor capable of perceiving its environment
- Contains a component capable of providing network connectivity, including Bluetooth and Wi-Fi
- Contains software running locally or remotely, including firmware and AI or machine-learning model weights that control the robot’s navigation and movement perception
Overall, robot vacuums themselves aren’t banned, but new models from companies based outside the US won’t get FCC approval and can’t be sold in the US. You don’t need to stop using any robot vacuum you have, but if you’re in the market for a new one, it’s better to shop sooner before availability starts to decline—and prices are likely to rise as supply falls.

How I Test Robot Vacuums
I test all robot vacuums in my three-story townhouse, where they clean across luxury vinyl plank (LVP); tile; carpet; and a large, low-pile rug. I have a dining table and four barstools to navigate, and both a cat and a child who create daily messes. I run the vacuum at least three times across the main floors of my home to assess its overall performance and note any recurring issues or errors it encounters. I do pick up my son’s toys, but I like to watch how the robot navigates the various chair legs and side tables throughout my home, and whether it sucks up the power cords beside my bed. I also like to see how much battery life is left after a run is complete on each level of my home.
I also set up an obstacle course of sorts. The first one is the corner test, created by three Cheerios placed in three tricky corners on the middle floor of my home: one in the corner of an Ikea Billy bookshelf toe kick, one underneath my countertops next to the fridge, and one next to a barstool chair leg. It’s how I test how well each robot vacuum gets into corners and underneath cabinetry.
I also create intentional spills for these vacuums to clean up. I use maraschino cherry juice to create two spill spots, then use a paper towel to smear and thin the stain to better replicate a spill you might not have seen on your floors. Many robot vacuums have AI that promises to detect these kinds of stains, but so far, no vacuum has stopped and scrubbed both spots on its first try.
Frequently Asked Questions
Can You Use Robot Vacuums on All Kinds of Floors?
You can, especially since there are so many mopping models now to better clean hard flooring. You can use these devices on anything from hardwood to LVP and tile, though I wouldn't recommend leaving smaller rugs out for these autonomous gadgets to get stuck on. Large, set rugs are fine, but bathroom and kitchen mats or any thin, easily moved rugs should be cleared out of the way and put in the wash instead of vacuumed by your robot vac.
How Often Do You Need to Maintain Your Robot Vacuum?
Taking good care of your robot vacuum will help it last. Here’s the debris-removal process you should follow for each robot vacuum style.
- If it has a charger-only base: This means the debris is stored inside the vacuum. You’ll likely want to empty it after each use. If your vacuum has a fill line you can watch, you can empty it when it reaches that line, but after each use is really best practice.
- If it has a self-emptying docking station: Each manufacturer will have different advice about when a self-emptying station needs to be emptied, but it’s usually between 30 and 60 days, depending on design and use. If you run your vacuum daily and have a lot of debris, like pet hair, you might need to aim for 30 days or less.
- If it has water tanks: Dirty-water tanks should be cleaned after each mopping run of your vacuum. Clean water can stay filled in the station.
Make sure to review your robot vacuum’s manual for any other steps the manufacturer recommends you take regularly to keep the vacuum running for as long as possible. Many brands also have replacement parts, so you can swap out individual pieces like brushes without needing an entirely new vacuum.
Do I Still Need a Regular Vacuum if I Have a Robot Vacuum?
I recommend keeping some kind of vacuum on hand, though that can vary based on your home. If you have stairs, you’ll definitely still want a hand vacuum or stick vacuum that can easily maneuver and clean your staircase, while pet owners might want a vacuum that can clean upholstery. I prefer my Dyson stick vacuums for a good carpet clean, but your mileage may vary depending on your preferences. Either way, I think everyone needs a companion vacuum of some kind with a robot vacuum.
Do You Need a Self-Emptying Dock?
You don’t need it, but a self-emptying dock makes using a robot vacuum much easier. You aren’t fumbling with debris every time it runs, and having a single bag to remove or a bin to empty is much easier than pulling debris out of the vacuum itself. I’d even recommend choosing a stick vac with a self-emptying dock, as it just makes the whole experience so much easier.
How Does WIRED Obtain Robot Vacuums? What Happens When We’re Done Testing?
Almost all the robot vacuums we test are provided to us as press samples with the understanding that there is no guarantee of coverage or type of coverage. Most companies don’t want a used vacuum back, so we either donate them locally or have the top performers long-term tested to see how they last.

In response to a new European Union law, AI platforms are implementing new schemes for watermarking the content they generate. Anthropic recently disclosed its future Claude models will use SynthID-Text, an approach Google created and released as open source. It uses a secret key that subtly changes the process a model uses for choosing the next word in a sentence. Whereas a top next word choice might be “cloudy,” the key might change it to “overcast.” Anyone who knows the key can determine if it was generated by the platform using it.
New research shows that SynthID-Text can change not just word selection but also the tools a model invokes and the chances it will adhere to or disregard safety guardrails it has been trained to follow. The threat can become greater in the face of an adversarial prompt, in which an attacker attempts to cause a model to carry out a harmful action, such as revealing a password or other sensitive information. Instructions that normally wouldn’t be followed will, in some cases, be performed once the watermarking is deployed. The finding underscores the need for developers to thoroughly test how their LLMs and agents behave when watermarking is in place.
Changing safety behavior
“As compared to the same models without watermarking, it is definitely going to change their behavior, especially when we place it under adversarial conditions, or we make these models call tools when they’re powering an agent,” Andrea Siposova, an AI security researcher at Lasso Security, told Ars. “Watermarking is made to not be perceptible to a reader, but we know that when we are changing anything about what the model is generating, it is going to cause some tradeoffs, it’s going to show up somewhere.”
Watermarking works by embedding a signal that allows output to be identified as AI generated, something known as provenance. SynthID takes the normal sampling process and adds a random seed generator, sampling algorithm, and scoring function to it. Instead of the process using an arbitrary random number generator for next-word selection, the watermarking uses a secret key. While the word selection is still random, people with knowledge of the key can check the sequence of words to determine the likelihood that the key was used.
A key feature of SynthID is something known as tournament sampling. Similar to a sports game, SynthID evaluates large numbers of next-word token candidates. It uses a secret key to assign them probability scores. A pair of tokens competes in a round. The one with the higher hidden score wins and advances to the next round. The process continues until a final winning token is determined. More about tournament sampling can be found here and here.
Siposova tested the “non-distortionary” configuration of SynthID-Text through Hugging Face’s unmodified SynthIDTextWatermarkLogitsProcessor. She fed harmful prompts into six open-weight models and compared the responses when the watermarking was used and when it wasn’t. The experiment revealed that the watermarking changed responses to harmful requests, particularly when they were made using prompt-injection techniques.
“Watermarking changes refusal behavior on bare harmful requests, but the effect is more pronounced when the same requests are paired with the prompt-injection technique,” Siposova wrote. “On several models, watermarking then makes the model more likely to answer harmful requests that it would otherwise refuse.”
The changes have important safety consequences because they influence not only the LLM responses but also subsequent actions of AI agents relying on the model.
“At the model level, this can change safety behavior, including whether the model refuses a harmful request and whether that refusal holds under prompt injection,” the researcher wrote. “At the agent level, the same sampled tokens can determine which tool is called and what arguments are passed to it. Prompt injection connects these two settings because a weakened refusal becomes more consequential when the model can also act through tools. Such a watermarking procedure can therefore affect both what the model says and what an agent does. We call this behavioral effect sampling drift.”
Also interesting: Model responses behaved differently depending on which secret key was used.
There are limitations to the research. It doesn’t test how Claude model responses change under the watermarking. Instead, it tests a half-dozen open-weight models, so the researcher has access to token sampling that could be enabled and disabled during tournament sampling while keeping other settings fixed. The experiments also tested the Hugging Face implementation of SynthID-Text tournament sampling and not the specific implementation Claude models will use.
Still, the results show that at least some forms of the watermarking approach may affect model and agent safety. It will be important for red-team hacking exercises to stress-test their platforms to ensure they perform as expected when SynthID is deployed.

Patricio Guzmán, the film-maker who chronicled Chile’s bloody 1970s political strife and its subsequent social and political turmoil in films such as The Battle of Chile and Nostalgia for the Light, has died aged 85. According to Chilean news outlet Emol, Guzmán died on Tuesday in Paris after a cardiorespiratory arrest.
Guzmán’s chief preoccupation throughout his career was the carnage unleashed by Augusto Pinochet’s coup in 1973 against Salvador Allende, Chile’s elected president. He later told the Guardian: “I’m a film-maker who was very marked by the ways of the dictator. It has remained with me for ever. I cannot leave it behind.” However, he resisted the idea that he was an activist, political film-maker, adding: “I’m not a sociologist. Neither am I a politician. I make films that are metaphorical and poetic; I interpret reality through my own personal way of looking.”
Born in Chile in 1941, Guzmán initially worked in advertising before studying film, first in Chile and then in Madrid. On his return to Chile, Guzmán responded to the febrile political atmosphere after Allende’s election in 1970, eventually completing the mammoth Battle of Chile documentary that chronicled Pinochet’s ultimately successful attempt to overthrow Allende, resulting in the latter’s suicide. Guzmán did not shrink from the brutality of the period, even including footage shot by camera operator Leonardo Henrichsen as he is shot dead by the soldier he is filming.
Guzmán was helped in the endeavour by French film-maker Chris Marker, who supplied film stock and connections that proved vital to make the film. Guzmán himself was arrested but eventually released, but the film’s cinematographer Jorge Müller was not so lucky – along with his girlfriend Carmen Bueno, he was arrested, tortured and “disappeared” in 1974.
Guzmán completed The Battle of Chile outside the country, releasing each of its three parts – The Insurrection of the Bourgeoisie (1975), The Coup d’État (1976) and Popular Power (1979) – through the rest of the 70s. Described by the Guardian as “an outstandingly photographed example of a newsreel film that captures the drama and volatility of the period”, it has continued to attract acclaim since then. Guzmán revisited the film in the mid-90s with Chile, Obstinate Memory, in which he returned to the country after a quarter-century of exile. In 2001 he completed The Pinochet Case, after the Chilean former dictator was arrested in London in 1998.
The director moved on to more metaphysical subjects with a trilogy of films starting in 2010: Nostalgia for the Light, The Pearl Button and The Cordillera of Dreams. They sought to explore Chile’s traumatic past by absorbing the country’s magnificent natural landscapes. His final film, My Imaginary Country, was premiered in 2022 and covered Chile’s dramatic 2019 street protests.

An egg retrieval is the culmination of several weeks of ovarian stimulation, as multiple follicles develop under the influence of fertility medicines, with the ovaries undergoing significant changes in response to hormonal stimulation.
The quality and number of eggs ultimately retrieved are influenced by several factors, including age, ovarian reserve, genetics and the underlying cause of infertility. A woman’s diet cannot alter these fundamentals, nor can any particular food guarantee better eggs or a successful IVF outcome. Nutrition can, however, influence the metabolic and physiological environment in which the body responds to treatment. For this reason, what a woman eats in the weeks preceding egg retrieval should be viewed as part of overall preparation rather than as a means of ‘boosting’ fertility.
Biology behind the preparation
Egg development is a prolonged process. Although the final stages of follicular growth occur during the IVF stimulation cycle, the oocytes have been undergoing maturation over a much longer period. This means that nutrition in the weeks before retrieval is unlikely to produce a dramatic change in egg quality on its own, but maintaining good nutritional status can support general metabolic health during a demanding treatment cycle.
During ovarian stimulation, the body is also adapting to changing hormone levels, increased follicular activity and, in some women, symptoms such as bloating, constipation, fatigue or changes in appetite. A balanced diet can help maintain energy levels and provide the protein, fibre, vitamins, minerals and healthy fats required for normal physiological function.
Among dietary patterns studied in relation to IVF outcomes, the Mediterranean-style diet has received some of the most consistent attention. A 2023 evidence-based review published in Frontiers in Nutrition, covering multiple IVF nutritional interventions, concluded that a Mediterranean-style dietary approach is the most consistently supported pattern for women undergoing ovarian stimulation. This diet is rich in vegetables, fruits, legumes, whole grains, healthy fats, and lean protein, with limited processed foods and refined carbohydrates.
What to eat more of
Protein is the macronutrient that most women underestimate in the lead-up to retrieval. Both animal and plant sources such as eggs, fish, lentils, chickpeas and dairy support follicle development and give the body the building blocks it needs during stimulation. Aim to include a source of protein in every meal.
Healthy fats, particularly omega-3 fatty acids, carry documented benefits for IVF outcomes. A review published in Reproductive BioMedicine Online found that supplementation with omega-3 free fatty acids may lead to improvements in both clinical and embryological IVF outcomes. Practical sources in an Indian context include fish such as salmon, sardines, and mackerel, as well as walnuts, flaxseeds, and chia seeds.
Folate belongs in this conversation for two reasons: it supports healthy cell division, and many women undergoing IVF are not getting enough of it through food alone. Dark leafy vegetables such as spinach, methi and palak are among the richest dietary sources. Iron from leafy greens, lentils, and lean meat supports the blood supply that developing follicles depend on.
Antioxidants such as vitamins C and E, selenium, zinc help protect developing eggs from oxidative stress, which increases during stimulation as the ovaries work at higher capacity. Berries, bell peppers, nuts, and seeds are practical sources worth building into daily meals.
Hydration matters more during stimulation than at other times. As follicles grow, the risk of bloating and fluid retention increases. Consistent water intake of at least two to three litres a day supports the body through this phase and helps manage stimulation-related discomfort.
What to limit
There is no single food that will undo an IVF cycle, but some patterns are worth avoiding in the weeks before retrieval. Highly processed foods, refined carbohydrates, and excessive added sugar affect blood sugar stability and create an inflammatory environment that does not serve follicle development. Alcohol should be avoided during stimulation. Excess caffeine, more than one to two cups of coffee a day, is worth reducing, as higher intakes have been associated with poorer IVF outcomes in some studies.
What patients should know
There is no fertility diet that guarantees better egg quality or a successful cycle, and any approach that promises otherwise is worth approaching with scepticism. What a balanced, nutrient-dense diet does is support your body through a physically demanding process the same way good nutrition supports any period of heightened physical demand.
The specifics of what your body needs during your particular stimulation protocol are best discussed with your fertility specialist, who can account for your individual clinical picture, any nutrient deficiencies identified through blood work, and whether supplementation is appropriate in your case.
(Dr. Shivika Gupta is a fertility specialist at Birla Fertility and IVF, Gurgaon Sec- 51. shivika.gupta@birlafertility.com)

The Clean Label Credibility Test India’s clean-label boom is facing its toughest test yet. FSSAI’s recent crackdown on health and purity claims is threatening the marketing language that helped many D2C brands grow. Can “healthy” food startups survive when every claim must stand up to evidence? The Label Under Fire: FSSAI’s recent notices to 20 legacy and D2C brands has brought claims such as “100% natural” and “healthy” under scrutiny. Brands built on “ingredient transparency” were caught using date powders and fructose while advertising zero added sugar. Rather than challenging the FSSAI's notices, several brands quietly opted to scrub these absolute claims and overhauled their packaging. But the situation took a sharp turn after the SC began questioning what a front-of-pack warning label should look like. SC Weighs In: The apex court accepted FSSAI’s proposed red hexagon warning for packaged foods high in sugar, salt and saturated fat. At the same time, it also sought more clarity on scientific thresholds, label size and possible confusion with existing food markers. The next hearing in the matter could establish a clearer path for how health warnings must appear, potentially reshaping packaging and product listings across India’s food market. Trust Needs Proof: Experts believe that the crackdown can potentially create a better opportunity for brands to demonstrate better ingredients, transparent formulations and verifiable nutritional claims. However, it will raise the cost of entering the category and will require the brands to rethink product formulations. So, will new-age food brands adapt or will this regulatory reckoning shatter consumer trust in "clean-label" promises? Celina Jaitly has shared an emotional throwback photograph featuring several of the people she has described as her most valuable treasures. The actor shared the picture on social media on September 17, reflecting on loss, family and the pain of looking back at moments that can no longer be recreated.
Celina Jaitly shares heartbreaking throwback picture with parents, brother and sons: “I have lost my most valuable treasures”
The photograph features Celina with her late parents, her brother Major (Retd.) Vikrant Kumar Jaitly, and her twin sons Winston and Viraaj Haag. Her younger son Arthur, who was not yet born when the photograph was taken, is absent from the frame. Sharing the picture, Celina wrote, “#alone : अभी उठा हूँ नींद से तुम्हारा ख़्वाब देख के…
 I am unsure which pain was worse.. the shock of what happened or the ache for what never will.”
She went on to reflect on the series of personal losses her family has experienced and how the photograph has taken on a different meaning with time. “I still cannot believe the tragedies that have struck our family. In the blink of an eye, I find myself staring at a photograph surrounded by my most valuable treasures ( only Arthur is missing he wasn’t born yet)”
Celina Jaitly reflects on family, loss and memories
The actor described the photograph as a reminder of a life that once felt ordinary, but has since been marked by significant changes and loss. “I find myself in a script I didn’t sign up for.. A story only possible in films..”
Celina also spoke about how everyday family relationships can sometimes be taken for granted, only for their importance to become clearer after loss. “We take our relationships for granted. Our parents, our siblings, our children… We go about our days complaining so passionately about the smallest things, never imagining that the ordinary moments we barely notice will one day become everything we long for.”
She added, “Then life hits, and the world we knew is gone. Yet there is the photograph. Those faces. That love. And the unbearable longing to step inside it, just once more.”
View this post on Instagram
A family marked by multiple losses
Celina has experienced the loss of both her parents within a span of less than a year. Her father, Colonel Vikram Kumar Jaitly, a retired Indian Army officer, died on July 2, 2017, following a prolonged illness. Her mother, Dr. Meeta Jaitly, a child psychologist and literature professor, died on June 8, 2018, after battling cancer.
The actor also lost her son Shamsher, one of her twin boys born in 2017. Shamsher died shortly after birth due to hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a severe congenital heart condition. His twin brother Arthur survived.
Celina has previously spoken publicly about the impact of losing Shamsher and has continued to remember him through social media posts.
Her recent family photograph comes at a particularly difficult period in her personal life. She is currently involved in divorce and custody proceedings with her estranged husband Peter Haag. Celina has publicly spoken about being separated from her three surviving sons, Winston, Viraaj and Arthur, who are in Austria. She has also expressed distress over missing important moments in their lives, including the beginning of the new school year.
Celina Jaitly’s ongoing family struggles
Alongside the custody dispute, Celina has also been seeking information and communication concerning her brother, Major (Retd.) Vikrant Kumar Jaitly, who has been detained in the UAE since September 2024. The Delhi High Court had considered her petition seeking assistance and communication with him. In March 2026, the court closed that petition after a statement attributed to Vikrant during a consular visit was placed on record saying he did not wish to communicate with his sister.
Celina has continued to speak publicly about the emotional toll of the circumstances surrounding her family. In a recent post about her brother, she referred to her parents no longer being alive and described him as someone whose absence has deeply affected her.
In her latest post, however, Celina's focus remained on the photograph and what it represents to her. Reflecting on questions that have remained unanswered, she wrote, “I don’t know whether this is karma from a past life or some incomprehensible journey of the soul. No answer brings me comfort. No explanation makes the absence easier to bear.”
Concluding her note, she said, “I have lost my most valuable treasures… and this, my heart cannot accept. 💔”

India and Pakistan summon diplomats after ships collide in international waters
- Published
India and Pakistan have summoned each other's top diplomats in Delhi and Islamabad after two of their naval vessels collided in the Arabian Sea.
Both sides blamed each other for the collision, which happened on Tuesday. They also accused each other of violating a 1991 bilateral agreement that requires either side to give advance notice of military exercises.
While India said the incident did not cause any major damage, the statement released by Pakistan did not make clear whether its vessel was damaged in any way.
The incident comes more than a year after the South Asian neighbours conducted military strikes against each other before agreeing on a ceasefire.
In its statement, India said it had lodged a strong protest with the Charge d'Affaires of the Pakistani High Commission in Delhi over what it called "unacceptable and unprofessional conduct" of the naval unit.
"The Charge d'Affaires of Pakistan was advised to convey to the concerned Pakistani authorities, the need for all military units to observe due care and respect the provisions of the relevant agreements between the two sides in order to prevent any repeat of such incidents," India's external affairs ministry said.
On the same day, Pakistan also summoned India's Charge d'Affaires in Islamabad, lodging its complaint against what it called a "highly provocative and unacceptable" action by India's naval vessel.
In its statement, Pakistan's foreign affairs ministry said that its navy was conducting its biennial exercise, SEASPARK-26, in its exclusive economic zone when the Indian vessel "carried out aggressive manoeuvres in dangerously close proximity" of its ship.
Pakistan also urged the international community to call upon India to "refrain from irresponsible actions that could further destabilise South Asia", saying that the region could not afford to be held "hostage to India's reckless pursuit of conflict and instability".
The Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Manoeuvres and Troops Movements - which both sides accuse the other of violating - was signed in 1991, external to prevent "any crisis situation arising due to misreading of the other side's intentions".
India specifically accused Pakistan of violating Article 10 of the agreement, which says that the two countries' naval vessels and submarines must not be closer than three nautical miles from each other so as to avoid accidents while operating in international waters.

Amid the ongoing debate over the introduction of MDR on select UPI transactions, the finance ministry’s Department of Financial Services (DFS) has said the move was not driven by “external pressure”. The clarification came after allegations linked the reintroduction of MDR on UPI to the US Trade Representative’s (USTR) 2026 National Trade Estimate Report, which flagged India’s digital payment policies as a barrier for foreign payment service providers. In a statement, the DFS highlighted two concerns raised in the USTR report — the inability of US payment service providers to participate in the UPI ecosystem, including credit card transactions, on a level playing field with RuPay, and NPCI’s proposed 30% market share cap for third-party application providers (TPAPs). Responding to the first concern, the DFS pointed to NPCI’s Tuesday’s (September 15) circular, saying credit card transactions on UPI continue to be permitted only through RuPay credit cards. According to the ministry, this is part of a deliberate policy to make RuPay the preferred credit card network among Indian users. On the TPAP market share cap, the DFS said NPCI introduced the 30% limit in November 2020, but it could not be enforced because smaller payment apps lacked a self-sustaining revenue model needed to compete with market leaders. The government said introducing MDR on select high-value UPI transactions would provide these players with a revenue stream and enable more domestic companies to expand their operations. It added that the move was aimed at protecting India’s sovereignty in the electronic payments ecosystem. The DFS also linked the policy to the government’s efforts to promote RuPay credit and debit cards as domestic alternatives to global card networks. RuPay debit-card payments will continue to remain outside the MDR framework. “The allegation that MDR has been introduced under any external influence is patently false and misleading,” the ministry said. The MDR Uproar Beyond the "external pressure" allegations, the new UPI MDR framework has drawn opposition from retailer and fuel dealer associations, capital-market platforms, and consumers over its potential cost impact. Retailer groups have raised concerns over the additional cost and its potential impact on UPI acceptance. “Small merchants will now think twice about whether to accept cash or UPI. During the festive season, a larger share of transactions cross the ₹2,000 mark, and the moment a fee attaches itself to digital payment, cash becomes the path of least resistance,” Retailers Association of India CEO Kumar Rajagopalan said. The framework provides concessional rates for certain sectors. Fuel, insurance, railways, telecom, and utility payments above ₹2,000 will attract a flat MDR of ₹5 instead of the standard 0.4% charge. However, the All India Petroleum Dealers Association (AIPDA) has sought the finance minister’s intervention over the payment processing costs arising from the framework. The association subsequently held discussions with senior officials at the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. Meanwhile, UPI transactions above ₹2,000 involving mutual funds, securities, and stockbrokers will attract an MDR of 0.02%, capped at ₹300. Zerodha and INDmoney have flagged the potential cost impact of the measure. Warning that brokers could incur charges on fund transfers without necessarily generating corresponding trading revenue, Zerodha cofounder and CEO Nithin Kamath called for the MDR on broking transactions to be capped at ₹5 or ₹10. A petition was also filed in the Supreme Court yesterday challenging the Centre’s framework. It contended that merchants could pass on the additional cost to consumers indirectly by raising prices. The government has repeatedly said consumers will not be charged a separate UPI fee and that merchants cannot levy a direct surcharge on customers. It expects the MDR revenue to support UPI infrastructure, cybersecurity, innovation, and customer service, along with a proposed fund for payment infrastructure and merchant onboarding in smaller centres. New Revenue Stream For Fintechs While merchant bodies and investment platforms have raised concerns, banks, payment companies, and TPAPs have largely welcomed the return of MDR, which has been a longstanding industry demand. Under the standard 0.4% MDR structure, the merchant will pay the acquiring bank, which will transfer 0.28% to the issuing bank as an interchange. The issuing bank will pay 0.12% to the payer-side payment service provider, which, in turn, will pay 0.08% to the UPI app provider. The framework will open a new revenue stream for companies operating in the UPI ecosystem. Following the MDR notification, PhonePe is looking to revive its IPO plans. Expensive flash drives: When and why it's worth paying more
Faster transfers are only part of the story when you're deciding whether a premium flash drive is worth it.
Flash drives aren't the first device you think about when considering the current sky-high cost of RAM and storage, but they've certainly been affected. Thanks to AI and data center demand, NAND flash prices have risen significantly. USB drives haven't absorbed those increases dollar for dollar, but cheap flash memory can no longer be taken for granted either.
That makes the price difference between various flash drives more interesting. While two drives of the same capacity may cost vastly different amounts, usually the extra cost brings something you'll notice: faster transfers, stronger security or hardware better suited to life outside a desk drawer.
Still, expensive doesn't automatically mean better. The trick is figuring out what you're actually paying for.
Faster transfers are a clear benefit of spending more
USB 3.0 was the first major successor to USB 2.0. It bumped the maximum theoretical transfer speed to 5 Gbps, compared to the earlier standard's 480 Mbps. From there, USB naming got complicated. The two following standards were initially called USB 3.1 and USB 3.2, but everything was retroactively changed to use "Gen" names.
The group behind USB now recommends using the max transfer rate for clarity, instead of "USB 3.2" followed by the generation — these cap out at 5 Gbps, 10 Gbps or 20 Gbps. Thus, if you see "USB 3.2" on a box, it doesn't necessarily indicate how fast that drive will be. You'll need to check the transfer rate elsewhere in the specs.
USB-C doesn't fix this problem either. USB-C is a connector type, not a performance promise, so USB-C devices can run at USB 2.0 speeds. What USB-C can give you is convenience. Having both USB-A and USB-C connectors on a single drive makes it easier to switch between older PCs and newer laptops, tablets or phones without having to carry an adapter around.
It's the actual read and write speeds that count. For example, Kingston rates its DataTraveler Max at up to 1,000 MB/s reads and 900 MB/s writes. In a 10GB transfer test, Tom's Hardware measured Samsung's cheaper Fit Plus at 319.7 MB/s reads and just 58.4 MB/s writes. That gap won't matter much when copying a PDF, but a folder full of 4K video is a different matter.
A USB driver's controller handles tasks such as error correction and write management, while the flash memory itself also influences performance. Unfortunately, flash drive manufacturers don't always disclose enough about those components to make them easy to compare. Actual speeds can also drop during long transfers, so anyone regularly moving hundreds of gigabytes should pay special attention to sustained write performance rather than assuming the largest number on the package is what you'll always get.
Sometimes you're paying for factors other than speed
A premium flash drive doesn't need to top a benchmark to warrant its cost. The Kingston IronKey Keypad 200, which focuses on security instead of speed, is a good example. It has a physical keypad, XTS-AES 256-bit hardware encryption, brute-force protections and FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validation. These are advanced features not found in basic flash drives that protect the device from physical tampering and technical attacks. Yet its fastest variants are rated at 280 MB/s reads and 200 MB/s writes. The idea isn't to make the progress bar disappear faster, but to make the files much more difficult to access if the drive goes missing from your pocket.
Capacity can push up the price too. While you can find 2TB flash drives, packing more storage onto your keyring doesn't guarantee strong performance. In the same 10GB test mentioned earlier, Tom's Hardware measured the tiny 1TB SanDisk Extreme Fit at 318.3 MB/s reads and just 82.52 MB/s writes. It also came close to blocking the adjacent USB-C port on the reviewer's laptop.
Ruggedness is another reason to consider spending more. Samsung rates its BAR Plus for protection against water, shock, extreme temperatures, magnets and X-rays. It also has a five-year limited warranty. That matters if your flash drive lives on a keychain, in a camera bag or anywhere else less hospitable than your desk.
None of those features makes an expensive flash drive a substitute for a proper backup, though. If you're looking for a USB drive for occasional documents, installers or file transfers, then a good, inexpensive USB 3.x drive might be enough. But if you're willing to spend big bucks for capacity and sustained speed, compare the price with top portable SSDs. External SSDs are often the better choice for regularly moving large amounts of data, or for extra storage that sits permanently attached to your computer.

Quick Answer
The iPhone Duo hides several firsts and oddities: horizontal rear cameras, vertical UI elements, top-mounted volume buttons, Apple Pencil support, titanium construction, Smart Take, a circular status bar, unusual USB-C placement, and no Action button or Pro camera controls.
Apple launched many devices at its recent Surprise and Shine event, but there was no doubting the star of the show. It was the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, and the device that many are expecting to do for foldables what the iPhone did for smartphones almost two decades ago. Small wonder then that the past few days have seen everyone and their grandmother discussing the iPhone Duo.
Debates have been raging over its animations, its crease, its cameras, its apps, and of course, its price. Some are hailing it as the coolest thing since sliced bread, while others insist it is a spawn of Satan in smartphone shape. But in all this debate and discussion, some important aspects and features of the Duo have either escaped attention or have not been adequately covered.
Here are ten things you might have missed about Apple’s first foldable.
Table of Contents
The first iPhone with horizontally arranged cameras on the back…selfie cameras on the corners
iPhones have been coming with multiple cameras (two or three) on their backs for a while now. However, they have always been arranged vertically, one below the other, or in the case of some Pro devices, with two cameras one below the other and the third one placed between them but slightly to the side, forming a triangle of sorts. The iPhone Duo thus becomes the first iPhone to have cameras placed next to each other horizontally, in what some would term a very Pixel-like style. The selfie cameras also get new locations – moving to the right corner of the external display and close to the right corner of the internal display (when opened), where it actually lies under the display. Regular iPhone users are sure to notice a change in perspective.
The dock, navigation, and even the Dynamic Island just got radically right, and utterly vertical
The cameras on the iPhone Duo might have gone horizontal, but some elements of the UI have gone vertical! While everyone has been focusing on the crease in the middle of the iPhone Duo and its visibility (it’s not easy to spot, by all accounts). Apple moved many iOS elements to the right side and gave them a vertical orientation. Lock screen controls, navigation buttons, the home screen dock, and even the Dynamic Island are on the right side of the iPhone Duo, and what’s more, are arranged vertically.
The Dynamic Island even slides open vertically to show information and updates. Evidently, this was done because of the width of the iPhone Duo (it is also the widest iPhone ever), which would have made it difficult to reach these elements. They have therefore been placed on the same side as the display unlock/power button, which is also a fingerprint scanner. This is pretty right-wing in UI terms, literally.
Volume buttons on the top
The iPhone Duo comes with a rather different volume button placement from other foldables. While it is conventional for most foldables and indeed, most ‘normal’ phones, to have volume buttons on the right or left side, the iPhone Duo actually has volume buttons on the top, aligned slightly towards the right. This is a volume button placement we have seen on the newer iPad minis but not on any other iPhones or iPads. It is a rather odd location in our opinion, and if opened and rotated clockwise, it would place the buttons on the lower part of the right side, and on the top of the left side if rotated anti-clockwise.
Camera Control? Present! Action button? Er…
While the iPhone Duo comes with a Camera Control button like other recent iPhones, it, rather surprisingly, does not have an Action button, which is generally seen on the left side of most iPhones and can be customized to carry out a number of tasks. It used to toggle Silent mode on and off, before being changed to an action button. Clearly, it was either not good enough to make the cut for the Duo or perhaps there simply was not enough space for it.
Apple Pencil support exists, but only for the Type-C one
The iPhone Duo is the first iPhone to come with Apple Pencil support. What’s more, it supports the Apple Pencil on both its internal as well as external display. But there is a catch – it only supports the basic Apple Pencil (USB-C). This means that while one can scribble and sketch easily, there’s no pressure sensitivity and no support for double taps. One will also need a Type-C cable to charge it, as it cannot charge magnetically. Given the price and potential of the device, it would have been good to have Apple Pencil Pro support on it.
Only new iPhone with Titanium
Remember how Titanium was the coolest thing in premium phones a few years ago. Well, while it still remains a very premium material, it has largely disappeared from the smartphone scene, with even Apple seemingly moving on to other materials, with only the iPhone Air using Titanium last year. This time around, it is the iPhone Duo that carries the Titanium legacy forward. While the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max use “forged aluminum” and ceramic glass, the iPhone Duo comes with a main chassis made with grade 5 Titanium, and 3D-printed titanium is also used for the hinge cover.
The only iPhone camera with Smart Take
Although its cameras might not seem as formidable as those on the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, the iPhone Duo has a slice of camera magic up its sleeve that no other iPhone has. This is Smart Take, which, with some AI magic, automatically works out when you are perfectly placed for a photograph and takes it without you needing to hit a capture button or prompt the device in any manner. It is supposed to work very well with individual and group selfies, and uses the rear cameras while showing you a preview on the cover display. While the feature is designed mainly for the fold form factor, it would be great to see it on “normal” iPhones too, although one might not be able to see previews!
A Type-C port placed under the cover display
In another case of rather unusual placement, the Type-C port of the iPhone Duo is actually placed on the base of the cover display or the upper panel. In many foldables, the charging port is placed on the lower panel, so that the phone can be opened without moving the charging cable. That is clearly not going to be possible on the iPhone Duo.
The status bar is closed…and is now a circle
The move to a foldable form factor has led to a redesign of some UI elements on the iPhone Duo. Perhaps the most surprising of these is the status bar. Until now seen in the top right corner, and displaying signal strength, Wi-Fi, and battery, it has now been changed to a circle, with the battery life and signal strength being on the circumference and Wi-Fi being at the center. It is not really as intuitive as its predecessor, but we guess users will get the hang of it.
No Pro controls in the camera
The iPhone Duo comes with two 48-megapixel cameras on the back – a new Fusion Main camera, and the same ultrawide that is on the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. But while these pack in a lot of features such as three photographic styles, smart focus tracking, next-generation portraits, macro photography and more, the iPhone Duo’s camera app does not come with the Pro Controls seen on the 18 Pro and Pro Max, which let users play around with shutter speed, white balance, and aperture. This l is a bit of a pity, especially given the vast viewfinder the open Duo can serve up. But well, to be fair, this was never meant to be a camera phone.

GURGAON: A group of men were seen rallying in cars in support of Gurgaon hit-and-run accused Kalyan Singh Bainsla on Friday, days after a video of the incident went viral.
A video showed several cars driving together on a flyover in Haryana.
"Full support to Gurjar Kalyan Bainsla. Come face-to-face once and call him a thug, bro," a post said on X. A mahapanchayat was called in support of Bainsla.
Bainsla is accused of chasing and ramming a biker, Shivani Chauhan, on Golf Course Road on Sunday. Police said he was allegedly returning from a club with his friends when the incident took place.
Bainsla, his cousin and other friends had gone to The Empire club at MGF Metropolitan Mall on MG Road on Saturday. He had borrowed a Maruti Ciaz from a friend for the outing. Police are yet to ascertain whether the accused were drunk.
Police said Shrikant, an associate of Bainsla, was also in the car at the time of the incident. According to sources, co-accused Lavnish allegedly instigated Bainsla to chase Chauhan and also allegedly abused her during the incident.
Investigators said the accused followed Chauhan for around 2km. They said Bainsla had asked her to stop. When she did not and instead signalled the car driver to move away, the accused allegedly rammed her motorcycle.

Waymo says it will launch a robotaxi service in Singapore in 2028, as the Alphabet-owned company continues to eye overseas markets for expansion.
Waymo says Singapore will be its next international robotaxi city
The Alphabet-owned company says it will launch a commercial robotaxi service in Singapore in 2028.
Waymo’s vehicles will begin arriving in Singapore in “the coming months,” the company says, in preparation of mapping and autonomous testing with human safety drivers behind the wheel in 2027. Waymo says it is “working toward offering fully autonomous ride-hailing to the public” by 2028.
Waymo will need approval from Singapore’s Land Transport Authority (LTA) before it can begin accepting passengers. The city-state requires all autonomous vehicles to undergo a safety assessment conducted at the Centre of Excellence for Testing and Research (CETRAN) before they can be deployed on public roads. The tests have been developed by LTA and CETRAN, with input from the Traffic Police. But Waymo isn’t totally unknown in Singapore. The company established a corporate entity there earlier this year and participates in Singapore’s Steering Committee on Autonomous Vehicles.
Singapore has become a hotbed for autonomous vehicle testing. The local authorities have green-lit autonomous freight delivery and road-sweepers, as well as self-driving buses for airport workers. Motional, a US-based company majority owned by Hyundai, conducted a robotaxi pilot in Singapore in 2016.
In addition to Singapore, Waymo has said it plans on launching a robotaxi service in London by the end of 2026, and Tokyo in 2027. The company has also said it will bring its robotaxis to Munich, Germany, in late 2027, marking its first expansion in the European Union.
“Singapore has built one of the safest, most efficient, and most forward-thinking transportation ecosystems in the world,” Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana said in a statement. “Their focus on reliability, sustainability, and human-centric progress directly mirrors how we have built Waymo’s technology and service.”
This year, Waymo has announced several new domestic markets, including Nashville, Denver, San Diego, and Las Vegas. The company has around 4,000 vehicles operating in about 15 US cities.
But regulatory hurdles and political opposition have kept it out of some of the US’ most important cities, including New York City, Chicago, and Washington, DC. As the robotaxi debate continues to rage on in America, Waymo has signaled that it intends to keep growing overseas — with no signs of slowing down.

Carrick 'not bothered' by pressure - but should he be after this latest mess?
- Published
Sir Alex Ferguson was St Mirren manager the last time Manchester United lost at Old Trafford having taken a 2-0 lead.
That is the context to the shocking Carabao Cup third-round exit his old club suffered against Brighton on Wednesday.
It is a period of time that encompasses the legendary Scot's dynasties at Aberdeen as well as United. The Class of '92 were in nappies when John Pratt scored the winner for Tottenham on 4 September 1976.
After holding protests inside and outside the ground before Sunday's loss to 10-man Manchester City, United supporters made their feelings known about their latest embarrassment in three ways.
- Most fans simply left as the players embarked on their post-match lap of appreciation.
- Some of those who remained booed, as they had done when their side fell behind 21 minutes from time.
- By the time they approached the tunnel, close to United's 'singing section', supporters were asking Michael Carrick and his players 'what was that?'. Their wording was somewhat more colourful.
It is not certain where 15-year-old JJ Gabriel was while all this was taking place, but nothing happened that would make him think he had got it wrong by turning his back on the club.
Indeed, it is quite possible, probable indeed, that the promised senior debut would have been scrapped given the game situation - and the fact skipper Bruno Fernandes was among the experienced players introduced in the frantic final stages.
"Of course we can turn it around, we have got some really good players," said Carrick. "It feels bad because we haven't had a great week or two, or three weeks."
- What next for Gabriel and Man Utd? 
  - Published8 hours ago
- 'Let's go, let's go' - inside catastrophic derby VAR mistake 
  - Published9 hours ago
Carrick's side have won twice this season, against newly promoted Ipswich at home after falling behind, and Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK in the Champions League. They have now lost on three occasions, more defeats than he experienced in 17 matches after replacing Ruben Amorim in January.
He has been around Manchester United long enough to know the pressure losing runs can build.
"I don't feel under pressure," he said. "Either way, that doesn't bother me one bit.
"I understand what goes on outside and how the world works, but it doesn't bother me. What bothers me is winning games, having a good feeling around the place and a good feeling around the group to know we're moving in a good direction."
The problem is it doesn't feel as though they are moving in a good direction. There were certainly not many positives to take from this mess.
The obvious one was Shea Lacey, who marked his first senior start with a well-taken eighth-minute goal. It meant he became the first teenager to score on his first United start since Marcus Rashford in February 2016.
Lacey was one of eight changes made by Carrick. Defensively, those changes were not a success.
Diogo Dalot was one of the three players to keep their place. His form has deserted him. Noussair Mazraoui is the back-up left-back, which only heightens the debate over the wisdom not to buy one before the transfer window closed. Leny Yoro and Ayden Heaven looked like the inexperienced defenders they are. In midfield Manchester United were overrun.
Yet again, Rashford threatened without managing a goal or an assist. He came closest to levelling when he sped beyond the Brighton defence, but his shot was saved by Jason Steele.
"The longer the game went, the more we had control," was the concise assessment of Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler. "I thought we deserved to win."
Carrick didn't dispute the assessment.
'Being here toughens you up'
His greatest sadness was for Lacey, who should have had his name in lights but instead was part of a team scuttling off the pitch to the sound of boos and harsher criticism.
"It's a shame that Shea's moment, such a great moment for him, for his family, his friends and the whole academy; to have an academy player come in and have a moment like that, gets a bit lost, unfortunately," said Carrick.
"It won't for him when things settle down but, as we sit here now, it feels that it was a long time ago."
Carrick also addressed the JJ Gabriel situation.
"He's a young boy, he's 15, and for me, definitely, and from a club point of view, looking after our younger players, their welfare, their wellbeing, their exposure, we've got to be really conscious of that in this situation," he explained.
But ultimately, for any manager, the assessment of their work comes through results.
"Being here toughens you up over a period of time," he said. "It depends how you deal with it. You've got to deal with it in a way where you can cope with it and you can bring out the best in yourself. However you do that, with your motivation and the confidence deep within yourself to know we can win football matches.
"We've gone out of the cup tonight, and the feeling around the place feels bigger than that. I'm honest enough to say that's how it feels. But it doesn't have to be like that. If we win football matches again, it can go in a different direction."
Manchester United have one more game before the international break, at Fulham on Sunday.
For the general wellbeing of the club, Carrick's team really need to win.
Speaking on Sky Sports, former England midfielder Jamie Redknapp said he wasn't sure they will.
"Right now, they're miles off it," he said. "It doesn't matter how good the manager is, if you don't have the right players it makes it really difficult.
"There's a reason why the other managers have struggled. Sooner or later the pressure's always going to come on.
"This weekend becomes a huge game. He doesn't need another poor result, otherwise all of a sudden you're going into the international break and everyone's talking about you. The winners tonight are the players who didn't play."

Nick Kroll said upcoming Netflix comedy series “A Hundred Percent,” which he co-created and stars in, is a “love letter” to Los Angeles — and he expressed hope that a “thriving” entertainment production community will bring “vitality” to the city.
The comedian, writer, producer, director and actor was a featured keynote speaker at the Variety Entertainment & Technology Summit presented by EY, held Thursday in L.A.
Kroll explained that “A Hundred Percent,” which is expected to debut on Netflix in 2027, was filmed in L.A. “I needed to make this show in L.A. It feels like it’s about people who live in Los Angeles. I’ve lived here for almost 20 years,” he said.
Popular on Variety
He co-created “A Hundred Percent” with his friend Gabe Liedman (creator of “Q-Force” and showrunner of the first season of “PEN15”), and stars in the show alongside Sam Richardson, Jason Mantzoukas and Vanessa Bayer, with Diane Lane joining the cast in a recurring role.
“We genuinely felt like it was a love letter to the city that we live in. And we really, honestly, have the best crew, had the best people, who were in such a happy mood making a show in Los Angeles,” said Kroll, who was interviewed on stage by Angelique Jackson, senior entertainment and media reporter at Variety. “It was an awesome experience, and I’m so grateful to the city for helping make that happen. I hope it continues to grow because I think all of the doldrums that we’ve all been feeling for so many years will hopefully begin to work itself out.”
Kroll continued: “The more that we have a thriving, ongoing shooting community here in Los Angeles, it will bring life back. Not only money, but just like it will bring a vitalization, a vitality to the city that I think I have missed from when I moved here, and like the dream of coming to Hollywood and making things and being around people who are making things.”
Kroll then quipped: “That said, I’m personally moving to Austin to start a podcast network.”
“A Hundred Percent,” Kroll said, is a “show about the world of thought leaders, self-help gurus, wellness influencers, and much of where they sort of live are on panels like this, in sad ballrooms” — he gestured to the Four Seasons room where he was speaking at the conference — “where you only get pitchers of water, tiny mints, and if you really search, a San Pellegrino, but that’s not what matters.”
Kroll said his goal with any project is “just trying to first and foremost work with the most talented people I can find.” In the case of “A Hundred Percent,” he said Liedman, the cast and the writers “I just think are the funniest people… It’s just an incredibly talented group.”
“Just surround yourself with quality people, because assholes — they’re just the worst, you know. So that’s what I would say,” Kroll said. He added, “That’s a pretty profound statement, if Variety wants to lead with that.”
In addition to his work on “A Hundred Percent,” Kroll is an executive producer of FX sitcom “Adults,” which follows five 20-something friends living together in Queens, New York (in one of the group’s childhood home). He also has served as EP and voice actor for several Netflix animated series, including “Mating Season,” “Human Resources” and the Emmy-nominated “Big Mouth.”
Kroll and “Adults” creators Ben Kronengold and Rebecca Shaw started developing the show several years ago, “and then we cast the next generation of incredibly funny comedic performers, and they fucking killed it.”
“Adults” comes under Kroll’s longrunning first-look deal with FX going on more than 15 years. He said he loves making fun of FX’s “fearless” tagline but said it’s true that “they are genuinely incredibly innovative in how they launch stuff and how they’re willing to take shots. And in the case of ‘Adults,’ Season 1 found an audience, but it wasn’t as big an audience as everyone wants. And so we shot this prequel episode to give a new way into the show.”
Kroll said about Season 1 of “Adults,” “Audiences found it, really responded to it, and then were able to understand the show and the characters in a way that they entered into the rest of the season and stuck around.” In Season 2, bucking typical TV trends, the show’s ratings grew by 40% domestically and 100% internationally. “It’s a testament to FX and and John Landgraf at the head of it to trust us to build something to keep with something that they know is quality and that’s what it comes down to.”
About creating engaging TV shows, Kroll said, “I really think it’s such incredible competition for people’s attention that you really have to figure out a way to grab them, but also hold them gently, so that they don’t run away. And that’s the hard thing to figure out. That’s the game we’re all in right now.”
At the beginning of his talk, Kroll riffed on the previous panel about AI in the entertainment industry — in which there was a sentiment expressed that humans will always find a way to keep the tech in check — Kroll commented, “Don’t underestimate the ability of machines to find a way to destroy us as well,” adding, “I say that generally without much alarm.”

Georgia district hopes to install license-plate capturing cameras to fine drivers passing school buses
Officials estimate that drivers in the state illegally pass school buses over 9,000 times a day
A Georgia school district is looking to install stop-arm cameras on school buses to dissuade drivers from illegally passing — a move that warrants a $1,000 fine in the state.
DeKalb County Schools is looking to find a vendor to add cameras to over 1,000 school buses in the district. The buses already have cameras inside, but the stop-arm cameras would show what’s happening outside, CBS Atlanta reported.
“The goal of DeKalb County School District is to ensure we’re protecting 100 percent of our students 100 percent of the time by providing safe and reliable consistent transportation to and from school each and every day,” Director of Student Transportation Bernando Brown said.
The district, which transports about 45,000 students, says it plans to get cameras with multi-angle video, license plate recognition, GPS tagging and automatic activation. Data collected with the cameras would automatically be sent to law enforcement.
“The camera will actually be mounted right on the side of our bus,” Brown said. “Directly up under our stop arm. As long as no one passes the bus, there’s nothing to worry about.”
However, cars that pass buses will be tracked by the camera the entire time, Brown said.
A survey from the Governor’s Highway Safety Association found that 46 percent of children riding the school bus have had a close call with a dangerous driver.
The data also found that 53 percent of parents believe dangerous driving continues because motorists think they won’t get caught.
Georgia officials estimate that drivers in the state illegally pass school buses over 9,000 times a day.
“It’s pretty frequent,” Brown told the outlet. “We have certain areas in DeKalb County where it’s almost every time a bus stops, you’re going to see it.”
In Georgia, the fine for passing a school bus starts at $1,000.
The district says it hopes to install the cameras no later than January.
