NASA satellite discovers a new crater on the moon that's bigger than the Colosseum
'This event constitutes a statistically rare, effectively once-in-a-lifetime observation,' scientists write
Scientists have discovered a crater on the moon that's bigger than the Roman Colosseum and is the result of a powerful impact two years ago that initially went undetected.
The steep-sided hole — 222 metres across and up to 43 metres deep — is the solar system's biggest known impact crater carved out in recent times.
Such a large-scale event is estimated to occur only once every 132 years, researchers said, making this a treasure trove of information as NASA prepares to build a base for astronauts on the moon.
"This event constitutes a statistically rare, effectively once-in-a-lifetime observation," the scientists wrote in one of two studies appearing on the subject Wednesday in the journal Science Advances.
NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) spotted the crater on the moon's near side in May 2024 soon after it was formed by an incoming fragment of an asteroid or comet. The moon strike escaped real-time detection by telescopes on Earth and in space.
LRO's wide-angle images were not identified in the crush of data until August 2025. The spacecraft gathered more detailed pictures last fall, followed by confirmation of the discovery early this year.
The crater is named for the late Thomas McGetchin, a former director of Houston's Lunar and Planetary Institute.
Like gardening
Pockmarked since ancient times, the moon bears some of the solar system's largest impact craters, including one that stretches more than 2,400 kilometres across.
This latest impact churned the lunar surface for more than 100 kilometres. Dust and rocky soil were hurled away at a higher angle than expected, according to Mark Robinson, chief scientist for the LRO's cameras who works at Intuitive Machines. Robinson was the lead author for one of the studies.
- Here's the mark a SpaceX rocket crash left on the moon
- Astronauts' movement increased subsurface temperatures on the moon, study finds
A separate study identified a seven-kilometre-wide cold spot around the new crater, consistent with a loosening of the moon's topsoil. Co-author David Paige of the University of California, Los Angeles, likens it to gardening.
"We're now thinking of impacts as a way to garden the regolith — churning the sediments and putting stuff above that's usually below the surface," Paige said in a statement. (Regolith is the term for the loose, solid material on top of bedrock.)
The LRO's numerous crater discoveries since its launch in 2009 show that the moon's top two centimetres of soil is being overturned by ejected material every 80,000 years, faster than previously thought, according to Robinson.
Contrary to the popular belief that the Apollo moonwalkers' dusty lunar footprints will last forever, they will "definitely be long gone in that time frame," Robinson said in an email.
The next step is to calculate the risk of ejected crater material striking NASA's planned moon base, he added.
"That information will help engineers harden structures so one won't have to worry about damage, or maybe worry less."

The political dominance of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which appeared almost unassailable after 2014, is beginning to show cracks. The 2024 general election was an important setback: the party lost its parliamentary majority and had to depend on its allies to form the government. Since then, disillusionment has acquired greater political salience through youth protests, rising prices, unemployment and failures of governance, particularly irregularities in the education and examination systems. To these can be added the defeat of the Constitutional Amendment Bill on delimitation and women’s reservation in April, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protests that led to the resignation of the then Union Education Minister and the complete washout of the monsoon session of Parliament, as both the Prime Minister and Home Minister stayed away. Questions over accountability for the excessive police action against student protesters on July 20, compounded by the absence of the two leaders from Parliament, reinforced the impression of a government unwilling to answer for its actions.
But these setbacks do not by themselves amount to an erosion of hegemony. The BJP remains a formidable political force, retaining a substantial electoral base and considerable ideological appeal. What is now at issue is whether the forces that produced the BJP’s dominance are beginning to encounter limits. Uttar Pradesh is where this can be most clearly tested.
The citadel of the party’s power, 2024 result
U.P. is not merely India’s most populous State; it is the citadel of BJP power, central to the party’s rise to national prominence. In the 2014 general election, the BJP won 71 of the State’s 80 seats, establishing it as a crucial pillar of its national power. In the 2019 general election, it won 62 seats on its own despite the formidable alliance of the Samajwadi Party (SP) and the Bahujan Samaj Party. The State’s electoral weight was thus instrumental to its successive parliamentary majorities at the Centre. U.P. is still the crucible of the BJP’s majoritarian politics and its Hindu-Muslim mobilisation. A weakening of the BJP here would therefore have implications far beyond the State.
The 2024 general election strongly indicates that the BJP had lost ground in U.P. Its tally fell from 62 seats in 2019 to 33, while the SP won 37 and the Congress six. The sharpest erosion occurred in Awadh, once the heartland of the Ayodhya temple movement. In 2022, the BJP won 101 of Awadh’s 154 Assembly seats. In 2024, it was leading in only 51 of those Assembly segments — 50 fewer than the number it had won in 2022.
The timing made the 2024 general election result extremely significant. It followed the inauguration of the Ram temple in Ayodhya, which was the culmination of a political and cultural project that had animated the BJP and the wider Hindu right for decades. Yet, the inauguration did not produce the electoral impact that might have been expected: most strikingly, the BJP lost the Faizabad seat, which includes Ayodhya itself. It also lost in many constituencies around it. This does not mean that Ayodhya or the majoritarian politics surrounding it has ceased to matter. The consequential point is that it was no longer enough to win elections even in the movement’s heartland. The fact that the erosion was most visible in this region adds to its significance, given the subsequent controversy over donations to the temple. The episode, whose effects are still being felt across the State, showed that even powerful ideological symbols are not beyond questions of integrity.
This matters because the BJP’s political hold in U.P. has rested on a combination of communal mobilisation, a durable electoral base and social coalitions built around the temple campaign. The 2024 general election showed that this alignment could be disrupted. Its longer-term implications will depend on whether that disruption proves temporary or marks a lasting shift in the electorate’s preferences and expectations.
Some of the prominent fault lines
The 2024 result also suggests that voters are becoming less willing to let a single dimension of politics overwhelm all others, especially when claims of economic performance do not match the realities on the ground. U.P. remains among the poorer-performing economies of the north and east — as it has for decades. Its economy has grown, but growth has not fundamentally altered its relative economic position or generated enough productive employment. The gap between the rhetoric of transformation and economic experience on the ground is particularly visible in the State’s industrial clusters. In Kanpur, Firozabad, Bhadohi and Moradabad, exporters have faced serious disruption from the tariff regime of the United States, and the duties raised on Indian goods, with falling orders, shrinking market access and risks to employment, principally among temporary and contract workers.
The frustration among young voters is strikingly evident in the precarity of employment and recruitment. Many were actively involved in the anti-National Eligibility cum Entrance Test protests earlier in the year. U.P. has seen repeated examination leaks and cancellations. In 2024, the police constable examination, taken by around 48 lakh candidates for 60,244 posts, was cancelled following a paper leak. The Review Officer/Assistant Review Officer examination was similarly cancelled amid allegations of irregularities, where out of a total of 10.76 lakh registered candidates, about 6.8 lakh candidates appeared, competing for just 411 posts. For a generation that invests years in its preparation for scarce government jobs, such failures are not merely administrative lapses. They can mean the loss of money spent on coaching and applications, income and opportunity in a State where government employment remains a highly valued path to economic security.
The battle lines are being drawn
In these circumstances, the 2027 U.P. election is likely to be more closely contested than those that the BJP has faced in the State in recent years. The party remains the strongest contender, but the 2024 result has opened space for the Opposition and revealed strains at various levels that were barely perceptible in earlier elections. The government is working overtime to address the gap on several fronts, reflected in a slew of measures to promote local entrepreneurship and provide stipends for students in corporate and technical institutions.
It is also set to introduce new schemes for women, such as the Mahila Udyami Credit Yojana, under which around one crore women associated with self-help groups are expected to receive interest-free credit of up to ₹1 lakh in stages. The Opposition, too, sees an opening. Both the SP and the Congress are seeking to strengthen their appeal among younger voters, with their leaders, Akhilesh Yadav and Rahul Gandhi, focusing on student unrest, unemployment and widening caste fault lines, particularly divisions among upper castes and between them and the Other Backward Classes. Convergence between the two parties, as in 2024, could bolster the Opposition’s chances in the 2027 U.P. election.
The 2027 election will therefore reveal more than the BJP’s ability to recover lost seats. It will show whether the political template that carried the party to power from Lucknow to New Delhi still commands the same electoral force. The 2024 result has already shown that this template is no longer invulnerable in U.P. The 2027 election will determine whether the shift revealed in 2024 becomes more durable. What happens in U.P. could therefore alter the political balance on which the BJP’s national dominance has rested.
Zoya Hasan is Professor Emerita, Centre for Political Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University.

“DealShare is today an empty vessel with $90 Mn in cash.” That’s how an investor who is aware of the company’s financial status, describes the startup. Once valued at $1.7 Bn, this is what DealShare has been reduced to, and the company is actively looking for a potential acquirer, with many names reportedly close to acquiring it at a 95%-plus haircut. Truemeds is said to be one such suitor but the proposed acquisition is not a done deal yet, according to another investor aware of the development. Active discussions are ongoing, but Truemeds’ existing investors are not necessarily aligned with the deal. DealShare is also in talks with other potential buyers, the investors added. Captain Fresh is another name that had surfaced in connection with a possible acquisition but Inc42 has learnt that the company is not pursuing the transaction. The talks for an acquisition at a distressed valuation come after years of restructuring and attempts to find a viable business model for DealShare, which once enjoyed unicorn status. But as the company’s current situation shows, a lot of that was down to the timing of DealShare’s fundraising spree when VCs were investing at valuations that seemed unsustainable. Questions sent to DealShare, WestBridge and Truemeds didn’t elicit any response at the time of publishing the story. For investors, that raises an old question related to distressed investments but with renewed urgency: what should be done with the roughly $90 Mn still sitting on DealShare’s balance sheet? The DealShare 2.0 Plan Tanks The first few years of DealShare’s existence were all about proving that its hybrid B2B and B2C model would be able to compete with the startups that were making inroads into B2B supply chain as well as ecommerce marketplaces. DealShare was pitched as the ecommerce and supply chain destination for consumers and small retailers or kiranas in Tier II, Tier III and beyond. By January 2022, it already had major investors on board and turned unicorn after raising $165 Mn from AlphaWave, Tiger Global and others. The startup raised its next round in rather quick time and was all set to enter the private label business towards the end of FY23. However, the business struggled to gain traction or show growth in the next year. Much of the money was spent in acquiring customers on both sides and by August 2023, DealShare exited the B2B vertical to focus only on B2C ecommerce operations. The company’s net loss crossed the ₹500 Cr mark in FY23 against a revenue of ₹1,963.5 Cr, despite raising more than $200 Mn in the previous year. After two years of struggle, where the company saw the departure of founders Vineet Rao, Sankar Bora and Sourjyendu Medda, DealShare was a shadow of the unicorn it once was. Towards the end of 2025, there emerged a new plan and a so-called DealShare 2.0 vision. Investors brought in Kamaldeep Singh, a former Big Bazaar executive, to run the company and build the next phase of DealShare. DealShare’s FY25 numbers also showed the strain. Revenue fell 13.4% YoY to ₹432.4 Cr, while net loss narrowed to ₹87.7 Cr from ₹167.7 Cr a year earlier. The idea behind this new DealShare was to return to the B2C value commerce, but with a different delivery model. While DealShare was never a quick commerce platform, with its reinvention it tried to reduce the delivery time to a two hour delivery. DealShare realised in comparison to 10-minute deliveries, standard fulfilment timelines would give the startup more room to curb delivery costs while continuing to serve customers looking for lower priced groceries and everyday products. As per sources the startup already had 40 dark stores and was doing about 25,000 - 30,000 orders a day. It focused primarily in cities such as Jaipur, Ghaziabad, Lucknow and Kolkata. The two-hour delivery timeline was a conscious choice. The startup did not want to spend heavily trying to match the delivery times of Blinkit and Zepto. “The 10-minute delivery model was not sustainable,” a source familiar with the operations at the time said, arguing that the economics of quick commerce made it difficult to generate profits after delivery and fulfilment costs. While DealShare did touch close to 38,000 orders a day at some point, another source added that gross margins in this business were around 5%-6%, leaving little to no margin for the company after subtracting costs. A separate industry source said DealShare’s online business faced high customer acquisition and fulfilment costs. “The new leadership had an offline retail background and lacked the technology, product and marketing know how needed to build an online-first business, which is why the company was forced to change tack again,” one of the sources said. By April 2026, DealShare had started cutting back its online operations, and turned to a physical store network as its next bet. The person familiar with the startup said the online business began going through changes from April onwards. At the same time, DealShare was expanding its physical store network, moving from around eight stores to 22. Sources said around 8-10 stores were profitable and that the offline business began generating revenue soon after opening. DealShare had plans to open more stores, including in markets such as Lucknow and Ajmer. Another industry source said DealShare had around 15-20 stores in Jaipur and was preparing to open another 15 stores in Lucknow and Kanpur. The stores were doing “decently well”, as per the source who has seen the numbers. The shift to offline, however, did not settle the question of what DealShare should become. The company considered several versions of the business, including an offline-only mode, retaining the online operation and an omnichannel setup where stores would fulfil online orders. “Multiple variations of AOPs (annual operating plan) and things were discussed, and nothing was sort of closed on by the board,” sources said. One person familiar with the discussions said the board, which was led by WestBridge and Alpha Wave was unable to agree on which business model to pursue. “The board was not able to decide on which way we should go forward with the organisation,” the person said. Investors Struggle To Agree On DealShare’s Future The majority institutional stakeholder in DealShare, WestBridge holds roughly 18.4% of the company, whereas Alpha Wave owns around 16.39% stake in the startup. For investors, the problem was not simply choosing between online and offline. It was finding a model that could make the remaining capital work. The startup had already spent years and hundreds of millions of dollars trying to build a growing business. This online vertical was struggling with low gross margins and high customer acquisition and fulfilment costs, while the newer offline business was still being tested. The indecision became harder to sustain with roughly $90 Mn, or around ₹800 - ₹900 Cr, still sitting on DealShare’s balance sheet, according to another investor familiar with the startup. One source said investors had been discussing how to salvage the remaining money for the startup. “The plan is to sell the startup off to someone who can take the money which we have in a bank account to fund their operations,” the person said. Sources told Inc42 that the talks between Truemeds and DealShare were primarily driven by WestBridge, which is a mutual investor in both the startups. That is where DealShare’s strategic uncertainty meets its acquisition talks. The strategy changes have also coincided with a steady churn in the organisation. Having come to steady the ship, new CEO Singh himself is on his way out. The person familiar with the startup said Singh is serving his notice period. CFO Ashish Shah is also close to the exit door. Besides this, several key employees have also left the startup. As per sources, the company has not carried out a blanket layoff, with employees leaving of their own accord. At the same time, DealShare’s online business has come to a complete halt. The startup began cutting back its online operations around April 2026 and eventually stopped fulfilment from its warehouses. The physical stores continue to operate, but the online business is now “next to zero,” according to the source. The app remains available and sources said around 30,000 users open the app every month, although many leave without placing an order. Roughly 22 DealShare stores are currently operational, but plans to add more stores in Lucknow and Kanpur have been put on hold. The result is a business that looks very different from the one investors were trying to build less than a year ago. The two hour delivery model has effectively been shut down, offline expansion has stopped and the management team brought in for DealShare 2.0 is changing again. Truemeds Talks Put The Cash In Focus The acquisition discussions with Truemeds come against this backdrop. Truemeds has emerged as the frontrunner, but the potential transaction is still subject to investor alignment, according to a person aware of the development. DealShare is also speaking with other potential parties. The roughly $90 Mn cash balance is likely to be a key part of any transaction, and sets the floor for the deal. But another source put it more bluntly. “Why will Truemeds buy a grocery business? It’s just an acquisition of DealShare’s cash reserves,” the source said. It seems that DealShare’s leftover VC backing will be the only thing worth buying. The same source questions whether investors in the potential buyer would be comfortable with such a transaction, particularly if the deal involves issuing shares and diluting their holdings. That is also why the Truemeds deal cannot yet be treated as a done transaction. There are many moving pieces here that may result in the deal falling through. DealShare’s investors appear to be looking for a way out after years of backing a business that has struggled to find a model that can deliver any meaningful growth or returns. For a startup that has raised $400 Mn in funding and touched a valuation peak of $1.7 Bn just over four years ago, the turn in fortunes is nothing short of astounding. The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has announced the first-ever Korea visit by Alfonso Cuarón, alongside a dedicated spotlight on nine films from European women and genderqueer filmmakers.
Cuarón, who has won the Academy Award for best director twice, for “Gravity” (2013) and “Roma” (2018), also holds the Venice Film Festival’s best screenplay prize for “Y Tu Mamá También” (2001) and a Golden Lion for “Roma.” He first caught Hollywood’s attention with “Y Tu Mamá También,” a portrait of youth and desire, before taking “Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban” (2004) in a moodier, more personal visual direction than the series had gone before, and later used extended long takes in “Children of Men” (2007) to pull audiences directly into a world at war. He is expected to appear at BIFF’s opening ceremony and will sit down for an extended conversation with festivalgoers about the camera language and instincts behind his films. An Imax screening of “Gravity,” co-written with his son, filmmaker Jonás Cuarón, will also be at the festival.
Jonás Cuarón’s latest feature, “Campeón Gabacho,” will have its Asian premiere in the World Cinema section, followed by a post-screening Q&A. Since writing on “Gravity,” the younger Cuarón has built his own filmography with “Desierto” (2015) and “Chupa” (2023). “Campeón Gabacho,” starring Juan Daniel García Treviño, Leslie Grace, Rubén Blades, Eddie Marsan, Rosario Dawson and Cheech Marin, follows a Mexican immigrant building a life in the United States, and was produced by Jonás Cuarón alongside his father and Gabriela Rodriguez under their Esperanto Filmoj banner, with Nicolás Celis also producing.
Popular on Variety
Elsewhere at the festival, BIFF is showcasing “Europe! Voices of Women+ in Film,” a program run with the European Film Promotion (EFP), spotlighting nine officially selected films through targeted promotion and industry networking. The lineup spans period drama, documentary and contemporary narrative work built around questions of freedom, memory and family, with four of the nine as feature debuts. May el-Toukhy‘s “Woman Unknown,” winner of the Golden Lion at Venice, anchors the group; el-Toukhy became the first Danish woman filmmaker to take that prize, while Mathilde Arcel won the Volpi Cup for best actress in the same film. Also included are Marine Atlan’s debut “La Gradiva,” Pegah Ahangarani’s “Rehearsals for a Revolution,” Sandra Wollner’s “Everytime,” winner of the Un Certain Regard Prize at Cannes, Margherita Ferrari’s debut “Föa – Once Upon a Future,” Isabelle Stever’s “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming,” Marie Kreutzer’s “Gentle Monster,” Shahrbanoo Sadat’s “No Good Men” and Sarah Arnold’s debut “Too Many Beasts.” Judith Godrèche’s “A Girl’s Story,” part of this year’s gala presentations, joins Angela Schanelec’s “My Wife Cries,” Janay Boulos and Abd Alkader Habak’s “Birds of War,” Jacqueline Lentzou’s “A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra,” winner of the Horizons Award for Best Director at Venice, and Konstantina Kotzamani’s “Titanic Ocean” among the additional selections.
Five directors from the program, el-Toukhy, Godrèche, Ferrari, Lentzou and Kotzamani, will travel to Busan to present their films. Godrèche will also take part in a Cine Class session, “Women, Rewriting the Screen,” and BIFF and EFP will co-host a Talk-to-Talk panel, “Women Directors: Taking the Scene,” bringing together Ferrari, el-Toukhy and Lentzou alongside Iranian director Marjan Khosravi (“Dreams of the Wild Oaks”), Chinese director Michelle Zhou (“Big Little Things”) and Afghan director Zainab Entezar (“771 Days”).
BIFF programmer Seo Seunghee said that in reviewing films for this year’s festival, she noticed European women directors becoming more prominent among the strongest titles under consideration, in both volume and quality. “Moreover, the fact that four of the nine invited films are feature debuts is also an indicator of the generational shift taking place in European cinema,” Seo said. “Our ongoing collaboration with EFP has become a reliable channel for discovering and validating outstanding films and filmmakers, and the results are fully reflected in this year’s lineup.”
EFP managing director Irina Ignatiew-Lemke said the “Europe! Voices of Women+ in Film” initiative lets EFP and its member organizations “join forces to give distinctive European voices greater international visibility.” She added, “Busan is an important platform for bringing these filmmakers and their works into dialogue with audiences and industry professionals in Asia. By combining the festival’s selection with EFP’s targeted promotion and networking, we are proud to support underrepresented voices and create opportunities for the next generation of women+ filmmakers.”
The program runs in collaboration with BIFF, the Sydney Film Festival and Festival do Rio, with support from the Creative Europe – MEDIA Programme of the European Union. This year’s participating national film promotion organizations are Austrian Films, Cinecittà, the Czech Film Center, the Danish Film Institute, German Films and Unifrance, with Cineuropa serving as media partner.
The 31st Busan International Film Festival will run Oct. 6-15 at the Busan Cinema Center and venues throughout Busan, with the 21st Asian Contents & Film Market held Oct. 10-13.

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."

With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

Flock CEO Garrett Langley has said the company made its first license plate cameras in his Atlanta home, permanently scratching his dining table with drill marks. A decade later, where the company assembles its signature—and fiercely debated—product has become more of a mystery.
For years, Flock touted publicly that its devices were produced in the United States. But more recent marketing materials from the company reviewed by WIRED no longer specify where its cameras come from. One US manufacturer that previously identified Flock as a customer quietly removed a mention of the company from its website earlier this year as public backlash against the company’s surveillance technology grew.
The startup has become the subject of a nationwide protest movement that has prompted dozens of local governments to abruptly stop using its cameras. Congress is also considering legislation that would cut federal funding to states that fail to limit use of Flock and other license plate readers. While police have argued the cameras are crucial tools for deterring and solving crime, activists have criticized Flock for enabling officers to track the cars of their exes, share footage with immigration authorities, and follow the movements of pedestrians.
But Flock’s manufacturing supply chain has received scant attention, even though where its hardware is produced could have implications for US national security. WIRED spoke with current and former Flock employees and supply chain analysts, reviewed data from US import records, and watched past marketing videos featuring Langley to piece together the first account of how its hardware pipeline has evolved.

Flock’s cameras largely rely on suppliers around the world that provide non-custom parts, which are also used in products from other companies. “Our value is in the aggregation and the packaging of all of these things … in a nice waterproof, consumer-friendly device,” Langley said in one marketing video from 2021.
Import records collected by ImportGenius show the company has been increasingly bringing “commodity” cameras, radar systems, and other components over from Primax Electronics in Thailand. Primax is based in Taiwan, but has manufacturing facilities in China, Thailand, and elsewhere.
“My understanding is that these are components, but it looks like Primax manufactures whole security camera solutions,” ImportGenius’ analyst Lynn Hughes says. “Quite a few shipments include ‘Radar’ in the product description which might be related to the radar sensor pods they're attaching to their cameras.”
Flock didn’t respond to most of the detailed questions WIRED asked for this story, though it did provide some general information. “All products that Flock builds are National Defense Authorization Act compliant,” Flock spokesperson Paris Lewbel said in an email, referring to a US law that effectively bars government contractors from using parts made by a handful of Chinese tech companies over security concerns.
Cris van Pelt, creator of the anti-Flock advocacy project Have I Been Flocked, says that while where the cameras are made may have relatively minor implications for US communities, the lack of transparency about their origins underscores a broader problem.
“It all speaks to the fact that there is no real oversight, and that tens of thousands of literal and figurative black boxes are being installed on American roads,” van Pelt says. “If any part of the supply chain is compromised, we would never know. That’s a much bigger problem than where the final product is assembled.”
“Aggregation”
The earliest Flock prototypes were made using cameras ripped out of Android phones bought on Alibaba, which were then attached to batteries and soldered onto a solar panel, Langley recalled in one video. The goal was to prove that a useful device could be created from parts collectively costing between $200 to $300. (WIRED reported earlier this week that Flock’s cameras continue to use smartphone-style processors and leave significant data unencrypted.)
As Flock began securing contracts with homeowners associations, it shifted into a corporate office that also doubled as an assembly line. Langley described the setup as fun, but also unprofessional and arduous—pallets of parts shipped in from China had to be dragged a quarter of a mile through the building multiple times a week.
Around 2020, Flock moved its assembly line to a WeWork-style warehouse facility in Atlanta, according to a marketing video produced by the space’s operator. A handful of Flock employees cranked out as many cameras as they could, with engineers assembling the main camera device and less technical staff attaching solar panels and mounts.
Rather than opening up warehouses, Flock stored cameras in self-storage locations across the country for its installation crews to retrieve as needed, according to two former employees. One described the system as “janky,” noting it may have left cameras more vulnerable to tampering than they would have been if kept in more secure locations operated by Flock itself.
In marketing materials from 2019, Flock touted its cameras as “manufactured in the United States.” The following year, it said they were “made in the USA.” In 2021, it got more specific, telling potential customers that assembly was done by “Flock Safety in Atlanta, GA.”
Over the next couple of years, Flock began shifting final assembly to contract facilities in North Carolina and Wisconsin operated by East West Manufacturing and Plexus, according to a person familiar with the matter. It also opened up its own warehouses.
The person says Flock wanted to keep assembly in North America, both to ease security concerns—particularly about potential Chinese surveillance—and to keep factories close enough that it could quickly customize products in response to customer needs.
A Flock marketing brochure from 2023 described its cameras as “designed & manufactured in the U.S.” By 2024, Flock’s manufacturing partners were capable of producing 500 cameras a day, a ten-fold leap from several years prior, one of the people familiar with matter says. Parts still largely came from Asia.
In mid-May, as backlash against the startup swelled, East West removed reference to Flock from a list of case studies on its website, according to archived versions on the Wayback Machine. (A video from East West promoting its work for Flock shared on LinkedIn in late 2021 remains online.)
East West and Plexus didn’t respond to requests for comment.
WIRED was unable to determine where Flock’s cameras are assembled now. A Flock marketing presentation from this year does not mention a location.
In July, the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration cited Flock for allegedly failing to promptly report a June incident in which an employee was hospitalized for a leg amputation, according to records from the workplace regulator. The records indicate the injury happened at a Flock “audio and video equipment manufacturing” site in Houston, Texas. It’s possible that the location is actually the site of a camera, and the injury came during an installation or maintenance procedure. Flock and OSHA did not respond to WIRED’s requests asking for clarification about the nature of the site and what work may occur there.
Flock is contesting a proposed penalty of about $9,500, saying it reported the injury quickly after learning about it.
Even if Flock’s manufacturing supply chain remains in the United States, it may do little to calm bipartisan backlash against the company.
“Domestic manufacturing is no substitute for accountability over how these systems are built, sold, and used,” says Matthew Guariglia, senior policy analyst at the civil liberties advocacy group Electronic Frontier Foundation. "The multi-billion dollar industry churning out mass surveillance technology is not safer or more acceptable based on where it is assembled.”
Flock’s top competitors vary in terms of how much they disclose about their manufacturing. Motorola Solutions has described its license plate cameras as being assembled at its own facility in Richardson, Texas. Axon has said little about where its Outpost cameras are produced, but has noted it assembles other products in Scottsdale, Arizona.
Motorola and Axon didn’t respond to requests for comment.
US-Made Drone
Flock has been more upfront about the manufacturing of its new surveillance drone. Last October, it announced the opening of its own facility in Smyrna, Georgia to assemble drones and solar panels, as well as refurbish various other products. US law now largely restricts foreign-made drones, including the models from China-based DJI that Flock has been deploying. No similar US rules apply to license plate cameras.
It’s unclear how well the Smyrna operation is faring. Flock repeatedly postponed the timeline for launching its first so-called Alpha drone, which finally “hit the field” in May, according to a company executive. This year, Flock told Berkeley, California officials it would swap out DJI drones for the US model “within two years.”
Lewbel, the Flock spokesperson, says it continues to “bring more Alpha drones online.”
Additional reporting by Caroline Haskins.

Aerospace propulsion startup DheyaTech has raised ₹43 Cr (around $5.1 Mn) in a funding round led by Avaana Capital, with participation from Unimech Aerospace and Manufacturing. The Bengaluru-based startup plans to use the fresh capital to scale production, establish an integrated testing facility for its gas turbine engines, and work with domestic and global OEMs to accelerate commercial deployments. DheyaTech is targeting flight trials of its engines in Q4 2026. The startup said it has already secured orders from Indian and global OEMs, without disclosing their names or the value of the contracts. Founded in 2018 by aerospace engineers Gurushankara KC, Abhinav Alva, and Chetan Kumar, DheyaTech develops indigenous small gas turbine engines for advanced aerial platforms and energy systems. Its engine portfolio spans thrust capacities ranging from 20 kgf to 400 kgf. The startup said the engines are now entering the commercial deployment stage after years of research and development. DheyaTech claims to have built the entire product development pipeline in-house, covering engine design, development, assembly, and testing. It has also developed a proprietary adaptive engine control unit (ECU), which manages and adjusts an engine’s operation. The startup claimed that it is the first Indian private company to pursue independent airworthiness certification for its gas turbine engines under the guidance of the Centre for Military Airworthiness and Certification (CEMILAC), a DRDO laboratory. Beyond propulsion, DheyaTech is expanding into hydrogen-based technologies and distributed power-generation systems. In collaboration with the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) Bengaluru, DheyaTech has also developed a hydrogen-based flexi-fuel combustor for its 60-kW turbogenerator. A turbogenerator combines a gas turbine with an electrical generator to produce power. DheyaTech’s fundraise comes amid growing investor interest in Indian aerospace and spacetech startups developing indigenous hardware and propulsion technologies. In January, aerospace propulsion startup D-Propulse raised ₹25 Cr from IAN Alpha Fund to develop indigenous propulsion systems based on rotating detonation engine technology. Meanwhile, spacetech startup InspeCity raised ₹100 Cr in August in a round co-led by Ashish Kacholia and Speciale Invest. It plans to use the capital to fund four in-orbit missions and advance its satellite-servicing and propulsion technologies. Advanced hardware and technology startups, including aerospace, defence, semiconductor, and robotics ventures, raised $365 Mn across 66 deals in the first half of 2026.

Last year, the District Child Welfare Committee in Chennai dealt with a case where a 15-year-old girl from Nepal had married a 28-year-old man working in Chennai, the two having met on Instagram. With the help of friends, they got married in Chennai.
A month into the marriage, the girl was traced after she made a call to her sister in Nepal. The girl’s family lodged a complaint with the police following which India Child Protection, a civil society organisation working in the area of child protection, intervened to rescue the girl.
Social media and online dating are increasingly exposing vulnerable girls to greater risk of child marriage.
“With advancement in digital communication, the modus operandi in child marriage is changing, making more children vulnerable,” says Bhuwan Ribhu, a child rights activist and founder of Just Rights for Children.
Bhuwan Ribhu says trafficking is a borderless crime, and it requires a borderless response. Online methods of enticement or grooming for marriage, sexual abuse and trafficking have become possible irrespective of distance and geography.
In a study taken by NGO Save the Children, they observed that girls in India faced greater online risk of child marriage and trafficking during the pandemic. The agency continues to work with children and teachers to raise awareness about staying safe online.
According to the National Family Health Survey (2019-21), the national average in India for child marriage is 23%. The prevalence rate in India for child marriage has fallen by 10 per cent. The Bal Vivah Mukt Bharat campaign launched by the Central Government in November 2024 promises to make India child marriage-free by 2030 and is seeing various state governments running different initiatives.
A dedicated CMPO needed
Natharsha Malim H, state coordinator - Tamil Nadu, India Child Protection, says while Tamil Nadu has been making steady progress in reporting and stopping child marriages, gaps continue to exist.
Tamil Nadu, he says, does not have Child Marriage Prohibition Officers (CMPOs) that are appointed to prevent marriages, gather evidence, raise awareness and report data. The District Social Welfare Officer (DSWO) is notified as the Child Marriage Prohibition Officer of the concerned district.
“This is an additional role that the DSWO takes up. We have been asking for a dedicated person to be appointed as many other states have done based on a Supreme Court recommendation,” says Malim.
For example, in Karnataka, the Department of Women and Child Welfare has included pre-university (PU) college principals as child marriage prohibition officers, whose responsibility is to prevent any girl child studying in their college from marrying before 18 years.
Dedicated officials tasked with curbing this practice is particularly required in places such as Salem, Dindigul, Namakal and Cuddalore which has reported maximum cases of child marriages, says Malim. Grama panchayats have to be empowered in these districts to curb child marriage
A rule book for intervention
Malim notes that State Governments have to draw up a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for elimination of child marriages.
“The Supreme Court came out with a landmark judgement on child marriages in October 2024, but Tamil Nadu is yet to come out with an SOP,” he says.
Panchayats that make an earnest effort to stop child marriage should be rewarded; and the bravery of young girls that resist coercion by family into child marriage should also be acknowledged.
Bhuwan Ribhu cites the example of a study done by India Child Protection in 2025, wherein cases in Assam dropped by 84 percent following a continuous crackdown by law-enforcement authorities.
How to report a child marriage
File a complaint with
* Child Marriage Prohibition Officer
* District Magistrate
* Nearest police station
* District Child Protection Unit
* ASHA Unit of District Legal Services Authority
* Bal Vivah Mukt Bharat portal https://stopchildmarriage.wcd.gov.in
Source: Ministry of Women and Child Development
Although Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 has been in existence for decades, enforcement leaves a lot to be desired.
“With amendments to the law and judgments by the Supreme Court, we have been able to see much impact on the ground, along with greater awareness,” says Ribhu, adding, “awareness needs to be supplemented with the enforcement of policies, accountability of institutions, and the use of technology for monitoring.”
Residents association in Chennai hails UN declaration
On September 4, 2026, when the United Nations General Assembly declared November 27 as the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage, a residents group in Anna Nagar celebrated the announcement.
A small number of residents, close to 150, of Kambar Colony in Anna Nagar gathered at the park in the neighbourhood to watch the live proceedings of the United Nations General Assembly on the designation of November 27 as the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage.
The programme was organised by the ICWO Tamil Nadu and Kambar Colony Welfare Association. The designation is a significant global commitment to strengthening awareness, prevention and action against child, early and forced marriage. This is a victory for children and civil society organisation that have been fighting to end child marriage.
Awareness banners and charts were displayed, and the gathering concluded with an oath-taking ceremony to strengthen the community’s commitment to end child marriage.
ICWO is a partner agency with Just Rights with Children in Chennai, working with educational institutions and communities on rights concerning children.
A.J. Hariharan, founder secretary, ICWO, says reporting is the key to preventing child marriage. He notes: “we work closely with schools and colleges to help eradicate child marriage. All what we ask them is report any cases of child marriage to the helpline number or a teacher.”
ChildLine Helpline 1098 can also be dialled to report a case.

At Uber, AI does everything from answering employees' questions in Slack to writing the response you get when you message customer service during a ride.
Six recently laid-off employees who spoke with Business Insider pointed to several ways that AI became more prevalent in their jobs over the past few months. Some said that they were prompting AI to do substantial portions of their work.
Uber declined to comment for this story. Earlier this month, the company laid off about 3,300 people, including all of the employees Business Insider spoke with for this article.
CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said at the time that the layoffs aimed to cut "management layers" and reduce the number of teams where managers had as few as one or two direct reports. Khosrowshahi didn't cite AI as a motivation in a memo announcing the layoffs.
At the same time, the employees who spoke with Business Insider said that the company has pushed ahead with implementing AI in a wide variety of uses.
One employee said that in the weeks before being laid off he was using an AI tool that reduced the time it took to do his job to one-fifth of what it used to be.
"AI definitely feels like the dynamite under the bridge for a lot of us," the employee said.
'Don't be using ChatGPT to do your work for you'
A laid-off employee in Uber's advertising business said that managers were increasingly urging them to use Gemini and ChatGPT to prepare for client meetings.
"We were asked to use AI all the time," the employee said. "It was part of our day-to-day work."
In many internal Slack channels, Uber uses an AI chatbot called Genie, which provides "prompt responses with proper citations from Uber's internal documentation," the company wrote in a blog post last year.
The chatbot provides answers to questions that employees post, the employee said, providing a lot of guidance that previously came from managers.
"If anybody else had an answer for you, then they replied," the employee said. "But it was usually AI replying to us about any questions we had."
Another employee who worked in customer service said that they used Glean, a similar tool trained on internal company documents, to respond to help requests from Uber drivers and passengers.
The tools were meant to help customer service agents find information, the employee said. They often copied and pasted answers from the tools directly into the chat.
"It wasn't what we were supposed to use, but it was a tool available to use when our knowledge base wasn't working," the employee said.
Other Uber employees said that their managers cautioned against that sort of AI use.
"We're also getting guidance like 'Don't be using ChatGPT to do your work for you,'" Kori X, a former evaluation specialist on Uber's GenAI team said.
"I think they're struggling with why they are paying these people if they're just using ChatGPT," X said.
Uber saw 'real tailwinds' from AI productivity
Another laid-off employee said that they didn't feel pressured to use AI at work.
The company took a measured approach to implementing AI compared to other tech companies, this employee said, offering office hours, explaining to employees what AI could and couldn't do, and curbing the use of AI-generated pictures in external communication.
Uber previously said it has used forward-deployed engineers in "agentic pods" to identify uses of AI across the company, from finance to HR.
Uber started cutting off or reducing credits to services like Claude in the first half of this year, the employee said.
Uber executives said around the same time that they had already spent their Claude budget for the year and that the company wasn't seeing productivity gains commensurate with what it was spending on AI tools.
In a presentation at an industry conference last week, Khosrowshahi cited some of the same justifications for the layoffs as in his memo the previous week.
Uber wanted to "have more doers versus managers," he said, and reduced the number of "micro-teams" where managers had as few as one or two direct reports.
At the same time, Uber saw an opportunity with the restructuring to take advantage of "real tailwinds as it relates to productivity, whether it is AI or general productivity technology as well," he said.

16-year-old girl gang-raped by 4 teens, found stabbed to death days later in Delhi
The girl knew one of the suspects, a 17-year-old, and had gone to meet him on Saturday evening.
Four teenagers have been apprehended for the gang-rape and murder of a 16-year-old girl whose body was found stabbed and hidden beneath leaves in a field in north Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar, police said on Thursday.
Police said Shivam Ganesh (19) was arrested in connection with the crime. His accomplices, the three minors aged 17 and 16, have been taken into custody. The two knives used by the suspects and the clothes that they allegedly wore at the time of the crime have been seized at their instance.
The girl, a school dropout who was living on her own and searching for work to help support her family, was found dead on September 13. Police said the body had about six to eight stab wounds.
Also read: Minor boy rapes Class 8 student in Delhi's Narela; friends film sexual assault
The crime
The girl knew one of the suspects, a 17-year-old, and had gone to meet him on the evening of September 10. “He raped her and when she threatened him, he called his friends who also raped her. They were all under the influence of alcohol. We have already taken their blood samples. After they committed rape, they took her to a field and stabbed her more than six times early on September 11. They tried to hide the body under leaves and mud. They later fled in the tempo,” a police officer said, citing initial investigations.
Her decomposing body was found on September 13.
Deputy commissioner of police (Outer North district) Shobhit Saksena said further investigation was in progress to establish the complete sequence of events, ascertain the individual role of each apprehended person, verify all available forensic and technical evidence, and examine the involvement of any other person in the offence.
Also read: Bihar teacher held for alleged rape of 17-year-old student, abetment of suicide
“The recovered exhibits have been preserved for forensic examination and necessary legal action will be taken accordingly,” Saksena added.
How police cracked the case
Police said the girl was found stabbed to death in an open field near Kushak Road, Swaroop Nagar two days later. Police said they lodged a case of murder, rape and causing disappearance of evidence on the basis of their initial investigations and the autopsy report.
A team led by additional DCP (Outer North) Lokeshwaran R and assistant commissioner of police Ravinder Ahlawat found that none of the locals had spotted the girl on Saturday night or Sunday. More than 50 CCTVs were scanned and then a tempo was spotted moving near the field around the time of the incident.
Also read: 40-year-old man held for abducting, raping 9-year-old in Delhi's Swaroop Nagar
Investigators said the registration number was not clearly visible in the footage due to darkness but the vehicle was finally identified with the help of CCTV mapping,
Police said they picked up the driver of the tempo, who revealed that his younger brother, 17, often took the vehicle.
“The footage also revealed the presence of four young boys inside the tempo. The boys were soon identified but had fled from their home,” said an investigator.
DCP (outernorth) Shobhit Saksena said the team had analysed the movement of the tempo across multiple CCTVs and used the footage along with local inquiry to establish the route taken by the accused.
“On the basis of the developed leads, a night-long search operation was conducted during the intervening night of Tuesday-Wednesday. The tempo was traced in Khadda Colony, Swaroop Nagar. Its driver was identified and questioned. Further investigation led to the apprehension of four persons,” the DCP.

US sanctions boost China’s science-driven innovation by over 70%, study finds
US tech restrictions have driven Chinese firms to expand and deepen their scientific research sourcing through citations and research
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Sanctioned Chinese companies are increasingly turning to open-source research to innovate and reverse-engineer restricted foreign technology, with a 72 per cent surge in scientific literature citations in their patent applications, according to a new study.
While the United States said it expanded its Entity List to safeguard national security and preserve its technological edge, an analysis of Chinese patent filings over the 12 years until 2022 showed that US restrictions on access to technology had driven Chinese firms to widely source publicly available scientific knowledge and conduct more of their own research.
“Our analysis reveals that US trade sanctions, such as the Entity List, have generated consequences that US policymakers may not have fully anticipated,” the researchers wrote in a policy article published in the peer-reviewed journal Science on Friday.
“Though hindering the targeted firms’ short-term operations, sanctions may also catalyse these firms’ development of internal capabilities and drive strategic shifts, potentially leading to the emergence of separate technological systems that compete with, rather than integrate into, the current global innovation ecosystem,” they wrote.

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

No fire alarms or sprinklers at Pakistan neonatal unit where fire killed 14, report finds
- Published
An official inquiry into a Pakistan hospital fire that killed 14 babies last month has found the neonatal unit lacked fire alarms and sprinklers, while firefighters reported that escape routes were "locked or obstructed".
One firefighter, who asked to remain anonymous, told the BBC he had heard from other rescue workers that entering the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) hospital in Islamabad was "extremely difficult".
"The doors were locked so they had to break through the windows to enter. Even after getting inside, the doors leading towards the ward were locked."
PIMS has not provided a comment on the report and its findings.
The firefighter said he arrived once the blaze had been put out.

- Inside hospital after fire kills 14 babies in Pakistan

For many inside the hospital on the morning of 26 August, the first warnings were shouts.
Abdul Ghafoor was in a nearby ward with his mother, who was a patient, when he heard someone warning that a fire had erupted. He went upstairs to see if he could help.
"The entire ward was filled with smoke, we could not see anything," he told the BBC.
CCTV from the corridor outside shows how quickly the fire spread. According to the report, the first indication that something was wrong came at 06:38 when a nurse can be seen running from the ward to get help, returning 20 seconds later with a security guard.
Another nurse, Razia Noreen, is then seen rushing into the ward, emerging seconds later with one of the babies who turned out to be the only one to survive.
Within a minute, the report says, dense smoke had obscured the camera.
Hivsa Walid, her newborn niece and sister-in-law were in the ward next door. Hours later she told the BBC that they had heard a loud commotion and then realised it was a fire when they saw smoke emerging from the unit where the babies were sleeping.
"In that moment, I couldn't understand what was going on. We just focused on getting downstairs and saving ourselves."
On the day of the fire, authorities suggested the fire had started from a spark in the ward's air conditioner.
The report agrees that this was the most probable source of the fire, due to an overheating electrical supply cable - although it remains unclear what exactly the electrical defect was.
The fire then spread quickly, igniting plastics, equipment and bins.
Several babies in the ward were on oxygen support, but the report says that while oxygen may have intensified the fire, there isn't evidence that it created a pathway for it to spread.
The air conditioning units had undergone maintenance, but the report says this is not the same as a safety check. Back in 2018, the hospital's air conditioning units had been approved to be replaced and upgraded, but eight years later this hadn't happened.
The report states that there was no functioning smoke detection, fire alarms or sprinkler system. It found no evidence that the staff in the unit had been trained or had ever rehearsed how to evacuate the ward of newborns, many of whom were premature or "medically fragile". It also found staff had not been trained on how to isolate the oxygen supply in the case of an emergency.
Several people described chaos and confusion in the hospital.
"There should have been fire extinguishers and protocols, but no one was doing anything," Walid said. "Everyone was just running."
Ghafoor said that he was part of a group of seven or eight who tried to find a way to relieve the thick smoke; they managed to break glass panels at the end of the corridor before firefighters arrived.
The emergency services weren't notified about the fire until 06:54, the report says, nearly 20 minutes after it first began. It says the first rescue workers arrived at 07:01.
Like the firefighter who spoke to the BBC, Ghafoor also said rescue staff struggled to get through some of the hospital's doors.
At the time, the hospital's executive director had told BBC News that the door to the newborns' ward was not locked, but guarded, because of previous incidents of baby abductions from government hospitals.
The report says that while "ordinary access restrictions may be legitimate for security purposes… they cannot render designated emergency routes inaccessible when needed."
The report also found that the hospital had received previous warnings about fire risks. A month before, a fire had broken out at its nursing hostel, raising issues with smoke detection, alarms and general fire preparedness.
It says that the hospital and its senior management "bear the principal institutional responsibility for failing to convert known risks, prior warnings and assigned duties into an effective safety system".
Pakistan's prime minister has directed the inquiry's short-term measures to be implemented within the next three months and ordered fire safety audits of public and private offices and buildings.
He has also suspended eight officials and asked for criminal proceedings to be initiated against them.

Boks power & All Blacks of old - what did we learn from series?
- Published
South Africa further cemented themselves as the world's best team with a 3-1 victory over New Zealand in the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series.
After losing the opening Test in Johannesburg, the world champions won three straight games, comfortably claiming the series with a 43-28 win in Baltimore.
The fourth Test, played in the United States, came after three Tests in South Africa where the All Blacks continued to show promising signs under Dave Rennie.
With the Rugby World Cup next year, what did we learn from the series, which replaced this year's Rugby Championship and will be played again in 2029?
Power remains Springboks' trump card
New Zealander Tony Brown's arrival as attack coach in 2024 pointed to South Africa's ambition to dominate in all facets of the game.
The former Highlanders head coach, who will join the All Blacks in 2028, is known for creating a cohesive attacking shape built on sharp ball movement.
But having been outscored in terms of tries over the first two Tests, the Springboks flipped their pack-power trump card - pivotal to their back-to-back World Cup successes - to prevent a repeat of New Zealand's victorious 1996 series win in South Africa.
Nothing illustrated that more than a monster maul that started just inside New Zealand's 22 and ended with Malcolm Marx peeling off to score the decisive try under the posts.
That came after a penalty try from a scrum in the first half. In Baltimore, their power again proved too much.
"South Africa have tried to play expansively a couple of times when we have dominance after hurting teams in the maul or scrum," Schalk Brits, a 2019 World Cup winner, told BBC Sport.
"New Zealand didn't have that dominance in the forwards, but people said they played beautiful rugby. I don't care if it is beautiful or not.
"Beauty is in the eye of the beholder and I love a maul and scrum."
Fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, who was injured at the end of May, returned to start all four Tests. He was initially named on the bench for the second match, only for Handre Pollard to withdraw.
Despite improving as the series went on, the 24-year-old lacked his usual flashes of individual brilliance.
It remains to be seen whether South Africa turn back to 32-year-old Pollard, as they did in 2023, on the biggest occasions to close out games.
Rassie Erasmus' experienced back-to-back World Cup winners - Marx (32), Eben Etzebeth (34), Pieter-Steph du Toit (34), Siya Kolisi (35), Damian de Allende (34), Cheslin Kolbe (32) - all remain regular starters.
The world champions have proven they can also play an exciting brand of attacking rugby, but appeasing the masses will not matter if a familiar formula can bring them three straight World Cups.
All Blacks return to what made them great
Scott Robertson's dismissal in January after two years as head coach sunk New Zealand to a new low.
Rennie, not the flashiest appointment, had to hit the ground running, and a stunning Test win over South Africa at Ellis Park was a case of doing just that.
The 33-16 victory injected jeopardy into a series which many had the Springboks winning comfortably, given their home advantage and recent dominance.
Hurricanes half-backs Cam Roigard and Ruben Love, both aged 25, were trusted by Rennie to instil a return to the All Blacks way - the ability to score from transition from anywhere on the field and compound scoreboard pressure.
Four or more tries in each Test in South Africa showed just that, with the third Test all square at half-time.
"Scott Robertson was a good culture coach but maybe not a brilliant technical coach. Dave Rennie is a brilliant technical coach," former England wing Ugo Monye told Rugby Union Weekly.
"After the Nations Championship, you could see the structures and how they want to play. I think the All Blacks' backline is the most skilled in World Rugby."
Love struggled to have the same commanding impact in Tests two and three, with fly-half Richie Mo'unga returning for the Baltimore game, his first Test since the World Cup final.
The 32-year-old Mo'unga, who is back after a stint in Japan, was not at the standard that made him one of the best fly-halves at the 2023 World Cup.
However, getting him back up to speed will be an All Blacks goal over the next 12 months.
Former England scrum-half Danny Care said: "Imagine what New Zealand would do with a platform and some dominance. It is great for the game that they are coming back to be the All Blacks of old, and the next 12 months will be fascinating."
World Cup rivals: France 'can play multiple styles', and be 'careful of Ireland'
South Africa live for must-win games. That is when, according to Brits, the Boks "come alive".
Defeat at Ellis Park cost them their world number one status - which was quickly regained - but also exposed a vulnerability.
South Africa, who lost matches in the pool stages of the past two World Cups, are currently the favourites to win next year's tournament in Australia, bringing a pressure they have not experienced previously.
"We hate being the favourite, we almost have to have our backs against the wall," Brits said.
"We prefer not to have the eyes on us and move under the radar. I think that is the best way for any team."
Back-to-back Six Nations champions France sent a weakened side to Christchurch in July and lost 34-32 to New Zealand.
When matched against the Springboks last November, France were beaten emphatically, 32-17.
Brits believes France are "the most settled" and offer tactical flexibility similar to that of the world champions.
"I feel like South Africa have an advantage as they can play multiple styles, and it feels like most other nations don't have that capability," Brits said.
"The only team that can play multiple styles is France, as they can grind it out with the forwards, play the kicking game and the expansive game as well."
He added that England still need to become what they are "supposed to be" and to keep an eye on Ireland, who are travelling "under the radar" after peaking in previous World Cup cycles prior to the tournament.
"Ireland still have amazing rugby players and coaches – the best coaches out there - and a top-four squad," Brits added. "Be careful of Ireland."
