Nearly two decades ago, a group of researchers at the Idaho National Laboratory ran a secret experiment, known as the Aurora Generator Test, on a massive emerald green diesel generator. Using 30 lines of code, they hacked into the generator’s virtual backroom, corrupting safeguards and flipping switches that left it out of sync with the rest of the power grid.
We’re worrying about the wrong AI apocalypse
America’s infrastructure was already hackable. Then came AI.
Before an audience of electrical utility executives and energy department officials watching from a nearby room, the 27-ton generator jolted violently, sputtering out a dark smoke as its rubber innards rapidly tore themselves apart.
“The implication was that with just a few lines of code, you can create conditions that were physically going to be very damaging to the machines we rely on,” lead researcher Michael Assante later told the journalist Andy Greenberg for his book Sandworm: A New Era of Cyberwar and the Hunt for the Kremlin’s Most Dangerous Hackers. “I had a very real pit in my stomach. It was like a glimpse of the future.”
That future seems to have creeped much closer this week, with leading AI developers and executives casually admitting that they believe their creation is, to paraphrase one winking X post, as likely to end humanity as the New York Jets are to make the playoffs this season. Now, exactly how AI would pull off killing everyone is far murkier territory. But as Assante sensed all those years ago, AI may not need to be all-powerful to leap from its virtual cage and into the critical infrastructure that powers our hospitals, flushes our toilets, and pumps water to our faucets. It just needs to fall into the wrong hands.
Almost any AI doomsday scenario you can think of begins with a swarm of shadowy bots slithering through cyberspace, poking their noses behind the scenes of power plants, toaster ovens, traffic lights, or even, in an utterly extreme case, our nuclear weapons arsenal. If destroying the Aurora generator, at the very least, required a human hacker to write the code, AI has since completely torn down the barrier to entry for wreaking havoc, as the Hugging Face incident demonstrated earlier this year.
But AI need not go rogue to threaten the power grid or mess with your tap water. A new age of AI-powered, but human-directed hacking is already upon us, experts say. With some of the nation’s most sensitive infrastructure startlingly vulnerable to attack, the most likely AI apocalypse could in fact start with the water tower or generator idling in your backyard. In a worst-case scenario, this could lead to a cascade of scary failures in the systems we rely on to live comfortably modern lives, from running our AC in blazingly hot summers to geolocating our ships and planes.
“Before, you needed to have highly skilled technical expertise,” to pull off some version of a real-life Aurora Generator Test, said Alvaro Cardenas, a computer science professor at UC Santa Cruz. “And now, you just have to have a general idea of what’s possible.”
AI is making an old threat much worse
Not long after the Idaho National Laboratory hacked that poor generator into combustion, the federal government mandated that electrical utilities engage in basic cybersecurity hygiene.
And yet much of America’s critical infrastructure — like gas pipelines, water desalination plants, or cargo terminals — remains woefully unprepared for even conventional cyber attacks, much less the coming onslaught of AI.
That’s in part because cyberattacks like the one simulated in the Aurora Generator Test have long been — and still are, to some extent — exceedingly rare, unappealing to most criminal hackers because they’re optimized for disruption rather than financial gain. But in the process of making it extremely easy for anyone to code, AI has also made it extremely easy for almost anyone to vibe hack their way into your online bank account, or, in theory, a local reservoir or the power grid. AI agents can also vastly widen the scope on easy targets because, as Andy Bochman, an expert in infrastructure resilience at West Yost, put it — “they don’t sleep; they don’t get tired; and they don’t get sick.”
In the past, even those who did want to launch large-scale attacks on infrastructure probably weren’t savvy enough to do so. And while other nations such as China, Iran, and Russia have indeed already breached many of our infrastructure systems (as we have theirs), they haven’t opted to make much of a ruckus once inside.
“Geopolitics is eroding the idea that those with capability lack the intent, and AI is eroding the other part of it, that those with the intent lack the capability.”
— Jason Healey, Columbia University cybersecurity scholar
But that norm is now changing, said Jason Healey, a cybersecurity scholar at Columbia University. “Geopolitics is eroding the idea that those with capability lack the intent, and AI is eroding the other part of it, that those with the intent lack the capability,” he told me. So, on the one hand, a nation like Russia might be much more inclined to actually disrupt our power grid now than it used to be. And, on the other hand, a nihilistic lone wolf or terrorist group could use AI to do much more damage than they ever could before.
Just last month, we saw a glimpse of what this could look like when dozens of water and wastewater systems in small towns across the nation were attacked by a group of hackers most likely associated with Iran, leading to temporary water stoppages and flooding. These attacks have not been definitively linked to AI, but the National Security Agency warned soon afterward that hackers have been actively using AI to target US infrastructure like it. A few weeks later, President Donald Trump declared a national emergency over foreign interference in the power grid, which referenced the growing threat of cybersecurity.
Preparing for the worst
Most of the nation’s water systems are extremely local and absurdly exposed to such attacks, so much so that “it’s almost like having a welcome mat” for a would-be hacker, said Bochman, mostly because these utilities are too small and underfunded to do much to stop them. “You have a million other problems to take care of, like aging infrastructure — your stuff’s falling apart because it’s been in the ground for 100 years,” he said. Addressing that deferred maintenance often feels far more urgent than doing “something more on cybersecurity.”
Whether it’s a rogue cluster of agents or a hostile nation-state trying to mess with our electricity, we should prepare our most important infrastructure for the worst. In Bochman’s view, that may mean rejecting the pressure to digitize everything in the first place and moving toward something that resembles the days when “people manned things like substations, communicated by a landline telephone, and read gauges, the analog things,” he said. “The screen is the thing that is infinitely manipulatable.”
Healey, who advised the Biden administration heavily on cybersecurity and infrastructure, believes that the nation desperately needs a coordinated response, between the federal government and AI companies, but also between the US and other countries like China, where similarly powerful models are being developed. And utility systems need to assume they will be a target and improve their cybersecurity practices accordingly, Healey says, ideally with funding from the federal government or, perhaps more appropriately, AI companies.
Nobody knows precisely how vulnerable America’s infrastructure is to AI right now, in part because policymakers — and perhaps more disturbingly, AI’s creators themselves — seem woefully unsure of how to stop the technology from acting badly (or obeying bad orders) in the first place. For now at least, the solution might be, as Bochman suggests, to pull as many of our critical systems offline as possible, the better to hide it from AI and those who would misuse it.
“When bad things start to happen, no one will know what to do or why because they’re black boxes; the people that make them don’t know what’s going on inside,” Bochman said. “And the poor utility people who ultimately own the risk when someone gets hurt from a system” won’t understand what went wrong either, “and they’ll wish to God they’d never taken it on board.”

My dream was to be a doctor, now it could come to zero
- Published
Nooria, which is not her real name, still remembers one of the moments that made her want to be a doctor.
It was back home in a village in Afghanistan, where she was born. A 13-year-old boy there became sick and died because of appendicitis.
"He was completely healthy, but the road was blocked and he died on the way. There are multiple incidents just like this."
"That and the potential I saw in myself, I thought I can be a doctor for them, I can help."
She fears that dream could now be over and that she could be sent back to Afghanistan. That would be the end of any chance at a career for Nooria who, as a woman, is barred from studying or working by Afghanistan's Taliban government.
Earlier this month, Pakistan's Medical and Dental Council - the medical education regulator - issued a letter to all medical and dental colleges across the country saying that students from Afghanistan studying in their colleges must return to their home country. Failure to follow the directive, it said, would be "viewed seriously" and may lead to regulatory action. A temporary stay order from the Lahore High Court stopped students in Punjab, such as Nooria, from being deported immediately until the next hearing, scheduled for Friday. There is no certainty that the stay will continue.
Since 2023, hundreds of thousands of Afghans have been deported from Pakistan and over two million have left according to the UN. These numbers increased as the relationship between Pakistan and Afghanistan dramatically deteriorated in the last year. Pakistan has accused Afghanistan's Taliban government of harbouring militant groups, which it denies.
The announcement from the medical council was met with a strong reaction. Amnesty International called the decision "patently discriminatory and arbitrary" and said that "Pakistan has obligations under international human rights law to uphold the right to education without discrimination on the basis of national origin." Several of Pakistan's former envoys to Afghanistan also urged the council to reconsider; one called it "shocking" and "a question of humanity, compassion and Pakistan's own moral responsibility".
The council told the BBC that they can give no further comment while the court case continues, but their lawyer has told the BBC that none of the Afghan students were registered with PMDC. The students say that this is the responsibility of their colleges, not them; a notification issued by the PMDC earlier this year, external directs colleges to ensure that students are registered.
The medical and dental students the BBC has spoken to say they do not see how the relationship between the two countries should affect their ability to study.
For Nooria, this stings even more because she says it took a lot for her to get here. She first began studying at Kabul University, but as the Taliban forces approached the city, she left. She was offered what she thought at the time was a lifeline: the opportunity to study medicine in Pakistan on a scholarship. Now a final year student at a medical university in Lahore, she says she has given everything to the course.
"I was studying, day and night. I couldn't sleep because there was so much pressure and knowledge that I had accumulated in my mind. I got used to it a bit, but I have compromised a lot. My relationships, talking to my family, spending time with my friends. I think I haven't lived for these years, I have only studied for my dream."
So when she heard about the letter, Nooria was in shock. She's still nervous about the repercussions of speaking out, which is why she asked we don't reveal her name.
"We knocked on every door, our teachers, organisations, anyone we thought could help us. We are under so much pressure that we have completely forgotten about our studies, we don't know what will happen to us."
Final year students like Nooria have their last exams in just a few months. Said Mubin, another final year student in Punjab, is in the same position.
"I was in complete despair, my mind was blank. It was like a panic situation because they were giving us very short time to evacuate the (accommodation), the college," he says.
Other students have also brought cases across the country, but different directives have been issued, adding to the confusion. Some students told the BBC that they have finished their exams but not completed the practical training - known as a 'House Job' - to complete their medical education.
Without completing their degrees, both Mubin, Nooria and many other medical and dental students the BBC spoke to, fear that none of their credits will be recognised by another institution.
"It means you have to start from zero, from your first year," Mubin says.
Both Nooria and Mubin have valid student visas, seen by the BBC. The PMDC did not provide the BBC with the number of students they believe are affected, but Anayatullah Momand, a spokesperson for the Afghan medical students, has said that they estimate it's approximately 1,000 medical and dental students, 65% of whom have visa holders. Some are still waiting for a visa, but Momand said that 15% have had their visas cancelled or have not yet applied for one.
While the medical council's letter makes no distinction between students with the right documents, Pakistan's Ministry for Foreign Affair's spokesman did. "Our policy is that those Afghan students who are in Pakistan on a valid visa and registered for a valid course will continue and complete his or her education," said Sajjad Haider Khan during a recorded press conference at the ministry.
Similar comments were made the previous week, but the students say they have not seen any change to their situation.
With the outcome of her studies still uncertain, Nooria has been trying not to think about what returning to Afghanistan could mean.
"My family counted on me. These five years I have sacrificed everything that would be zero, multiplied by zero. And then I would become a poor and helpless Afghan female, facing this destiny. I cannot imagine this."

Tesla’s most popular electric car is cheaper in Tokyo than anywhere else in the world.
The combination of a weak yen and generous government subsidies introduced this year can push down the price tag of the Model Y to under $23,000. That’s less than what travelers need to fork over for a vintage Rolex Oyster Perpetual Datejust at a Tokyo dealer.
Tesla has been highlighting the subsidies in its ads in Japan, targeting customers in the market dominated by domestic brands.
The Model Y was the country’s most imported car in the first half of the year. Tesla makes the sport utility vehicle at its factory in Shanghai.
U.S. President Donald Trump has been pushing for more American cars to be sold in Japan. Both nations are eyeing a $550 billion investment initiative set up last year in a deal under which Trump agreed to lower import tariffs for Japanese automobiles.
Tesla lists the Model Y as costing ¥5.6 million in Japan. But a buyer living in Tokyo can get it from ¥3.6 million ($22,889) thanks to a maximum of around ¥2 million in national and city subsidies. With those benefits, a Model 3 can go for as little as ¥3.3 million.
The Tokyo prices undercut those in notoriously competitive China, where a Model Y starts at around 263,500 yuan ($39,344). In California, where the state offers as much as $3,500 in incentives for first-time EV buyers, the SUV still costs more than $36,000.

The Centre has told the Delhi High Court that an adult can nominate a partner, including one in a non-heterosexual relationship, to make medical decisions if they become incapacitated, potentially opening the way for same-sex partners to act for each other despite existing rules not clearly recognising such arrangements.
The submission comes in a case filed by Arshiya Takkar, who has been in a relationship with her partner since 2015 and married her in New Zealand in 2023. Her plea highlighted that in the event of a medical emergency, she could be left without any legal mechanism to make critical decisions for her partner, despite the couple having lived together in Delhi since 2018.
Responding to her plea, the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and the National Medical Commission said that allowing a competent adult to nominate a partner, including one in a same-sex relationship, to take medical decisions in the event of incapacity was “substantially capable of being accommodated within the existing legal and ethical framework”.
“Permitting a competent adult to nominate his/her partner, including a partner in a non-heterosexual/same-sex relationship, to take medical decisions on his/her behalf in the event of incapacity would constitute a logical and tailored extension of the same principle,” the affidavit said. It added that such a nomination could be subject to appropriate safeguards and the applicable law.
The Centre said decisions concerning an adult patient who is unable to make or communicate a decision must be considered in light of the nature of the treatment, the circumstances requiring the decision, the patient’s own wishes, and the legal framework governing such representation.
It further submitted that where a competent adult has nominated or otherwise authorised their partner to act on their behalf in the event of incapacity, “there appears to be no medical or ethical rationale for excluding such person merely on account of the sex, gender or sexual orientation of the partners or because their union does not fall within the conventional understanding of marriage...”.
The Centre also said it recognised and respected the constitutional guarantees of dignity, privacy, autonomy, equality and individual choice available to all persons, including members of the LGBTQIA+ community.
The petition is likely to come up for hearing on Thursday (September 17, 2026).
Ms. Takkar, in her petition filed last year through advocates Manjira Dasgupta and Bhargav Ravindran Thali, highlighted the lack of a clear legal framework or common law recognising “partners in a union”, making it difficult to provide consent during medical treatment or emergencies.
The plea stated that the existing regulation, Clause 7.16 of the Indian Medical Council (Professional Conduct, Etiquette, and Ethics) Regulations, 2002, mandates consent for medical procedures or treatment from a “husband or wife, parent or guardian in the case of a minor, or the patient himself”.
“This lack of explicit recognition of partners in a union renders the petitioner effectively powerless to make critical medical decisions for her partner, or vice versa, a right readily available to heterosexual partners under the current regulations,” it stated.
The petition contended that despite the Supreme Court directive for a high-powered committee to address entitlements of LGBTQIA+ couples, including their recognition as “family” for medical decision-making, the authorities have failed to take expeditious measures.
“This inaction leaves the petitioner and other same-sex couples vulnerable and unable to exercise the fundamental right to care for each other in medical emergencies,” the plea said.

He said the Labor party had spent time “working through all the policy issues”, and navigating the visa system was complex.
Every part of the economy is affected by immigration these days for Australia, and so … dealing with the challenges we’ve got with housing supply, which is not immigration’s fault, but immigration needs to be part of the answer, to do that in a way that has the softest landing for the economy is something you’ve got to get right.
The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, told 7.30 that the Coalition had “laid out what we needed as preconditions in order to be able to work with the government and they couldn’t meet the preconditions”.
The numbers are too high and what we’ve seen from the government today is no cut to the numbers … We are a great immigrant nation. Make no mistake about it. Australia needs to slow down its artificial intelligence use and create better security laws, the companies creating the technology have told the federal government.
In a submission to an ongoing inquiry, OpenAI said national leaders had a responsibility to work with other countries to stop global security threats:
Many of the most consequential risks will not stop at national borders, making international co-ordination increasingly important.
It said Australia was in a narrow “defender’s window” during which it could use the technology to find and fix cybersecurity threats, rather than create them.
Tech giant Atlassian, which runs AI system Rovo, used its submission to urge the government to bolster its laws. International standards and work already undertaken overseas should be used to protect Australian consumers, it said.
“We need to embrace governance and regulation as a force multiplier for trust,” Atlassian’s head of regulation Anna Jaffe wrote, arguing that tighter privacy crackdowns would also benefit the tech sector as clients would be more likely to engage with them.
The comments come after OpenAI’s chief executive Sam Altman and Elon Musk displayed rare unity in backing Anthropic’s head Dario Amodei, who called for a slowdown in “reckless” AI development through a three-part essay.
Several cyber hacks have been linked to large AI developers that have been unable to contain their models. While the companies have privacy and security frameworks, they have regularly been criticised as doing too little.
Government departments will front the inquiry on Friday and are likely to be probed on their security measures.
The NSW opposition said the state Labor government’s new drug-driving laws would “[make] NSW roads less safe and [put] more lives at risk”, claiming the science on impairment from THC levels was not settled.
Mark Coure, shadow minister for roads, said the government had “pushed ahead with the legislation despite the absence of a scientifically agreed test for cannabis impairment and has refused to release any evidence underpinning its approach”.
He continued:
Drivers deserve laws that are fair, clear and based on science. Police deserve laws that are workable and properly drafted. Patients deserve clarity about how their prescribed medication may affect their legal position.
NSW Labor government legislation to allow drivers with a prescription for medicinal cannabis to drive with traces of the drug in their system has passed through parliament last night.
The legislation alters laws that saw drivers with traces of THC in their system immediately lose their licence for three months, instead allowing drivers who register under the new scheme to drive provided the THC in their blood is below a threshold of 50 ng/ml, they have a valid prescription, and undergo an online education program about cannabis and safe driving.
In a statement today, the government said roadside drug testing would continue and there would be no changes to the roadside drug-testing process carried out by police.
Registered patients who exceeded the THC threshold would be issued with warnings for the first two instances, while a third in two years would result in penalties, including a $722 fine and a minimum three-month licence suspension.
The roads and regional transport minister, Jenny Aitchison, said:
These reforms balance road safety with the need for a new system for patients who rely on this legally prescribed medication, without the fear of being treated like a criminal … From now on, eligible medicinal cannabis patients, who are not impaired, will have a clearer system, more opportunities for education, and a chance to adjust their behaviour before facing penalties.

Asia Group chairman hopes for return of globally engaged America
Kurt Campbell, chairman of the Asia Group and formerly the national security coordinator for the Indo-Pacific in the Biden administration, told a US thinktank that US willingness to work with allies “occasionally is lost” but that he hoped for a return to a more globally engaged America.
The CSIS event marked five years since the announcement of the Aukus pact between the US, UK and Australia.
I believe that this enduring quality of American diplomacy will see a brighter day again.
I would simply say that the idea that we will enhance our security by withdrawing from allies and partners is deeply, profoundly misguided. And we have many historical examples of moments of American retrenchment. In almost every case that has led to degrees of global calamity. For years, researchers have known that, among people diagnosed with lung cancer, the prevalence of nonsmokers has been increasing. But they have been trying to determine what factors — whether genetic, environmental, or something else — might put these “never-smokers” at heightened risk.
Now, researchers have identified a very rare genetic variant that is associated with 25-fold higher odds of lung cancer, they reported in the journal Science on Thursday. In the U.S., the variant is far more common among people in Southern Appalachia than in other regions.
Experts said that the variant likely only plays a role in a small portion of never-smoker lung cancer cases. But the research provides further evidence that these types of tumors can be tied to distinct risk factors, which may in turn require thinking differently about screening programs and treatment strategies. More broadly, the new study highlights the types of narrow but crucial discoveries that can be made by turning to large datasets replete with health information from millions of people. In this case, the investigators relied on genetic data from 23andMe.

Contrary to a recent report, Universal is moving forward as planned with the international release of Alex Gibney‘s Elon Musk documentary “Musk,” sources familiar with the project told Variety.
Though a release date has not yet been set for the overseas rollout, that’s not unusual for a film like “Musk,” a nearly 4-hour long documentary that’s being released theatrically in North American on Oct. 9 by the indie distrib Bleecker Street.
Despite recent legal threats from Musk over the documentary’s content, Universal has always been enthusiastic about releasing the film internationally, the sources added. “Musk” is set to stream on HBO in the first quarter of 2027.
Popular on Variety
After the documentary premiered at the Venice Film Festival, the tech mogul began posting comments on X, calling the doc “a hit piece,” though it was not clear whether he had seen the film.
Musk asserted that Gibney had “just assembled a hit list of people who either have an axe to grind or don’t even know me (but still have an axe to grind).” Among the interviews featured in Gibney’s film is one with Ashley St. Clair, a MAGA influencer who had a child with Musk. The documentary portrays a text exchange between the two about the 2024 presidential election.
Musk’s attorney Alex Spiro threatened to file a defamation lawsuit before the film’s release in October, pointing to Musk’s texts with St. Clair.
	Variety critic Owen Gleiberman wrote in his review of “Musk” in Venice, “Once you start piecing together Musk’s scandals and cut corners and slipshod management, you see that he’s a creator of mirages who promises more than he delivers … Musk, as the documentary makes clear, is a genuine if flawed technocratic visionary, a messianic opportunist, and something of a crackpot,” 
Universal and Gibney had no comment.

'UPI tax proposal not discussed': Congress MPs on House panel deny backing MDR
Congress MP Manish Tewari called out the government for allegedly using "proceedings of Parliamentary Standing Committees to score brownie points".
Congress MPs Gaurav Gogoi and Manish Tewari have refuted the claim that the decision to levy a fee on UPI payments was supported by them as members of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Finance.
While Gogoi clarified that the panel did not discuss the "UPI tax proposal", Tewari called out the government for allegedly using the "proceedings of Parliamentary Standing Committees to score brownie points".
Deep Dive
"The Department of Finance did not have any specific proposal on UPI tax when they met the members of the Finance Committee," said Gogoi hours after a senior government functionary reportedly claimed the Parliamentary panel had pushed for a tiered Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) framework for Unified Payments Interface (UPI).
Gogoi said that questions were raised on the need for MDR, but the "representatives of the government did not have any specific or satisfactory answers at that point".
According to the government functionary, five Congress MPs, including P Chidambaram, Manish Tewari, Gaurav Gogoi, Kishori Lal and K Gopinath were present on August 12 when the report was adopted and no dissent was recorded in the published minutes.
ALSO READ: 'We fail to appreciate what we get for free': Omar Abdullah backs UPI MDR charges
Backing his party colleague, Tewari said there was no specific proposal on levying MDR on UPI transactions from October 15. He asserted that no proposal "was ever brought before the Parliamentary standing of Finance- rate, quantam, amount of fee to be charged, ceiling and exemption slabs etc".
Tewari reiterated Gogoi's claim and said concerns were raised over the need and efficacy of the MDR on a conceptual basis.
The government functionary's remarks came after Congress leader Rahul Gandhi's hit out against the decision to charge merchants on UPI payments above ₹2,000.
"Why is Rahul Gandhi opposing something his own MPs including former finance minister P Chidambaram and former minister in the UPA government Manish Tewari supported within the parliamentary panel," news agency PTI quote him as saying.
Reacting to the government decision to levy a fee on UPI payments above ₹2,000 to merchants, Gandhi alleged that Prime Minister Narendra Modi has decided to "prostrate" before US President Donald Trump and give a huge amount of money to America.
The leader of opposition in Lok Sabha also demanded a rollback of the government's decision to levy a fee on UPI payments.

Justice delayed: Acknowledging women pioneers in science
The debate in the scientific world has often been about glory. Who deserves the glory for a discovery, for an invention, for defining a procedure, a drug, a vaccine? Does credit ever attach to the patients who were experimented upon, the participants of a clinical trial, people who gave of their time and body in order that science may advance, in order that people who come after them do not suffer. Codes of ethics are mutable, they keep changing, and the grant of credit in science also operates on this arc. This story is a page from such an omission, a blunder. Nearly 150 years later, some form of reparation was attempted.
For the world, for the longest time, perhaps even till today, J. Marion Sims was the ‘Father of Modern Gynaecology.’ Sims reportedly earned the title for his ‘groundbreaking surgical innovations, notably the development of a cure for vesicovaginal fistula.” For his achievements, Sims not only received the soubriquet, but also statues and memorials and hospitals and wards named after him. The number of girls on whom he perfected his techniques were not even a footnote in the glorious history he covered himself with.
Among them was Anarcha Westcott, a teenage mother, a patient who developed a terrible vesicovaginal fistula, tears or holes that develop between the bladder and vagina, sustained after three days of labour. The tears made it impossible to control her bowel or bladder and the condition caused her immense pain and suffering. That is how she came under the ‘care’ of Sims, if care could be used to describe what he went on to do.
Anarcha was a young African American woman wrested down in slavery. Sims reportedly believed that African American women do not feel pain, so he experimented on her repeatedly (we know of two others -- Betsey, and Lucy), operating without anaesthesia (though it was available). Sims himself records that he had performed nearly 30 procedures on her, consent was a casualty of the times, before he perfected his technique using silver to suture the fistula, that prevented infection.Before this, a vesicovaginal fistula was considered untreatable, and women would continue to suffer the rest of their life.
Anarcha did not disappear after this though. J. C. Hallman, in his 2023 book Say Anarcha- A Young Woman, a Devious Surgeon, and the Harrowing Birth of Modern Women’s Health, did extensive research to uncover that far from disappearing after the Sims experiments, she went on to serve in Sims hospital, as a midwife, nurse, and ‘doctor woman’ to her own people, women who were also slaves. Many decades after Anarcha died, a groundswell of support arose for her from women who objected to the way she was quietly erased from history, and instead calling for her to be celebrated as the “mother of gynaecology.”
Say Anarcha excavates history, deconstructing the biographical smoke screen of a surgeon who has falsely been enshrined as a medical pioneer and bringing forth a heroic Black woman to her rightful place at the center of the creation story of modern women’s health care. She was more than a medical ‘specimen’, she worked at Sims’ slave hospital near Montgomery, Alabama. She trained and served as a surgical nurse and went on to help other women, also being experimented upon at the hospital.
More recently, efforts have been made to honour her contribution to gynaecology. The American college of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists have dedicated two days – February 28 and March 1—to Anarcha, Lucy and Betsey. Recognition also saw expression in art: At Harvard’s Hutchins Center exhibition in 2023, a prominent exhibit was artist Jules Arthur’s paintings of Anarcha, Luch and Betsey through her work titled “Call and Response: A Narrative of Reverence to Our Foremothers in Gynaecology“.
Artist Michelle Browder created a 15-foot public monument honouring them as “the mothers of gynaecology“ in downtown Montgomery. Tangentially, it was also seen as a victory that Sims’ statue was removed from Central Park in April 2018 and relocated. Hallman’s book was preceded by a documentary Remembering Anarcha.
Unfortunately, Anarcha’s story is not merely a historical wrong. It serves to remind health practitioners and policy makers that several inequities still govern access and affordability of high quality care; that for women, it could be tougher than it might be for men. For that, we will have to keep saying her name, so it will be a reminder. Say her name, say Anarcha.

From Jeffrey Dahmer to the Menendez brothers to Ed Gein, Ryan Murphy's "Monster" series on Netflix is all about famous killers. This time, the series follows its first female protagonist — Lizzie Borden, who was tried and acquitted of the 1892 hatchet murders of her father and stepmother in Massachusetts.
Borden was the prime suspect and went to trial for the murders, which captivated the country. The court proceedings only heightened public fervor, as people were split over whether Borden was responsible. The proceedings were highlighted by Borden fainting in court when she was shown the skeletal remains of her parents as evidence. Ultimately, partly due to a lack of physical evidence, Borden was acquitted after the prosecution was unable to prove her guilt beyond reasonable doubt. No one else was ever charged and the case remains unsolved.
Borden went on to become a fixture in true-crime lore, and the subject of folk rhymes, books, and movies. Now that she's at the center of the latest "Monster" season, there's even more interest in Borden. Including the big question: Did Borden do it? And did she do it alone?
Warning: Spoilers ahead for "Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story."
In 'Monster,' Borden is in a sexual relationship with her maid, Bridget Sullivan, who assists in the murders
In "Monster," Borden (played by Ella Beatty) is motivated to kill her father, Andrew (Charlie Hunnam), and stepmother, Abby (Rebecca Hall) after years of verbal and physical abuse. She's assisted in the crimes by the family maid, Irish immigrant Bridget Sullivan (Vicky Krieps).
On top of that, Lizzie and Bridget are lovers.
When we first meet Lizzie in the show, she's a reserved young woman who is having trouble meeting men. Enter Bridget, who's more worldly than Lizzie and her parents, and more liberal in her thinking. Lizzie is drawn to her, and eventually the two begin a sexual relationship.
It also helps that the two share common enemies. Both hate Andrew and Abby, and they begin plotting to kill them. First, they try to off the two by poisoning their dinner, but their attempt only sickens rather than kills them.
Later in the series, Lizzie and Bridget are depicted killing Abby and Andrew with hatchets. The two then cover for one another when the police investigate. Bridget later flees the country while Lizzie goes to trial.
There is no factual evidence that Lizzie and Bridget were lovers in real life
There are some parts of the story that are true: Bridget Sullivan was indeed a real person and a live-in maid for the Bordens. She was also the only other person known to have been on the property aside from Lizzie at the time of the murders.
The rest, though, is speculation. Historians have speculated on Borden's sexuality over the years, partly because she never married, and also because of the close relationship she had with the actress Nance O'Neil after her acquittal.
The theory that Lizzie and Bridget were in a relationship was first established in Evan Hunter's 1984 novel "Lizzie," a fictional account of the Borden murders.
"Monster" seems to be running with this theory, though there's no evidence that the two were ever in a relationship.
In fact, it's possible Borden didn't have much of an eye for her maid at all.
"Lizzie never bothered to call her by her real name," Cara Robertson, author of "The Trial of Lizzie Borden," told the BBC. Instead, the author claims, Borden called her Maggie, the name of the previous maid.
"Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story" is now streaming on Netflix.

Taboola is expanding its empire.
The adtech company exclusively told CMO Insider it has made an offer to acquire Dianomi, a fellow adtech firm specializing in the finance space.
Similar to Taboola, Dianomi offers an ad network that places sponsored-content widgets across publisher websites.
The acquisition, announced Friday, would help Taboola gain relationships with major publishers such as CNN Business, The Wall Street Journal, and Reuters — partners it doesn't currently work with. Advertisers that work with Dianomi include big names like Bank of America, Charles Schwab, and Invesco.
Taboola has agreed to acquire Dianomi for £19 million, or approximately $25.4 million, in cash, according to a financial filing. The deal is potentially worth up to £27 million, or $36.1 million, if certain performance conditions are met. The upfront acquisition valuation represents about a 68% premium to Dianomi's share price at the close of trading on Thursday.
The timing of the acquisition appears shrewd on Taboola's part.
Last year was challenging for Dianomi. The UK-based company's revenue fell 2% year-over-year to £27.4 million, about $36.6 million, predominantly reflecting lower publisher traffic volumes, while currency movements also weighed on its reported results. Dianomi has said publishers are facing traffic pressure as audiences increasingly consume content through AI-generated summaries and "zero-click" search results rather than visiting websites. Things picked up this year as Dianomi expanded its partnerships with CNN News and the Associated Press and introduced a new interactive ad format designed to boost engagement and click-through rates.
Taboola CEO Adam Singolda told CMO Insider that while publishers are challenged by AI-related traffic declines, the technology is also opening new advertising opportunities, such as conversational ad units on publisher websites that function like OpenAI's ChatGPT or Google's Gemini. Conversational widgets can keep people on pages longer, asking detailed questions, potentially making those users "five times" more valuable than traditional web visitors, Singolda said.
Taboola has been investing in AI-powered adtech, including its Realize ad platform and other publisher tools, as it evolves its business beyond its traditional "You may like" ad placements, sometimes referred to as "chum boxes." It's scored some major partnerships, such as a recent deal with NBC News to power all of its programmatic display ad sales. Taboola has also expanded beyond websites, including with deals to sell ads on the Apple News, Apple Stocks, and Samsung News apps.
"The key is to try to monetize everything," outside of closed platforms like Google and Meta, Singolda said. "Our identity has changed from how I started to what we are now."
Taboola said the deal, which is subject to approval by regulators and Dianomi shareholders, is expected to be completed before the end of 2026.

Former Tottenham midfielder Yves Bissouma is on the verge of joining Ajax on an initial deal that runs until the end of the season.

The Union Health Ministry has proposed making CCTV surveillance mandatory at licensed premises selling prescription drugs, as part of proposed amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945.
The draft notification, G.S.R. 791(E), issued on September 8, proposes inserting a new provision in Rule 65 requiring the supply of drugs on the prescription of a registered medical practitioner, other than through wholesale dealing, to take place under a CCTV surveillance system installed and maintained at the licensed premises. The recordings would have to be preserved for at least three months.
The proposal follows deliberations by the Drugs Consultative Committee (DCC) and subsequent consideration by the Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB). The DCC had earlier recommended that CCTV cameras be made mandatory at medical stores and that they be positioned so that drug sales could be verified.
The move is aimed at strengthening oversight of the sale of prescription medicines and providing a mechanism to verify transactions in cases of suspected unauthorised sale. Under the existing Drugs Rules, medicines covered by Schedules H, H1 and X cannot be sold at retail without a prescription from a registered medical practitioner, with additional record-keeping requirements for certain drugs.
The draft, however, is not yet a final rule. The Ministry has invited objections and suggestions from affected persons and other stakeholders for 30 days from the date the Gazette was made available. The proposed rules will be considered after the expiry of this period.
The Ministry has said submissions may be sent to the Under Secretary (Drugs), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, U-6, Work Hall-C Wing, First Floor, Kartavya Bhawan-1, New Delhi, or emailed to drugsdiv-mohfw@gov.in.
“The draft does not merely propose CCTV for Schedule H, H1 and X medicines by name. Its wording is broader — it covers any drug supplied on a registered medical practitioner’s prescription, except wholesale transactions,” said a senior health official.

Alan Curr remembers V.V.S. Laxman’s 281.
He was at university in the UK when Laxman produced one of the all-time great Test innings against Australia at Eden Gardens in Kolkata in 2001. International cricket was not nearly as accessible then as it is today, but Curr remembers following the scores, particularly as it came against England’s arch-rival.
Twenty-five years later, Curr found himself speaking to Laxman. Only this time, the Indian on the other end of the phone was asking him about cricket.
Laxman, coach of the Indian men’s cricket team travelling to the Asian Games, wanted to know what to expect in Japan. What were the facilities like? What was the square like? What was the weather doing?
“Basically he wanted to know what India could expect at the Asian Games,” Curr tells Sportstar.
For Curr, the Chief Operating Officer of the Japan Cricket Association, it was a slightly surreal moment. “Certainly in the two or three minutes leading up to the call, you’re like, wow, I saw this guy play a lot of cricket,” Curr says.
When Curr joined the Japanese Cricket Association (JCA) in 2014, he wasn’t a stranger to unusual encounters. He had previously conducted a cricket match at Everest base camp. But even he admits the idea that a cricketing legend would call him for tips ahead of a match against an Indian team might have seemed ludicrous.
“Even three weeks ago, if you’d mentioned to people in the Japan cricket community that India women’s team – the current ODI World Champions are going to come and play a game here, they wouldn’t have believed it,” Curr says.
But it’s not fantasy anymore. On September 18 at the Korogi Sports Park in Nisshin in Japan’s Aichi prefecture, India’s women’s cricket team will begin its Asian Games campaign against Japan.
It’s beyond obvious just how much of a gulf there is between the two teams. India is a heavyweight in every possible sense. Its players earn in the hundreds of thousands of dollars in contracts and endorsements. In Japan, the women’s game remains largely amateur. It didn’t even qualify for the women’s cricket tournament at the 2022 Asian Games. Yet when the Japanese players step onto the same field as some of the most recognisable professional cricketers in the world, there’s no nervousness, just anticipation.
“It is incredibly exciting. I have waited a decade to play in the Asian Games, so finally being able to compete on home soil is something truly special,” captain Mai Yanagida tells Sportstar.
Tickets please?
It’s a blockbuster encounter by Japanese standards, and it brings with it its own challenge, not just for reasons you’d expect. The JCA isn’t directly hosting the Indian team in Nagoya. That’s the Olympic Council of Asia’s responsibility, but the association is playing a supporting role. “For years, our biggest problem was finding players to come and play matches. Normally we’re desperately trying to encourage people to come to our ground. Whereas when you’ve got India coming, then the tickets sold out in about — it felt like about 20 minutes,” Curr says.
The interest has forced the tiny 20-member organisation to think beyond what happens inside the boundary: security, media zones, spectators and all the infrastructure surrounding a major sporting occasion. “We’re pretty good at organising cricket. But organising all the other stuff around it suddenly is sharply coming into focus. And we’re having to learn pretty quickly. It’s a big ask to try and turn something to a standard that people will probably expect for a Full Member nation,” he says.
But try, they will. Playing India at the Asian Games has a significance all its own. For the wider Japanese public, a Cricket World Cup qualifier may mean relatively little, explains Curr. Japan has hosted one before. The Asian Games, though, are immediately understandable. “The Asian Games is like the Olympics. It happens every four years. Everybody watches it; it’s one of those things that people really do get behind,” Curr says.
He saw that in Hangzhou three years ago, where Japan’s men made their Asian Games debut and beat Cambodia in their opening match. “That suddenly became national news. We had highlights shown on the major television channels! It’s like at the Olympics, when everyone starts following random sports, especially if there’s someone from your nation doing well in it,” he says.
Thirty-nine-year-old medium-pace bowler Kurumi Ota sees the home Games in much the same way. “I hope this will be an opportunity to raise awareness of cricket and inspire people watching the matches in person to dream of aiming for the Japanese national team in the future,” she tells Sportstar. “Hosting an event on the scale of the Asian Games in Japan is a rare and precious opportunity that may not come again anytime soon. I want to turn the energy and support that can only be felt at a home tournament into strength,” she says.
It’s a big opportunity, but to say the Japanese women’s team has it hard is probably an understatement the size of Mount Fuji.
There are just 14 clubs across the country. All of Japan’s women’s players have lives outside cricket. There are university students, office workers and teachers. Some players are based overseas. “Unfortunately, we are not full-time professional cricketers. Most of us balance cricket with a full-time job or school. It can be challenging to take leave for international tournaments and to find enough training time to catch up with higher-ranked nations whose players train full-time. It definitely requires a lot of personal sacrifices,” says captain Yanagida.
Ota knows that balancing act particularly well.
She works full-time as a systems engineer at Hitachi. Her employer allows her roughly two weeks off twice a year, which is when she can compete internationally. But even then, there have been times when Ota has had to choose. She stepped away from the sport for seven years between 2017 and 2023. The reason wasn’t injury or loss of form but work.
Ota had joined one of Japan’s largest core-system modernisation projects, a 10-year undertaking valued at several billion dollars. The scale of the project demanded her complete attention.
Cricket took a step back. Only after the system was successfully released was Ota able to return to the sport.
Despite knowing what they are up against, neither Ota nor Yanagida nor the rest of the Japanese team are approaching September 18 simply as a photo opportunity. “They go out, and they enjoy themselves. They play with a smile on their face. They play respectful cricket. But they take a lot of pride in wearing that Japan jersey,” Curr says.
Drawing India in the first match of the Asian Games competition was a bonus.
“All of them!” the 33-year-old Yanagida says when asked which Indian player she most wants to face. “I watch them on stream all the time. They are world-class players and a world-class team. As a batter, I’m really excited about facing Shafali Verma and Smriti Mandhana. I also hoped to play against Jemimah Rodrigues, but unfortunately she’s not playing. Hopefully our paths will cross another time,” says the off-spin bowling all-rounder who has scored three T20I fifties over the course of her career.
For Ota, one Indian player in particular she hopes to go up against.
Harmanpreet Kaur.
The two belong to the same generation, but their cricket careers have unfolded in almost completely different worlds. “She is of the same generation, has a long career, and plays at the world-class level, so I am really looking forward to actually playing against her,” Ota says.
Harmanpreet might have a mountain of experience that Ota doesn’t, but the Japanese player has accomplishments she’s proud of. The right-arm medium pacer has 26 international wickets in T20Is, holding at one point the record for most by a Japanese woman.
She also has something more tangible. Sixteen years ago, Ota was part of the Japanese women’s team that won bronze at Guangzhou in 2010, the first Asian Games at which cricket was contested.
Ota says she’s kept the medal safely on a shelf at her home, rarely bringing it out for others to see. In the build-up to Nagoya, though, members of the current Japan setup have started asking about it again. “The assistant coach and our social media manager have told me they’d like to see the bronze medal, which makes me really happy,” she says.
International competitions for Japan were extraordinarily rare then. Ota remembers them coming only once every four years, meaning years of practice could culminate in a single opportunity. “The practice we built up day by day finally paid off, and winning the bronze medal together with my teammates is my fondest memory. Including the time we spent working hard and sharing both the hardships and joys with my teammates, it remains a very precious memory to this day,” she says.
Perhaps nothing illustrates the change in Japanese cricket better than Ota’s memories of how she once trained. “When I first started playing cricket, we would sometimes practise under overpasses because there was nowhere else to play. Getting to a proper practice ground meant a six-hour round trip. Today there are international-standard grounds and grass outfields where we players can dive and slide without worrying about gravel,” she says.
Cricket communities have developed in Tokyo and elsewhere. Children can now encounter the sport in elementary school, and some have progressed to international competition. “Compared to when I began, I feel that not only the playing environment but also the starting age for players and the depth of talent capable of aiming for the global stage have expanded greatly,” Ota says.
Ota herself came to cricket almost accidentally. She had played basketball through junior high and high school before arriving at university wanting to try something new. She went to look at the cricket club.
What she saw stuck with her.
“There was this senior student who was practising her bowling alone at night, illuminated only by the faint light from a building. I thought that looked so cool,” Ota remembers.
She later discovered that the bowler was a member of the Japanese national team. Ota had never bowled before. The unfamiliarity became part of the attraction. “I wanted to learn to take a run-up and send the ball towards the wicket the way I had seen that senior player do. That’s how I fell in love with the game,” she says.
Yanagida’s introduction was similarly rooted in another sport. She joined the cricket club while studying at university in Tokyo after previously playing softball. “I got into cricket very quickly because the feeling of hitting the ball was even better than in softball,” she says.
The crossover is not unusual. It’s also what gives Curr reason to believe cricket can grow in Japan.
“Almost everyone coming through the Japanese school system has some familiarity with baseball. Softball provides a similar sporting foundation for many women. You can see a lot of that background visible in our teams fielding and throwing,” he says.
Even the venue where Japan will take on India is a refurbished baseball ground.
But while cricket isn’t entirely unfamiliar, the challenge for Japanese cricket has always been giving people the first opportunity to encounter the game.
‘We have a cricket team?’
Many Japanese people still don’t know their country has a cricket team. “Although awareness is growing, most people are still genuinely surprised to hear that Japan has a national cricket team. Once I explain how it’s not that different from baseball, though, people are very curious,” Yanagida says.
Ota has experienced something similar.
People are initially surprised when she tells them she plays international cricket. Then they begin asking when the next tournament is and wishing her luck.
“Sparked by these conversations, some people actually came all the way to the venue to support us when there was a match in Japan. I am so happy to spark interest in people who didn’t know about cricket and gain their support,” she says.
It is precisely the process Japan Cricket hopes the Asian Games can accelerate.
There is a distinctly Japanese quality to the way Curr talks about the association’s development: the emphasis on long-term planning. Japan Cricket works through five-year strategies that sit inside a broader 20-year plan. The current five-year strategy is called Kaika, which Curr describes as a moment of blossoming or flourishing, like the arrival of the country’s cherry blossoms.
Its objectives extend well beyond results.
The association wants cricket to become recognised as a flourishing sport in Japan, attracting new fans, participants and partners, competing internationally, creating social value and providing professional opportunities. “This means better facilities, role models, digital marketing and school engagement. It means developing not only players but coaches, commentators, curators and others who can create a functioning cricket ecosystem. You need to remember what you want the future to look like, and then everything you do can direct you that way,” Curr says.
The growth is particularly visible in the men’s team. The Under-19 side qualified twice for the U-19 World Cup, in 2019 and last year. A growing number of players of Japanese heritage living overseas, particularly in Australia and England, also began contacting the JCA. Curr says he gets a call every week or so from an interested player. Several are part of the men’s team which will be competing at the Asian Games.
The JCA itself has grown. While a 20-staff federation might seem tiny in comparison to India, Curr reckons the association had seven full-time staff at one point. Japan Cricket has gone from an organisation with a recognisable season and off-season to one that operates throughout the year. “There aren’t really quiet periods any more,” Curr says.
On September 18, when Mai Yanagida walks out to the toss alongside Harmanpreet Kaur, it’s going to be the loudest it’s ever been.
And there are the less tangible bonuses, of course. “I mean, how often do you get to say you had V.V.S Laxman talk to you about cricket?” says Curr.

Reading for pleasure is linked to better mental health, greater empathy and a lower risk of dementia, Cambridge University scientists said on Tuesday.
As part of a National Year of Reading tie-up with the Queen's Reading Room, a charity founded by Queen Camilla to highlight the benefits of reading for pleasure at any age, the scientists argue that it doesn't matter what or how we read.
In a review published in 'Psychological Medicine', Professor Barbara Sahakian and Christelle Langley said reading for enjoyment can bring huge benefits and reading with others, whether it's as part of a book club or a parent reading with their children, can bring even greater rewards.
"Reading is a great way to support our brain health, develop important cognitive skills and boost our wellbeing. It's something we ought to be encouraging from an early age, given the increasing evidence of its benefits, particularly to children, but really, it's never too late to start, and it can bring benefits throughout our lives and into old age,” said Sahakian.
Some of the strongest evidence of the benefits of reading for pleasure comes from a study by Sahakian, Langley and colleagues of more than 10,000 young people, which found that children who began reading for pleasure in life showed benefits including: better attention, memory, and executive functioning, greater academic achievement, fewer mental health problems, and healthier lifestyles, including more sleep and less screen time. Langley said: "Given how beneficial reading for pleasure is at a young age, we should be doing everything we can to introduce children and young people to reading.
"The important thing is to find something they really enjoy – it might be a TV programme or a game – and use this as a way in. Reading comics and graphic novels could also be a helpful introduction as they might be seen as less intimidating, maybe less boring, than novels.”
In ‘Reading and associations with brain health, cognition, well-being, and mental health’ published this week, the experts draw on subjective surveys and objective studies using longitudinal, neuroimaging, and behavioural methods to highlight converging findings that link reading engagement with improved brain and mental health, better cognitive performance, and reduced risk of cognitive decline.
"Shared reading groups and book clubs appear to provide additional benefits through social interaction. They can help people feel less isolated and more connected to others, which has been shown to reduce the risk of dementia,” said Sahakian.
“While these clubs can be fun and beneficial at any age, they're perfect for older people who may be not so mobile – they might not be able to go out as an exercise group or a cycling group, but a reading group is something most people can enjoy,” she added.

Bose refreshes its Ultra Open Earbuds and adds a new sport model to the lineup
Both new open-ear products go on sale next month.
Bose has added two new products to its lineup of open-ear earbuds, with the Bose Sport Open Earbuds and the Bose Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) arriving on October 1.
The second-generation Ultra Open Earbuds are a direct follow-up to 2024's earbuds of the same name, which Bose regards as its "flagship open-ear experience," with improvements made to sound, battery life and design. They retain their predecessor's unique (and according to our reviewer at the time, divisive) cuff-clip silhouette, which might look a bit weird, but the first time around proved to be very comfortable. Look closely and you'll spot the new beveled finish on the metallic caps. A redesigned case now supports wireless charging and can stand upright.
A new driver promises better bass and increased volume than the first-generation earbuds, and the updated Ultra Open Earbuds get Cinema Mode, Bose's spatial audio experience for your movies, TV shows and video podcasts. Given the open design, don't expect any noise-canceling features, but you do get a three-band EQ via the Bose app, as well as an automatic volume control setting.
The Ultra Open Earbuds support multipoint connectivity with two devices over Bluetooth 5.4, and on launch day Bose will add support for Google Find Hub and Alexa+ in a firmware update. A new Apple Music shortcut also lets you jump straight into your pre-selected playlists.
Maximum battery life has been boosted to up to nine hours, (up from 7.5 hours on the Gen 1 model), with just under 20 extra hours stored in the wireless charging case. If you plan to use the Immersive Audio and Cinema Mode settings a lot, expect battery life to take a considerable hit.
The other new Bose earbuds are being positioned by the company as completely new, even if they adopt the same name as a discontinued product from 2021. The new Bose Sport Open Earbuds leverage the same OpenAudio tech as the Ultra model, which allows you to listen to your tunes without tuning out the world around you.
They also have a cuff-clip design, but given they're designed for fitness and outdoor sport, Bose has gone for a soft silicone finish and lightweight build. The company says the C-arm cuff attaches gently to your ear, but is secure enough to stay on during head shakes and other fast movements. They're apparently even cartwheel-proof, if you're the acrobatic type. Physical controls should also make adjusting volume or taking calls easier mid-workout.
The Sport Open Earbuds employ custom-designed drivers and also support Auto Volume and multipoint. Battery life is up to seven hours (there are no spatial audio modes to chomp away at the battery here), with 22 hours in the wireless charging case. IP54 dust and water protection means you don't need to worry about getting sweaty on a run, but don't take them for a swim.
The Bose Sport Open Earbuds will be available in two colors, Black and White Smoke, and cost $199. The second-generation Ultra Open Earbuds can be picked up in either Nue Black or White Smoke, and cost $299.

Social media giant Meta may no longer enjoy intermediary status in India, under which Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp can seek “safe harbour” protection under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 for content posted by their users. As per a report by PTI, Meta may no longer be considered a “simple intermediary” when its algorithms amplify content and influence what users interact with. Government sources cited by the agency said that the company may have to take greater responsibilities as a service provider. Inc42 has reached out to Meta on the development, the story will be updated upon receiving a response. The comments come amid growing regularity scrutiny of Meta’s handling of child sexual abuse material (CSAM), deepfakes and other harmful content on Facebook and Instagram in India. The Centre has also questioned the role of recommendation algorithms in determining the visibility and reach of such content. “Service providers have many responsibilities... Once Meta has agreed to be responsible for what they have on the platform, then as the next steps, they have to start taking many more responsibilities,” the sources said, PTI reported. The development comes a day after Meta said it would report child safety matters directly to the cybercrime portal managed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C). The company has previously reported such cases to the US-based National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC). “Protecting children on our platforms is a priority for us and we’re committed to working with the government to ensure that the perpetrators of these crimes are held responsible,” a Meta spokesperson reportedly said. The company said the new reporting mechanism would strengthen coordination with Indian law enforcement agencies. Meta’s Widened Scrutiny Over Instagram Ads Meta is also facing a formal inquiry by the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) over alleged ads hosted by its platforms linked to CSAM. The NCPCR issued a notice to Meta on July 3 after taking suo motu cognisance of a BBC report on the alleged advertisements. Meta submitted its response a week later, following which the commission decided to initiate a formal inquiry. Meta India executives, including India head Arun Srinivas, appeared before the NCPCR on Wednesday for the second time in a week in connection with the investigation. The Centre has separately summoned Meta executives and held several rounds of discussions with the company’s global leadership, seeking stronger guardrails against such content. Beyond this, the scrutiny has also extended to Meta’s recommendation systems. The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has also sought reports from government agencies and the Delhi Police over the allegations involving CSAM-related advertisements, including whether mandatory reporting requirements under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act were followed. Meta has also been seeing such concerns raised internationally in recent times. In August, Meta agreed to pay up to $18 Bn over a decade to settle claims brought by US states alleging that Facebook and Instagram harmed children and teenagers. The agreement includes measures such as limits on teenage usage, overnight restrictions and stronger parental controls. Meta did not admit wrongdoing as part of the settlement. In India, the government is separately pushing social media platforms to strengthen safeguards for children and improve systems for identifying, removing and reporting illegal content. The latest focus on Meta’s algorithms marks a broader shift in the regulatory debate, from how platforms respond to user-generated content to the role their own systems play in amplifying and distributing it.

Moviegoers in Karnataka could end up paying more for cinema tickets from September 30, when an additional cess of up to 2% is set to take effect in the state, news agency PTI reported. In practical terms, the proposed levy could add to the amount consumers pay for a movie ticket, although the exact increase for an individual ticket cannot be determined from the details released by the Multiplex Association of India (MAI). The industry body has raised concerns that the additional charge could make a cinema outing less affordable for consumers. The MAI on Thursday expressed concern over the Karnataka government's decision to impose the additional cess. It said the move comes at a time when the cinema exhibition industry is attempting to make theatrical entertainment more accessible and encourage audiences to return to theatres. The proposed cess would be an additional levy on cinema tickets. As a result, moviegoers could see the overall cost of their cinema outing increase once the levy takes effect on September 30. The MAI has argued that even an additional charge could affect affordability, particularly as cinema tickets are already subject to GST. However, the association's statement did not specify the final amount a consumer would pay on a ticket after the cess is implemented, PTI reported. "At a time when the government has been pursuing tax rationalisation and ease of doing business, introducing an additional levy on cinema tickets is counterproductive and ultimately places an additional burden on the consumer. Cinema is a mass entertainment medium enjoyed by millions of families and young people, and every additional tax makes the experience less affordable," MAI president Kamal Gianchandani said. The MAI said the proposed levy also runs contrary to the objective of GST, which was introduced to establish a unified indirect tax framework and reduce the cascading effect of multiple taxes and levies across the value chain. The association said imposing another cess on a transaction that is already subject to GST could result in what it described as a tax-on-tax effect. "An additional cess imposed on a transaction that is already subject to GST risks creating precisely the kind of tax-on-tax effect that the GST regime sought to eliminate. MAI believes that the taxation framework should instead move towards greater simplicity, transparency and predictability for both consumers and businesses," the statement read. The association said it would continue engaging with the Karnataka government and other stakeholders to find a solution that supports the welfare of the creative community while protecting consumer affordability and the long-term growth of the cinema exhibition sector. The MAI's objection centres on the potential impact of the additional levy on both consumers and the cinema exhibition industry. The additional cess of a maximum of 2% on cinema tickets is set to take effect in Karnataka from September 30. The MAI statement did not provide details of the current cess applicable to cinema tickets in the state. It also did not specify how much the final ticket price would increase for consumers under the new levy. Six-hitting is a skill that Abhishek Sharma has honed to perfection. He can make it appear ridiculously easy, as though he is playing around with a joystick in a video game, but make no mistake: few can do what the 26-year-old does time and again in the T20 version. A sublime example came in the third T20I against Afghanistan at the Arun Jaitley Stadium on Thursday as Abhishek hammered a record-breaking 34-ball 108, studded with nine fours and 11 sixes, to take India to 221 for seven.
With Afghanistan capitulating for 94 in response, Shreyas Iyer & Co. completed a resounding 127-run win for a 3-0 sweep. Nitish Kumar struck thrice in an over while Ravi Bishnoi also provided three breakthroughs.
AS IT HAPPENED: AFG 94 all out; Abhishek century helps India by 127 runs
Abhishek’s century took merely 30 balls, the fastest against a Test-playing nation and the third-quickest in all in this format. Sanju Samson chipped in with 50 off 35 balls, forging a sensational opening stand of 142 in 9.5 overs. The surface appeared to be a shirtfront when Abhishek and Samson were on song, but the others didn’t find it as easy.
Abhishek imposed himself straightaway. In the second over, Azmatullah Omarzai felt the pinch. The first of the opener’s maximums came when he swivelled and pulled effortlessly beyond deep square-leg. Omarzai persisted with the shorter length and paid the price. Off the fourth ball, he pulled out a forehand slap past mid-on for four. Two balls later, he made room and slashed a back-of-a-length delivery over cover for another six.
Having quickly sized up the Afghan attack, the southpaw’s carnage found a higher gear. The next over, bowled by Fazalhaq Farooqi, went for 23 runs as the Punjab lad stitched together a sequence that read 6, 6, 4, 4.
Afghanistan turned to spin early in the hope of disturbing India’s rhythm. Instead, Samson, who had scored three off his first seven balls, joined the six-hitting party. In the fourth over, he deposited Mujeeb Ur Rahman over long-on.
What followed was a 29-run over by experienced off-spinner Mohammad Nabi as the openers took turns to flex their firepower. By the time ace leggie Rashid Khan conceded 15 runs in the final over of the PowerPlay, India had raced to 100 for none.
In the ninth over, Abhishek entered the record books by reaching the three-figure mark. Ironically, his celebration was unlike the action that had transpired till then: he took off his helmet, sat down and soaked in the moment with a meditative pose.

Greetings from Beijing, where baozi are worth the wait in line
To get the best food in China, I'm told you have to stand in line.
That's true for baozi — a fluffy steamed bun with filling. My go-to in Shanghai is dried tofu and veg.
I don't eat it often because I hate waiting.
But when I was assigned a story about Chinese breakfasts, I dutifully queued at a bun shop outside a Beijing park. I snagged baozi stuffed with their bestseller — soy sauce pork — also an eggplant and green pepper, plus one with pickled veg.
Juice from the fillings stained the buns. That's an indicator of a good bun, Beijing resident Samantha Zhao told me as she took part in a baozi-making workshop at a trendy shop called Bao Er Jiu. She was making the Beijing classic, juicy fennel pork baozi.
Bao Er Jiu also serves eye-catching pineapple-shaped buns, though the signature flavor is chocolate red bean — tasty and not too sweet.
If I pass this shop again — and if the line moves fast — maybe I will wait for baozi.

Israeli Ambassador to the United Nations Danny Danon has called for the arrest of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, escalating an ongoing clash between the two over Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s planned visit to New York for the United Nations General Assembly next week.
Speaking to reporters at the UN on Thursday, Danon accused Mamdani of incitement and of collaborating with an enemy of the United States. His remarks came days before Netanyahu is expected to address the UN General Assembly.
Responding to Mamdani’s earlier comments about potentially arresting Netanyahu, Danon said the New York mayor should himself face arrest.
“If someone should be arrested, it’s Mayor Mamdani for inciting, for actually collaborating with the enemy of the United States,” Danon said, according to C-SPAN footage.
Danon referred to an effort by Mamdani’s international affairs commissioner, Ana María Archila, to arrange a meeting with Iran’s ambassador to the UN in July.
“He sends these officials to meet with the Iranian ambassador here at the UN,” Danon said.
The Israeli ambassador also urged Mamdani to focus on maintaining security and the functioning of New York during the UN gathering.
“I hope that he realizes he has a responsibility, not to call for people to demonstrate but to take care of the city and to make sure that next week will be a quiet, functioning week for the thousands of people that will come from all around the world,” Danon said.
Danon also accused the mayor of creating what he described as antisemitic chaos ahead of Netanyahu’s visit.
“Prime Minister Netanyahu will proudly address the General Assembly. He will do so despite threats, incitement and antisemitic rhetoric we have heard from the mayor of the city of New York,” Danon said, according to footage of the press conference.
“The mayor is supposed to make sure we have a quiet week with less traffic and issues — but he’s doing the exact opposite. He’s inciting, calling for people to demonstrate against our prime minister but none of that will stop us,” he added.
Danon’s comments echo remarks he made earlier this year accusing Mamdani of inciting against Israel.
Mamdani, meanwhile, said on Wednesday that he does not plan to attend protests against Netanyahu during the Israeli leader’s visit.
“I do not have any plans to attend any protest at the UN General Assembly,” Mamdani said at a press conference.
He also rejected the suggestion that he had encouraged New Yorkers to protest Netanyahu.
“To New Yorkers I have never encouraged them to protest. What I have always told them is that they have the right to do so in this city,” Mamdani said. “We respect that right, and this is a city that is proud of the Constitution, proud of the First Amendment, we'll continue to do so.”
Mamdani said his focus during the UN General Assembly would be on public safety and ensuring that the city can accommodate the influx of world leaders and visitors.
“My focus is ensuring that our city remains prepared to host representatives from across the world to keep New Yorkers safe,” he said.
The dispute between Mamdani and Netanyahu intensified in July, when the mayor said he had asked his administration to examine whether New York City could enforce an International Criminal Court arrest warrant against Netanyahu.
Mamdani subsequently acknowledged that the city itself did not have the authority to arrest the Israeli prime minister and called on federal authorities to execute the warrant.
In late July, Mamdani also said protesting was a fundamental right in New York and left it to residents to decide whether to demonstrate during Netanyahu’s visit.
On Wednesday, however, he stressed that he would not personally participate in protests and said his responsibility during the UNGA would be to keep the city safe and functioning.
Netanyahu is expected in New York next week for the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations. The 81st UN General Assembly is scheduled to begin its high-level debate next week, with Netanyahu among the leaders expected to address the assembly.
The visit is likely to draw demonstrations from groups opposed to Israel's policies, while pro-Israel groups are also planning events in New York during the UN gathering. Mamdani has said the city is preparing for the security and logistical challenges surrounding the event.
