Verified video shows wreckage of Saudi fighter jet shot down over Yemen
- Published
Footage verified by the BBC shows the wreckage of a Saudi F-15 fighter jet which the Iran-backed Houthi group says it shot down over Yemen.
The US-made aircraft was "downed using a locally manufactured surface-to-air missile" as it "conducted hostile operations" over the Marib region, according to a Houthi statement on Wednesday.
Experts have told BBC Verify the incident is a "propaganda coup" that shows the Houthis' military capability has advanced and they are prepared to further escalate its conflict with Saudi Arabia.
Using satellite imagery to match features in the landscape seen in the footage, BBC Verify was able to pinpoint the crash site to an isolated location in the hills west of the Yemeni city of Marib.
The long-running conflict between a Saudi-led military coalition and the Houthis has escalated in the last week after the armed group launched an offensive against pro-government forces.
This led to the Houthis seizing key territory near the south-west coast, close to vital international shipping channels in the Bab al-Mandab strait.
In one of several video clips released by the Houthis, men with assault rifles can be seen at the crash site inspecting the wreckage. The fighters celebrate as they lift the jet's almost-intact tail fin which features the Saudi flag and a four-digit serial number.
The fate of of the crew is not known.
The Houthis also released a thermal video clip - which cannot be fully verified due to a lack of visual details - that appears to show a fighter jet in mid-flight being struck by a missile.
BBC Verify has contacted the Saudi Ministry of Defence for comment.
Baraa Shiban, Yemen analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, told BBC Verify the incident showed it was "very clear the Houthis have been taking advantage of advice and technological support" from Iran.
"They continue to develop their military arsenal and capabilities to make it more and more painful on Saudi Arabia," he said.
Downing the F-15 is also a "propaganda coup", said Yemen expert Adam Baron from the Washington-based New America think tank, as Saudi air support is considered to be "key to any significant pushback" against recent Houthi gains.
"An eye-for-an-eye has been a huge element of the group's public messaging. This is partially to show that air support will come at a price," he added.
BBC Verify used the position of the sun and satellite imagery to locate the distinctive landscape seen in the footage - including cliff faces and hills - to an isolated mountainous area about 25 miles (40km) west of Marib.
Satellite imagery published on Wednesday also shows a new dark shadow at the same location, which appears consistent with scorch or burn marks at a crash site.
The aircraft in the wreckage has been independently identified by Nick Brown, a weapons expert from military intelligence company Janes, as an F-15 Strike Eagle. He based his analysis on distinctive elements seen in the footage including the tail fin arrangement, radar antenna and missile warning system sensors.
The four-digit tail number visible on the wreckage also appears to be consistent with that of an F-15 Strike Eagle operated by the 55th Squadron of the Royal Saudi Air Force based at King Khalid Air Base near the city of Khamis Mushait in south-west Saudi Arabia.
This base, about 245 miles (392 km) from the crash site, was targeted last week by what the Houthis described as a "barrage of missiles and drones". Satellite imagery analysed by BBC Verify appears to show damage to at least three aircraft hangars or shelters.
The base is one of a series of high-profile Saudi targets struck by the Houthis in recent days including an oil refinery in the city of Jizan.
Saudi Arabia said on Wednesday it had destroyed a Houthi drone close to the Islamic holy city of Mecca on Tuesday, which the Houthis have denied targeting.
The group said on Thursday that Saudi Arabia had launched 40 air strikes against Yemen over the past 24 hours.

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

India's government on Thursday told the Supreme Court it was open to tougher red warnings on food packaging after health activists said its earlier proposal was too easy on companies, in a potential blow to the $100 billion food industry.
After years of delays, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) last month suggested a two-phased labelling programme, starting with red-coloured hexagonal warning labels on products that exceeded limits in at least two of three categories — added sugar, salt or saturated fat. Stricter rules would be introduced in a second phase, it said.
The announcement came as India's federal and state food regulators pursued an aggressive enforcement drive, with surprise raids on eateries uncovering poor hygiene and leading to many forced closures, stoking anger among consumers.
Health experts criticised the FSSAI proposal, however, saying the two-nutrient approach was an "industry-friendly loophole" that disregarded public health, as many products would escape scrutiny.
Supreme Court Justice J.B. Pardiwala questioned why the FSSAI was taking a two-phased approach, as he questioned a government lawyer during Thursday's hearing.
"It has to be sugar and salt. Only then will you ask them to put a label?" Pardiwala said, stressing the word "and".
The FSSAI's lawyer, Additional Solicitor General of India Brijender Chahar, responded that after hearing the court, it was now suggesting it could roll out the phases "in one go."
That would effectively mean foods high even in one of the three nutrients — added sugar, salt or fat — would have a red hexagon.
The Supreme Court has been hearing a plea by health group "3S And Our Health" demanding stricter labelling, drawing the FSSAI and the industry to court.
The nationwide debate on food safety has intensified since Reuters reported last month that India's government opted for a weaker labelling regime after lobbying by Coca-Cola and groups backing Nestle and PepsiCo, which argued warning labels were ineffective. Many companies, however, have implemented such measures voluntarily in European markets.
Food industry raises concerns
India's food and drinks market is key for foreign players including Nestle, Unilever, Mondelez and Mars, whose food products compete in a thriving industry that also includes big Indian firms such as ITC and Dabur.
On top of that, thousands of smaller businesses sell snacks and sweets, which remain hugely popular among millions of Indians.
All India Food Processors' Association, which represents dozens of Indian and foreign food giants, has called for a review of the planned health labels on packaging, saying many staples risk being covered in warnings that will tarnish the image of Indian food globally.
During Thursday's hearing, the group's lawyer held a food packet to explain its position, saying "nobody can eat 100 grams of pickle", and so the warning labels should be decided on a per-serve basis, not by analysing salt and sugar in 100 grams of a product as the authorities have proposed.
The United States, for example, has proposed per-serve front-of-pack labelling, which Indian industry favours, though many other countries use the 100-gram benchmark.
Rising obesity rates and the consumption of fatty foods are a growing concern among health experts and the Indian government. Some 450 million Indians could be obese or overweight by 2050, according to a recent study published in the Lancet medical journal.
"We are concerned with the health of people, more particularly growing children. We have taken it up very seriously. We expect one and all to extend their cooperation to a cause which is in national interest," the Supreme Court said on Thursday.
The judges said they will issue a written order before Friday.

Ukraine-Russia war latest: Poland says Putin is planning to launch drone or missile attack on a Nato country
Russia will pretend strike was accidental to 'paralyse' Nato response, says Donald Tusk
Polish prime minister Donald Tusk says Russia is planning hybrid strikes with drones or missiles targeting Nato countries supporting Ukraine, potentially including Poland.
The warning came as “a massive attack on the western part of Ukraine – very close to the Polish border,” took place, with Poland repeatedly forced to scramble its aircraft.
While Poland’s airspace was not breached, Tusk warned that Russia was planning to strike Nato territory and then pretend the attack was "accidental".
This, he told the parliament, would be in a bid to "paralyse or at least weaken the motivation of Nato countries" to rush to the defence of the member state coming under attack.
Earlier on Thursday, Russian forces carried a barrage of attacks on Ukrainian cities, including a strike on an industrial park west of Kyiv that killed one person, a local official said.
And in Russia, a Ukrainian drone attack damaged an oil refinery in the city of Yaroslavl, Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed.
Polish air traffic authority says airports in Lublin and Rzeszow halt operations
The Polish Air Navigation Services Agency said on Friday that airports in Lublin and Rzeszow in southeastern Poland suspended air operations due to military aviation activity.
Putin doesn't budge on his war goals despite dip in approval ratings
Vladimir Putin acknowledged the attacks from Ukraine on Russian oil refineries and warehouses inflicted significant damage but insisted the economy can weather it. He said Ukraine had opened a "Pandora's box," inviting massive retaliation.
Russia intensified attacks on Kyiv and other cities with missiles and new jet-powered drones, exploiting Ukraine's shortage of defensive interceptors. Moscow also dramatically stepped up its barrage on Black Sea ports, disrupting Ukrainian exports of grain and other agricultural products, a key source of revenue.
Amid the escalation, fears mounted that the Kremlin was mulling a massive mobilisation.
A partial mobilisation of 300,000 reservists in 2022 prompted hundreds of thousands of Russians to flee abroad, undermining domestic stability. Since then, the Kremlin has relied on volunteers to fight, offering comparatively high wages and other benefits. Military experts warned, however, that the flow of volunteers has ebbed while massive losses have continued.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky repeatedly claims the Kremlin is considering a post-election mobilisation, which Putin dismissed as "nonsense".
At a 5 September Kremlin meeting with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and a subsequent call with president Donald Trump, Putin said Russia holds the upper hand on the battlefield, signalling he will keep to his maximalist demands for striking a peace deal.
Economic damage for Russia mounts from summer attacks
A summer marked by Ukraine's long-range drone strikes brought the war home for millions of Russians.
The attacks exacerbated problems for the economy, which has plunged into stagnation after an initial boost from massive military spending. The government raised taxes and increased domestic borrowing to keep the growing budget deficit under control.
Strikes on Russian oil refineries sparked a severe fuel crisis that peaked in June, eased for a few weeks and then returned in August.
Adding to the pain was a series of attacks on warehouses of online retailers Wildberries and Ozon. Hundreds of thousands of individual sellers lost their merchandise, sending a shock wave through the economy.
All this dampened the public mood.
Polls recorded a dip in Putin's approval ratings, even though they remained high, with the independent Levada Center showing it at 76 per cent in August, down from 87 per cent in September 2025.
Even some senior members of Russia's elite openly expressed discontent.
Andrei Klepach, chief economist of the state VEB.RF bank, warned of possible internal turmoil.
"We won't win the competition in this war of attrition," he said at a seminar. "Our costs are mounting. I'm almost sure that we will come to face a social crisis."
Wartime parliamentary election in Russia includes illegally annexed region
For the first time, the election in Russia includes residents of four Ukrainian regions that Moscow illegally annexed after the invasion.
Ukraine has called the vote illegal.
"Your choice and resolve will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our fighters, that we are a united people, bound by shared values, historical memory, and love for the Motherland," Putin said in an address before the vote.
With the result predetermined and Vladimir Putin's political dominance under no immediate threat, analysts say the Kremlin sees the election as a key effort to mobilise public support for the war and legitimise its action.
The Kremlin has stifled even the slightest signs of dissent before three days of voting that began Friday in Russia's Far East.
The only party that dared to criticise the war was unceremoniously removed from the ballot, and a few anti-war politicians have been imprisoned or forced to flee abroad.
Russia strikes Nova Poshta facilities near Ukraine's Odesa, defence ministry says
Russian drones have hit Nova Poshta's logistics hub near the Ukrainian Black Sea port city of Odesa as well as a cargo vessel in the nearby port of Chornomorsk, the Russian defence ministry said on Telegram, citing the use of both for military purposes.
Regional polls open in Russia
Regional polls have opened in Russia for the first parliamentary election since the country's war on Ukraine that began four years ago.
They come amid plummeting approval ratings for Vladimir Putin, mounting casualties on the frontline and minimal territorial gains in the grinding war.
The country’s electoral system is tightly controlled and Putin’s United Russia party is expected to retain its majority in the State Duma, which comprises 450 members. It currently has 310 seats and needs to win at least 300 in order to retain its supermajority.
Night strike on Odesa damages apartments in 19-storey residential building
Russian barrage on Ukrainian cities leaves one dead in Kyiv
Russian forces carried a barrage of attacks on Ukrainian cities on Thursday, including a strike on an industrial park west of Kyiv that killed one person, a local official said.
Russia's military had previously carried out most of its attacks at night, but in recent weeks it has expanded them to daylight hours.
Vitali Bunechko, governor of Zhytomyr region, said the industrial park strike occurred near the town of Korosten.
The Ukrainian capital underwent a series of air alerts through the day and its mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said one strike hit a non-residential building, injuring one person.
In the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia, regional governor Ivan Fedorov said Russian forces attacked a market, triggering a large blaze.
Pictures posted on social media showed the fire reducing the area to charred ruins. No casualties were recorded.A Russian attack also caused a fire in the southeastern city of Dnipro, injuring two people.
Outgoing UN chief Guterres warns of Security Council paralysis
Due to leave office at the end of this year, UN secretary-general António Guterres has warned that the "huge geopolitical divide" and paralysis in the Security Council have created an environment of impunity, with powerful countries flouting international law and the UN Charter.
He cited the invasion of Ukraine by Russia and the attacks on Iran by the United States, both veto-wielding council members, as examples.
"Many countries say, 'If superpowers can violate the law, why can't we?"' the secretary-general said.
"And so what we are seeing around the world is more and more situations in which countries simply do not care. They do whatever they want, knowing that there will be total impunity."
The violations and impunity have caused death and enormous destruction, he said, and the combination of the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the broader Middle East conflict are having "a dramatic impact" on the world economy.
Food and energy prices are going up, interest rates are rising and developing countries face enormous difficulties in responding to the needs of their people.
He expressed hope that these problems will force people to realise that the obstacles can't be eliminated alone and require international cooperation.
Russia will not indulge in peace talks ‘without total capitulation of Ukraine’
Polish prime minister Donald Tusk said at the moment Russia was not ready for any peace talks "without the total capitulation of Ukraine."
"They are convinced the winter will be tragically critical for Ukraine," Tusk said. He said last winter Poland stepped in with deliveries when Ukraine's energy infrastructure came under attack, but if border crossings are destroyed, it will be much harder for Warsaw to offer such help this upcoming winter.
"Russia's goal is to destroy as much as possible the economy and logistics of Ukraine," Tusk said, adding that intelligence indicates continuous attacks of "very high frequency and intensity" on six main Ukrainian cities should be expected in the near future.

Assam Foreigners Tribunal member accused of demanding bribe for bail arrested
The Foreigners Tribunal is a quasi-judicial body in Assam that determines if an individual is an illegal immigrant, and has the power to order their detention
A member of the Foreigners Tribunal (FT) in Assam’s Udalguri district has been arrested on charges of demanding a bribe to release a person on bail, a senior police officer said on Thursday.
Bhupen Chandra Pegu was arrested on Thursday on the basis of an investigation into the complaint received against FT member Bhupen Chandra Pegu on August 29, Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP), Udalguri, Padmanabh Barua said.
The Foreigners Tribunal is a quasi-judicial body in Assam that determines if an individual is an illegal immigrant or a foreigner, and has the power to order detention of suspected foreigners in a designated camp.
Assam has about 100 such functional tribunals.
Police said Pegu, who has been a member of the tribunal since 2018, was accused of demanding a ₹15,000 bribe from a person whose case was pending before the tribunal on August 29.
A first information report (FIR) was lodged against Pegu at the Mazbat Police Station under Section 308(2) (extortion) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) along with Section 7(a) (obtaining or attempting to obtain undue advantage to perform public duty improperly or dishonestly) of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
Police did not identify the complainant or the person who filed the complaint. A police statement said it took action after receiving information from an informant.
Baruah said Pegu was arrested on Monday and produced before the local judge.
Not the first case
Sishir Dey, a former member of the tribunal in Karimganj (now Sribhumi), said it was a dangerous trend.
He said he remembered allegations of efforts to influence tribunal proceedings in 2018-19. In this case, a member was subsequently suspended, he said, adding that similar accusations have been made from time to time.
“This recent case has raised the concern again, and if the allegations are true, the entire system needs to be scrutinised because FTs deal with citizenship and once a genuine Indian loses it, there are provisions for pushback,” he said.
According to social activist Kamal Chakraborty, though FTs are quasi-judicial institutions, their opinions on a person’s citizenship carry severe consequences.
“These opinions decide whether a person is Indian or an illegal migrant and we know many genuine Indians were declared foreigners by these FTs,” he said.
Former FT member and lawyer Dharmananda Deb said that if Pegu actually tried to manipulate the judicial process, he must be handed out exemplary punishment.
Senior advocate Hafiz Rashid Ahmed Chowdhury raised questions about the selection process of FT members.
“The state government selects members and most of them are ordinary practising lawyers,” he said, suggesting that the government should opt to appoint retired judges to tribunals instead of young lawyers.
Because of this lack of expertise and understanding of the law, the Gauhati High Court and even the Supreme Court have set aside many orders of FTs, he added.

The US has announced visa restrictions on some South Africans as Donald Trump’s administration continues to claim that South Africa’s government racially discriminates against white minority Afrikaners.
The announcement did not specify individuals who were barred from the US. Trump has spent his second term falsely claiming there is a “white genocide” in South Africa and railing against its affirmative action policies.
Since the start of last year, the US has cut aid to South Africa, barred it from this year’s G20 summit in Miami and set up a refugee programme for Afrikaners and other South African racial minorities. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has been dismantling refugee and asylum programmes for people fleeing war and persecution.
“The South African people are being failed by a government that is destroying its economy through an obsessive pursuit of racial grievance against the Afrikaner minority,” the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said in a post on X.
“The South African government has consistently failed to adequately address rural crime, violent and dehumanising rhetoric, and race-based discriminatory policies against Afrikaners and other minority populations.”
The US visa restrictions would target “foreign nationals who enact or enable policies that promote race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa”, Rubio added.
The US ambassador to South Africa, the conservative media activist Leo Brent Bozell III, said on X: “As has been made absolutely clear, the time for endless ‘dialogue’ has run its course … This visa restriction policy is only the first step in a series of escalatory measures that will show America’s firm resolve in this matter.”
Spokespeople for South Africa’s presidency and foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Afrikaners, who are descended from Dutch and French settlers, ruled South Africa during apartheid. The regime discriminated against and repressed the country’s black majority, while keeping white people safe and wealthy.
Since Nelson Mandela took office as South Africa’s first black president in 1994, South African governments have tried to redress the country’s racial inequality, including through Black economic empowerment policies and buying land to redistribute.
These efforts have had limited impact. White South Africans typically have 20 times the wealth of Black people, according to a 2023 article in the Review of Political Economy, an economic journal.
Nonetheless, some white South Africans claim they are now the victims of racial discrimination, allegations that US conservatives have long promoted.
Rubio’s visa restrictions announcement criticised land expropriation without compensation. South Africa introduced a law last year that allows the government to seize land without paying for it in specific circumstances, including if it is abandoned or only held for speculation. There is no large-scale expropriation of land.
Among white South Africans who think they are discriminated against, many cite the far-left opposition leader Julius Malema’s repeated use of apartheid-era chant “Kill the Boer”, Boer being another word for Afrikaner. A video featuring the chant was played by Trump when he met South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, in the Oval Office last year.
The ruling African National Congress party has disavowed the chant, which South African courts have ruled is not meant literally and therefore not hate speech.

For years, many of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley have argued that the US is locked in an AI arms race with China, and that the consequences of losing would be disastrous. But over the past week, those same executives have started emphasizing a different message. AI has the potential to become so dangerous, tech leaders say, that the two countries urgently need to work together to slow the race down.
“Global pacing will require cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in a blog post published Saturday titled “We Must Pace the Frontier.”
China’s government and AI companies have made it clear that they’re deeply skeptical of Amodei’s proposal, but not because they want to keep blindly racing ahead or don’t believe the technology poses serious risks. The problem the Chinese government and Chinese AI companies see is far simpler. They think they’re being offered a bad deal.
“The AI safety community in China is growing and shares many of the same concerns that American labs do,” says Kevin Xu, founder of the technology hedge fund Interconnected Capital and a former White House staffer under President Barack Obama. “The gulf lies between an Anthropic-led vision that would only subjugate and restrict China first to maximize leverage before talking. Meanwhile, China would only talk if it’s being treated from a position of equals.”
Amodei wrote that a “key part” of the slowdown strategy should be ensuring that the US and other democracies maintain “as large as possible” a lead in AI development over autocracies like China. To do that, he urged the US to take steps including cracking down on chip smuggling and preventing unauthorized model distillation by Chinese companies.
“His essay specifically says the pacing of AI is conditional to increasing the lead over China," says Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis and a digital fellow at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI, “which makes the proposal feel inauthentic to Chinese readers.”
Amodei went on to make what might seem like a heroic leap in logic: He argued that weakening China’s AI industry would somehow give the US more leverage and make “an agreement more likely in the future.” How, exactly, that is supposed to entice Beijing to come to the negotiating table is left unexplained. (To Amodei’s credit, he later admitted in a television interview that he has “no idea how to negotiate with China.”)
The government officials, AI researchers, and other prominent commentators in China who responded to Amodei haven’t argued that AI poses no risks. But many of them clearly resent the idea that their country should simultaneously be treated as an essential governance partner and a competitor that needs to be constrained.
When asked about Amodei’s blog post on Monday at a press conference, Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, didn’t mince words: He described the proposal as “fear-mongering, confrontation, and vicious competition” that would only hamper global AI cooperation efforts. The next day, the ministry also stressed that “China puts equal emphasis on development and security in terms of AI.”
The mixed comments are reflective of another reason that Beijing may be less receptive to the Anthropic CEO’s warnings than other audiences. Unlike many of the loudest voices in Silicon Valley, China’s leaders are not primarily concerned about so-called existential risks from AI, such as the possibility that a rogue agent could kill everyone on Earth. Like in many other policy areas, Beijing’s prevailing anxiety is that AI could disrupt domestic social stability or threaten the Chinese Communist Party’s grip on power.
“Beijing finds it difficult to take these calls at face value partly because it’s skeptical of the possibility of achieving AGI and doubtful of the narrative that AI poses extreme risks to humanity,” says Michelle Nie, a visiting fellow at the Center for a New American Security focused on national security and artificial intelligence. “Although Beijing is starting to recognize loss-of-control risks, the risk that Beijing seems most worried about is the threat AI could pose to CCP rule.”
In a recent essay, China’s minister of state security Chen Yixin warned that AI could fuel political disinformation, cyberattacks, espionage, social unrest, and new military threats. He spent far less time on the kinds of doomsday scenarios that frequently preoccupy people at US frontier AI labs.
“Chinese policymakers tend to read US companies’ calls for AI safety as instrumental,” says Nie. “They believe that US companies are seeking to inflate their own value ahead of potential IPOs or to slow down their competitors, which are primarily Chinese companies at this point.”
That skepticism is also shared by many people who work in China’s AI industry, which has broadly focused on releasing lower-cost, open-weight models. In a widely shared essay published on Sunday, a researcher at DeepSeek said he believes AI could move human society to one of two extremes. In the first, powerful AI is broadly available and raises living standards. In the second, a handful of tech companies control the most advanced systems and the resources that come with them, making it even harder for everyone else to catch up.
“That is why I still believe the most advanced intelligence should be made available to everyone in an open and inexpensive way,” the DeepSeek engineer wrote. “I do not trust Anthropic or OpenAI to do that. And I especially do not want Anthropic to control the most advanced artificial intelligence or AGI.”
None of this means that US-China cooperation on AI safety is doomed. Preliminary negotiations between the two countries are reportedly already underway ahead of Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s planned visit to Washington later this month to meet with US President Donald Trump.
There are plenty of reasons to be hopeful that these discussions will result in some progress, even though it may be incremental. Both governments have expressed worries about some of the same things, including cybersecurity threats, the misuse of powerful models, and the possibility that increasingly capable AI systems could behave in unexpected ways.
“There are people who genuinely care about AI safety on both sides, and there’s a possibility they could engage in good-faith discussion in narrowly scoped issues,” says Nie. What might move the needle most, she says, is designing a credible way for each country to verify that the other is abiding by its commitments.
Still, others worry that rhetoric from Amodei and other US tech leaders about weakening China could erode the fragile trust that diplomatic talks depend on. Kristy Loke, a research fellow at the AI safety nonprofit MATS Research, says that Amodei’s missive may ultimately backfire. “Dario is undermining one of the few available levers for reducing the very risks he professes to take seriously,” she says.

On stage at Davos in the Swiss Alps earlier this year, Bill Gates, before an audience of the global do-gooding elite, announced a $50 million partnership between his foundation and an unlikely new ally, OpenAI, aimed at improving healthcare in Rwanda.
Can AI save global health? Bill Gates is betting $1 billion that it can.
AI can’t fix all the infrastructure aid cuts broke. But maybe it can help.
Just a month earlier, the Gates Foundation had released a harrowing report about widespread global health cuts and collapsing foreign aid infrastructure, documenting a rise in child deaths for the first time this century. But at Davos, even as the US hemorrhaged funding for vaccines, maternal healthcare, and HIV treatment, the Microsoft co-founder struck an optimistic tone.
“Using innovation, using AI,” Gates told Reuters, “I think we can get back on track.”
As it turns out, the partnership was just an opening salvo for what’s become a wholesale embrace of AI by the world’s largest global health philanthropy. A $200 million partnership with Anthropic came just a few months later. And then, on Tuesday, the Gates Foundation announced a plan to dole out a jaw-dropping $1 billion over the next two years for scaling up AI interventions across healthcare, education, and agriculture around the world.
The sense that AI will soon change everything, and mostly for the worse, has perhaps never felt so pressing and alarming as it does right now. But this hefty new commitment is premised on the idea that AI could eventually make our lives much better too. In a country like America, AI requires massive investments and buildout — in the grid, in power, in technology, in water. In many parts of Africa, already infrastructure-poor, the foundation is effectively betting that AI can compensate for some of the infrastructure that isn’t in place or that has been lost — and offer a new layer that can help in education, in delivering healthcare, and more.
The Gates Foundation’s new commitments include projects to improve how farmers analyze their crops, how doctors diagnose patients, and how students learn. Some have already proven to be quite effective, according to the foundation, with one tool improving the accuracy of medical diagnoses by 16 percent across several Kenyan clinics. “In poorer countries with enormous health worker shortages and lack of health systems infrastructure,” Gates wrote on his blog earlier this year, “AI can be a game-changer in expanding access to quality care.”
Last year’s foreign aid cuts were unfathomably destructive for some of the world’s poorest countries, shuttering thousands of clinics and perhaps hundreds of thousands of classrooms in places where critical workers and supplies were already stretched thin. No, AI cannot deliver a baby, administer a vaccine, or manage a classroom — not yet, at least — but it can, the Gates Foundation hopes, help ease the burden and augment the quality of care for nurses and teachers now tasked with serving far more people than any one person should.
“This is the most transformative technology of our lifetime,” Mark Suzman, CEO of the Gates Foundation, told me, and while there are “very real risks and challenges” surrounding AI, it also presents genuine opportunities to tangibly improve many people’s lives.
It is a tantalizing premise: We can’t afford to build clinics, hire teachers, or lay new power lines, but perhaps AI could create the digital infrastructure needed to help billions of people do more with what they have — or rather, with what’s left. The question is, can the right layer of innovation help bolster a buckling system, even as the physical and logistical infrastructure surrounding it crumbles?
Is AI really what global health needs right now?
Most Americans have yet to see AI improve their lives in meaningful ways, much less those living in poverty or in countries where only a sliver of the population has ever used ChatGPT.
But those numbers in the developing world are slowly changing, a shift enabled in part by other global health funders convinced that as foreign aid dries up, AI could soon help the world do more with less. The Trump administration itself is on board with this thinking, so long as it benefits American tech companies. Last year, the State Department announced a $150 million partnership with the drone company Zipline to transport medical supplies in several countries.
To Zipline’s credit, an NPR reporter in Rwanda last month found that the company’s drones were already saving lives in places with poor road infrastructure, where driving to the nearest hospital can take hours on winding hills, but where drones can deliver crucial blood transfusions within minutes.
And yet, for Rwandans to benefit fully from these high-tech deliveries, they need staffed clinics to visit. As a result of foreign aid cuts, some of those literal landing spots are now on the verge of closing in some of the nation’s most vulnerable rural corridors. “Without the underlying infrastructure, like roads, energy and power and unless there is accessibility, rural and otherwise,” Enoh Ebong, president of the global development department at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told NPR, “then all of these solutions will stop short.”
But just as medical delivery drones still need a clinic to fly to, most of these interventions require some layer of physical infrastructure — roads, schools, power, and quite obviously, broadband — to function. Satellite imagery shows that some rural communities in sub-Saharan Africa quite literally went dark in the aftermath of USAID cuts. It will be much harder for their kids to prompt an AI math tutor, or for a local farmer to download a weather app.
“We’re seeing this very much as a both/and,” Suzman told me, calling more traditional funding for education and healthcare “the bedrock for long-term economic growth,” which AI is meant to supplement, not replace. But, in practice, foreign aid cuts have left serious cracks across much of that bedrock, which could make it harder for state-of-the-art solutions to function as intended.
It is obviously not incumbent on the Gates Foundation to pay for all of this alone – nor would it even be feasible for them to do so. And for the record, plenty of the foundation’s other grant programs are not AI-related at all. But this tension does speak to a broader question that may be felt most acutely in a context like global health, but ultimately one that touches us all: Do we spend our scarce resources on the digital infrastructure of the future at the peril of our needs right now? Could you justify buying the new $1,999 folding iPhone if you can barely afford to buy groceries?
The answer is not actually always an easy one. It is not for us to say, for example, that just because a community lacks reliable running water, its people should be excluded from the benefits (and encumbrances) of the smartphone, especially if that smartphone can connect them to health advice they could never access otherwise, or guidance that could help them survive a drought.
In some parts of the world, digital forms of banking arrived long before local brick-and-mortar branches did, instantaneously connecting countless people to a cheap and secure way to save and send their cash to family and friends in need. It is certainly possible that AI, or at least the kind of applications the Gates Foundation funds, could one day have a similarly transformative effect on how people access personalized levels of care, education, and other services in places without the resources to do so otherwise.
That is the hope, but it is also hard right now to believe uncritically in a technology that, as Gates himself blogged just last month, “will either be the greatest equalizer ever invented, or the worst source of injustice,” ushering in “one of the most turbulent times in human history.”
In an interview with the New York Times soon after, he seemed convinced that AI will likely do more harm than good. “I don’t like bringing bad news to people, and I don’t like saying that innovation may be a net negative,” he said. “But that’s where we are.”
Now he wants billions of people around the world to use it? Yes, Suzman said, because if not, then inevitably the best parts of AI — the potential for exponentially better cancer treatments, for example — will go only “to those who can pay for it,” while the worst parts of it will fall, as they so often do, on those who benefit the least. “These decisions are being made now,” he said, “and the decisions being made now will then probably shape the following two decades.” Here’s hoping they’re good ones.

F-16 fighter jet crashes in Michigan and bursts into flames with residents told to evacuate
A witness described seeing a big plume of black smoke and said ‘explosions kept happening’
An F-16 fighter jet has crashed in rural Michigan, sparking an evacuation order for anyone within one mile of the crash site.
The pilot of the fighter jet ejected before the crash and was rushed to the hospital, according to Sgt. Derek Gutierrez, a public affairs specialist with the 149th Fighter Wing. Citing military protocol, Gutierrez declined to provide further details about the pilot’s injuries or identity.
The Grand Traverse County Emergency Management warned anyone within a mile of the crash site to evacuate.
“Evacuate away from the intersection of Co Rd 633 and Jefferson Pl. Follow instructions from emergency personnel. More information to follow,” officials wrote.
The aircraft, from Texas, was taking part in training drills based out of Alpena, Michigan's National Guard Base, according to the military.
Witnesses reported a loud impact and photos on social media platforms showed a tall column of dark smoke rising from the crash site.
Wendy Sobeck said that she and her spouse heard a "very loud crash" down the street from their home.
"We thought there was a car accident outside our house. We saw big billowing black smoke. We couldn’t tell what it was, so my husband got into his pickup truck and saw what happened," Sobeck said. "You could see the plane debris in the field. Explosions kept happening."

Srinagar, Sept 18: Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha on Friday handed over appointment letters to newly selected candidates of the Jammu and Kashmir Police (Gazetted) Services at Lok Bhavan, Srinagar, saying the appointment is not merely a government job but a call to serve and protect the people of Jammu and Kashmir.
Addressing the newly selected officers, the Lieutenant Governor said the appointment letters carried the “burden of the faith of the whole of Jammu and Kashmir” and represented a commitment towards the security, dignity and future of the people.
“I do not consider it just an appointment letter, but I see it as an invitation to service. This invitation is a call to accept the responsibility of the security of Jammu and Kashmir. It is also a promise that their security, their honour and their future will be in a position of honesty and duty,” he said, as per the news agency—Kashmir News Observer (KNO).
Sinha congratulated the selected candidates and their families, saying they had successfully cleared a rigorous selection process that tested their intelligence, patience, character, discipline and ability to withstand adverse situations.
“You have faced tough competition among the talented youth of your generation. You have gone through such a difficult process, which has not only tested your intelligence, but also your patience, character, discipline and strength to withstand adverse situations,” he said.
He told the officers that receiving the appointment letter was “not the end of your journey” but the beginning of a new one, in which their responsibility would shift from personal achievement to protecting others, serving the people and upholding the rule of law.
“You are about to embark on a new journey. Now you have to enter that struggle, whose purpose is not to achieve success for yourself, but to fulfil the responsibility of protecting others, to serve the people and to protect the rule of law in Jammu and Kashmir,” Sinha said.
‘PSC selection process strengthened faith in merit’
The Lieutenant Governor also congratulated the Jammu and Kashmir Public Service Commission (JKPSC), saying the commission had, in recent years, strengthened the principles of impartiality, transparency and merit in its selection process.
“At a time when doubts are being expressed on institutions many times, I understand that the protection of Jammu and Kashmir Public Service Commission’s impartiality and trust is like a holy lamp,” he said.
Recalling the earlier system of government recruitment, Sinha said merit-based employment had now become an established practice in Jammu and Kashmir.
“I do not need to tell you what used to happen here. How did you get a job? A complete book can be written on it. The people sitting here know more about that book than I do,” he said.
“But employment with qualifications has been prepared in such a heritage of Jammu and Kashmir, where a government job can only be obtained with your qualifications, hard work and talent,” he added.
Recalling the 2022 Jammu and Kashmir Employment Festival, Sinha said people had begun to believe that children from ordinary and economically weaker families could also aspire to become government officers.
“I remember that in 2022, the Jammu and Kashmir Employment Festival was celebrated with the qualification of a government job. At that time, for the first time, people said that the son of a vegetable vendor can also be a KAS officer,” he said.
“This time has come to Jammu and Kashmir. Even a father can see his son becoming a government officer. Perhaps after a long time, this arrangement was established,” he added.
Sinha said recruitment should be based on merit rather than recommendations and again congratulated the JKPSC for what he described as an impartial and trustworthy selection process.
“In Jammu and Kashmir, a job will not be obtained with a recommendation, but with the qualifications and qualities of a young man,” he said.
‘Uniform is a symbol of service, not power’
The Lieutenant Governor told the selected officers that their responsibilities after completing training would extend beyond a conventional career.
“The responsibility you will take after this training is not just a career, but a mission,” he said, adding that their training at the Sher-i-Kashmir Police Academy (SKPA), Udhampur, would give them an understanding of that mission.
He said discipline, hard work, rigorous training and leadership would become integral parts of their professional lives.
Sinha said the badge on a police uniform should not be seen as a symbol of power over the people, but as a symbol of service and responsibility.
“The badge on your uniform is not a symbol of power on the people of Jammu and Kashmir, but a symbol of the service and responsibility of the people,” he said.
Changing terrorism, radicalisation pose new challenges
The Lieutenant Governor said the security environment in Jammu and Kashmir was changing rapidly, with terrorism increasingly extending beyond traditional methods.
“Today’s Jammu and Kashmir is facing such challenges that the police officers of a decade ago may not have been able to imagine,” he said.
“The form of terrorism is changing and the war is not only being fought with traditional weapons. The virtual world has faced many challenges. Radicalisation is also leaving a strong and deep impact,” Sinha said.
He said methods of terror financing had also evolved, with cryptocurrencies, money laundering and other emerging mechanisms posing new challenges.
“The means of financing for terrorism have also changed. Instead of the traditional methods, cryptocurrencies, money laundering and these new methods have emerged,” he said.
Sinha said the newly inducted officers would therefore have an important role not only in maintaining security in Jammu and Kashmir but also in the broader national security framework.
‘Police will stand as wall between terrorists and citizens’
After completing their training, the officers would have to act as a protective shield between terrorist forces and ordinary citizens, he said.
“When you wear a khaki uniform, you will become a strong wall between the terrorist forces, terrorist organisations and ordinary citizens. You will protect the dreams of every citizen. This is not a small responsibility,” Sinha said.
He said ensuring the security of every citizen was among the biggest responsibilities entrusted to officials in a democracy and expressed hope that the officers would help instil confidence among people to live without fear.
Sinha also asked the officers to learn from the experience and sacrifices of their seniors in the Jammu and Kashmir Police.
“The Jammu and Kashmir Police Force is considered to be a symbol of duty, dedication, love and sacrifice. This is the only force in the country that has faced every challenge related to security with full determination and courage,” he said.
He said the sacrifices and determination of police personnel over the past decades had contributed to establishing peace and urged the new officers to draw lessons from their leadership and experience.
‘Duty not limited to fighting terrorism’
Sinha stressed that the officers’ responsibilities would not be limited to countering terrorism but would also include enforcing the law, protecting citizens’ rights and maintaining social harmony.
“Always keep in mind that your responsibility is not limited to fighting terrorism. You have to keep the law in place. You have to establish the rule of law. You have to establish social harmony. And you have to play a very important role in protecting the rights of every citizen,” he said.
He said the true test of democracy lay in protecting its weakest citizens and called upon the officers to combine authority with compassion.
“The real condition of democracy is that it ensures the protection of its weakest citizen and its prosperity. After training, you will have power and you will have to add the values of compassion to that power so that there is human compassion in all your actions,” he said.
Sinha reminded the officers of the long-standing principle of the J&K Police: “Do not touch the innocent and do not leave the culprit.”
He urged them to take pride in the uniform while ensuring that their conduct remained rooted in honesty, courage and humility.
‘Choose truth and duty, whatever the situation’
The Lieutenant Governor asked the newly selected officers to commit themselves to upholding truth and duty, regardless of the circumstances.
“No matter how difficult the situation is, you will always choose truthfulness and duty on the basis of priority. Always remember that the uniform is respected only because of the honesty, courage and determination of the officers who wear the uniform,” he said.
“Only the uniform is not respected. So move forward with honesty, courage and humility,” he added.
Sinha said the appointment also represented the hopes and aspirations of the people of Jammu and Kashmir and called upon the officers to use their authority for justice.
He also expressed gratitude to the parents and relatives of the newly selected officers, saying they had supported their children through the difficult journey and shared their dreams.
“All of you have prepared your children for the service of Jammu and Kashmir. You have supported them in their struggle. You have lived their dreams as your own dreams,” he said.
“India and Jammu and Kashmir will always be grateful to you for this contribution,” Sinha added.—(KNO)

The Best Android Phones
Featured in this article
The best Android phone means something different to everyone. It's hard to find one that caters to every need, but chances are there's a new smartphone that comes close to what you're looking for. From the bottomless pit of phone choices, my favorite Android handsets include the Google Pixel 10a, Pixel 11, and Galaxy S26 Ultra. The phones we've selected have specific advantages, and I've laid them out here based on extensive testing.
See our other mobile buying guides for more, like the Best iPhones, Best Cheap Phones, Best Samsung Phones, Phones With a Headphone Jack, Best Pixel Phones, and Best Folding Phones.
Updated September 2026: We've added the Motorola Razr Ultra (2026), Google Pixel 11 series, Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8, and Fairphone (Gen. 6+), alongside other options like the Galaxy S26 FE, Nothing Phone (4a) Pro, and Motorola Edge 2026.
Is Now a Good Time to Buy?
Yes. All the major smartphone makers have released their devices for the year. Prices will dip during major sale events like Black Friday and Cyber Monday, so those are often the best times to upgrade if you're hunting for a bargain.
Buy an Unlocked Phone
We recommend unlocked phones in this guide. When a phone is sold unlocked, it means you can use it on multiple wireless carriers and networks. When you go into a carrier store and buy a phone, usually on a payment plan, it often comes locked to that network, and they'll try to get you to pay for a host of unnecessary accessories and features.
Carriers are legally required to unlock a phone upon request so you can switch networks, but it's a big hassle, and they may have terms about how long you have to wait to ask. Try to pay full price for your phone, or make sure it specifically says it's unlocked. Buy it from the manufacturer or an authorized third-party retailer, or check your carrier's unlocking policy if you bought a device on a payment plan that requires you to use its network. An unlocked phone is also less of a hassle when you travel and want to switch to an international SIM card or eSIM.
Android Specs to Look For
If none of the smartphones in this guide strike your fancy and you want to continue searching, keep these specs in mind.
Display: Gone are the days of shoddy phone displays—almost every smartphone uses an OLED panel now. Cheaper phones still use LCD, which won't have as deep blacks and poppy colors, but even phones under $300 can sport OLED. You'll see some variations, like AMOLED or Dynamic AMOLED 2X, but that's mostly marketing jargon.
Screen size: You hold a smartphone all the time, so make sure whatever you pick fits your palms. Most small Android phones are around 6.1 to 6.3 inches (measured diagonally), whereas larger phones typically top out at 6.8 or 6.9 inches. Foldable phones will have a smaller outer screen and a larger display when opened. For example, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 we recommend has a 5.5-inch screen when closed and a 7.6-inch display when unfolded, but sizes vary by manufacturer.
Processor: Most smartphones use a Qualcomm or MediaTek processor. Google phones use the company's in-house Tensor chip, and some Samsung phones utilize Samsung's Exynos processor in select markets. It's hard to say how reliably a processor will perform without looking at reviews and benchmark results, so do your research. For reliable performance, try to stick to Qualcomm's Snapdragon 7 series or higher, or MediaTek's Dimensity 7000 series or higher. The 2026 flagship chip is the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5.
RAM: You'll want at least 8 GB of RAM, though 12 GB is better. This lets you juggle multiple apps more seamlessly and run more intensive AI tasks.
Cooling: High-performing phones can be ruined if they get too hot because the processor throttles, causing slowdowns. This mostly applies to folks who game a lot, but it's worth checking whether the phone has a dedicated cooling system. You'll want to look for language like “heat pipes” or “vapor chamber cooling.”
Refresh rate: Most phones used to come with 60-Hz refresh rates, meaning the display refreshes at 60 frames per second. Nowadays, even cheap phones offer 90- or 120-Hz screens. The more frames refreshed in a second, the more fluid everything looks and feels. It might sound small, but it can make a big difference in whether your smartphone feels buttery smooth. We have a broader guide that explains this technology. Flagship phones have screens with variable refresh rates ranging from 1 to 120 Hz, which often makes them more battery-efficient (look for LTPO or LTPS).
Battery capacity: Smartphone batteries are measured in milliampere-hours (mAh). A big battery doesn't necessarily mean better battery life, because it depends on screen size and other technologies the phone is powering. Most phones should have 4,000-mAh cells or higher, and you typically won't see much above 5,500 mAh. Some phones now use silicon-carbon batteries, a new technology that allows them to be denser but thinner.
Charging speeds: Most Android smartphones can charge fast, but certain companies offer shockingly fast recharge times. That's usually because they require a proprietary charging brick. You can find charging speed information on a phone's product spec page. Just remember that these days, most smartphones do not come with a charging brick, just a cable. We have more details in this fast-charging guide.
Software updates: Software support is crucial. Your phone stays secure longer, and you'll get new features over time. Even if you trade in your phone, it may end up in someone else's hands, and a long update policy means the phone will continue to be supported. The gold standard in Android is seven years right now, thanks to Samsung and Google. However, if you replace your phone every two or three years, the shorter update policies of other Android makers might not be a deal-breaker.
Cameras: Camera specs are very misleading. A phone with a 108-megapixel (MP) sensor doesn't mean it will take better photos than a phone with a 50-MP sensor. The only way to know for sure is to read reviews. If the camera matters to you, check whether it has a versatile system. The best camera phones offer a primary wide camera, an ultrawide, and a telephoto zoom (usually 5X). Cheap phones tend to come with a lot of cameras, many of which are useless.
Extra features: Don't overlook the secondary features. Does the phone have a near-field communication sensor (NFC) so you can make contactless payments? Does it have a good IP rating that can survive a drop in the pool? (You'll want IP67 or IP68!) What about wireless charging (Qi2 or Qi)? Or a microSD card slot, dual-SIM tray, or headphone jack? Vet the phone's specs if you're after something specific.
5G service: Nearly all smartphones support 5G, the current generation of network connectivity. 4G LTE isn't disappearing, and you may still fall back to LTE when 5G isn't available. Avoid smartphones that don't offer 5G at all.
How to Switch Between Phones
The best way to switch phones is to follow the setup prompts when you first boot up your new device. Make sure you transfer data from an old phone via a cable. It's much faster than doing it wirelessly, though that's an option too. Some manufacturers, like Samsung, will suggest you download a proprietary data transfer app on your old device, like Smart Switch, and you should. It means less work for you—whether it's fewer apps you need to sign into or fewer icons you need to rearrange. If you're coming from an iPhone, you can use Google's official Android Switch app, though Apple and Google have improved the transfer process to make things smoother.
Check out our tips on setting up your new Android phone, and our steps on backing up an Android and how to factory reset it.
How We Test Smartphones
I put my personal SIM card in every smartphone I test and use it for at least a week, if not two or three. I stress-test performance by playing mobile games and running benchmark tests, like Geekbench and Antutu, while also monitoring thermals. I make calls to test the smartphone's microphone quality, since, you know, it's still a phone.
I often test the cameras by bringing a competing phone along and analyzing photos side by side on a larger, more color-accurate screen. I've been reviewing smartphones for close to a decade—not just flagship devices either. I'm always testing cheap phones to see what innovations are trickling down.
Other Phones to Consider
We test a ton of Android phones. We like the ones below, but you'll be better off with one of the options above. Check out our Best Cheap Phones and Best Folding Phones guides for more.
Nothing Phone (4a) Pro for $499: This midrange phone from Nothing (7/10, WIRED Recommends) strikes a good balance of features and price, and you won't find another smartphone that looks this distinct. You may have some carrier compatibility issues on AT&T and Verizon, and I don't love that it's only IP65 dust- and water-resistant and lacks wireless charging. Still, performance is good, the screen is bright, and battery life is reliable. There's a triple-camera setup with a 3.5X zoom telephoto, and the Glyph Matrix display on the back is weird, light-hearted fun that will surely be a conversation starter.
Samsung Galaxy S26 FE for $700: Like most consumer electronics, Samsung has hiked the price of its midrange Galaxy S26 FE (6/10, WIRED Review), which stands for “Fan Edition.” Some features have even gotten worse, like how it now only supports USB 2.0 instead of USB 3.2. Still, if you want a Samsung but don't want to spend big bucks on the flagship S26 range (the Galaxy S26 doesn't cost significantly more, so look for the S26 FE on sale), the FE is a capable handset with a good triple-camera system, a great screen, and good battery life.
Motorola Edge 2026 for $600: Are phones too heavy for you? You might appreciate the Edge—it has an amazingly lightweight 160-gram frame and a fairly compact 6.3-inch screen. It's great to use one-handed. Performance is more than capable, and there's even a handy triple-camera system, though it doesn't quite match the quality of our recommended picks above. Disappointingly, Motorola only promises two Android OS upgrades and three years of security updates, which is hard to accept at this price. Buy it on sale!

DOGE bros have a new role — making an AI-powered site for Trump that handles basic government services
Some Trump administration officials reportedly hope that America.gov will help boost Republican congressional candidates in the midterm elections
Former members of Elon Musk's controversial Department of Government Efficiency — including one known as “Big Balls” — are reportedly developing a new government services website for the public that will be powered by artificial intelligence.
The planned America.gov site is set to be unveiled by the end of September, with some Trump administration officials hopeful it will give Republican congressional candidates a talking point to boost their campaigns ahead of the crucial midterm elections, The Washington Sun reported Thursday.
The site is slated to feature a chatbot interface and allow users to perform tasks that include filing tax returns and renewing passports, the Sun said, citing unidentified current and former officials familiar with the plans.
The tax-filing feature would essentially replace a free online program, called Direct File, that the Biden administration launched in March 2024 for the 2023 tax-filing season. The Trump administration canceled Direct File in November 2025.
“There’s a real need for simple, integrated services. We actually built one, Direct File, and people loved and trusted it, but it took careful work,” former Direct File deputy Merici Vinton told the Sun. “Then DOGE killed it.”
Vinton, now a senior fellow at the progressive Center for American Progress think tank, also noted the complexities of the tax code and warned, “In a moment where the public is already skeptical about AI in government, this could undo trust instead of building it.”
Neither the White House, Treasury Department, State Department nor General Services Administration immediately returned inquiries Thursday from The Independent. The Sun said the White House declined to comment for its report.
The America.gov website is being developed by the White House's National Design Studio, led by Airbnb co-founder and former DOGE official Joe Gebbia, according to the Sun.
Other National Design Studio projects, including the TrumpRx and Trump Gold Card websites, suffered from early accessibility problems, the outlet said.
The America.gov team reportedly includes 20-year-old Edward Coristine, a college dropout and early DOGE staffer who made headlines in part due to his “Big Balls” nickname.
Coristine — whose father, Charles Coristine, is CEO of the LesserEvil snack company — also had a limited work history that reportedly included getting fired from a cybersecurity internship for allegedly leaking inside information to a rival company.
Officials are considering using the federal Login.gov identity-verification website for access to America.gov, which would be overseen by the General Services Administration, according to the Sun.
Another former DOGE official, Sam Corcos, is reportedly involved in Login.gov and was recently given several roles at the GSA.
Musk initially claimed DOGE would cut as much as $2 trillion in government spending, but its online “Wall of Receipts” listed only $215 billion in estimated savings before the ad hoc government agency was shut down in July.
Last month, the Government Accountability Office said that it couldn't verify 96 percent of DOGE's reported savings and that DOGE's claim of having saved $110 billion on contracts, grants and leases was artificially inflated because some leases “were already in process for termination.”
Another GAO report released Tuesday also said a DOGE-inspired drive to reduce the federal workforce paid government employees about $9.5 billion not to work, with $6.7 billion going to people who eventually retired or resigned.
Billionaire Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has also criticized a move by Musk, who has an estimated net worth of $939 billion, to effectively shut down the U.S. Agency for International Development, which had a budget of about $40 billion a year.
“The picture of the world’s richest man killing the world’s poorest children is not a pretty one,” Gates told the Financial Times last year. Musk called Gates a “huge liar” in response to the accusation.
