Amazon Prime Day events are some of the most confusing shopping occasions in existence: It’s not even a single “day" anymore. Amazon promises “millions of deals”—but the displayed discounts are often misleading, and while it’s advertised as a members-only event, some deals are available to people who don’t subscribe to Prime. Add in the frenzy of limited-time Lightning Deals and you’ve got a perfect recipe for spending too much money on stuff you don't even really want.
Fear not! I've been covering deals for over a decade and am here to help. WIRED’s Reviews team is familiar with common shopping pitfalls, and we closely track the best Prime Big Deal Days prices. What time do sales start and end? How do you tell whether a deal is actually a deal? We pooled our collective expertise to get you prepared for the latest Amazon Prime Day Event, which is technically dubbed “Amazon Prime Big Deal Days” and will be on October 6 and October 7 this year.
When Is Amazon Prime Day?
Amazon Prime Day has a main sale in the summer and a secondary sale—called Prime Big Deal Days—in the fall. This year, Prime Big Deal Days will take place on Tuesday and Wednesday, October 6 and October 7.
When Do Prime Day Deals Start?
The event kicks off at 3:01 am Eastern time (midnight Pacific) and runs for 48 hours. New deals will drop three times each day of the event, at 3 am, 11 am, and 4 pm ET, with Lightning Deals going live sporadically as well. WIRED will cover the best deals from both Amazon and retailers that have competing sales.
Are Prime Day Deals Only for Prime Members?
That's the official line: You need to be an Amazon Prime member to shop Amazon Prime Day deals. There is a free 30-day trial available for eligible new accounts. (Prime membership comes with a lot of perks, and we've rounded up all of them here.) The trial will let you get in on the sale—just remember to cancel your membership to avoid any subsequent $15 monthly renewal charges.
However, there are usually plenty of discounts available if you're not a subscriber. Other major retailers like Best Buy, Target, and Walmart typically hold competing sales during Prime Days. The prices are often close to what Amazon is offering on the same products, and sometimes the competing sales match the Prime Day price exactly. This is a good way to save even if you object to shopping on Amazon.
Is Prime Day Worth It?
It depends. For some items, Prime-exclusive event prices tend to be among the lowest we see all year. That's especially true for Amazon hardware, like Kindles, Fire tablets, Fire TV sticks, and Echo devices. The kicker is that prices on nearly everything fluctuate throughout the year, and some products are discounted on a frequent basis. Even if the price is good, a deal on a product that goes on sale all the time diminishes the overall quality of that offer.
The sheer volume of deals promoted by Amazon during sales like Prime Day is a blessing and a curse. The truly standout discounts can be difficult to pinpoint—there's so much stuff on sale that just browsing the site can feel overwhelming. But if you're in the market for something specific, there's a good chance the item you want will be discounted. We've seen some fantastic Prime-exclusive discounts in the past, ranging from dirt-cheap Kindles and video doorbells to elusive price drops on gaming consoles and office furniture. The tricky part is finding the diamonds in the rough.
WIRED covers legitimately good deals all year long, including during Prime Day. Our policy is to only cover deals on products someone from our team has personally used and would buy or has bought themselves, to avoid promoting cheap junk. Maybe it'll be a product we've reviewed or an item we use in our day-to-day lives. We also only cover actual deals—if the price isn't lower than it normally is, we don't include it. We aim to provide pricing context as well. Our tips below will help you find those great discounts on your own—in the same ways that we would. No gatekeeping here.
How Do I Know Whether a Deal Is Good?
ABC: Always be checking (prices, that is). Researching an item's price is the most important aspect of determining the quality of a discount. Don't fall prey to deceptive marketing language and inflated MSRP prices. The easiest step is to take a second to Google the items you're considering so you can see the price across multiple stores. Amazon product pages now feature a Price History link to see up to 365 days of pricing history, though it may not always be accurate.
One tool we use is CamelCamelCamel, which tracks Amazon's prices over time. Paste the Amazon link or ASIN (found in the Product Information section on the Amazon product page) into CamelCamelCamel's search bar to see the item's lowest recorded price and its average price, and how frequently the price fluctuates. Some deals, such as Lightning Deals, are excluded from the pricing history, but this works for most items. It's useful to see what an item has sold for in the past. And while Amazon's Alexa for Shopping chatbot has price history information, it isn't always reliable and often misses context (as evidenced by our personal testing). We also like Keepa, which has an extension (available for multiple browsers) that shows the recent price history for products directly on the Amazon page so you don't have to open a new tab. When in doubt, check multiple sources.
Keep in mind that these services may not work all the time. But being able to see how much a product costs right before the sale starts (and whether the MSRP happened to increase) can be helpful. Putting these tools together can help you deduce whether a deal is worth your money.
WIRED always fact-checks deals to determine their quality. Of course, I'm biased, but you can check out our ongoing deals coverage to find roundups of the best discounts available—during Prime Big Deal Days and beyond.
What Are Lightning Deals?
Lightning Deals are limited-time deals that Amazon runs for only a few hours. They're not restricted to Prime Day, but they're especially prevalent during major sales events. Once an item sells out, you may be able to join a wait list, but not always.
Put bluntly, the Lightning Deals selection is often full of impulse buys, like makeup, skin care products, or toys. Prime members can browse upcoming deals on Amazon's website and in the mobile app. The app can also alert you before a Lightning Deal begins. We'll share some of our favorite Lightning Deals in a live blog during the event this year.
Be sure to also keep an eye on Amazon Haul, Amazon's discount page featuring novelties, fashion accessories, and gadgets starting at $1. Additional discounts are rumored to be dropping on holiday decor and tailgating items.
Are There Other Ways to Make Sure a Deal Won’t Sell Out?
If you know what time a deal begins, make sure to pay attention to the product page around the starting time. You may also be able to add an item to your cart before the sale starts, so you can refresh the page and snag it right away. With the Amazon app (Android, iOS), you can set up personalized deal alerts to get notified when items you have searched for recently are on sale, but only if you're a Prime member.
It's smart to create an account at trusted retailers so you can save your credit card information and shipping details ahead of time. This will make the checkout process as fast as possible. It's also a good idea to clear your web browser cache before you start shopping during sales events like Prime Day. Just be sure to log back in to those retailers afterward.
If a deal does sell out, there's a high chance another store will be offering a similar or matching discount. Check other stores, especially big-box merchants like Walmart, Target, and Best Buy. Sometimes expired deals can come back in stock, too.
You may also be able to use Amazon's Alexa for Shopping AI assistant to set deal alerts. But keep in mind that sometimes the notification system is dodgy. It can be useful, but if you're set on getting something specific, you should keep a close eye on it regardless of any AI tools you use.
Should I Buy It?
It's easy to fall into a trap during events like Prime Day. You might see a great deal on a product you don't really need. Don't do it. Make a list of items you've actually been wanting to buy ahead of the event and save those links. When Prime Day begins, take a look around to see whether they're on sale, and use the aforementioned practices to make sure it truly is a good deal. Don't buy a product just because it has a nice price.
This isn't your last chance to score a great deal this year—there's always Black Friday and Cyber Monday, which take place around Thanksgiving weekend. You might see even bigger price drops then.

US president Donald Trump has threatened the European Union with “serious tariffs” and a cut to trade after the bloc proposed to make Canada its first ever associate member, calling the idea “laughable”.
Suggesting the move was a “hostile act”, the US president told reporters he could put “very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe”. He added: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe.”
European Commision president Ursula von der Leyen insisted yesterday that “this is not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength,” and deputy chief spokesperson Olof Gill repeated this line this morning in response to Trump’s overnight threats.
Canadian prime minister Mark Carney – fresh from watching Everton’s Carabao Cup win over Wolverhampton Wanderers in Liverpool – will address the European parliament late morning. Let’s see if he has anything to say on this.
Separately, our attention is increasingly turning to Germany, where embattled chancellor Friedrich Merz is set to join the campaign trail today in Berlin ahead of this weekend’s two state elections that just could determine his political future.
Powerful German state leaders from his party have rallied behind the chancellor as speculation builds that his days in office may be numbered, and he cancelled his trip to the UN general assembly next week.
Our Berlin correspondent Deborah Cole will be joining us just after 11am to answer your questions about Merz’s future,the two state elections, and what’s next for Germany. You can post your questions to her below the line from 9am.
Lots for us to cover today.
It’s Thursday, 17 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
'Not up to the US to choose political and geopolitical direction of the Europeans,' French minister says
Back to Trump’s threats over the proposed “associate membership” for Canada overnight, France’s Europe minister Benjamin Haddad said in response that the EU has no power to veto EU’s geopolitical choices.
“It is not up to the United States – or anyone else – to choose the political and geopolitical direction of the Europeans. Once again, we have a relationship with Canada, and we are fully entitled to seek to deepen it,” Haddad said in an interview on Public Senat TV channel, reported by Reuters.
Ask your questions: Q&A on Germany, Merz, state elections and what's next
Our Berlin correspondent Deborah Cole will be joining us later this morning to answer your questions on Germany’s embattled chancellor Friedrich Merz as he braces for two more tricky state elections this weekend.
Our comments section is now open below – post your questions and Deborah will answer them after 11am this morning.
Earlier this week, Merz cancelled his planned visit at the UN general assembly in New York next week, saying he needed to be in Berlin. It’s never a good sign when a political leader feels he needs to do that.
Roland Paris, the director of the Graduate School of Public and International Affairs at the University of Ottawa and a foreign affairs adviser to the former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau, saidthe term “associate member” has taken too much focus and “doesn’t really matter” in the long term.
“My hunch is that von der Leyen was hoping to rally supporters of much closer cooperation with Canada by using that label. In the end, what I expect is that we’re going to see a collection of agreements rather than membership in any institutional sense,” he said.
Carney’s decision to formalise close ties with Europe however prompted outrage from Conservatives at home.
Pierre Poilievre, the Tory leader, posted on social media that he feared Canadians “struggling to pay their rent” would have to pay more taxes “to fund the European Union’s heavy bureaucracy”.
“The welder from Welland didn’t elect a Eurocrat to regulate our steel. The farmer from Saskatchewan and the fisher from the Atlantic provinces didn’t choose a Brussels food regulator who has never seen our prairies or our coasts,” he wrote. “We will NEVER be the 51st American state. And we will NEVER be the 28th state of the European Union.”
Another, Jamil Jivani, posted that Conservatives “will NEVER support Mark Carney’s Liberal plan to have Canada join the hopelessly run, over-regulated, and self-destructive EU”.
Paris said no Canadian leaders “would be interested in formal EU membership if it involves subordinating Canadian law and regulatory structures” to Europe.
“I don’t think that’s on the table right now. There has long been a bipartisan push in Canada to deepen trade connections between Canada and Europe,” he said. “We’re now seeing now is a logical extension of those trade discussions into other areas.”
The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, although it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, allowing deep economic integration with these countries, who follow many EU rules.
It remains to be seen what associate membership means, including for Canada’s relationship with the EU single market. When the UK was negotiating its departure from the bloc and post-Brexit relationship, EU officials repeatedly said there was no status that enabled a foreign country to be half in and half out of the single market.
The phrase itself took EU insiders by surprise since von der Leyen had not used the term when she briefed senior EU diplomats ahead of her speech last Friday.
One EU diplomat said member states were “generally very supportive of ambition” in the EU-Canada relationship, but had been slightly worried in recent weeks that von der Leyen was overpromising on Canada.
“‘Associate membership’ sounds like a nice headline but in reality 10 member states have still not ratified Ceta,” the person said, referring to the EU-Canada trade agreement that was agreed 10 years ago.
A second EU diplomat described associate membership as “an empty phrase”.
Martin Leng at the Brussels Institute for Geopolitics thinktank said a world in flux was “pushing the EU towards far greater flexibility in its relations with third states”.
He said von der Leyen’s speech, with its focus on different sectoral areas of cooperation “points to the ambition and strategic breadth of the associate membership which the parties have in mind but also suggests that, in reality, Canada’s ‘membership’ may consist of ‘plugging in’ to existing programmes and frameworks, such as the European Defence Agency, rather than joining the union in any traditional sense”.
US president Donald Trump has threatened the European Union with “serious tariffs” and a cut to trade after the bloc proposed to make Canada its first ever associate member, calling the idea “laughable”.
Suggesting the move was a “hostile act”, the US president told reporters he could put “very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe”. He added: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe.”
European Commision president Ursula von der Leyen insisted yesterday that “this is not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength,” and deputy chief spokesperson Olof Gill repeated this line this morning in response to Trump’s overnight threats.
Canadian prime minister Mark Carney – fresh from watching Everton’s Carabao Cup win over Wolverhampton Wanderers in Liverpool – will address the European parliament late morning. Let’s see if he has anything to say on this.
Separately, our attention is increasingly turning to Germany, where embattled chancellor Friedrich Merz is set to join the campaign trail today in Berlin ahead of this weekend’s two state elections that just could determine his political future.
Powerful German state leaders from his party have rallied behind the chancellor as speculation builds that his days in office may be numbered, and he cancelled his trip to the UN general assembly next week.
Our Berlin correspondent Deborah Cole will be joining us just after 11am to answer your questions about Merz’s future,the two state elections, and what’s next for Germany. You can post your questions to her below the line from 9am.
Lots for us to cover today.
It’s Thursday, 17 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

Warm words on Canada's EU 'associate membership' but no guarantees
- Published
Is Canada about to join the EU? Headlines across Europe indicate a lot of confusion right now.
The EU constitution rules that possibility out as Canada is geographically outside Europe.
But in a speech on Thursday to the European Parliament, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said: "Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities."
Mark Carney was responding – extremely warmly – to an invitation by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for Canada to become the EU's first associate member.
The EU and Canada already have a far-reaching trade deal (Ceta) in place but Carney insisted additional cooperation on energy and economic security, on critical and raw materials, education, tech and AI innovation, and defence would help safeguard all countries involved.
Canada and the EU feel increasingly squeezed by the superpowers USA on the one side and China on the other – and by tech giants, too, that seem to operate supranationally.
The idea of associate EU membership, Carney emphasised, would not be to form a third superpower or to create a bloc against anyone else.
"We do not pursue zero sum deals," he said. Instead he suggested like-minded nations should club together to create a new form of multilateral global governance in an increasingly turbulent world where – in the minds of some others - might is right.
Only by countries joining forces and shunning isolationism, Carney suggested, could they close key capability gaps, build strength and ensure national sovereignty.
This last may have been a nod to upcoming elections across Europe and the continent's increasingly powerful nationalist politicians. Their slogans – whether "Italy First" or "France for the French" or "Make Poland Great Again" – echo Donald Trump's call to Make America Great Again.
Carney's words were hopeful and warm; the applause in the European Parliament rapturous and apparently heartfelt.
- What could EU associate member status mean for Canada? 
  - Published3 hours ago
- Canada welcomes EU proposal to become 'associate member' 
  - Published6 hours ago
Not so across the Atlantic. On Wednesday, Donald Trump dismissed the EU associate membership proposal out of hand, threatened to impose "very heavy tariffs" if the agreement came to fruition and warned he may view it as a "hostile act".
But the US president is the unintentional matchmaker for this EU-Canada love-in.
Traditionally, America is trade partner and defence ally number one for Canada and the EU.
But Ottawa is currently embroiled in what it calls an escalating trade "war" with the White House. Both Canada and the EU have been stung by what they view as Washington's weaponisation of trade tariffs.
They also fear they can no longer fully rely on the US to have their back in terms of security and defence.
Canada is not alone among Europe's far-flung allies, now seeking to cosy closer to the EU, as they worry the US is becoming too unpredictable a partner. Japan and South Korea show an interest in sheltering under the EU umbrella too.
For its part, the EU has recently hastened to secure a list of trade deals – with India, Indonesia and Japan for example – to intentionally diversify relationships.
But there is no guarantee Canada's associate membership of the EU will ever get off the ground, never mind become a blueprint for other countries, like the UK wanting closer relations stopping short of full EU membership.
Any deal would have to be approved by each one of the EU's 27 countries.
No legal precedent exists, negotiations would be lengthy and potential conflicts of interest loom, over steel tariffs for example.
A suggestion in May by Germany to make Ukraine – a country desperate for full membership of the European Union as soon as possible – an associate member was rejected by others in the EU.
Some, including France's government, want to avoid EU non-members securing "too good" a deal. They fear eurosceptic forces at home and abroad could then encourage voters to clamour to leave the bloc.
In the end, "associate membership" is just a label. Buffeted by adverse winds – from China, the US and Russia, the normally rigid rules-based EU is coming under serious pressure to show more flexibility in accommodating countries wanting to stand by its side.

New Delhi: Indonesia has entered a new chapter in its naval history with the arrival of its first aircraft carrier, the former Italian Navy vessel ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi, at Tanjung Priok port in North Jakarta on Friday, September 18. The 41-year-old warship was transferred by Italy after being retired in 2024 and is now being prepared for service with the Indonesian Navy.
The carrier sailed from Italy on August 24 and travelled through the Suez Canal before making port calls, including in Sri Lanka. After entering Indonesian waters, it was escorted by Indonesian Navy frigates KRI Brawijaya-320 and KRI Prabu Siliwangi-321 before reaching Jakarta.
The vessel has been identified by the Indonesian Navy as KRI Sriwijaya, named after the historic maritime kingdom of Sriwijaya. Its arrival makes Indonesia only the second Southeast Asian country to operate an aircraft carrier, after Thailand.
Why Indonesia Wanted The Aircraft Carrier
Unlike traditional carrier operations focused on projecting fighter power far from home shores, Indonesia has said the ship will primarily support Military Operations Other Than War (MOOTW).
Its intended roles include humanitarian assistance, disaster relief, maritime security, command-and-control and logistics. With Indonesia spread across thousands of islands and frequently affected by floods, landslides, earthquakes and forest fires, the carrier is expected to provide a large mobile platform from which helicopters, drones and relief equipment can be deployed.
The Indonesian government has also described the vessel as a platform for responding to disasters and supporting operations across the country's vast archipelago.
A 41-Year-Old Italian Warship
The Giuseppe Garibaldi was built for the Italian Navy by Fincantieri and entered service in 1985. Named after Italian military and political figure Giuseppe Garibaldi, the vessel spent nearly four decades with the Marina Militare before being retired in October 2024.
It was Italy's first purpose-built ship designed to operate fixed-wing aircraft and helicopters from a continuous flight deck. Its design centres on STOVL Short Take-Off and Vertical Landing operations, allowing compatible aircraft to take off over a ski-jump and land vertically or at short distances.
The carrier was originally classified as an aircraft-carrying cruiser because of Italy's legal restrictions on aircraft carriers at the time. It was later operated as a conventional light aircraft carrier.
How Big Is Giuseppe Garibaldi?
The ship measures approximately 180.2 metres in length, with a beam of around 33.4 metres. Its full-load displacement is roughly 13,850 tonnes, rising to around 14,000 tonnes following its mid-life modernization.
Its flight deck stretches for about 174 metres and features a ski-jump at the bow for short take-offs. The vessel also has a large internal hangar served by two aircraft elevators.
Despite being considerably smaller than the giant aircraft carriers operated by the United States and other major naval powers, the Garibaldi was designed as a compact, versatile aviation platform capable of carrying a mix of fixed-wing aircraft and helicopters.
Four Gas Turbines, 30-Knot Top Speed
The Giuseppe Garibaldi is powered by a COGAG (Combined Gas And Gas) propulsion system using four LM2500 gas turbines. Together, the engines produce roughly 60,000 kW, or more than 80,000 horsepower.
The propulsion system drives two shafts and gives the vessel a maximum speed of around 30 knots, equivalent to roughly 56 kmph.
Its range is estimated at approximately 7,000 nautical miles at 20 knots, giving the ship the endurance required for extended deployments.
Built To Carry Aircraft And Helicopters
The defining feature of the Garibaldi is its aviation capability.
During Italian service, the ship was designed to operate AV-8B Harrier II/Harrier II Plus STOVL aircraft, along with a variety of helicopters. Depending on the aircraft mix and configuration, the vessel could accommodate roughly 16 to 20 aircraft.
Its helicopter operations included platforms such as the SH-3D Sea King, EH101/AW101, NH90 and AB212.
The flight deck does not use catapults. Instead, the ship's ski-jump arrangement enables compatible STOVL aircraft to launch from the forward section of the deck.
For Indonesia, however, the aviation component is expected to evolve around its current operational requirements, with helicopters and potentially unmanned systems expected to be particularly important.
More Than An Aircraft Carrier
The Garibaldi was not built simply as a floating runway. During its Italian service, it also carried command-and-control, surveillance, communications and maritime warfare systems.
Its original configuration included air-search and surface-search radars, electronic warfare equipment, sonar and defensive weapon systems. Some of its earlier offensive systems, including Otomat anti-ship missiles, were removed during its 2003 modernization as additional space was made available for aviation and communications capabilities.
What weapons, sensors and electronic systems the ship will ultimately carry under Indonesian service will depend on the country's ongoing refit and modernization programme.
Crew, Hangar And Operational Capacity
In its Italian configuration, the carrier could operate with a complement of roughly 780 to 830 personnel, including the ship's crew, aviation personnel and command staff.
The vessel's hangar is approximately 110 metres long, providing substantial space for aircraft and aviation support equipment. Its internal facilities and flight deck were designed to allow aircraft to be moved, maintained and deployed rapidly.
Indonesia has also begun preparing personnel for the ship's operation as it transitions from Italian to Indonesian service.
From Italian Flagship To Indonesian HADR Platform
The transfer marks a major change in the Garibaldi's role. After almost four decades as an Italian naval aviation platform, the vessel is now being adapted to Indonesia's requirements.
The Indonesian government has repeatedly highlighted humanitarian assistance and disaster relief as a central mission. Its large flight deck and ability to operate multiple helicopters could allow the vessel to function as a mobile base during major disasters, carrying relief supplies, personnel and aircraft closer to affected areas.
The acquisition has nevertheless triggered debate in Indonesia over the costs of modernising and operating an ageing carrier. While Italy transferred the ship as a grant, Indonesia will have to bear the expenses associated with refurbishment, systems integration, training, aviation assets and long-term operations.
For now, the Giuseppe Garibaldi represents something new for Indonesia: not just a larger warship, but a mobile aviation, command and logistics platform designed to operate across one of the world's largest and most geographically dispersed archipelagos.

Hyrox athlete apologises and forfeits victory after defecating during race
Joanna Wietrzyk said she is ‘deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption’ that her defecation caused during a Hyrox event in Beijing
An Australian Hyrox athlete who went viral after soiling herself during a race in Beijing - before going on to win - has apologised and forfeited her victory.
Joanna Wietrzyk defecated during the global indoor race event in Beijing, and initially responded to her win with a post on Instagram stating “Go hard or go home they say… a win is a win.”
However, after the fallout from the now-notorious incident continued, she has now announced she will “retroactively withdraw” from the race and forfeit the points she won during the event.
“I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the Hyrox organisers for what happened during the race in Beijing,” she wrote.
“I felt completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness. Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognise that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused,” she added.
The 22-year-old holds the Hyrox women’s solo world record, and on Saturday completed the Beijing race in 1 hour, 1 minute and 23 seconds.
Hyrox is a gruelling indoor fitness event that combines running with functional exercises like sled pushes, rowing, burpee broad jumps, and wall balls. Unlike a traditional marathon or obstacle race, every Hyrox event uses the same format and distances, allowing competitors around the world to compare their times directly.
Facing backlash over the incident, Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste apologised to “everyone directly or indirectly affected”.
“Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race. In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents and I did not,” he said in a statement posted on Instagram.
Fürste said that Hyrox had also begun “ improving event processes, plus making rulebook changes immediately”.
“As of this moment, there are new rules and procedures in place to prevent situations like this from happening again. We learn and try to get better everyday.”
The revised rules will allow a race director to withdraw an athlete on medical grounds if their “blood, vomit, urine, or faeces poses a welfare or contamination risk to the racer or to other racers”.
Wietrzyk added in her statement: “I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected. I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away.
“On reflection, I have decided to retroactively withdraw from the race and forfeit the points I earned.”

‘Hindi can’t be barred from Tamil Nadu’: SC on Navodaya schools, gives state 3 months
The Supreme Court refused to recall its Navodaya school order, giving Tamil Nadu 3 months to identify land in every district.
Tamil Nadu cannot take the position that Hindi will never be taught on its soil, the Supreme Court said on Thursday while refusing to recall its earlier direction requiring the state to identify land in every district for setting up Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas.
A bench of justices BV Nagarathna and AG Masih, while urging Tamil Nadu and the Centre to resolve their differences over the schools through dialogue, gave the state three months to comply with its December 15, 2025 order and identify suitable land for the proposed schools.
‘Change your mindset’
The exchange came during the hearing of Tamil Nadu’s plea against a Madras High Court direction to establish Navodaya Vidyalayas in every district. The state has resisted the schools, among other reasons, on the ground that their three-language model, including Hindi, conflicts with Tamil Nadu’s two-language policy.
Also read: Supreme Court directs ED, Delhi Police to submit details of cases against Unitech directors
“You have to change your mindset. It can’t be that Hindi will not be taught on the soil of Tamil Nadu,” observed the bench, as it also sought to dispel the state’s apprehension that accepting the central scheme would amount to surrendering its educational autonomy.
“We are saying in addition to all the good things you are doing in your state, having something in addition will not bring down your standards. Coming from Delhi will not lower the standards of Chennai. People in Chennai should not alienate Delhi and vice versa,” it said.
What Tamil Nadu said on school order
The court’s intervention came after senior advocate Jaideep Gupta, appearing for Tamil Nadu, argued that the state’s opposition was not merely a matter of mindset but concerned its constitutional authority to frame education policy.
Gupta said the state was not opposed to Hindi as such but objected to what he described as the insistence on Hindi as the predominant language in the Navodaya system. He also argued that the central scheme was optional and that the court could not issue a mandamus compelling a state to adopt a particular policy.
“This kind of unification is not the purport of the Constitution. There is an adamancy that Hindi must predominate,” Gupta said.
Court's response
The bench, however, maintained that the state could continue with its own educational institutions and policies while allowing another model of school to operate in Tamil Nadu. “Today it is education, tomorrow it will be something else. You have to relax this rigidity in your mind,” said the bench, stressing the need for cooperative federalism.
Also read: ‘How can there be a blanket ban?’ Delhi HC to cops over protest refusal at Jantar Mantar
The court made clear that it was not directing Tamil Nadu to immediately acquire land or committing the state to a particular expenditure. It said its December 2025 direction only required the state to identify suitable land in its government plan. “Comply with our earlier order. We are not asking you to acquire land. We are only asking to identify,” it added.
In its 2017 order, the had held that the proposed schools did not violate Tamil Nadu’s law on Tamil learning and that a blanket refusal to facilitate them deprived students of the choice of accessing the central scheme.
Tamil Nadu then approached the top court, contending that education being in the Concurrent List did not mean the state could be compelled to adopt an optional central policy, particularly when the Navodaya model followed the three-language formula.
In December last year, the Supreme Court directed the state to identify the land required for establishing the schools in every district within six weeks. Tamil Nadu subsequently sought recall of that order, citing, among other things, the change in the state government and the lack of progress in discussions with the Centre.
Three-month deadline
The bench declined to recall the direction on Thursday. At the same time, it gave the state another three months to comply and directed representatives of the Centre and state to continue discussions on the policy and its implementation.
The language question figured prominently in those discussions. The bench suggested that the state’s concerns could be addressed through negotiations and even indicated that Tamil could be accommodated in the language arrangement.
“If you want Tamil as a second language, it is a matter which can be considered,” said the bench, asking the state and Centre to engage at the level of their respective education secretaries.
Gupta said discussions had already taken place but the Centre had remained firm on Hindi. He nevertheless agreed to another round of consultations. The state also raised a financial objection, claiming that the Centre had failed to release funds under existing education schemes and that Tamil Nadu could not take on additional financial liabilities.
Additional Solicitor General KM Nataraj, appearing for the Centre, countered that the State’s primary obligation under the Navodaya scheme was to provide land, while construction and other expenditure would be borne by the Centre.
The Centre also submitted that the schools were at a nascent stage and construction would take several years, leaving sufficient time to resolve the language-related differences. The bench said the financial and language issues could be discussed separately and emphasised that the establishment of Navodaya schools would not prevent Tamil Nadu from continuing its own education system.
“Ultimately everybody must work together,” the bench said.
The state, however, maintained that cooperative federalism could not operate in only one direction and that the court should not enter the policy debate.
The bench responded that the central scheme should not be viewed as an attempt to displace Tamil Nadu’s educational model.
“We are not alienating you and we are not alienating them. Some more type of schools come in your state also which will only enhance the high standard which we are aware of. This is not going to lower your standards. It will provide more opportunity,” said the bench.
In its order, the bench recorded Tamil Nadu’s explanation that the change in government and lack of material progress in discussions with the Centre had contributed to its non-compliance with the December 2025 direction.
“Be that as it may,” said the bench, directing the state to comply with the earlier order insofar as identification of land necessary to establish a school in each district was concerned.
The matter has been posted for December 14, by when the state and Centre are expected to have had further consultations.

ICE agent appears in Minnesota court to face charges in the shooting of a Venezuelan immigrant
Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer Christian Castro made his first appearance in state court in Minneapolis today in connection with the shooting of a Venezuelan man last January during a surge that brought thousands of federal agents to the Twin Cities area.
Castro, handcuffed and in an orange jumpsuit, said very little during the hearing. He did, however, sign a pre-waiver of extradition, agreeing to immediately return to Minnesota if he violates his conditions of release.
"The state of Minnesota certainly has an interest in not being back in the frustrating situation we were in last month," Senior Assistant Hennepin County Attorney Joshua Larson said in court Thursday.
Castro had traveled to Minnesota from Texas, where authorities released him from jail in August. The Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension arrested Castro, 52, Wednesday afternoon in Minneapolis, ending a months-long standoff between the two states. Minnesota authorities charged him with several counts of assault and falsely reporting a crime in connection with the shooting of Julio Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan immigrant.
In court, one of Castro's lawyers, Daniel Gerdts, said that Castro had planned to self-surrender to Minnesota state authorities at the lawyer's downtown Minneapolis office, but was arrested before he could do so.
"You do not get to dictate how you are taken into custody," Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said at a press conference following the court appearance.
On Jan. 14, Castro allegedly shot through the front door of a house Sosa-Celis had entered while fleeing. The bullet passed through Sosa-Celis' leg and lodged into the wall of a child's bedroom, state authorities say.
In the immediate aftermath of the shooting, the Justice Department initially charged Sosa-Celis and another man with assault, but later dropped the charges after acknowledging that the officers involved, including Castro, had made untruthful statements about the incident.
Castro then became the center of a months-long extradition fight between Minnesota and Texas. Minnesota authorities issued a nationwide warrant for his arrest, not knowing where he was in the country.
In May, Castro was found in Texas. Texas Rangers, along with DHS agents, arrested him. Castro remained in a Texas jail for three months as Gov. Greg Abbott delayed signing an extradition warrant. Last month, Minnesota officials sued Texas over the extradition, alleging that Texas' refusal to send Castro to Minnesota at Gov. Tim Walz's request was illegal. A federal judge declined to intervene. Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison announced at a press conference following Thursday's court appearance that it had dismissed the lawsuit.
Federal prosecutors have also charged Castro for lying to investigators about the shooting, though they did not bring any civil rights charges against Castro for the shooting itself.
Castro is expected to appear in federal court Friday. He remains in a Minnesota county jail. One of Castro's attorneys, Rolando Cantu, says Castro plans to plead not guilty to the federal and state charges.
"We just wanted to stress, you know, we're anxious. We're ready to fight this case in court, so we're looking forward to it," Cantu told NPR.
Castro's next appearance in state court is set for Nov. 3.

In early September, two teenagers got into a Waymo, but then ended up in the back of a police car. The robotaxi company said it detected “a violation of our terms of service involving a firearm,” pulled the car over, and alerted emergency services, according to the Los Angeles Times. Police arrested the passengers after allegedly finding a loaded AR-style “ghost gun” in the vehicle.
Your robotaxi might be a narc
Waymo notified the police when it detected a gun during a ride, leading to the arrest of two teenagers. The incident exposes the limits of privacy in an autonomous vehicle.
Your robotaxi might be a narc
Waymo notified the police when it detected a gun during a ride, leading to the arrest of two teenagers. The incident exposes the limits of privacy in an autonomous vehicle.
The arrests exposed a lot of unanswered questions about privacy and autonomous vehicles, including what they are recording, what they do with the footage, and how much privacy riders should expect while riding inside them.
Waymo’s camera-covered cars have already been drawn into the debate over privacy and surveillance. On a number of occasions, law enforcement agencies have obtained search warrants for footage captured by its cars, according to Bloomberg. Last year, the LAPD obtained footage of a hit-and-run that was recorded by a nearby Waymo vehicle. During anti-ICE protests in Los Angeles, five Waymos were vandalized and set on fire amid questions about whether the vehicles could be capturing images of protesters that might be used as evidence to identify or arrest them. Waymo does not publicly disclose how many law enforcement requests it receives or how often it complies.
Those concerns echo the backlash against Flock’s network of automated license-plate readers, which have given police the ability to track cars across jurisdictions and have prompted growing fears about government surveillance and misuse. Unlike fixed Flock cameras, Waymos move through cities carrying cameras both outside and inside their vehicles.
The latest case of the arrested teens takes those concerns a step further. Police did not approach Waymo after a crime looking for footage its cameras happened to capture. Waymo detected something inside the car and initiated the police response itself.
Waymo spokesperson Julia Ilina told The Verge in an email that the company uses its internal cameras to help enforce its terms of service, including detecting prohibited items and behavior. She said it uses automated technology to help Waymo’s teams identify potential violations, such as the presence of firearms inside the vehicle. “If Waymo detects a firearm in the vehicle, we may reach out to local law enforcement,” she added.
Waymo did not explain how its automated system determines whether something may be a firearm, how confident it has to be before something gets flagged, what role humans play between an automated alert and a call to police, or what other violations of its terms of service might prompt a police response. Those are important omissions. This wasn’t a human taxi driver deciding to call 911. It was a driverless car, equipped with cameras and an AI brain, escalating a situation involving its passengers to police.
Bob Somers, a former engineer at autonomous vehicle company Zoox and technical adviser to the AV-safety nonprofit SAVE-US, said he would expect Waymo’s system to look for a range of potentially dangerous weapons and behaviors. The software may not need to decide with certainty that it has seen a firearm. It could instead flag something that resembles one for further review, he said.
“If there is a certain set of objects detected, then that would probably loop in a remote operator to take a look at what’s going on,” Somers said.
Phil Koopman, a Carnegie Mellon University professor emeritus who researches autonomous vehicle safety, said computer vision systems can be trained to recognize objects and potentially dangerous situations.
“If there is a certain set of objects detected, then that would probably loop in a remote operator to take a look at what’s going on.”
— Bob Somers
“If you can train a computer to look at the road and decide how to drive, you can train a computer to decide if somebody’s holding a gun,” Koopman said. But, he added, those systems are “never 100 percent accurate.”
That’s where the unanswered question about human review becomes important.
A human taxi driver who sees a passenger holding something has context. They’ve been in the car for the entire ride. They can hear what the passengers are saying and ask questions. They can decide whether the object is a real gun, a toy, or something else entirely. Back in July, Waymo reported two teens to the police for underage drinking and shooting a toy gun loaded with water beads from the vehicle. It was not clear whether the teens ultimately faced any charges.
A remote worker brought in to review a flagged moment might not have all of that context because they haven’t experienced the entire ride the way a human driver would. Waymo says its interior microphones are generally active only during calls with Rider Support or when riders enable them, meaning a reviewer may not be able to hear what preceded the flagged moment. As of earlier this year, Waymo has about 70 “remote assistance agents” on duty at a given time in the US and the Philippines, who “provide advice and support to the Waymo Driver but do not directly control, steer, or drive the vehicle.” Waymo has not said whether the people reviewing possible violations inside its cars are among those agents.
“It’s really important that Waymo gets it right when they alert the police to something dangerous,” Koopman said. Beyond undermining riders’ trust in robotaxis, a false alarm could put passengers at risk during a police encounter.
Then there’s the question of what Waymo tells riders to expect. Without a driver in the front seat, robotaxis can feel more private than they actually are. In 2023, the San Francisco Standard spoke with four people who said they had hooked up or had sex in Cruise robotaxis, despite the cameras inside them. The publication could not find anyone who said they had done so in a Waymo, but the episodes illustrate how readily passengers can mistake the absence of a human driver for the absence of a witness.
Waymo’s terms of service requires riders to comply with applicable laws and prohibits them from creating a dangerous condition, carrying weapons “or anything that resembles a weapon, e.g. toy gun,” or using drugs. Riders must be at least 18 to ride alone in San Francisco. The two riders arrested this month allegedly violated both the age and weapons restrictions.
The terms say Waymo can suspend or terminate a rider’s access if it believes the rider has violated the rules. Earlier this year, Waymo suspended the account used to book a ride after three boys were photographed hanging out the windows of the vehicle and taking selfies. But they do not plainly tell passengers that the company may call the police based on what it sees inside the car.
“It’s really important that Waymo gets it right when they alert the police to something dangerous.”
— Phil Koopman
Waymo’s public camera policy says its interior cameras can be used to “check that in-car rules are being followed” and “promote safety and security.” It says Waymo Support may review recorded video after an issue is brought to the company’s attention and, in urgent circumstances, access live video during a trip.
The policy also says Waymo may share certain data with law enforcement as needed to comply with legal requirements, enforce agreements, or protect the safety of riders and others. But it doesn’t specify that automated monitoring inside the vehicle may trigger Waymo itself to contact police.
Hayley Tsukayama, director of state affairs at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, called Waymo’s public policies “very broad.” Riders shouldn’t have to infer from language about “safety and security” that their behavior could result in a police response, she said, adding that Waymo should clearly disclose that possibility before passengers get into the car.
“I’m not condoning illegal behavior in rideshares,” she said, but “if they’re going to share it with authorities, then that should be clearly stated in the policy.” As it stands, Tsukayama said, “it is outside of the expectations of consumers.”
Then again, robotaxis themselves are outside the norm. As they become more common, riders may have to develop a new set of expectations about what happens inside them. A human driver can decide how to respond to what happens in their car. In a robotaxi, cameras and software can flag what happens inside, remote workers may become involved, and the vehicle can pull over while police are summoned.
Waymo’s system may have helped police recover an illegal firearm in this case. But the incident also raises a more basic question about what kind of space a robotaxi is: a ride with cameras for safety, a continuously monitored space, or a system that can call the cops on its own passengers.
That question is already showing up in fiction. Robotaxis are making their debut as villains in Road Rage, an upcoming short film about a driverless car that turns against humans. One of the film’s more unsettling ideas is that a robotaxi could end up acting less like transportation and more like law enforcement. This month offered a glimpse of what that might look like.

Kash Patel Refuses to Take a Republican’s Lifeline
The FBI director allowed a Senate hearing to turn into a discussion of bestiality.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
President Trump appointed Kash Patel to lead the FBI not because of his brief experience in law enforcement but because he is a political brawler. The problem, as Patel demonstrated yesterday, is that he is not a very good one: No skilled political messenger would have allowed nearly every headline about a Senate hearing to connect their name and agency with bestiality.
Yesterday’s Senate Judiciary Committee hearing was Patel’s first appearance on Capitol Hill since a raucous visit in May. (At that hearing, Patel and Senator Chris Van Hollen verbally agreed to each take a self-screening test for alcohol abuse. Van Hollen posted his results the next day, but his office said it never heard back from Patel.) It was also Patel’s first hearing since CBS News revealed changes to FBI hiring standards, which reportedly now allow the bureau to consider applicants who have hired prostitutes fewer than three times, stole from an employer more than three years ago, or engaged in sex with animals before the age of 18.
Democrats were eager to press Patel on the changes, but the hearing’s buzziest exchange turned out to be between Patel and Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana, a Republican. During his questioning, Kennedy seemed to be doing everything he could to offer Patel a chance to defuse the story—but Patel, unable or unwilling to recognize the openings, didn’t take them.
The ranking Democrat, Senator Dick Durbin of Illinois, asked about the new requirements first. Patel said the bestiality change was designed to ensure that people who had been forced to engage in sex with animals were not shut out of an FBI job. “We did not want to punish victims of bestiality,” Patel said. “We are not going to target victims.” Whether this is accurate is unclear. The memo laying out the new standards has not been made public, but sources told CBS News that the rules “do not distinguish between candidates who were coerced into sexual activity with animals, as opposed to those who engaged in such acts willingly.”
Kennedy was the next senator to quiz Patel, and he tried to do some cleanup. “I’m really trying to understand,” he said, rubbing his face. “’Cause I listened to the exchange between you and Senator Durbin, and I’ve read a few news accounts, and I’m confused.” He asked Patel, almost rhetorically, to affirm that the FBI still had hiring standards, and Patel argued that changes had been necessary to ensure the quick hiring of good agents. As for bestiality, the old rule had “automatically disqualified any individual who participated on either side of it.”
Kennedy, a bit of a ham, couldn’t resist a jibe: “So you disqualified the animal?” But he was also losing patience. “I’m trying to understand why you did this,” he said, and then offered an unusually frank description of how many Senate hearings work today: “I understand the game. People try to make you look bad. We do the same thing when the other party’s in office.” He gave Patel another shot. The director replied that sometimes human traffickers force victims to engage in bestiality, and that the FBI did not want to disqualify victims—even though, again, the guidelines reportedly don’t make such a distinction.
An exasperated Kennedy wasn’t buying it. “Someone came to you and recommended” this? he asked. “And when you saw bestiality—I say this with respect—the person who recommended it, why didn’t you just say, ‘What planet did you parachute in from? Why do I wanna lead with my chin and get into bestiality?’”
One answer is that Patel just isn’t very politically astute. It’s hard to claim you’re cleaning up and reforming the FBI, as Patel has, when you’re allowing johns and people who stole from their employers to apply. As for bestiality, more careful wording of the FBI memo that first laid out the new standards would have avoided the controversy. Better preparation for the hearing might have given him a clearer explanation than what he offered. And sharper instincts would have told Patel that Kennedy was trying to help him out. Any high-level appointee should be able to get through a congressional hearing without bestiality becoming the main topic. Instead, Patel takes his cues from Trump, whose instinct is always to push back. But what works for Trump doesn’t work for others. It’s not even clear whether it works for Trump anymore.
Patel may have felt a need to loosen qualifications for agents because the FBI has experienced an exodus of staffers since he took over. More than 1,100 special agents, who had an average tenure of almost 22 years, left in 2025 alone, according to data from the Office of Personnel Management. Durbin has alleged that more than 5,000 nonpartisan civilian staffers departed last year. Some left of their own accord, and others were fired who were involved in investigations that Trump and Patel don’t like, such as those looking into the January 6 riot. This spring, my colleague Sarah Fitzpatrick reported that Patel’s colleagues had been concerned about what they described as Patel’s excessive drinking, repeated absences, emotional outbursts, and impulsive behavior. (Patel denied the allegations and sued Fitzpatrick and The Atlantic for defamation, demanding $250 million.)
If Patel doesn’t have the skills and temperament to run the FBI well, isn’t really cleaning up the bureau’s ranks, and can’t even get through a standard Senate hearing without things going off the rails, one might wonder why he’s in the job at all. Lower hiring standards apparently start at the top.

US President Donald Trump said on Thursday he is approaching a “big decision” on the next phase of the Iran war, as the conflict enters its seventh month and fighting involving Iran-backed Houthi forces and Saudi Arabia adds another layer of uncertainty to the regional crisis.
In an interview with Axios, Trump said his next move would be influenced by discussions with leaders of six Gulf countries whom he is due to meet in New York next Tuesday on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.
“I have a big decision coming up,” Trump reportedly told the news outlet. He also indicated that he was weighing whether to resume major military action against Iran.
Trump is scheduled to meet leaders from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman at UN headquarters in Manhattan next week.
The meeting is expected to focus on the next phase of the Iran conflict and US plans for the post-war regional order, according to Axios.
Trump said he wanted to hear directly from the Gulf leaders before determining his next steps.
“I want to find out where they are and how they are doing. We have been very protective of them,” he told Axios.
The meeting comes as Gulf states face growing economic and security risks from the expanding conflict, including attacks on energy infrastructure and disruption to key maritime routes.
Trump separately told reporters on Wednesday that he hoped the nearly seven-month war was approaching its end.
“Well, hopefully we are towards the end of the war. They want to make a deal, we’ll see how that works out,” Trump said, according to Reuters.
Trump also said he had communicated with Tehran “directly”, but did not provide details about when the contact took place, who was involved or what was discussed.
Asked whether a deal with Iran was possible, Trump again said: “They want to make a deal, and we’ll see how it plays out.”
However, Reuters reported that no negotiations between the United States and Iran to end the war have taken place since an interim agreement reached in June subsequently collapsed.
The diplomatic uncertainty comes as the conflict has spread into Yemen, with Iran-aligned Houthi forces and Saudi Arabia exchanging strikes.
The Houthis have made major territorial gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and captured positions overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key maritime chokepoint connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. Reuters reported that the advance has created new risks for Saudi oil exports and global shipping.
Saudi Arabia has carried out airstrikes in Yemen, while the Houthis have launched missiles and drones towards Saudi territory. Reuters reported that Saudi authorities announced the first civilian death in the kingdom from the latest Houthi attacks.
The escalation has also triggered a fresh humanitarian crisis, with more than 100,000 people displaced inside Yemen, according to the UN refugee agency cited by Reuters.
The fighting has also threatened an important alternative route for Gulf oil exports.
Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline, which transports crude from the kingdom's eastern oilfields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, was temporarily shut after drone attacks damaged pumping stations. Reuters reported that three pumping stations were hit and that the pipeline normally handles around 4 million to 5 million barrels of oil per day.
Saudi Arabia has sought to offset the disruption by arranging additional crude shipments through Oman's Sohar port using ship-to-ship transfers.
The Strait of Hormuz remains another major concern for global energy markets. Commercial vessel traffic through the strategic waterway has fallen sharply amid the conflict.
The US Navy has been attempting to guide ships through the strait, while Iran has said the waterway will remain closed until Washington lifts its blockade.

Claude is taking on a growing share of the work behind Anthropic's next-generation AI.
Anthropic said in a Thursday blog post that Claude now "leads" 26% of its AI research and development work, meaning the chatbot can complete most of a task from a high-level prompt while a human supervises. The company said that the figure was below 1% in March.
"The share of work at or above 'AI collaborates' is above 90%," Anthropic said, adding that "Claude is not operating fully autonomously for any measured subset of AI R&D work."
The figures could help indicate how close the industry is to recursive self-improvement, which Anthropic described as "a model fully autonomously building its successor."
"Models accelerating their own development could make it more challenging for humans to understand or control these systems," Anthropic said. "It is therefore important to share these metrics to understand how close the world is to reaching recursive self improvement."
Anthropic's report comes amid an ongoing debate over AI safety and how quickly the models are improving. An Anthropic researcher resigned last week and accused leading AI companies of "gambling with our lives" by pushing ahead with increasingly capable models. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has since called for frontier AI companies to coordinate on slowing development to give safety measures more time to catch up.
Anthropic said in its report that the company's AI actions are reviewed by automated monitors. Anthropic said 0.002% of more than 1 billion decisions analyzed in August, which amounts to about one in 47,000, were blocked. Roughly 50 high-priority cases are escalated for human review each week.
Anthropic said other frontier labs could publish the same figures and allow third parties to verify them.
"We are reporting these measurements because they give the public, third parties, and governments better visibility into the pace of AI development inside frontier labs," the company said. "This means better measuring the development of AI, reporting on it publicly, and giving society an opportunity to decide how to use this information."

The EU plans to ban chatbots from simulating emotions or interpersonal relationships in interactions with anyone under the age of 18 as the bloc tries to stop children from developing emotional dependencies on the technology.
The rules will be part of the EU Kids Act, proposed on Thursday, which includes similar restrictions on minors’ access to social media and video-sharing platforms. Children under 13 will be banned from accessing chatbots without their guardians’ supervision, and digital platforms will have to build child-safety protections into their products or face fines of up to six percent of total worldwide turnover, according to a draft of the legislation seen by WIRED.
Chatbots operating in the EU will also not be allowed to retain memory of interactions between separate conversations under the new rules, since the Commission worries this could lead to systems accumulating sensitive data of minors over time and potentially reinforcing harmful interaction patterns.
Providers of online social networking sites, video-sharing platforms, and games should not automatically activate or encourage the use of AI chatbots on their services, the proposed law will also stipulate. That includes not pinning AI companions and general conversational chatbots at the top of a minor’s contacts list, it says—as had been done by Snapchat.
The proposal is limited to AI companions and general conversational chatbots seen by the Commission to pose serious risks to minors health, safety, and well-being. Simeon de Brouwer, a policy adviser at the Brussels-based advocacy group European Digital Rights, welcomes the chatbot measures, but tells WIRED it doesn’t make sense to restrict them to young people only. “Don’t we all deserve to be protected from AIs designed to be addictive, from AIs which create emotional dependencies, or from AI features which are activated and pushed by default onto users?” The EU says its Digital Fairness Act, due to be unveiled later this year, is expected to propose clamp downs on addictive design more widely.
In documents seen by WIRED the European Commission says it is worried that dependency on chatbots may negatively impact a child’s development and its relationships with other humans. It’s also concerned by chatbots giving minors dangerous advice, including on their mental health and personal development, which it said can shape and encourage risky behaviour.
“Platforms have been playing fast and loose with children’s mental health,” President Ursula von der Leyen said in a press conference on Thursday. Around half of Europeans aged 11 to 25 have discussed intimate or personal matters with AI chatbots, according to an Ipsos BVA survey across France, Germany, Sweden and Ireland. Australia and the UK are both attempting to restrict minors’ access to chatbots through their social media bans.
It also highlighted the harms of deepfakes generated by chatbots, which von der Leyen nodded at in Wednesday’s State of the Union speech: “We do not have to accept that girls have their photos used for AI-generated sexualised images … Europe has the power to act.” While the EU AI Act has required synthetic content to be labeled as AI-generated since August, the rules currently only apply to deepfakes generated for commercial use.
The Commission also blames digital distraction for a decline in basic skills in young people. Children who say they use AI chatbots for schoolwork get lower test scores than those who don’t, according to research spanning 91 countries by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Concerns about cognitive impacts and deskilling “expose the absence of children’s rights from the design of GenAI’s tools,” researchers from independent network EU Kids Online wrote in a report.

Former Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, Justice Ali Mohammed Magrey, on Friday described teachers as the “quiet architects” of a child’s character and called for greater investment in their dignity, professional development and well-being.
Addressing the Dronacharya Awards for Teachers 2026, organised by BMS Academy for Professional Courses under the aegis of the BMS Educational Trust at BMS College of Engineering in Bengaluru, Justice Magrey said teachers do much more than impart academic knowledge.
“A teacher does not merely transfer information from a textbook to a notebook,” he said, highlighting the role of teachers in encouraging students, building confidence and shaping their character.
Justice Magrey said education in its true sense goes beyond marks and examinations, encompassing curiosity, integrity, resilience and empathy.
“It is the teacher who instils the discipline to keep trying after failure, the courage to ask an honest question, and the values that will guide a child's conduct long after the syllabus is forgotten,” he said.
Reflecting on his experience as a judge, Justice Magrey said that long before law, family and society leave their imprint on an individual, teachers play a crucial role in shaping a child's character.
He said that behind the success of doctors, engineers, scientists and judges, there is often a teacher who believed in them before they believed in themselves.
Describing teachers as “nation-builders”, Justice Magrey said India’s aspirations for growth, knowledge and innovation are closely linked to the collective efforts of teachers working in classrooms across the country.
He also commended the BMS Educational Trust and BMS Academy for Professional Courses for instituting the awards and bringing attention to the contribution of teachers and principals.
As part of the event, 100 teachers and principals from State, CBSE and ICSE schools were felicitated.
Justice Magrey said the contribution of teachers could not be fully measured by awards, adding that their real impact is reflected in the lives and confidence of their students.
He urged parents, administrators, policymakers and civil society members to view the occasion as a reminder of their collective responsibility towards teachers.
“A society that wishes to prosper must invest in its teachers: in their dignity, their continuous learning, their working conditions and their well-being,” he said.
Justice Magrey also traced the educational legacy of the BMS Educational Trust, recalling its origins in 1946 and the establishment of B.M.S. College of Engineering by Late Sri B. M. Sreenivasaiah.
He said the legacy was subsequently expanded by his son, Late Sri B. S. Narayan, into institutions covering law, science, commerce, architecture and management.
Concluding his address, Justice Magrey said the “true Dronacharya award” would continue to be given silently in classrooms through the lives of students whose teachers helped them understand difficult concepts, overcome challenges and dream bigger.
He congratulated the award organisers and paid tribute to the teachers and principals honoured at the ceremony.

AI-assisted air traffic control is coming to some of the nation’s busiest skies
The software will initially serve only as a real-time decision tool during unexpected disruptions, though it is eventually designed to predict traffic flows and map routes days ahead
Federal officials plan to launch an artificial intelligence-powered system in the Washington, D.C., area as early as Monday, the first step in a broader push to modernize U.S. air traffic management.
The software — known as Smart, or Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories — is designed to analyze flight schedules, weather forecasts, airport runway capacity and operational limits to predict traffic flows and spot potential bottlenecks ahead of time.
Developed by Air Space Intelligence under an $875 million, 12-year government contract awarded earlier this year, the tool is intended to function as a central intelligence center for the nation’s airspace once fully operational, as reported by The Wall Street Journal. The primary goal is to help the Federal Aviation Administration and major carriers navigate schedule disruptions, cutting down on delays and cancellations.
Though industry insiders previously anticipated a broader initial release after months of planning, government officials told the publication that the rollout was always meant to begin on a limited scale.
In its current phase, Smart will serve as a decision-support tool during operational disruptions. Future iterations are expected to handle complex tasks, such as managing flight arrival intervals and mapping out routes days in advance.
As part of the launch, federal authorities plan to open a centralized office for the program at the Transportation Department’s headquarters on Monday.
The initiative comes amid a broader push by the Trump administration to modernize the country’s aging aviation infrastructure through multi-billion-dollar technology investments and expanded controller hiring to address persistent staffing shortages.
However, the transition presents coordination challenges. The FAA has been holding talks with commercial carriers regarding schedule alignment, though industry representatives have raised concerns over how the automated system will operate amid intense market competition for peak flight slots.
During Senate testimony earlier this year, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford addressed the need for structural change in airspace management.
“The way we manage traffic today is chaotic, and we can do better,” Bedford said. “We need to manage that at the FAA, rather than rely on commercial airlines to simply schedule however they want.”
Despite operational questions, industry advocates have welcomed the technology. Airlines for America, a trade association representing major domestic carriers, told The Wall Street Journal that the software offered significant potential to boost safety, expand airspace capacity and enhance overall efficiency.
The organization described the project as “one of the most exciting and bold initiatives taken on by the FAA in decades.”

While the Tokyo Deaflympics in 2025 helped boost public awareness of the sporting event, issues regarding public perception have remained almost a year on.
The Yamaha Motor Foundation for Sports conducted a survey before and after the Deaflympics, an international sporting event for deaf athletes, on the public’s recognition of it. A total of 2,060 responded to the part of the survey conducted before the event, and 1,400 responded to the part conducted after.
According to the survey, 24.3% of respondents age 20 and over said they knew of the Tokyo Deaflympics, before the competition was held last November. The recognition rate rose to 55.4% in 2026.
The rate of recognition among Tokyo residents after the event stood at 72.4%, jumping from 33.3% before the tournament.
“As the tournament approached, I felt there was an increase in people who knew about the event,” said Rina Komokata, who won gold in the women’s tennis doubles and bronze in the singles event at the Tokyo Deaflympics, at a recent seminar in Tokyo for media organizations hosted by the foundation.
“There was a surprisingly large crowd of spectators,” she said, adding that the survey results “made sense.”
While the event was significant for making progress toward an inclusive society, the survey also highlighted issues remaining after the Tokyo Deaflympics.
The proportion of respondents who felt the bias against those with hearing loss had gone, and that such people were a familiar presence in their daily lives, fell to 40.8% from 45.7% before the tournament.
The survey also showed a decline in the proportions of those who wanted to learn sign language and those who thought they could play sports with other people regardless of whether they had hearing difficulties.
Tokyo’s hosting of the Deaflympics “was a positive thing in terms of boosting public interest,” University of Tsukuba professor Mayumi Saito said.
“On the other hand, (the event) has not been enough to bring changes to (public) attitude,” she said, citing as a reason a lack of competitiveness in the Deaflympics.
There may have been a gap between people’s high expectations for deaf sports and what they saw during the Deaflympics, Saito added.
Meanwhile, Komokata highlighted a need for steady work to help develop deaf sports and enhance understanding for people with hearing loss.
One of the four Grand Slam tennis tournaments, the Australian Open, has an event for deaf athletes.
“Creating opportunities where those with disabilities could shine helps garner public interest,” Komokata said. “I hope that we’ll see more of such chances.”
