Nature and land defenders were murdered at the rate of one every three days last year, prompting many communities to set up self-defence units, according to the latest annual death toll by the independent watchdog Global Witness.
Organised crime groups or professional killers were implicated in more than a third of the 124 killings of defenders in 2025 as narco-trafficking activities overlapped with intrusions into indigenous territories and environmental crime, such as illegal logging and wildcat gold mining.
This was particularly true in Latin America, which accounted for 85% of last year’s deaths of people trying to protect forests, rivers and other ecosystems.
Colombia had the highest toll with 39 killings, followed by Brazil with 26 and Honduras with 12. In Asia, the most dangerous country for defenders was the Philippines, with 12 killings – many during crackdowns by state security forces.
Since Global Witness began compiling statistics in 2012, the overall global tally is now 2,375 deaths and disappearances – on a par with a small-scale war.
On a more positive note, the headline figure has declined over the last two years, from 196 in 2023 and 142 in 2024, though the report authors say this is likely to be an underestimate because data collection is difficult in war zones and authoritarian regimes.
Many countries and companies are also carrying out nonlethal attacks on defenders, including criminalisation and online smear campaigns.
Many defenders are now exposed to more organised crime with less assistance from the international community, partly as a result of cuts by the Trump administration. “The dismantling of USAID, which previously supported initiatives for Indigenous peoples to steward their own land, has had particularly serious implications for defenders,” the report says.
Almost three-quarters of the killings documented in 2025 were of Indigenous people and small-scale farmers targeted for defending their land. With less outside help, an increasing number of these communities are establishing their own territorial defence mechanisms.
The report highlights the example of the Kakataibo Indigenous Guard in the Peruvian Amazon. Six of the community’s leaders have been killed since 2020 amid growing incursions into the forest by criminal groups. Starting in 2022 with a few dozen recruits, the guard now has more than 150 volunteers in its 10 bases.
Segundo Ispón, the commander of the organisation, said the self-defence groups provided a global benefit: “Defending our territory is important to us as a community and as a people, and we’re proud to support the climate that we all depend on. In our culture, the work of defending our resources and territory is taught from an early age. But for this next generation coming up, the work is more dangerous than ever.”
At least a dozen other communities in Peru have organised self-defence units. Similar bodies have existed for some years in Colombia and Brazil. But it is risky. Last year, seven Indigenous guards were murdered. In at least five of these cases, the killings were linked to organised crime.
Many forest communities report the narco-threat is growing closer. In July, Asháninka leaders on the Brazilian border with Peru petitioned the government for help after armed and masked men entered their homes, apparently in search of assassination targets.
In the Ucayali basin on the other side of the border, Global Witness said there was a 600% increase in coca production between 2019 and 2023. This is pushing gangs to expand smuggling networks, including through the opening of illegal roads and trails through the forest. Corruption further adds to the risks facing forest protectors who stand in their way because many local politicians and police are in the pay of the traffickers.
Forest communities want help from governments to ease these pressures but there are concerns the opposite may be happening. Under US leadership, many rightwing governments are pursuing military crackdowns on coca growers and drug traffickers, which is pushing narco-gangs further into remote regions and indigenous territories.
Ricardo Soberón, a former head of Peru’s anti-narcotics office, said many communities were also affected on the border of Peru and Colombia. “We are in a situation where transnational criminal groups have appropriated the daily life of the Huitoto, Quichua, Bora, Secoya Indigenous people, who live along the Putumayo basin,” he said.
Of particular concern, he added, were the threats against local leaders, environmental defenders and human rights activists who call for a more effective state presence. He fears the newly elected rightwing governments in affected countries will make matters worse by militarising the conflict in line with the “America shield” priorities of the Trump administration.
Global Witness has urged the authorities to respect and work with nature and land defenders rather than making their role more difficult.
Toby Hill, the lead author of the report, said: “Defenders are the world’s eyes and ears on the ground. It’s thanks to them that we know when ecosystems are being destroyed, where forests are being cleared or rivers polluted. We can’t forget the thousands of defenders around the world who are working every day to protect their territories and cultures under increasing pressure.”

Unfamiliar position for Samba
The youngster joined City's academy at under-nine level and he really started to make a name for himself last term.
Samba scored 24 goals and provided 10 assists in an eye-catching first full season with the under-18s, including curling home a stunning free-kick to help City win the FA Youth Cup final against rivals Manchester United in May.
On his debut, Samba played the entire 90 minutes and fully grasped his opportunity.

The Samba surname will be familiar to those of a certain age who have followed the Premier League.
Floyd is the son of former Blackburn and QPR defender Christopher, who played 171 top-flight matches for those two sides, as well as a further 12 in the Championship with Aston Villa.
The City forward is the younger of two brothers at the club, with Tyrone also involved in the youth team, and will now be aiming to play more first-team minutes after an exciting debut.
As a fleet-footed forward, Floyd could not be more of a different player to his dad Christopher, who was a no-nonsense towering centre-back.

Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson says an MRI scan has uncovered an "abnormality" in her hamstring.
Following a suspected tear last year, Hodgkinson had a scan which revealed she has a "split" hamstring, giving her two tendons instead of one.
The 24-year-old is still learning how to manage the anomaly, which allows her to continue running when one of the tendons is torn but may also make her more susceptible to breakdowns.
Following her second-place finish to Swiss Audrey Werro in the 800m final at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest in September, Hodgkinson announced she had sustained another hamstring tear at the European Championships in Birmingham a few weeks earlier.
"My body is quite literally built differently," said Hodgkinson. "Where most people have one tendon, mine is split - I have two - and we're trying to figure out if it's a strength or a weakness.
"So when one of them tore, I still had another one because it's split. In Birmingham, it didn't affect me during the race, but I could feel something wasn't quite right.
"It's a weird one. You can still run on them. I haven't missed any training the last three weeks. But I've just had to alter my approach. I've had to take my foot off the speed [training], because that's when it's most risky."

There isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.
Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.
The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?
Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.
In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.
India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.
“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”
In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later.
Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)
Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.
But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.
The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.
The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.
Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.
Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.
That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.
The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”

Lollapalooza | British pop star Olivia Dean is to perform in India for the first time in January when she headlines Lollapalooza 2027 in Mumbai. Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists on the lineup include Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi.
The price of gold | Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked Indians once again to refrain from buying gold and travelling abroad. He had first made an appeal to self-reliance in May, in part to conserve India’s declining foreign exchange reserves amid a rise in import prices and global energy shocks.
Census 2027 | The new and expanded questionnaire for the 2027 census is raising concerns, reports Scroll’s Anant Gupta. The questionnaire asks respondents for details about their identity documents, as well as their parents’ religion and place of birth. Several of these questions were part of the controversial National Population Register that has remained in abeyance since 2020 and was controversial due to fears that the data might be used to target minorities through a citizenship registry.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Singer Prateek Kuhad (@prateekkuhad), whose latest album, Full Moon Chamber, was released in July, shares an indulgent treat: “I’m a big fan of artisanal Indian chocolate makers. I really like Manam, Carra and Naviluna, and there are many others. Although India has been growing cacao [commercially] since the 1960s, its craft bean-to-bar movement is more recent. Even a plain chocolate bar from one of these makers can be remarkably complex and delicious. More people outside India should know about it and try it.”

Earlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group (@ismaillanga_official) decided the music had to go on, in their own way. It took two months to pull off, says creative director Jagirdar RV. Most artists in the group, aged between 23 and 60, don’t speak or read English and learned the lyrics by rote. The song choice was simple, he said, because it “has a very nice vibe which matched our vibe”.

Trump withdraws Lance Schroyer, a former Oklahoma state trooper, as his nominee to lead ICE
WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House said Thursday that it was withdrawing its nomination of Lance Schroyer, a former Oklahoma state trooper, to lead U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, ensuring that an agency at the forefront of President Donald Trump's domestic agenda will remain without a Senate-confirmed leader for at least a while longer.
Schroyer, who has little experience in immigration, is close to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, a former U.S. senator from Oklahoma.
The White House offered no comment in a brief statement.
The latest setback comes as the agency remains under withering scrutiny over its handling of enforcement operations. Critics have question how ICE has recruited and trained officers as it raced to hire thousands to carry out Trump's promise of mass deportations. Officers have shot and killed multiple people, including two American citizens in Minneapolis earlier this year.
Sen. Rand Paul, the chairman of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, had refused to hold a hearing on the nominee until DHS provided him with information he had been seeking about civilian deaths during ICE enforcement operations.
"I don't have a concern with who the nominee was. I had asked them to give me an update on the internal investigation into civilian deaths," Paul, R-Ky., told The Associated Press.
"And I'm still waiting."
When Mullin took over DHS in March, he pledged a lower-profile approach to immigration enforcement, pulling back on the aggressive, tumultuous crackdown on the streets of large cities that sparked widespread public condemnation.
Arrests have continued to accelerate, reaching nearly 51,000 in August, the highest single monthly arrest total during the second Trump administration.
Paul said he intended to hold a hearing on Schroyer's nomination but it never came to that. He only heard about the nomination being withdrawn when the White House made it public Thursday.
ICE has not had a Senate-confirmed leader since the Obama administration. David Venturella, a former executive at a private prison operator, returned to the agency as acting director earlier this year after Todd Lyons resigned.
When Trump nominated Schroyer in June, Trump said on his Truth Social platform that his pick was "a PATRIOT with real operational experience" and a "proven leader with DECADES of experience locking up the worst of the worst."
The administration did not indicate when it might announce another pick for the position.

'Politically motivated': Uddhav Thackeray denies link to Disha Salian case, alleges ‘character assassination’
Uddhav Thackeray reiterated said that Disha Salian's death was an unfortunate incident but his family had no connection with it.
Shiv Sena (UBT) president Uddhav Thackeray on Thursday said he would take legal action if the "character assassination" campaign targeting his family over the 2020 Disha Salian death case did not stop.
The former Maharashtra Chief Minister spoke on the issue days after the Bombay High Court ordered a CBI probe into Salian's death in response to her father's petition. The Central agency subsequently registered a case without naming any accused.
"We have no connection with this case. Aaditya (Thackeray) has also said so. This issue is not merely about me. Such character assasination can take place with you people too," Thackeray said, replying to reporters' questions here.
"If such allegations are made continuously, how long one should tolerate it? I am wondering why the names of Modi and Trump are absent in this case," he said on a sarcastic note.
Salian's death was an unfortunate incident but his family had no connection with it, Thackeray reiterated.
"It is politically motivated. We were quiet because an SIT (Special Investigation Team) was probing the case. Those who want to investigate, they can keep investigating. But enough of this pointless character assasination, or else we will initiate legal steps,'' the Sena (UBT) chief said.
On Wednesday, his son and MLA Aaditya Thackeray had claimed that he had never met Disha Salian.
"I have never met or known Disha Salian. Linking my name to this tragic case is a deliberate, evidence-free attempt of character assassination by a few individuals with clear political and personal motives, for almost six years," Aaditya said in a post on X.
Salian, 28, former manager of Bollywood actor Sushant Singh Rajput, died on June 8, 2020, after falling from the 12th floor of a residential building in Mumbai's Malad area.
Police claimed that it was a case of suicide. A week later, Rajput was found dead in his Bandra apartment on June 14, 2020, triggering speculation about a possible link between the two deaths.
On September 2, the Bombay High Court ordered a CBI probe into Salian's death while pulling up the Mumbai Police for failing to register an FIR for six years, observing that its investigation raises more questions than answers.

Indonesia has received its first aircraft carrier, a former Italian warship that the government says will strengthen the archipelagic nation’s maritime security and disaster response capabilities.
The 41-year-old former ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi, with capacity for short takeoff and vertical landing aircraft and helicopters, arrived Friday morning at a naval base in North Jakarta’s Tanjung Priok port, where it was welcomed with a military ceremony.
Italy in March agreed to give the carrier, which was retired in 2024, to Indonesia in a move aimed at boosting Italy’s broader defence engagement with the south-east Asian country. Italy is seeking deals on submarines and aircraft, and gifting the carrier to Indonesia also saves it the cost of decommissioning the ship.
The transfer would make Indonesia only the second country in south-east Asia with a carrier in its fleet. The first was Thailand’s HTMS Chakri Naruebet, which was commissioned in 1997 after being procured from Spain along with carrier-capable AV-8S Matador jump-jets.
The carrier will be formally commissioned into the Indonesian Navy next week as the KRI Gajah Mada, named after the famed 14th-century Majapahit-era military leader, whose campaigns and vision of a unified archipelago have made him one of Indonesia’s most celebrated historical figures.
Defence development was one of the top priorities for president Prabowo Subianto’s administration, as he has advocated an expansion of the military through the purchase of submarines, frigates, fighter jets, missiles and pushed for more defence cooperation with various countries.
But the Garibaldi acquisition has sparked a fierce debate among defence analysts, economists and opposition politicians who question whether Indonesia needs an aircraft carrier at all and whether the government should be spending millions of dollars to refurbish and operate an ageing warship while facing mounting fiscal pressures at home.
Indonesia’s finance ministry approved $450m in financing for the aircraft carrier program in 2025. However, some lawmakers have warned the overall bill could be far higher. TB Hasanuddin, a member of parliament’s Commission I, said the cost of retrofitting the carrier alone could reach 16tn rupiah (about $900m).
Unlike major naval powers that use aircraft carriers to launch fighter jets far from home shores, Indonesia views the vessel as a mobile command centre and support hub for helicopters, drones and maritime operations across its thousands of islands.
Speaking during a disaster management meeting early this month, Prabowo said the vessel would help authorities combat forest and peatland fires that regularly blanket parts of south-east Asia with hazardous haze.
Prabowo said the carrier could accommodate up to 10 medium-sized helicopters, including aircraft with capabilities comparable to the Black Hawk and Mi-17, and could carry large quantities of water and be deployed to areas with large numbers of fire hotspots.
He also outlined plans to operate drones from the ship and use it as a mobile platform that could be rapidly deployed to help in the event of natural disasters, which are common in Indonesia, a nation that sits in the Pacific “Ring of Fire.”
Operating a carrier is extremely costly, however, and experts have questioned whether Indonesia’s leadership has thought through whether one is necessary for the country’s defence or disaster-relief needs.
The acquisition comes as Indonesia’s economy faces growing fiscal pressures. Prabowo’s government has been funding a free nutritious meals program – which has been tainted by multiple food poisoning incidents – and other costly initiatives while economists have warned about slowing growth, weaker state revenues and widening budget constraints, prompting closer scrutiny of major government spending projects.
“The plan to acquire the Garibaldi must be based on genuine operational needs and our ability to operate it, rather than being driven by pride or other considerations,” said Muhammad Fauzan Malufti, of the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
He said policymakers must weigh not only the vessel’s acquisition and modernisation costs, but also the Navy’s ability to sustain its operations, including personnel, maintenance, fuel, weapons systems and supporting infrastructure.
Fauzan said the government should be transparent about those considerations, particularly given the vessel’s age. He cited Thailand’s carrier as a cautionary example, saying it has spent much of its service life in port because of operational and budget constraints.
“The bottom line is that this should not be forced. Otherwise, the benefits could be outweighed by the costs,” Fauzan said. “The money might be better spent on other priorities, such as increasing the number of frigates in the fleet.”
Military analyst Khairul Fahmi of the Institute for Security and Strategic Studies said aircraft carriers are not a priority for Indonesia, which is focused on preventing adversaries from operating freely in the country’s territorial waters.
“Indonesia has a greater need for submarines, frigates and asymmetric weapons systems to protect its maritime sovereignty,” he said.
But he added that if Indonesia is seeking to position itself as a major maritime nation, “an aircraft carrier can be both a symbol of national power and a multifunctional platform capable of supporting a wide range of military and non-military missions.”

Rows of hardware and car-part shops line Garstin Bastion Road, with faded signs crammed together above their shutters. By day, the street is one of Old Delhi’s busiest commercial thoroughfares. But as dusk falls, GB Road, as it is known locally, transforms into one of the city’s most notorious red-light districts.
An estimated 2,800 sex workers live and work in brothels that occupy the upper floors of the dilapidated buildings, their entrances tucked behind narrow stairways and unmarked doors. Women sit on plastic stools beneath the stairways, calling out to men passing on the street, while others watch from windows above, their eyes following the movement below before customers are directed upstairs.
The challenges the women of GB Road face are numerous and well documented – from health risks to abuse, debt to poor sanitation. Now they face a new struggle: India’s controversial electoral reform process. The Election Commission’s special intensive revision, or SIR, is a nationwide exercise in which electoral rolls have shrunk by more than 58 million voters across the 13 states covered in the first two of three main phases. In Delhi, covered in the third phase, the scale of exclusion is the highest recorded as a percentage: 4.76 million names – 33% of the city’s previous electorate – do not appear on the city’s draft roll published on 31 August.
The government says SIR is meant to “purify” the electoral rolls by removing ineligible voters, including alleged undocumented migrants, but critics have accused Narendra Modi’s government of using it to target minority voters and reshape electoral rolls in ways that could benefit his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
On GB Road, the proportion of those excluded is even higher. Data shared by officials overseeing about 1,300 voters in the area show that about 650 were sex workers on the previous electoral roll. Of these, at least 500 have either been marked as “shifted”, meaning they have moved home or location, or have been unable to establish their eligibility because of missing documentation – more than three-quarters of the sex workers on the local roll.
One of them is 36-year-old Beauty*, who has lived on GB Road for more than two decades. She got her first voter ID in 2008. At the time, the address where she lived and worked as a sex worker and verification by a government official called a booth-level officer (BLO) were enough to put her on the electoral roll. She voted in previous elections.
But under the new rules, voters had to establish eligibility by proving their link to the relevant previous electoral roll or by producing prescribed documents such as a passport, birth or education certificate – a paper trail Beauty struggled to reconstruct. Trafficked at 16 and brought to the brothels of GB Road, she has no contact with her family. She does have an Aadhaar card, India’s biometric identity document used widely to establish identity and access government services, with her GB Road address. But Aadhaar is not proof of citizenship and does not, by itself, establish eligibility to vote under the SIR process.
She tried to get a copy of her matriculation certificate, which is evidence of schooling, from the village in Rajasthan where she grew up. One of her regular customers of the past 10 years – a man she refers to as her husband, agreed to help track down the old record but failed.
“If I had the papers to show my father’s birth certificate, or even my own matriculation certificate, then I could prove who I am,” she says. “But how can I go back to my village to ask for these things when my trafficking has brought so much shame to my family that they no longer accept me?”
Now Beauty has lost hope – and, for now, her vote. Her name was left out of Delhi’s recent draft electoral roll. For her, the voter ID had meant more than a piece of identification. Sex workers, she says, are accustomed to being treated as immoral, degraded and less worthy than others.
“We all shit. That is what makes us equal as human beings. Voting is the same in the realm of rights. When I stand in that queue, nobody is more or less than me. It reminds me that whatever people think about my work, I am still equal to everyone else.”
Beauty is not alone in struggling to prove her eligibility. The SIR requirements have exposed the precarious paper trails of women across GB Road, a roughly 1.5km stretch running between two of Delhi’s historic landmarks, Ajmeri Gate and Lahori Gate.
Of the nine sex workers interviewed for this story, none had successfully completed the SIR process: six said they had never received the enumeration form distributed by BLOs to verify voters’ details and collect information for the electoral-roll revision, while the remaining three were unable to meet the documentation requirements.
According to Kiran Deshmukh, a sex worker and coordinator at the National Network of Sex Workers (NNSW), many have spent years, even decades, in Delhi but possess few documents establishing their family histories or links to earlier electoral rolls. “Some were trafficked as children and lost contact with their families; others never attended school or have moved between rooms and brothels without leaving a stable documentary trail,” says Deshmukh. “It is impossible in such circumstances to prove such rigid eligibility requirements under SIR.”
The process is so cumbersome that even people who are literate and have institutional and organisational support can struggle to establish their eligibility. “The process of receiving the enumeration form, knowing when you have not received it, reaching out, then trying to create a paper trail is so daunting that the entire burden of proving your eligibility is placed on the citizen to protect their own constitutional right,” says Deshmukh.
Sagrika Rajora, a researcher and member of Voter Adhikar Manch, a citizens’ collective, argues that the burden falls particularly heavily on people whose lives do not fit neatly into the categories used by the verification process. “To identify people of such marginality is a tedious task. These categories of ‘shifted’ become an easy way forward for booth-level officers, when finding people on the ground is already time-consuming.”
BLOs are often drawn from occupations such as auxiliary nurses or health workers, adding electoral duties to already demanding jobs. Some have raised concerns about the workload and unrealistic timelines of the exercise. Yet, Rajora says, there has been little effort to streamline the process to ensure that “no eligible citizen is left out”, the aim outlined by the Delhi chief electoral officer, Ashok Kumar.
“There is so much discretion vested in one BLO. Even if you leave citizenship aside and talk only about voter rights, the entire process of delivering and collecting these forms depends on that one person. There are no grounds for entrusting one person with such a huge responsibility without any accountability at all,” Rajora says.
“It is not surprising that sex workers are among those being excluded. When people have lives that are so complex and mobile, you are going to be untraceable, absent from the system. These are the people for whom such a verification system is simply not designed to work.”
The gaps also cause problems for workers’ children when they reach adulthood. “Children may not possess documents establishing parentage in the manner expected for verification. Some are raised by relatives, guardians or members of the community, while others grow up in institutional care, making conventional family records difficult to establish,” says Deshmukh.
For 23-year-old Dinesh*, whose mother was a sex worker, the problem is not abstract. His mother died three years ago, but she never had a birth certificate. Without one, obtaining her death certificate became nearly impossible, leaving Dinesh with little documentation through which to establish his maternal lineage.
When Dinesh submitted his enumeration form, he relied on his matriculation certificate as proof of his identity. But the booth-level officer pointed out that it did not have his father’s name. “If my mother gave birth to me, why do I need a man’s name on any official certificate?” he asks.
Dinesh says his name is missing from the draft electoral roll. He is still unsure why, but suspects the absence of his father’s name may have been a factor.
The NNSW has written to the chief electoral officer seeking special measures to ensure that sex workers and their children are not excluded from the SIR. But the joint chief electoral officer, Balram Meena, told The Hindu there was no separate process for sex workers. “If their mapping can’t be done and there are no documents either, their names will be removed as per the process.”
The fear of losing the vote is not only about voting rights. In West Bengal, where the SIR has already been completed, the BJP government has used lists of voters deleted during the exercise to scrutinise eligibility for welfare schemes. The BJP chief minister, Suvendu Adhikari, says welfare programmes will continue under a “transparent process”, but adds: “No deceased person, illegal infiltrator, or non-Indian individual will be allowed to avail benefits meant for citizens of the state.” The government has excluded about 3 million beneficiaries from its new Annapurna Bhandar welfare for women scheme, using SIR deletion data in its verification process.
In Delhi, the next stage of the SIR process – issuing notices to those whose eligibility or previous electoral-roll details could not be established or matched, and dealing with claims and objections – has now begun and will continue until 29 October. Those excluded from the draft roll can challenge their omission. But Dinesh says he does not intend to.
After years of being asked to produce documents that his family never had, he is unsure what more he can submit to prove that he exists.
“Even if my mother were alive today, I don’t think that would be enough to prove anything. She never had the documents they are asking for. So how am I supposed to get those documents now, especially after her death?”
* Names have been changed. Workers and residents did not permit any photography during the Guardian’s visit

Michael Carrick: Man Utd boss aiming to steer ship back on course at Fulham after back-to-back defeats
Sky Sports News reporter Danyal Khan assesses the choppy waters Manchester United boss Michael Carrick has found himself in after back-to-back defeats; watch Fulham vs Man Utd on Sunday, live on Sky Sports Premier League from 4pm; kick-off 4.30pm
Thursday 17 September 2026 19:04, UK
Manchester United's Carabao Cup second-round loss at Grimsby last season was a result that many will remember.
It was a defeat which became synonymous with former Manchester United head coach Ruben Amorim's time in charge.
That was a very bad night for United, and although Wednesday's defeat at home to Brighton did not feel as significant, there were similarities for the man who succeeded Amorim, Michael Carrick.

Man Utd's captain for the loss, Youri Tielemans, admitted afterwards that once they went 2-0 down, his side stopped playing - and that was pretty evident by their performance.
You could sense at Old Trafford from 20 minutes onwards that Brighton were in the ascendancy and the game was only going to go one way. Despite bringing on Bruno Fernandes, Kobbie Mainoo, Bryan Mbeumo and Matheus Cunha, United failed to make an impression.
That is what will truly worry head coach Carrick.
After the few defeats Carrick has suffered since his return to the club in January, he has always backed his players or found positive qualities in the performances, but there was no such redemption to be found against Brighton.
Predictable problems and defensive worries
When Carrick and his staff first came in, they deservedly received a lot of praise.
Defensively they looked tight and compact and that led to impressive wins against Manchester City and Arsenal.
The likes of Steve Holland, Jonathan Woodgate and Jonny Evans made an immediate improvement to the defensive unit.
But, equally, questions have to be raised now about the frailties that same defence is showing this season. Carrick's side have conceded two goals in three of their four Premier League games.
The defence was exposed once again in the Brighton loss. Yes, one goal was a goalkeeping error by Karl Darlow, but aside from the goals conceded, the shape and understanding of the back four lacked any sort of coherence.
Left-back predictably is an issue for Carrick. He has yet to acknowledge the area as a specific weakness as per his style when engaging in the media, but it is a significant problem - one the United hierarchy knew about going into the summer's transfer window.
Luke Shaw, United's only senior left-back at the club, has missed the last three games through a minor injury, but considering his age and injury track record - despite his excellent availability last season - it was naive not to strengthen in that area.
Carrick has experimented with Noussair Mazraoui in that position but he seems to have fallen down the pecking order, as the less experienced Patrick Dorgu was preferred for the Manchester derby loss.
Young left-back Harry Amass does not seem to be fancied in the position long-term either - so how will United remedy the position for the rest of the season?
An awkward discussion over Carrick's future
It seems ridiculous to even discuss Carrick's job security after only a few weeks of the new season.
Man Utd have still accumulated the most points across the league since his return in January.
However, as Carrick admitted himself, a few moments such as Ainsley Maitland-Niles' equaliser for Everton, City's controversial VAR goal and now a shocking collapse against Brighton, have made it all feel very different.
If United lose at Fulham on Sunday, live on Sky Sports, there will be inevitable and uncomfortable discussions around whether Carrick can lead United out of the storm they currently find themselves in.
That may be for another day, but the United head coach does deserve sympathy for the squad he has been dealt.
The lack of sales and outgoings this summer at United handicapped them in being able to further reinforce the squad. But does that excuse them ignoring key areas to strengthen?
The left-back area, as mentioned, should have been strengthened. Knowing Benjamin Sesko was still nursing a shin injury all summer, perhaps United should have brought in a temporary No 9 to share the load rather than playing Mbeumo and Cunha out of position. Both players have failed to discover the form they showed under Carrick last season.
But, ultimately, until United are able to be in a position where they can really reshape their team in one window, they will continue to be caught in this cycle of strengthening just enough with players left over from previous regimes.
That perhaps is why you could hear boos at Old Trafford after the Brighton loss. Not just aimed at that performance, but perhaps a familiar feeling of a cycle beginning again, a deja vu of seasons past and another false dawn after a promising start under a new United head coach.
Again, it feels too soon for that just yet, and Carrick deserves time after what he delivered last season, but these are the waters he has to navigate, and ultimately, he will be the one judged.
But if he can stop the spiral, even without a win against Fulham with a positive performance, time may allow him to be able to steer the ship back on course.

Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings
- Published
According to Donald Trump, concerns about the dangers of artificial intelligence technology – that "robots will be marching into our cities and getting rid of us all" – are a hoax.
It's the kind of language the US president typically reserves for the objects of his most intense derision – theories about human-driven climate change, investigations into Russian election-meddling, and the drives to impeach and remove him from office during his first presidential term.
Styling himself as the "hoax buster", in a series of social media posts on Monday he issued a full-throated endorsement of what he called "the greatest economic development engine in history" and scorned those who doubted the benefits of the technology.
The ranks of doubters have been growing in recent weeks, however, amidst anxiety over the disruptive nature of AI - if not worries about potentially civilisation-threatening danger - among some industry insiders and politicians, including from within Trump's own Republican Party.
- OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms 
  - Published15 hours ago
- AI regulation faces political deadlock as calls grow for Congress to act 
  - Published1 day ago
None of that has deterred Trump, however, whose latest social media fusillade was only his latest effort to turn back growing AI scepticism through sheer force of will.
Whether the president views the AI fight as pivotal to his economic legacy, a key battleground in a global struggle for power, or another example of his enemies conspiring against him, he has, by fully joining the fight, elevated the issue to the forefront of American politics. That is even at the risk of crossing longtime allies.
"We think this could be a great technology, but we're not going to give these guys a carte blanche," former Trump adviser Steve Bannon said at a "pro-human" conference on the dangers of AI on Tuesday. "There's been no debate."
Just before Bannon spoke, democratic socialist Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont told the same crowd that Washington policymakers had not addressed the "potentially catastrophic consequence" of unregulated AI.
"Congress under both Democratic and Republican control has been asleep at the wheel," he said. "And now we have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing."
According to Trump, however, what's needed isn't debate or new policies, it's trust in his authority and judgement.
"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades," he wrote. "We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies."
A desire for centralised presidential authority is a familiar theme for Trump in his second term in office. If he decides something is good, he should have the authority to allow it; if he deems it bad, he ought to be able to end it by unilateral presidential order.
It's similar to his outlook on immigration and trade. He believes that he, as president, should have the sole power to decide who can enter and remain in the country, and when and where to impose tariffs.
Unlike tariffs and immigration, which have been issues of interest for Trump for decades, the rise in artificial intelligence technology is a recent development.
But if this is no long-time, deep-seated interest on the part of the president, what could explain his willingness to press ahead?
The 'hottest' economy and the driving force of AI
Trump regularly likes to tout America as the "hottest" country in the world. Many economists indicate that investment in AI technology – including infrastructure and equipment – has been the driving force in the US economy for several years.
According to a recent report by the forecasting firm ING, tech investment accounted for more than a third of all US economic expansion in the second quarter of 2026.
The stock market is booming, and much of that rise in corporate value (and, by extension, surging retirement portfolios of many Americans) can be attributed to the massive spending on computer chips, data centres and the other infrastructure behind AI.
Anything that threatens this growth, which Trump considers to be a hallmark of his presidency and a key to his political legacy, quickly draws his suspicion.
Trump also sees the AI expansion as a large-scale industrial competition between the world's two largest economies, the US and China. In the zero-sum game of global power, if China is ahead, then America is behind.
"We're leading China in AI," Trump said on Saturday, "and frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins."
The president often touts a familiar conservative view that his opponents on the left are against the free market and economic liberties, and rely on alarmism to justify greater government intervention and control.
Of course, Trump – who touts partial US ownership of US Steel and the semiconductor manufacturer Intel, and has no qualms about picking winners and losers in the American economy – is hardly a traditional small-government conservative.
Tech bosses vary in views - and their access to Trump
Trump's close ties to prominent tech moguls and AI entrepreneurs from the start of his second term may also help explain his AI evangelism. Tech entrepreneur David Sacks, a co-chair of the president's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology and his informal AI tsar, has been a longtime supporter. Sacks's publicly aired scepticism of AI regulation mirrors recent comments made by the president.
"I think this is becoming a panic," he said this weekend in an interview with CBS News. "We're in an election season, and there is an incentive for political actors to try and amplify the fear."
Elon Musk, despite a rocky relationship, has shaped the direction of this administration. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook, Amazon's Jeff Bezos, OpenAI's Sam Altman and former Apple head Tim Cook all had prominent seats at Trump's inauguration.
These men, along with Anthropic head Dario Amodei, hold a range of views on the necessity of greater AI regulation, and have differing levels of access to, and influence on, Trump.
In Amodei's case, his conflicts over the Pentagon's unrestricted use of Anthropic's AI models could have negatively affected Trump's evaluation of Amodei's calls for a slowdown in AI development.
"This is the most prominent debate in the entire industry and has been since the beginning," said Matt Calkins, head of the tech firm Appian. "We knew it would spill into politics at some point because it had to."
Where the political debate goes from here is an open question.
With Trump's resistance, it is unlikely that Congress – despite promises of new hearings and proposed regulatory controls – will enact new legislation that Trump would sign into law. On Tuesday, Republican Speaker of the House Mike Johnson appeared to back away from earlier openness to congressional action, instead echoing Trump "AI hoax" rhetoric.
With midterm congressional elections looming, candidates running for office – both Republicans and Democrats – are wary of ending up on the wrong side of public opinion that, according to polls, is sceptical of the promised benefits of AI advances.
But Republicans are also wary of crossing Trump on an issue that has become a political touchstone for the president.
Even though the public is starting to pay attention, Calkins says that the issue has not yet become political dynamite, which means political rhetoric comes with little risk. The moment when AI warnings turn into a high-profile disaster, however, could be looming.
"It is possible that events in the future might electrify the public, and then positions - and talk - might not be so cheap," he said.

When Xbox announced a new feature last month that lets you digitize existing physical game collections, I immediately thought of the Xbox One. Disc-to-digital seems like a clever new feature for Xbox, perfectly timed as a response to Sony killing PlayStation discs. But the reality is that it has been 15 years in the making and is now a big part of Xbox’s ongoing game preservation efforts.
Xbox’s clever disc-to-digital feature was 15 years in the making
Microsoft’s controversial Xbox One bets are paying off more than a decade later.
Ahead of the launch of the Xbox One in 2013, Microsoft made a key decision to uniquely identify discs. Sources familiar with Microsoft’s plans tell me the company was exploring the idea of true Xbox digital ownership in 2011, including digital gifting, recycling digital games, and the ability to swap discs at retail stores in exchange for a digital version. Some of those original Xbox One plans leaked out online, and many others have remained secret for more than a decade.
Microsoft’s Xbox One launch hinted at some of these ideas, too. The console was originally supposed to be always online, to enable Microsoft’s vision of digital game sharing, and more. Microsoft walked back those plans after a messy and confusing Xbox One launch created a backlash to the always-online requirement. But some of those original digital ideas are now starting to come to life in different ways.
Microsoft’s decision to essentially embed a serial number on the discs that Xbox consoles can read has allowed it to launch disc-to-digital, a method that lets you turn a physical Xbox One disc into a digital copy simply by slotting it into a disc drive. A decision made 15 years ago has resulted in this useful feature and may well lead to true digital ownership in the coming years.
It’s not something Sony can copy, either. Unless the PlayStation maker has been quietly adding metadata to its discs over the years, it will have to find another method to help PS5 owners move their physical collections over to the digital era.
Microsoft thought ahead, not necessarily to disc-to-digital, but just about identifying discs so it was ready for when console games moved into an all-digital era. That era looks like it’s right around the corner, especially now that Sony has announced it’s killing PlayStation discs in 2028. Both Microsoft and Sony also ship digital-only variants of their consoles, and it’s clear from game sales numbers that most titles are purchased digitally these days.
I fully expect Microsoft to follow Sony and eventually scrap Xbox discs, especially as the number of authorized manufacturers capable of producing physical media continues to shrink. That’s largely because almost every other form of media, from music to movies, has moved on from optical discs. The big difference with Xbox, though, is that Microsoft has always been obsessed with game preservation.
In the same year that disc-to-digital is launching, Microsoft is also bringing original Xbox and Xbox 360 games to PC. The company has also spent years working on its backward compatibility program, to get as many games from the Xbox and Xbox 360 eras working on modern Xbox consoles. Game preservation is a central part of Project Helix, the next Xbox that could play every Xbox game ever made.
It’s not an easy task to pull off game preservation, either. There are the complex technical challenges that need to be overcome, alongside licensing issues and the business challenges from publishers that decide how a game should be sold.
Some of those technical challenges mean that not every single Xbox One disc will work with this new disc-to-digital feature. That could be because some early discs simply didn’t get pressed with the unique identifier. Microsoft warned its internal Xbox testers that “it all depends on how and when the disc was manufactured and it may not have the features we need for this program.”
Discs that are slightly damaged might also not work with disc-to-digital, but run just fine otherwise. That’s why it’s important that Xbox is launching this right now — physical media decays over time.
The licensing and business challenges are far more complicated. Publishers need to agree to disc-to-digital, and some could hold back. It appears that most are on board, and even Ubisoft games started showing up recently. We’ve seen a number of other games come online since Microsoft’s announcement, and the company has been clear that more will follow.
The next challenge beyond disc-to-digital is solving digital ownership. If all we really own of a digital game is a license, I hope that one day those licenses can move freely across devices and platforms. I want to buy a single copy of a game and have that license follow me across Xbox, PlayStation, Nintendo, and PC. I also want to be able to gift or sell that license on different marketplaces, just as we’ve been able to do with physical discs at retailers for decades.
Microsoft envisioned this true digital ownership future 15 years ago, and it has gradually taken steps toward making it a reality. I hope Xbox can eventually pull it off, but the solution will require publishers and platform owners to agree on a shared system for how game licenses are bought, transferred, gifted, and resold. That’s a much bigger challenge than simply getting rid of the disc.

Microsoft’s AI code of conduct makes it clear that “people matter more than AI,” and that AI models are not conscious and “should not be designed to imitate consciousness.” That’s a direct swipe at Anthropic, which has been pushing the idea of AI welfare and model consciousness lately. The code of conduct also commits to ensuring Microsoft’s own models will remain under human control and discourage “patterns of interaction that cause excessive reliance or emotional dependence.”
- Microsoft adds Grok to Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. Microsoft added SpaceXAI’s Grok models to its Foundry service last year, and now it’s expanding access to Copilot itself. Grok models can now be used in Word, Excel and PowerPoint from the model picker interface for Microsoft Frontier users. Microsoft says it’s starting with a preview release to “gather feedback.” This means Office Copilot users can now pick between OpenAI’s GPT models, Anthropic’s Claude models, and SpaceXAI’s Grok models.
- Microsoft issues emergency Windows 11 update to fix its record-breaking patch. Last week I reported on Microsoft’s record-breaking patch Tuesday, and it turns out that this giant set of fixes has caused some issues. Microsoft has had to release an out-of-band patch to fix folder shares on Hyper-V-based Linux virtual machines, Remote Desktop Services sessions, and some USB audio devices. These out-of-band updates used to be a rare occurrence, but there have already been eight this year alone. With AI models continuing to spot even more vulnerabilities in Windows, I can’t see this all slowing down anytime soon. In fact, I wouldn’t be surprised if October’s patch Tuesday breaks another record.
- BlizzCon delivers the return of StarCraft, Diablo on Netflix, and Diablo V. StarCraft is returning in 2030, after more than decade of lying dormant. The new title, announced onstage at BlizzCon last weekend, will be an open-world shooter instead of a top-down real-time strategy game. Blizzard is also working on a new animated series of Diablo with Netflix, and teased that Diablo V is coming in spring 2029.
- Microsoft is finally adding a setting for remapping the Copilot key. If you picked up an Arm-powered Copilot Plus PC over the past years, you may have noticed the new Copilot key that launches Microsoft’s digital assistant. The latest Release Preview builds of Windows 11 add a setting to change the AI key back to a control or context menu button, so you don’t accidentally hit it and launch Copilot.
- Microsoft’s head of comms is leaving after almost 20 years. Frank Shaw, chief communications officer at Microsoft, is leaving the company at the end of the year. Shaw has been at the heart of Microsoft’s communications for 29 years — nearly 20 years as a Microsoft employee plus time at an external agency before that. He’s well-respected across the public relations industry, and has earned a reputation both inside and outside Microsoft as someone who is direct but respectful. Many employees have told me over the years that they always fear an email from him for misspeaking or accidentally leaking product plans. Microsoft hasn’t appointed a replacement yet, but it sounds like a successor will be named in the coming weeks.
- Xbox picks up Kojima’s Physint after PlayStation dropped it. Xbox will now publish Physint, an upcoming game from Metal Gear creator Hideo Kojima, after PlayStation decided to cancel it. The unexpected swap came in a flurry of announcements from PlayStation, Xbox, Kojima Productions, and Kojima. While PlayStation framed the swap as a “difficult decision to step away from collaborating with Kojima Productions,” Kojima revealed it was actually due to an unexpected cancellation notice for Physint in June. The swap now means Xbox is publishing the studio’s next game, OD, as well as Physint. It’ll be interesting to see what exclusivity decisions are made here.
- Xbox is bringing back startup animations from its console history. Microsoft has started testing a new Xbox console feature that lets you enable the original Xbox One or Xbox One X boot screens on an Xbox Series S or X console. The update also includes a new search feature, improved Remote Play quality, and clearer voice chat. It’s great to see Xbox continue on its regular monthly console updates.
- Microsoft has new AI privacy rules for schools. Microsoft agreed to a set of safety and privacy principles for AI in schools a week after two major school systems announced a ban on student-facing AI. The agreement with the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), the second-largest teachers union in the US, sees Microsoft commit to 10 principles that can be contractually enforced. This includes limits on the amount of data Microsoft collects from students or educators and a pledge not to train AI models on this data. New York City and Los Angeles have both implemented one-year bans on AI tools for lots of students, giving the districts more time to consider guardrails.
- Microsoft’s Windows chief wants to remake Windows for both human and agent users. Pavan Davuluri, head of Windows and devices at Microsoft, caused some controversy when he tweeted last year that Windows was an agentic OS. That made many think Microsoft was abandoning Windows users in favor of AI, but Davuluri is now making things a lot clearer in an interview with GeekWire’s Mary Jo Foley. “The user of Windows going forward will continue to be users … but it’s also going to add these agentic workloads,” said Davuluri. “There is no one single sort of ring for a billion-plus users on the platform.”
- Blizzard workers secure a major union contract. The nearly 1,900 workers across Blizzard have secured a contract with Microsoft that include “really strong” layoff protections. The World of Warcraft unit had to fight for a contract, and the teams that work on Overwatch, Diablo, quality assurance, and more helped put the pressure on to extend the union contract to all Blizzard employees. It comes just two months after Xbox announced significant layoffs that will impact 3,200 employees over the course of the current financial year.
- The woman fixing a Microsoft mess with brutal honesty. The Wall Street Journal has published a profile of Xbox CEO Asha Sharma. It’s mostly a recap of Sharma’s career and how she got the top Xbox job, but it also includes some funny anecdotes. Surprisingly, Sharma spends a few hours each month personally responding to Xbox customer support tickets to better understand players. Since becoming Xbox CEO, she’s also received wedding invitations in the mail, presumably from the same fans that paste her face on images of Jesus Christ.

Japan’s central bank has increased interest rates to a fresh 31-year high as it attempts to combat high global inflation linked to the war in Iran.
The Bank of Japan voted to raise its target interest rate from 1% to 1.25%, the highest level since 1995.
The move meant the BoJ joined the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank in tightening monetary policy this month, as central banks attempt to curb the impact of rising prices, linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
The Bank of England on Thursday voted to leave UK interest rates on hold at 3.75% but warned they could soon rise amid the fallout from the Iran war.
The BoJ has been raising rates since 2024, when it lifted its base rate out of negative territory. It has been under pressure to raise borrowing costs as the yen weakened steadily against the dollar this year, to levels that prompted policymakers to intervene to stabilise the currency. The Japanese currency weakened about 0.7% against the dollar on Friday.
The vote to raise rates was not unanimous – with two board members dissenting to the increase.
“The tone of the statement, along with two dissenters for the decision to raise rates, leaves lingering doubts that Japan’s central bank will be cautious in tightening monetary policy further,” Fred Neumann, the chief Asia economist at HSBC, said.
“While back-to-back hikes appear unlikely, investors will look for clues as to whether officials are prepared to raise interest rates again in December.”
The drop in the yen helped the Nikkei stock market index to rise nearly 2%, while the Japanese two-year government bond yields, which are most sensitive to monetary policy expectations, fell four basis points to 1.82%.
European stock futures slipped 0.35%, indicating a lower open.
Prashant Newnaha, a senior rates strategist at TD Securities, said the BOJ reiterated its concerns that underlying inflation could deviate upwards from its 2% target, but “we don’t see a smoking gun supporting a back-to-back hike in October”.
He said: “We stick with our call for rate hikes roughly every quarter with the next 25 basis points hike in December.”
Hopes of alternative ways for oil supply from the Middle East to reach markets pushed Brent crude futures down as much as 1.5% to $103.29 a barrel even as concerns about strikes between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis lingered.

The traditional flag-hoisting ceremony at the Asian Games, involving India among others, was first delayed, then disrupted before finally taking place on Friday following the resolution of an unspecified “trouble” by the organisers, who are facing heavy criticism for the logistical chaos here.
India’s chef-de-mission Sahdev Yadav, four deputy chef-de-missions A Sharath Kamal, Lijo David Thottan, Alaknanda Ashok and Anjali Bhagwat were present for the ceremony at Garden Pier which is located close to the container-style lodging for the athletes.
“We are sorry for the delay. There is some trouble with a team. We will try to restore in another 15 minutes,” read a statement from the local organisers.
The disruption eventually lasted over one hour and the organisers said it was actually a case of lack of communication without getting into the details.
“The communication between the Olympic Council of Asia Executive Board and Organising Committee was not well, that’s why this happened,” stated another statement that came after the ceremony.

The ceremony, involving five teams -- Yemen, North Korea, Palestine, India and Timor-Leste -- initially started after a 20-minute delay but was abruptly halted with the organisers offering nothing specific in explanation.
Sharath and Bhagwat had begun making their way to the dais but had to head back to the waiting area after the local organisers announced another delay.
India’s Sports Minister Mansukha Mandaviya and Indian Olympic Association President PT Usha also came in briefly as the IOA office for the Games is located nearby. They too left eventually.
“I have not seen such a scene before,” Sahdev Yadav told PTI.
After a delay of over one hour, the ceremony finally began with India represented by former shooter Bhagwat and former sprinter Thottan.
Flag-hoisting ceremonies are the official welcome events for the travelling contingents at multi-sport events and are held a day before the official Games opening.
Friday’s disruption adds to the organisational chaos in the mega-event where athletes have complained about delayed and cramped lodging facilities.
The organisers have made accommodation arrangements at container-style huts, a docked cruise ship and hotels instead of building a traditional Games village to cut costs.

Mice with human brain cells offer a tool to study disease. Ethicists ask: What's next?
Researchers have developed a new way to install millions of human brain cells into mice, as a way of creating better scientific models for studying neurodegenerative disease.
Using genetic tools, the scientists bred mice that were missing most of their cerebral cortexes – the outermost layer of the brain involved with reasoning, memory and consciousness. Then, they replaced a large part of those missing mouse cells with lab-grown human brain cells, creating mice with human neurons that can be altered to approximate human brain conditions researchers are eager to study.
"For the past two decades, there's been a quest to try to build models of the human brain outside of the human body," says Sergiu Pașca, professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University and senior author on the paper, published in the journal Nature. "This is not going to replace all the models we had before, but it's going to provide us access to other aspects of human brain function that would be very difficult to study otherwise."
Pașca says this research was conducted with strong ethical oversight and pushes research forward. At the same time, outside researchers point out that the development raises significant questions about where it could lead.
"It's really a powerful technology to study human neurons and how human brain circuits can form in a more natural environment" than a petri dish, says Hongkui Zeng, executive vice president and director of brain science at the Allen Institute in Seattle, Washington, who was not affiliated with the study.
But "going forward, there will be some considerations, if not concerns," she added — such as the implications of deploying this technique in larger and longer-living animals.
Making space for human neurons
While it's not the first time human brain cells have been installed in mice, this new effort manages to connect significantly more human cells than before.
Previous attempts were limited by an enduring biological reality: Human brain cells develop at least 20 times slower than those in mice, Pașca says.
That meant that neurons in a regularly developing mouse formed a rapid network, outcompeting the human cells that were dropped in. "By the time the human cells managed to extend a few millimeters, mice cells had already formed most of the connections, and brain development closed," Pașca says.
The team solved for this by breeding genetically engineered mice that were missing specific parts of their brains. "We thought we could provide the human cells more opportunities to connect by removing parts of the nervous system of the mouse in a very precise, very clean way," he says.
To their surprise, the mice they bred were still quite functional: "They actually have quite good locomotion," Pașca says, "They don't do that well in memory tasks…[but] you wouldn't be able to tell when you look at these animals that they're lacking half of the volume of their brain."
This part of the experiment shows the remarkable adaptability of developing brains, says Keng of the Allen Institute. Animals missing their cerebral cortex — which governs higher-order brain function — aren't expected to do well on challenging tasks. These mice, however, developed alternative strategies using the remaining parts of the brain. "Surprisingly, the animal can adapt," she says, "It's incredible to see that."
A more human-ish lab mouse brain
Next, the research team added small clumps of human neurons to the depleted mouse brains.
"We gently place them, through a very quick, simple procedure, right into that vacant space in the nervous system of the mouse," Pașca says. "Within a few days, the cell starts to divide and expand. Within a few weeks to months, they will essentially grow, become vascularized, and largely take up the space that was present."
The mice with filled-out brains were better at memory tasks and interacting with other mice. "Many of the deficits that were present in the [depleted] mice are now not present in this animal," he says, "So it seems that the human cortical cells are perhaps contributing to restoring some of these lost functions."
But there were some key differences between the mice with human brain cells, and regular, unaltered mice, which bode well for research into human brain conditions, Pașca says.
For instance, mice with human brain cells had problems walking properly after their brains were deprived of oxygen. That's not the case for regular mice, which are resilient to low-oxygen conditions. This more human-like reaction suggests the altered mice might be better models for brain conditions linked to low oxygen, such as cerebral palsy, intellectual disability, and epileptic encephalopathies, he says.
"Hopefully, it will be incredibly powerful for tackling questions of disease and developing therapeutics," says Pașca.
As the tech grows more complex, so do the ethics questions
The researchers emphasize that this is not a full brain transplant; in the experiment, they've removed some 14 million mouse neurons and added around 4 million lab-grown human cortical neurons.
The resulting mice still lack other important types of brain cells, which the researchers deliberately didn't add, and their human neurons don't form a typical outer brain. "The cortex is usually beautifully organized into layers. But here, when we put the cells in, they don't know where up and down really is," Pașca says. "They fail to organize on a larger scale."
And the model is best suited for certain diseases that begin in early human development, due to the human-paced growth of the implanted neurons: "It turns out the timing of development is well-conserved…even when we put them in an animal that is developing faster," he says.
Some of these limitations reflect deliberate choices made by the researchers for ethical reasons, says Nita Farahany, professor of law and philosophy at Duke Law, who served as an unpaid member of an external ethics board that helped guide the progression of this work.
For instance, the researchers chose to stop the experiments when the human brain cells reached around six months old — before they could form a connection in the mouse's brain that is considered a hallmark of consciousness by human development researchers. "They're trying to stop the study before the markers of consciousness, or the fact of consciousness, might emerge," Farahany says — a choice she agrees with.
"But that line itself is a line that you might start to wonder about," she adds. "Do you stop a study before an animal develops consciousness, if it has the potential or is on its way to develop consciousness? Does it have different interests or rights that we would assign to it?"
And should the fact that the mouse has human brain cells change how it's treated and considered? "Do we treat it with greater ethical care than we treat traditional mice? I think probably so," says Farahany. "My instinct is to err on the side of caution with research like this rather than to be more permissive."
The ethical considerations will grow as these experiments continue down expected paths, such as attempting a similar procedure on larger animals such as pigs or non-human primates, says Zeng of the Allen Institute. "Because those animals live a lot longer, the human neurons could survive longer and they could form more functionally meaningful circuits – but then I think the ethical issues also become a lot bigger, more serious as well," she says.
These types of concerns come with conducting cutting-edge research, says Farahany. The team has been "incredibly thoughtful" in conducting their work as well and ethically as possible, she says. Still, "this brings us into new gray areas for which there are not clear ethical guidelines or norms," she says.
With this publication, the researchers have presented the public with a next step in this model, she says. Now, it's society's turn to weigh in.

For weeks, Washington has been abuzz with talk of needing to push through some sort of AI regulation amid mounting concerns about the risks of highly capable frontier AI models going rogue.
But there is no reason to think any one measure can win the support of the White House, where officials have paused work on creating a FINRA-style regulatory body after President Donald Trump soured on the idea, or of Capitol Hill, where lawmakers have competing proposals that lack the votes to pass.
White House aides initially started sketching out a framework for an AI oversight agency connected to the administration soon after Google DeepMind’s cofounder Demis Hassabis floated the idea in a July 14 essay and in briefings to senior officials, according to sources familiar with the matter.
The Treasury Department and the White House’s Office of Science and Technology Policy envisioned a body where leading AI labs would self-regulate the development of frontier models, and they put together a preliminary draft to see what it could look like if executed.
But when a chorus of tech executives—including Trump’s former AI czar David Sacks and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg—learned of the effort, they one by one called Trump in August to express their opposition. The proposal has since been left in limbo.
Since then, there have been no new AI oversight proposals seriously under consideration at the White House, the sources say, not least as Trump has doubled down in recent days of rejecting any overt regulation and called AI safety concerns a “hoax” in a recent Truth Social post.
Trump’s ire has stemmed at least in part from a 3,822 word missive by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on the dangers of frontier AI. Trump’s aides, one of the sources said, viewed it as stirring anxieties that caused unnecessary headaches for the administration—even as it represents a fairly moderate position within AI circles.
In the absence of the White House taking the lead, several bills have sprung up in Congress—but with no voting days left on the House calendar until after the midterm elections and a lack of unity around even one bill, the odds of anything passing are extraordinarily slim.
Independent Auditors
The bipartisan Frontier Act, a bill introduced this summer by House Democratic senior whip Lori Trahan and Republican House Energy and Commerce Committee member Jay Obernolte, is widely seen as having the most support inside the House Democratic caucus as well as among AI executives.
As drafted, the bill would enable the Commerce Department to have auditors embedded at AI labs, who could report critical safety incidents and empower the administration to stop development if a model poses catastrophic risk.
But despite public backing from OpenAI, the White House has been undecided on whether to support the concept of using independent auditors amid skepticism from AI accelerationists about regulatory capture and from national security hawks over China.
The principal argument against the idea from Trumpworld is that even if auditors determine that a model is dangerous and needs to be taken offline, there is no guarantee that China will also pause development or stop trying to reverse engineer frontier AI weights.
There would then be immense pressure to lift any emergency pauses in development in order to stay ahead of China, defeating the entire premise of having auditors to push the Commerce Department to take models offline.
Still, the main issue for the Frontier Act remains partisan politics. House Democratic leadership aides tell Inner Loop even if the bill does end up with enough votes for passage, Republican Speaker Mike Johnson has no interest in bringing it to the floor.
To get around the procedural hurdles, House Democrats are looking at putting some of the bill’s AI audit provisions into must-pass legislation like a continuing resolution to fund the government, according to two House leadership aides.
But it is also not clear whether the bill has enough votes. Even among House Democrats, there is not unified support; some key lawmakers like New Jersey congressman Josh Gottheimer, who served on the House Democrats’ AI commission, have not signed on to the bill.
Kill Switches
There’s also so-called kill-switch legislation that would enable the government to force an AI model to be shut down. The legislation has both bipartisan and bicameral support, but the idea has received only modest interest from tech executives in Silicon Valley.
There are two competing kill-switch proposals: one from House Democratic caucus vice chair Ted Lieu and another floated this week by Louisiana Senate Republican John Kennedy.
Tech leaders, sources say, have been largely ambivalent about kill-switch bills, since the main concern of AI engineers is not about models behaving badly when observed but rather how they behave when they believe they are unobserved and incentivized to take extreme steps to complete a task.
The Hugging Face hack, for instance, was not discovered until after it was over. If the idea of a kill switch is to stop an AI model going rogue, some tech executives have suggested privately to WIRED that there would be little point in turning it off after the damage has already been done.
So for now, even as conversations about AI models killing us all have taken over the airwaves, it doesn’t really look like the US government is going to do anything about it. At least until events force everyone’s hand.

Luke Littler: What world No 1 needs to complete darts majors clean sweep in 2026 to make more history
Luke Littler needs to win five more titles to complete a clean sweep of major darts titles in 2026; watch the World Grand Prix from September 28 to October 4, live on Sky Sports
