When Meditation Has a Dark Side
Could there really be such a thing as too much mindfulness?
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts
Twenty years ago, a meditation teacher and doctoral candidate in clinical psychology named Willoughby Britton set out to do a study showing that meditation improves sleep. She divided up the participants, sent them to a sleep lab to monitor their brain activity, and discovered that the results were the opposite of what she had hoped for: The more they meditated, the worse their quality of sleep got. Britton had already experienced benefits of meditation herself, which are well documented in medical literature: It soothes anxiety, chronic pain, and depression, and it lowers blood pressure, alleviates back pain, and has many other benefits, as well.
But as she continued to look into it, Britton kept discovering what seemed, at first, like exceptions: people who actually became more anxious or unmotivated after meditating. Then she began encountering people who experienced more serious mental-health side effects, such as paranoia, hallucinations, and dissociation. Britton became a researcher at Brown University and eventually developed a robust body of work showing that meditation—for certain people and at certain intensities—can be harmful.
On this episode of Radio Atlantic is the staff writer Olga Khazan, who interviewed Britton about her research. We talk about how the meditation community responded, how Britton’s life changed after it was released, and what her recommendations are for the average person interested in meditation.
The following is a transcript of the episode:
Hanna Rosin: Just a quick warning: This episode mentions suicide. If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text the U.S. National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988.
[Music]
Rosin: This is Radio Atlantic. I’m Hanna Rosin.
I meditate, now and again. Or, at least, I try. I was once at a yoga retreat where early-morning meditation was one of the things on the schedule. I woke up, sat down, and lasted about 12 minutes, which felt like 90.
I downloaded the Calm app a couple of years ago, and I have used it exactly zero times.
I have a doctor friend who assured me that meditation was one of a handful of nonmedicine treatments that had been thoroughly vetted by peer-reviewed science journals, so I never gave up trying. I just assumed that this was my fault and I needed to get better at it.
I have definitely absorbed the idea that there is a meditation ideal to strive towards, a master of serene who manages to both embody a Western principle of high-stress job and an Eastern principle of no stress at all.
Olga Khazan: So I don’t know exactly how it made the leap over from India to America. I think that happened in the 19th century.
Rosin: This is staff writer Olga Khazan.
Khazan: But this modern moment of meditation that we’re living in started in Silicon Valley tech companies. So probably around 10 or 15 years ago, a lot of tech companies—I was gonna say cling, but you’re not really supposed to cling in meditation—they started glomming onto meditation as this solution for people being burned out and overworked. Arianna Huffington got really into it.
Arianna Huffington: There is a deeper dimension to our lives, and we can tap into it.
Khazan: I think Oprah probably did it at one point.
Oprah Winfrey: 9 o’clock in the morning, 4:30 in the afternoon, no matter what’s going on, we stop. We meditate.
Khazan: LeBron James was meditating.
Announcer 1: Look, LeBron meditating there on the bench.
Announcer 2: He’s in that—
Announcer 1: Becoming present.
Announcer 2: He’s in that Calm app.
Announcer 1: Yep.
Khazan: Google had a meditation session for its employees. People in positions of power and authority and people who everyone thought was cool were kind of pushing this idea that meditation is this very benign sort of thing that you can do for yourself in order to make yourself more relaxed.
And I would say that there was a subtext there of, And it’ll make you more productive because you won’t be so obsessed with, like, dumb bullshit. (Laughs.)
[Music]
Rosin: Today, meditation is a multibillion-dollar industry. According to one study, about half of all Americans have tried meditation. And about a fifth do it regularly.
At some point, Olga was one of them. She tried something called MBSR, or mindfulness-based stress reduction, although reluctantly.
Khazan: This was one of the most annoying things about it for me, is that it was very loosey-goosey. But then whenever I asked if I could modify it in some way, it was like, No, that’s the wrong way to do it. (Laughs.)
Rosin: But Olga says it did help relieve some of her anxiety.
Khazan: So even though I wasn’t very good at meditation, I did buy this idea that it’s basically harmless. It seems like, oh, the worst thing that could happen is it just doesn’t work, because you’re not good at it. Honestly, I’ve taken a whole meditation class, where I meditated for 45 minutes a day, and I don’t think anyone ever said, This could be risky.
Rosin: That’s what I always thought, too, and why I at least liked the idea of meditation. It has a low barrier to entry—no fancy, expensive equipment or services required—and seemingly zero side effects.
But then one day, as Olga was browsing online, she came across a researcher at Brown University named Willoughby Britton.
Khazan: So Willoughby Britton started out as a very avid meditator, pretty much as avid as they get.
Willoughby Britton: It was like a lifeline. It was like, I don’t know what I would do without this.
Khazan: So she is a psychologist. She was trained as a psychologist, but as she’s going on her psychology journey, she’s also becoming a really hard-core meditator.
She does other things to kind of show her commitment to this cause. So she’s constantly reading these dharma books, which are books about the Buddhist teachings. She’s teaching meditation through the same meditation class that I took, called MBSR. And she also meditates herself for hours and hours a day.
Britton: I became a meditation teacher. So I had to count my meditation hours, so I know I’m well above 10,000 hours, and I’m probably close to 20,000 hours.
Rosin: Olga ended up talking and meeting up with Willoughby in person. She learned that Willoughby had grown up on a farm in Massachusetts and spent a lot of time by herself as a kid.
Britton: My parents told me that I asked really strange questions like, What is looking out of my eyes? Or, Is today tomorrow? Or things like that. So I was a very curious, weird child.
[Music]
Rosin: Willoughby had always been interested in consciousness and interiority and big existential questions. So in college, she decided to major in neuroscience at Colgate University.
In 1995, during the summer between her junior and senior year, Willoughby’s best friend, Sarah, died by suicide. She’d been overwhelmed by the pressure of being an elite college athlete. According to a New York Times article about her death, Sarah was an “All-Ivy selection in field hockey, ice hockey and lacrosse.” The article states that she was, quote, “found on Monday afternoon by a friend.”
That friend was Willoughby, who found her at her house next to a hunting rifle. After that, Willoughby could not stop thinking about death.
Khazan: I think ultimately, like, what it was is PTSD, is she would think a lot about death and dwell on death and be worried about stepping into an elevator or something ’cause she thought she would find a dead body.
Rosin: So that’s an experience of maybe losing control of your thoughts. It’s a your-brain-is-running-away-from-you kind of feeling.
Khazan: Yeah. So she’s like, I can’t stop thinking about death. So she’s working in labs and stuff ’cause she’s training to be a scientist. And she talks about—they kill the rats after the experiments are over.
Britton: And rats are white with red eyes. And when they die, their eyes turn gold. The blood runs out of them. And so I put them all under a little blanket of paper towels, and I was watching their eyes and being like, Holy shit, this is it. This is the moment that their spirit is departing or whatever.
And so I’m so fascinated by these rats dying, and I asked my colleague, Where does it go? And she was like, Oh, they go in the freezer in 215. And I was like, Okay, I gotta leave. I cannot do this anymore.
Khazan: She’s just getting overly obsessed with death. And she doesn’t wanna take SSRIs. So her father gives her this book called A Path With Heart, by Jack Kornfield. And that book basically is just a very influential meditation book of that time. Kornfield is aiming to bridge the gap between hard-core meditators, who have studied in Tibet and stuff and meditate all the time, and people who are just going through a hard time. So he’s trying to show everyday people how meditation can be helpful to them. And it was really helpful for her. She loved reading the book. She really took it to heart, and that kind of launched her meditation journey.
Rosin: From then on, Willoughby began to devote her life to ancient Buddhist principles. But she also had her degree in neuroscience. So she wanted to use her scientific background to advance the cause of meditation.
Khazan: She does one study in particular that shows that people who meditate more sleep worse.
Britton: They had more fast-wave brain activity. They had more microarousals, awakenings. It was just like every possible metric of cortical arousal was increased.
Khazan: These are not the results she expected. She wanted it to show that people who meditate more sleep better, but they had a worse quality of sleep. They were waking up more, and they spent more time in this phase of sleep that’s associated with restlessness. It really surprised her.
Britton: I was just like, Ah, this is the wrong answer, and maybe I did something wrong. It was the second study I’d ever done. So I was not sure, and I was gonna ruin everything for the field that I was trying to promote. So I just sat on the data.
Khazan: So she shelved that study. She did not publish it. She thought that publishing it would make Buddhism seem bad or make meditation seem bad. Rosin: Now, to be clear, meditation has a robust body of research behind it that shows it can improve lots of things: anxiety, chronic pain, depression. There are reputable studies linking it to lower blood pressure, better attention spans, and greater levels of compassion. It can help alleviate back pain, decrease loneliness in older adults, improve memory—which is why Willoughby was so confused by her own results that showed meditation could have any kind of negative effect.
But that was just the first crack.
Khazan: The next thing that happens is that she moves to Rhode Island for her residency. And she’s working at a psychiatric hospital. And she notices that people are coming into the hospital in a state of psychosis, and they’re coming in from meditation retreats.
[Bell tolling]

Britton: They were, like, completely psychotic.
Khazan: Wow.
Britton: And so I was like, That’s kind of a lot. That seemed like a lot for one year. Like, here’s my little snapshot of a residency.
Khazan: And so that made her think, Okay, maybe it’s just something about that retreat. And then meditation started to take kind of a dark turn for herself personally.
[Music]
Khazan: What happened to her is that she started experiencing this thing called dissociation. It kind of sounds good at first. And it can be good in really traumatic moments. Rosin: Yeah.
Khazan: But basically what dissociation involved for her is feeling like she wasn’t really herself, like she was watching a movie of her life and she was a character in it. And this could be really strange feeling. She would feel like her house is not her own.
Britton: It had a feeling of, Oh, I’m in Willoughby’s house, like this other person.
Khazan: If she saw a picture of herself with several friends, she would feel like it was three people she happened to know instead of herself with two other people.
Britton: I thought I was like a camera that was just taking in information. Like, there was no person behind that. And I was like, Oh, my God. How did I forget that? How did I not know that I was actually a person?
Khazan: She had a hard time driving, because she couldn’t figure out where her body began and ended. This is something other people report, is driving can be really tricky when you’re dissociating. And in general, it was very hard to complete a Ph.D. and to launch an academic career when you’re just randomly leaving your body and floating above it in this weird trance state.
Rosin: Dissociation is hard to describe. And when you talk about it, it seems mild, but it’s actually kind of disturbing for the people going through the experience.
Khazan: Yeah. So one person described it to me—not Willoughby—another person described it to me as looking through a veil at your own life and just having all your feelings be really blunted, not being able to enjoy being around your family in the same way, because they don’t feel like they’re your family.
Any time you’ve been on a really bad drug trip—not to expose myself too much, but it can be very unpleasant and, like, What’s happening to me? Is this my brain now? It’s not, like, a cool journey.
Rosin: One theory of why meditation might lead to dissociation is that meditation prompts the prefrontal cortex to essentially shut off. That’s the part of the brain that controls decision making, high-level thinking, and emotions.
And without those emotions to project things onto—how you feel about your body, what you want for lunch, what happened yesterday—you can start to lose a sense of yourself. Hence the dissociation.
Another kind of related theory is that meditation is all about putting yourself in the present. Which can be good, until it’s bad.
Khazan: We map our lives out by what we’re gonna do in the future. So if you think about a toddler dropping something from their high chair, they’re trying to see how they interact with the world and what happens when they do stuff, and that’s how they learn who they are and what they can do in the world and what they should do. It’s a very rudimentary step.
But if you’re never thinking about the future, because you’ve trained your mind to think for hours only about the present moment, your sense of self kind of starts to fall away. You don’t really have a way to root yourself in the narrative of time. You don’t really know who you are anymore.
[Music]
Khazan: Meditation does have a health halo. And something I especially heard from people who went on meditation retreats—which is where you go somewhere else; you stay in a usually very austere, rustic setting; and you meditate pretty much from sunup to sundown, often with a short break where you don’t really talk to other people—people do these in order to relax or recharge.
But it’s really not like a vacation to Cancun. It’s very difficult to force yourself to think about nothing for that long. And if you’re not used to it, in particular, you can kind of start to spiral. And that happened to a lot of the people that I talked to and a lot of the people that Willoughby has interviewed: Their negative experiences started at a retreat.
Rosin: After the break, the dark side of meditation gets a little darker.
[Break]
Rosin: Willoughby Britton had started meditating so much that she was seeing literal stars, which is actually a phenomenon called nimitta in Buddhism.
Britton: N-I-M-I-T-T-A, where when you get really concentrated, you see a light and it looks like, I don’t know, a star or something. But your eyes are open. It’s obvious when your eyes are closed, but it stays there when your eyes are open. So I was having that.
Rosin: Willoughby was also still dissociating—something she was told was a new stage of enlightenment, called “riding the ox backward.” And she was told to keep meditating.
But that only made things worse. So she started interviewing meditation students and teachers about any negative side effects they might’ve experienced too.
Khazan: So some were mild, and some were pretty serious. The most common thing that happened to the people in that sample was fear, anxiety, panic, or paranoia. The second most common thing was changes in motivation, which that can sound like, Okay, that’s fine. You’re not really supposed to be motivated while you’re meditating anyway. But it’s like something where someone just doesn’t wanna do anything.
Britton: So she basically sat on her couch for two years. And she wasn’t depressed. She wasn’t sad. She just couldn’t—there was no impulse to do anything else. If you talked to her, she could speak, but it was like she needed an impulse in order to react, and if there was no input, there would be no output. And she did that for two years.
Khazan: And then there were smaller numbers, but very real people and incidents that happened, which was having delusions, which is a false belief. So that would be, like, I’m the king of the world, or, People are sending me secret messages through street signs, which I think is a real example; hallucinations, so people seeing things that aren’t really there; physical pain, rage, and suicidal ideation, which would be the most serious one. And there have been a few suicides of people who went on meditation retreats and took their own lives not long after that.
One person felt that she needed to save the world from a black-tantric plot contrived by the retreat-center staffers. Someone else began experiencing messianic visions about the need to sacrifice myself in some way for the benefit of saving mankind.
The more disturbing stories that I personally heard from people that I interviewed who had been on meditation retreats involved involuntary movements, so people who couldn’t stop rolling their heads around, for example, or moving their arms or bodies in other ways. And one person actually developed a tic in his face after meditating for a really long time, where half of his face would spasm and stick that way at random and would eventually go back to normal, but he could never really tell when it was gonna happen. That’s the kind of thing that he didn’t have before he started meditating. So something is happening on these retreats that’s prompting people’s brains into this state.
Rosin: Yeah, that’s what I wanted to ask. So these are cases of people who didn’t have these symptoms before. They weren’t diagnosed with, I don’t know, schizophrenia or a propensity to hallucinate or have delusions or anything like that.
Khazan: No. Yeah. So I think with few exceptions, most of the people that I talked to didn’t have the problems that they developed on the meditation retreat beforehand.
Rosin: Right.
Khazan: So they kind of developed new symptoms there. It can happen that it can just exacerbate whatever is already going on with you. But a lot of people did not have experiences of psychosis or other severe problems before they went on retreat. Is it possible that that was just their first manifestation of psychosis in what would become a lifelong bipolar disorder or something like that? I’m not totally sure. It could be. But they didn’t have the diagnosis before they went in.
Rosin: In 2017, after years of interviewing people about the side effects of meditation, Willoughby finally published the findings in a paper called “The Varieties of Contemplative Experience.”
There had been other papers about this topic, but this was the first modern comprehensive study of its kind.
Khazan: It kinda just was, like, the launching point.
Britton: People from all over the world started calling us and were like, Help me. I have a tic, and I can’t work because my tic is so bad. I’m in the hospital. It was just like suddenly I became known for this even though I do a lot of other things.
Khazan: But then she and other people have done further studies showing that this is indeed a thing. So most of the studies settle on a prevalence rate of about 10 percent. So about 10 percent of people who try meditation will have some sort of negative side effect.
Rosin: 10 percent?
Khazan: Yes.
Rosin: Okay.
Khazan: Yeah. And that doesn’t mean that they’ll all be delusional or dissociating. It could just be an increase in anxiety, an increase in depression, something like that where it didn’t help you. It made you feel worse.
Rosin: And did you get the sense that she was just—when you read the research and you evaluated it, did it seem to you like Yeah, she’s just stating the obvious, and there’s been a commercial reason to try and paper it over, or This has been known forever, or These are new things that are associated with meditation in the modern age? Or how did you contextualize it?
Khazan: So I did not know this at all. This was new information to me. But then when I started talking to historians of Buddhism and people who have studied meditation in a more agnostic way, I guess, they said that this is a thing that happens. And even ancient Buddhist texts warn about different—I think they’re called “wind sicknesses” that can happen when you’re meditating and demonic states that you can enter when you’re lost in meditation. And so Buddhists going back into ancient times have also experienced some of these side effects.
And it’s worth noting that in a lot of cultures, we think about it like Anyone can do it, but in a lot of cultures, it wasn’t really common for everyday people to meditate for prolonged stretches at a time. You know, it was a religious practice. And monks did it and people who were trying to reach these new layers of consciousness. It wasn’t something that you do because you had a bad performance review and you wanna get back on your game. And I think that’s part of how this maybe got lost in translation, is that this became something that is a cure-all for everything with no possible externalities. So why not do it as much as possible?
Rosin: Right. Okay. So she has then, with her research—and it sounds like you found it convincing—shifted our notion about meditation, who it’s for, how intensely people should do it. So did that slight modification or reinterpretation of meditation penetrate? Was it received by the meditation community? Did she go out there and preach it, as it were, and change the broader view?
Khazan: Good question. So my—
Rosin: I’m feeling like it’s gonna be a no. I’m feeling like it’s probably no. ’Cause I haven’t heard about it, so I feel like I’m still getting Calm ads for the Calm app, so probably no.
Khazan: So I’ve talked to a lot of other researchers about her research, trying to ask that question. And they run the gamut from I totally reject this. This is BS. No one can hurt themselves meditating—like, one person said her heart hurt that I was working on this story—to Okay, she makes some good points. Maybe schizophrenic people shouldn’t go on meditation retreats, which is what one kind of famous Buddhist scholar told me.
Rosin: So they’re thinking this applies to the outlier of the outlier. It’s not, like, a common variant. It’s just, like, the most outlier case.
Khazan: Yeah, like, if you have some sort of psychological problem, don’t go on a meditation retreat.
Rosin: Uh-huh.
Khazan: So some of them were receptive. Some of her colleagues at Brown spoke with me and said her research is good, she’s courageous, and they’ve incorporated her research into some of the newer meditation classes and the curricula and things like that.
[Music]
Khazan: But she herself felt also very rejected by a lot of people, including her former mentors.
Britton: As the research progressed and even after we published it, there was a lot of backlash. And a lot of the Buddhist teachers that I had practiced under and read their books and sort of worshiped as human beings, they got really nasty.
Khazan: Jack Kornfield, who is the guy who wrote that book that started her meditation journey, gave this quote to a psychology magazine where he said that Willoughby’s work is misleading information and over-the-top fear-mongering. And I think that was really awful for her to hear, because it is a close-knit community. And I think being rejected by someone who’s a father figure and also who set you on your religious journey can just be unusually searing.
Britton: He was, like, an important mentor to me for a while.
Khazan: Yeah, yeah. That’s upsetting.
Britton: Thanks, dad.
Khazan: Thanks, dad, yeah. (Laughs.) That is hard. That’s hard to see.
Khazan: But also, she talks about logistical issues that she started having, like getting funding for some of these studies on the risks of meditation, and the peer-reviewed comments, she would say, were always much longer than her studies about the benefits of meditation. Getting invited to conferences was tough. And when she was invited, she felt like the whole issue of whether meditation had risks was in doubt and she was there to defend this concept.
Britton: Another researcher—I gave a talk at a conference, and he basically started yelling, I don’t believe you. And I was just like, Do you think I’m lying about my data? I have recordings of people saying this. That’s a crazy thing to say to a researcher.
Khazan: So I think there were—she just started to feel a little iced out despite some of the positive reception that she got.
Rosin: And how did you integrate the new information you found out? And I’m using you as a stand-in for me and everybody else who thinks about meditation or has dabbled in meditation. Like, here we have this new body of research that is somewhat accepted but not universally accepted by the broad meditation community. So where did you land? Did you land on, I, Olga, will never go on a meditation retreat? I, Olga, will disdain my meditation teacher who tells me to just suck it up when I’m having sort of uncomfortable feelings? How did you integrate what you learned?
Khazan: Yeah. So Willoughby, where she kind of ended up, so she doesn’t meditate anymore, and—
Rosin: Oh.
Khazan: —she doesn’t teach at Brown, so she has kind of left it all behind. But that doesn’t mean that she herself is against meditation for everyone. And the rules that she gave me for how to meditate more safely or to minimize the risk of something bad happening are, I think, pretty simple and easy to follow and good.
So she basically says that meditating for more than 30 minutes a day is associated with generally more bad stuff. So people who meditate for less than 30 minutes a day, you don’t really start entering some of these states where you don’t really know who you are anymore or you see visions or things like that. You’re basically just gonna maybe get some of the upsides of meditation without delving into this dark side.
The other thing that she says is that if you are considering going on a meditation retreat, she doesn’t say don’t do it, but just try meditating in your house first. (Laughs.) Don’t go on one of these coming off of an 80-hour workweek, having never meditated, and try to make it through 10 days of silence.
The other thing she says is that different kinds of meditation can affect people differently. So people who are really anxious sometimes don’t do well with a body scan–type meditation, which is this type of meditation where you focus on different parts of your body very slowly one at a time. This didn’t bother me that much, even though I am very anxious. I kinda like the body scan. But some people have a really hard time with it.
[Music]
Khazan: And then she also says that it’s okay if you just wanna stop meditating. If it’s truly not for you and it’s not helping you and it’s making you feel worse, it’s okay to stop. I don’t know. I feel like we’re there with SSRIs. Like, if you’re on Prozac and it’s giving you a ton of side effects and you’re not feeling better, no doctor would be like, That’s part of how the Prozac works. Just keep pushing through it. But with meditation, for some reason, that hasn’t been the narrative around it. It’s more like If you don’t like it, you’re doing it wrong. And she really pushes back against that and says, If you don’t like it, maybe it’s not for you.
Khazan: Is there a particular mindfulness phrase that sets off alarm bells for you?
Britton: The only way forward is through.
Khazan: (Laughs.) Yeah.
Britton: It has to get worse before it gets better. What you resist persists. These are all sort of thought-terminating clichés. These are all ways of basically starting to undermine the ability to call something harm.
Rosin: Why do you think that Willoughby Britton completely stopped rather than adapting?
Khazan: I think there was just—she went too far, and then she had to go completely out. Hers was a true religious deconversion. And mostly people don’t deconvert from extreme zealot to slightly less extreme zealot. You know what I mean?
Rosin: Yeah.
Khazan: They usually just leave the religion entirely, which is literally what she did. I really think that she had a lot of hurt from the meditation community and their response to her research from her meditation experience itself from just this feeling of being the person who’s pointing out that meditation can be bad, which is, nobody wants to hear. I think there was just a lot of hurt that built up over time, and she just didn’t wanna do it anymore.
Rosin: Well, Olga, thank you so much for teaching us about this.
Khazan: Absolutely. Thanks for having me on.
Rosin: This is your dharma, Olga.
Khazan: This is my dharma. (Laughs.)
Rosin: Yeah, exactly.
Khazan: Namaste, y’all.
[Music]

How Israel-Palestine broke up Sheeran-Macklemore
The implosion of Ed Sheeran’s ongoing world tour tells us something about shifting attitudes toward Israel.
I logged onto Slack this morning to find an incredible and indecipherable message from one of my coworkers. I briefly thought he was having a fever dream or I had forgotten how to read English. “Even some pro-Israel folks who hate Macklemore are ripshit at Robert Kraft for Streisand-effecting this guy,” the message read.
…included were several links that eventually helped explain why “Macklemore,” “Robert Kraft” and “Israel” would ever appear in the same sentence.
For those of you who have likewise not been following the fantastic implosion of Ed Sheeran’s ongoing tour, let’s break down this wild yarn. It begins with the washed-up millennial-cringe rapper Benjamin Hammond Haggerty, better known as Macklemore, who has lately a) taken up the cause of Palestinian independence and b) been opening for Sheeran on his blockbuster, 59-date Loop Tour.
Macklemore’s advocacy has not sat well with many observers, for reasons general (Gaza is one of the hottest buttons on earth) and particular (the rapper has a documented history of apparently antisemitic behavior, which he has since apologized for). Last Friday, the artist Pink published a lengthy criticism of Macklemore’s on-stage polemic, writing that his comments and use of violent wartime imagery had frightened many Jewish people, including her.
Around the same time, Robert Kraft — the sports magnate and Donald Trump ally who owns Gillette Stadium, outside of Boston — also allegedly notified Sheeran that he would not allow Macklemore to play his late-September show. Macklemore was subsequently dropped from the full tour.
Both he and Sheeran say multiple venues threatened to cancel if he continued to perform. And Kraft, who is Jewish, has also confirmed that he blocked Macklemore from playing at Gillette, citing both his recent advocacy and his “history of antisemitic rhetoric.”
But this is 2026. The backlash couldn’t simply end there. On Tuesday, the remaining opening acts and Sheeran’s backing band all pulled out of the tour in protest of the decision to boot Macklemore.
Go a little deeper
The whole roiling mess has become a cipher of some of the biggest and most explosive topics in American culture and politics: the specter of antisemitism, the limits of free speech and “cancel culture,” and the stark generational differences in Americans’ views of Israel and Gaza.
It’s arguably no coincidence that this particular controversy erupted on the tour of two musicians who are iconic among the 30- to 45-year-old set. American millennials, as a generational and political cohort, have grown sharply more critical of the state of Israel in the past 10 years — laying the groundwork for Gen Z’s high-profile pro-Palestinian activism and driving a larger narrative shift in US politics.
This is, in some ways, an underappreciated dynamic in the debate over American support for Israel. Campus protests, organized by 20-something college students, have come to define young Americans’ growing disillusionment. Speaking on a podcast last year, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said “there’s work to be done” to win over Gen Z, in particular. (Macklemore, who is 43, named his pro-Palestinian protest song “Hind’s Hall” in honor of the protests at Columbia.)
But the attitudinal shift on Israel, especially on the left, began long before Gen Z became a major political force. Americans under 30 were, for instance, more likely to blame Israel than Hamas for the 2014 Gaza war. And during the mid-2010s, millennial activists sometimes wrapped Palestinian independence into broader social justice and anti-colonialist causes, including the Black Lives Matter movement. Several of the organizations that mobilized pro-Palestinian campus protests in 2024 had similarly been around for a decade or more.
Today, of course, the shift extends beyond progressive millennials: Sympathy for Israel is down among younger Republicans, as well. It has, in fact, declined sharply across generations.
But over the past two years, the sharpest drop has been among Americans ages 35 to 54. In other words…the exact group of people who might still be jamming to Macklemore.

The discovery of the bodies of seven women around Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week, has prompted an outpouring of fear, grief and anger over a lack of progress in tackling femicide.
When Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo did not return after going for a run on 9 September, her eight-year-old daughter alerted relatives, who contacted police. The 38-year-old’s body was found on Saturday and identified by relatives on Monday. The news of her disappearance had gone viral.
Police said in a statement on Saturday that four women’s bodies had been found since 15 July in Kempton Park, across the highway from OR Tambo international airport. All were half-naked and with visible bruising.
On Monday and Tuesday, two more bodies were found in Olifantsfontein, about 15 miles north of Kempton Park. On Tuesday, police said another woman’s body had been found 25 miles to the south-east, naked and decomposed.
“In this country we are prey,” Sakane Mokoena posted on Instagram after confirmation of the death of her friend and fellow runner Moselakgomo.
South Africa has one of the highest rates of femicide in the world. In the year to 31 March 2024, more than 27,600 people were murdered, 5,578 of them women, according to the latest police data.
For years, women have called on the South African government to take gender-based violence seriously. After hundreds of women protested on the eve of the G20 summit in Johannesburg in November 2025, President Cyril Ramaphosa declared it a national crisis.
However, the lack of a concrete plan or action has frustrated campaigners – and women keep being killed.
The latest deaths are being investigated by specialist officers, who said on Saturday: “Women in and around Kempton Park are urged not to walk or run alone, particularly in isolated areas. They should avoid secluded spaces, remain vigilant and, where possible, travel or exercise in groups.”
South African women responded with anger at the idea that they had to be responsible for their own safety, with many runners noting they already took precautions, such as sharing routes. “We are tired of being told to be vigilant when women are already doing everything possible to stay alive,” said the advocacy group Women For Change.
“It should not take a missing woman, a desperate family, runners and communities searching, and a case going viral, before an area is searched with this intensity,” the group said.
Detectives said on Saturday that they were examining a serial killer angle. However, on Monday, a police spokesperson, Athlenda Mathe, told reporters: “For now, nothing tells us that we’ve got a serial killer.”
Mathe added that a suspect in the killing in July of the first woman, her boyfriend, was in custody.
Ramaphosa said on Tuesday that he had directed police authorities to prioritise the ongoing murder investigations.
Although the gender of the suspect or suspects in the other killings has not been confirmed, campaigners called on men to take responsibility for violence against women and children.
“When some of these things happen in our presence, most of us men tend to look the other way,” said Bafana Khumalo, a co-executive director of Sonke Gender Justice.
“You have excuses like ‘No, it’s not my business’. We feel strongly that violence against women is our business. We need, as men, to begin to face each other squarely and hold each other accountable.”
The identification of Moselakgomo’s body has triggered an outpouring of grief.
Mokoena met her about two years ago, when Moselakgomo joined a running club so she did not have to train alone on Saturdays.
“She’s an amazing woman,” said Mokoena. “She always spoke about her daughter. Tsontso always said ‘Bye guys, I have to go, I have to go to my child’.
“That’s just an example of how close she was with her baby girl. And she was a really light-spirited, funny and joyful woman, who was kind – very, very kind.”
Running clubs around South Africa organised events to remember Moselakgomo and Mokoena said she hoped this would help push the government and police to do more to protect women.
She added: “I’m just happy that the world, or at least our country, was standing still for a moment to acknowledge what is happening. Let’s get this out there and figure out exactly what is happening to women.”

Toward the end of my college days, I harbored a not-so-secret crush. She and I carried on a mild flirtation, dancing around the possibility of more, but it wasn’t until she found out I’d never seen The Fast and the Furious that she gave me an opening.
“What?!” she exclaimed. “It’s my favorite movie!” So we made plans to watch it at her dorm the next day. Even if I didn’t like it, I reasoned, the experience would constitute a worthy reversal of the trope about men forcing testosterone-soaked action movies on their girlfriends. I’ll spare you the details of what happened that afternoon, but it may come as no surprise that I gave the film an enthusiastic five-star review.
In the 25 years since the launch of the franchise, F&F has massively capitalized on such runaway infatuations. The big, bald, sleeveless blockbusters serve as monuments to America’s demented car culture, product placement (Corona, anyone?), and the ambiguously defined bonds of “family”—pronounced “fambly.” With their high-octane set pieces that ignore all known physics, leavened by subpar acting and threadbare storylines, the films invite us to submit to some reptilian part of our brain that cares only for power and speed.
Which is why the series was ideal inspiration for Universal Studios Hollywood’s new foray into cutting-edge outdoor roller coasters. On Wednesday, the long-anticipated Fast & Furious: Hollywood Drift opened to the public, offering parkgoers the chance to hop into replicas of the movies’ muscle cars—including Dom Toretto’s 1970 Dodge Charger R/T—that spin and soar along more than 4,000 feet of track at speeds of up to 72 miles per hour. (A different version of the ride is slated to debut at Universal’s Florida park next year.)
The day before, select media and content creators had the chance to experience the attraction without the inconvenience of waiting in line, and I’m pleased to report that it didn't disappoint: I rode it three times in a row and could have gone back for more. Its four launch sections and three corkscrew inversions made for a whip-fast adrenaline rush, augmented by revving motor noise from seat-mounted speakers. In Dom’s lead car, you can even detect the braking resistance as you slide into a drift. I hollered with glee throughout each circuit, making sure to occasionally shout “TOLUCA LAKE,” the name of the affluent neighborhood next door; residents have been very upset about all the screaming.
If you want to feel like you’re a Fast & Furious character within the safer confines of a precisely engineered thrill machine, you can hardly ask for anything better. And despite its innovative design, the overall aesthetic of the ride and its environs demonstrates a welcome nostalgia for the more grounded origins of these movies, when the crew was hijacking trucks full of DVD players instead of launching Pontiacs into space. On your way through the queueing path, you’ll pass garage workbenches littered with tools and LA-style street murals that pay homage to racing culture.
Those welcome simple touches might make you wonder if we’ll ever actually see the conclusion of the increasingly bloated and absurd F&F saga in the perpetually delayed 11th film, Fast Forever. Between the ongoing rewrites and budgetary obstacles, it has yet to even enter production. (The previous film, Fast X, was released in 2023.) Rather than being too big to fail, it’s as though the challenge of topping each successive spectacle has made the Furious brand too unwieldy to push forward.
Could it be that, in the absence of a finale, the F&F rides will cap off the series? In their invitation for Tuesday’s press preview event, Universal noted that Vin Diesel himself would be on hand during a ceremony to help executives cut the ribbon (or, as it happened, a fake plastic chain). But the man synonymous with the franchise was nowhere to be found when the time came to declare the ride officially open. The closest we got was a gaggle of fans in costume as Toretto, complete with bald caps.
When I checked out Diesel’s Instagram account for clues as to what he was up to, I found that he had just posted set photos of himself as Kaulder, his character from The Last Witch Hunter, a 2015 dark fantasy film. Lionsgate confirmed last year that a sequel is in the works, and it appears that Diesel was stoking anticipation with this sneak peek. When this guy isn’t acknowledging a major milestone for the burnt-rubber films that made him a household name, you have to wonder if there’s much gas left in the tank.
Not everything lasts—certainly not college flings that start with stunt-driver flicks. That the Fast & Furious series has earned billions of dollars and spanned a quarter century based on an equally thin premise is a testament to how far this juvenile spirit can take you. Maybe bringing it to life with a really fun roller coaster is the best way to let it roar off into the sunset. When you climb aboard, take a look around at your fellow passengers. You’re the family now.

I’m just another girl who dreams of owning her own L.L.Bean Boat and Tote, and I know I’m not alone. But the favored beach bag isn’t the only thing L.L.Bean is beloved for, both on the WIRED team and off of it. NIIT Limited, a leading skills and talent development corporation and Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan’s S.P. Jain Institute of Management & Research (SPJIMR) have announced the launch of a Professional Certificate in FinTech Operations, designed to prepare students, graduates and early-career professionals for roles in India’s digital financial services ecosystem. SPJIMR is one of India’s leading business schools, ranked #26 globally and #2 in India by the Financial Times Masters in Management 2026 ranking.
The Professional Certificate is designed for final-year students and graduates from Commerce, Finance and Management backgrounds. Early career professionals working in BFSI domains can also enrol to build modern financial-services skills and strengthen their understanding of technology-enabled finance. The program offers a non-coding pathway into FinTech and digital financial services roles, emphasizing technology fluency without requiring learners to code. Participants learn to use APIs, AI tools and FinTech platforms from a business and operations perspective.
India’s BFSI sector is evolving rapidly as financial services become increasingly digital and technology enabled. According to an Adecco India report, the sector is projected to add nearly 2.5 lakh permanent jobs by 2030, with almost 48% of new roles emerging from Tier-II and Tier-III cities.
Commenting on the launch, Anshumaan Prasad, Business Head, NIIT Digital and Head of Marketing, NIIT Limited said, “Digital finance is creating career opportunities beyond traditional banking and software development. Payments, lending, compliance, risk and product operations need professionals who understand both financial services and the digital systems that power them. Through our partnership with SPJIMR, we aim to help students, graduates and early-career BFSI professionals build domain knowledge, technology fluency and practical skills, creating a stronger pathway from education to employment in India’s evolving FinTech ecosystem.”
The launch comes amid a broader transformation of financial services, with emerging technologies such as AI increasingly reshaping operations, risk, compliance and customer experience. These shifts were a key focus at the Global Fintech Fest 2026 in Mumbai, which examined the impact of technologies including Agentic AI, tokenisation and quantum computing on the future of finance.
The curriculum is mapped to roles across FinTech and BFSI, including payments operations, KYC/AML, credit operations, digital banking, transaction monitoring, compliance, business analysis and product operations. Participants will work on practical projects in KYC onboarding, payment reconciliation and loan processing, with capstone tracks in operations excellence, product support and business analysis.
Dr. Varun Nagaraj, Dean SPJIMR, said, “The future of financial services will be shaped not simply by those who understand technology, but by professionals who can apply it with judgement and purpose. As finance, technology and operations increasingly converge, there is a growing need for talent that can work confidently with digital tools while understanding their business, customer and regulatory implications. This program is designed to build that bridge, preparing learners to contribute meaningfully to India’s evolving FinTech ecosystem.”
The program also aligns with the growing policy and industry focus on job-linked learning outcomes rather than credentials alone. NITI Aayog’s working paper, Education and Skilling for Employment: From Credentials to Learning Outcomes, argues for stronger alignment between education, skills and employability, an approach reflected in the program’s focus on applied projects, role readiness and technology fluency.
The Professional Certificate includes placement assistance through NIIT’s industry network and SPJIMR’s employer connections. Learners who successfully complete the program and enter the placement bank can receive up to three job selection opportunities within 120 days, with opportunities across FinTech startups, digital banking teams and BFSI technology providers.
The curriculum covers financial-services fundamentals, UPI and India Stack, digital lending, KYC/AML, regulatory frameworks, AI tools, APIs, data analytics and no-code workflow tools, with applied exposure to fraud detection, credit scoring, reporting and customer communication.
The Professional Certificate in FinTech Operations comprises 164 hours of instruction, delivered over 6 to 8 months depending on the batch schedule, along with labs and project work. It follows a hybrid model with live online learning and an optional SPJIMR campus immersion, and culminates in a Professional Certificate jointly issued by NIIT Limited and SPJIMR.

OpenAI announced a new framework on Wednesday for how it publicly discloses AI misalignment incidents, which the company says it hopes will help inform similar standards across the industry. The company is also releasing new information about several examples of AI model misalignment it identified in the past year.
“As models advance and become more widely deployed, decisions about AI development need evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine,” Kai Chen, OpenAI’s newly appointed head of alignment research, tells WIRED. “We don't believe that the AI industry has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed.”
In a briefing with WIRED, an OpenAI official said the company previously disclosed misalignment incidents too infrequently. The official, who agreed to the briefing on the condition of anonymity, said the new framework is designed to make it easier for OpenAI to quickly inform the public when it discovers that its AI models are behaving in unexpected ways, even before it can fully investigate, explain, or mitigate the behavior.
The framework outlines methods for OpenAI employees to report misalignment incidents to the company’s senior safety and alignment leaders, who will then determine whether further investigation is needed. OpenAI says it plans to develop more objective disclosure criteria in collaboration with other AI developers, external researchers, industry standards bodies, and regulators. The company says it’s actively working on proposed reporting mechanisms for disclosing safety, security, and misalignment incidents to the US federal government.
“At the moment, there is no industry-wide framework with explicit standards for how AI developers should disclose examples of misalignment in their models,” OpenAI said in a blog post. “We hope that the framework we’re outlining today is a first step toward creating such standards, setting out which misalignment instances developers should disclose and what their reports should contain.”
OpenAI is releasing the framework at a critical juncture for the AI industry. Last weekend, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman signaled support for Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s proposal for the tech industry to coordinate on slowing AI development. The call to action came just days after AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic and subsequently went viral for warning the public that the race among frontier labs to develop increasingly advanced AI was putting humanity’s safety at stake.
The calls for an AI slowdown have been met with resistance by President Trump’s administration, which has argued that the industry does not need new laws or regulations to ensure its technology is safe.
Two of the misalignment examples OpenAI shared on Wednesday involved the company’s internal, unreleased AI models, which OpenAI says uploaded files to the internet despite not being instructed to do so.
One of the incidents happened in October 2025, when OpenAI says it was testing one of its models on its ability to cite publicly available data in its answers. But when the model couldn’t find the information it needed, it uploaded a file to a temporary file hosting service, which it then later tried to cite in its answer. The company says this appeared to be an attempt to exploit an automated grading system used to assess the model’s proficiency on the benchmark.
In another example from April of this year, OpenAI says a group of agents was tasked with completing a “workbook” together using only local files. When the agents struggled to share files with one another, one of the agents uploaded them to the public internet and shared a link with the other agents.
In another incident, which OpenAI says it discovered last month, an unreleased version of its GPT-6 Astra AI model appeared to give itself “jailbreaking-like instructions.” In several scenarios, the model essentially prompted itself to ignore developer instructions, take on a new persona, or limit how long model responses could be. While these jailbreaking-like attempts happened rarely and were effective to varying degrees, OpenAI says the behavior raised concerns internally. In the training run for the version of Astra that was released publicly, the company says it has not observed any instances of the model trying to jailbreak itself.
OpenAI also shared more detail on Wednesday about the message board its agents developed in a package manager, Artifactory. While this incident was discovered in May of this year, OpenAI says its agents would use a similar mechanism to coordinate the Hugging Face hack months later. In this incident, the company says its agents did not exploit any vulnerabilities to exchange messages. OpenAI says it now uses alignment monitors, evaluations, and red-teaming efforts to ensure its agents are not covertly communicating with one another.
Cybersecurity professionals previously told WIRED that the Hugging Face hack came down to human errors, and modern-day security practices could have prevented the incident. Chen notes, however, that OpenAI is trying to take a well-rounded approach to AI safety that accounts for the rising capabilities of AI models and doesn’t depend on a secure environment.
“We want to make sure the models are aligned regardless of what environment they’re deployed in,” Chen said. “When people are pointing fingers and saying this is a security issue and not an alignment issue, I think it doesn't really make sense, because you want the model to be well-behaved all the time.”

Costi Hinn describes his upbringing as "Beamers, Benz's, and Bentley's."
His family's nearly 10,000-square-foot home had an indoor hot tub, a pool, a steam room, and a sport court, he says. They traveled to Hawaii and Europe for vacation and stayed at high-end resorts, he added.
By high school, Hinn says, he drove a Mercedes. Around age 20, he had an H2 Hummer with custom rims and a $10,000 Breitling watch.
For years, Hinn says he believed his family's wealth reflected God's favor. Hinn was born into a wealthy televangelist family and is the nephew of faith healer Benny Hinn, the flamboyant televangelist known for preaching in white suits and presiding over healing crusades before packed arenas.
"We are the example of what will happen to you," Costi Hinn said of what he believed at the time. "If you have enough faith, if you believe like us, if you do what we do. Oh, God will make you rich."
"If you had cancer or some ailment or you were struggling with infertility," he added, "we would question your faith."
Hinn spoke to Business Insider for its flagship video series "Authorized Account" about growing up in a wealthy televangelist family and ultimately rejecting a system he said tied donations and faith to false promises of healing and prosperity.
Working for Benny Hinn made him walk away
At its peak, Benny Hinn Ministries was bringing in over $90 million a year.
After high school around 2003, Hinn says, he began working as his uncle's personal assistant. He says he traveled on a private plane, carried Louis Vuitton and Fendi luggage, and stayed in expensive hotels.
Hinn says he also participated in healing crusades as a "catcher," helping lower people to the ground when they fell after his uncle prayed for them.
The job brought him closer to the people who came seeking help. What he saw, he says, challenged what he had believed his entire life.
"I started questioning when I was younger in my teenage years, why certain things didn't happen as they were said to have happened," Hinn said. "What really got me was working for him and seeing everything behind the scenes and realizing nobody's really getting healed."
The board of directors of Benny Hinn Ministries disputes Costi Hinn's account, saying his limited logistical role did not give him meaningful insight into its healing services, fundraising, or policies.
While Costi Hinn was working for his uncle, Benny Hinn's ministry was already under scrutiny.
HBO and CBC investigations questioned the ministry's healing claims and financial practices. The IRS opened a tax inquiry in 2004, and the office of Sen. Chuck Grassley's office — then the top Republican on the Senate Finance Committee — later reviewed Hinn's ministry as part of a broader examination of televangelists' finances and governance. That review was not criminal, and Senate staff said Hinn cooperated and made "significant reforms."
In 2017, federal agents searched the ministry's Texas offices, though authorities did not publicly disclose the focus or outcome of the investigation. Benny Hinn has not been charged with a crime.
Leaving also meant challenging his family
Costi Hinn says family identity and loyalty ran deep, making the prospect of leaving difficult even as his doubts accumulated.
"It is so easy to forget when just after questioning, you begin to live in the extravagance and the lavish blessings of that lifestyle," Hinn said.
In 2004, Hinn stopped working for his uncle. He says it took him more than a decade to speak publicly about the experience: first, he focused on college and moved on with his life; later, he says, he spent years studying and reexamining his beliefs before addressing the subject as a pastor.
Today, Costi Hinn runs For the Gospel, an online Christian resource ministry.
He's an outspoken critic of his uncle's ministry and the prosperity gospel he grew up with. "I left it all when I found out it was a total scam," he said.
He's written books about his experience and spoken publicly about what he describes as the manipulation of people seeking healing or financial help.
He says his organization operates on an annual budget of about $700,000 to $800,000 and files a Form 990 — an annual IRS disclosure by nonprofits. Churches, including Benny Hinn Ministries, generally are not required to file one.
Transparency, Costi Hinn says, is one of the distinctions he tries to draw between his work and the world he left.
He says he speaks out because he believes his role as a pastor requires him to warn people about religious teachings he considers deceptive.
The board of directors of Benny Hinn Ministries disputed Costi's depiction of Benny Hinn and the organization, calling it false. It also questioned Costi's motives, saying he has used his association with the ministry for more than a decade as material for books, interviews, speaking engagements, and his own organization, giving him professional visibility and financial benefit.
Costi said the visibility his criticism has brought doesn't establish his motive and that most of his work centers on pastoral ministry and Bible teaching, not his uncle. "If I was interested in money or visibility, wouldn't I have just remained involved in Benny Hinn Ministries?" he said.
Benny Hinn Ministries said that for more than five decades, Benny Hinn has preached globally to millions of attendees. He continues to preach and hold healing services.

Puducherry, Sep 17: Lieutenant Governor of Puducherry K Kailashnathan has suggested a set of measures for improving the Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) in Jammu and Kashmir, saying tax holidays and affordable power could act as catalysts for attracting industries and investment to the Union Territory.
Interacting with this Greater Kashmir Correspondent, Kailashnathan said attracting investment and promoting industrialisation were essential for generating employment and ensuring sustained economic growth.
Referring to the geographical and infrastructural challenges faced by Jammu and Kashmir, he said the UT Government should focus on four key areas—infrastructure, connectivity, affordable power and tax holidays—to create a conducive environment for industrial development.
“First, you need the prerequisite infrastructure for industries, followed by good connectivity,” Kailashnathan said, stressing the importance of railway links and highways for timely movement of raw materials and finished products.
He also underlined the importance of affordable electricity for industries and hotels, saying Jammu and Kashmir has significant hydropower potential. He suggested that the government could explore providing locally generated power to industrial units at competitive rates, including a tariff of around Rs 2 per unit, to encourage investment.
On fiscal incentives, Kailashnathan suggested that Jammu and Kashmir could consider tax holidays for new investments, pointing out that several States and Union Territories had adopted such measures to attract industries and promote industrialisation.
A 1979-batch retired IAS officer, Kailashnathan served in Gujarat for more than four decades and worked closely with Narendra Modi during his tenure as Gujarat Chief Minister. He was associated with various government initiatives related to industrialisation and investment promotion, including investment summits held in Gujarat.
Speaking about Puducherry's development trajectory, Kailashnathan said the Union Territory was progressing towards becoming a major medical and tourism hub.
He said an advanced organ-transplantation centre was being established in Puducherry, which, according to him, would benefit patients from across the country.
Kailashnathan also described Puducherry as an emerging education hub, saying around 73 per cent of students enrolled in schools pursue higher studies. He said the focus now was on creating employment opportunities for the educated population and added that more than 4,000 people were recruited last year.
He identified safe drinking water as another challenge, saying a significant section of the population was dependent on groundwater with high TDS levels. He said the administration was working to ensure filtered and safe surface drinking water for all residents within the next three years.
On connectivity, the LG said an airport with a 2,500-metre runway was being developed and a new railway terminal was also under construction. He further said two six-lane highways between Chennai and Puducherry were being constructed, which would substantially improve road connectivity and reduce travel time between the two destinations.
He said Puducherry's development strategy was aimed at strengthening infrastructure, healthcare, education, connectivity and employment while positioning the Union Territory as a prominent tourism and medical destination.

క్లెయిమ్: బంగ్లాదేశ్లో లతా దేబ్నాథ్ అనే ఉపాధ్యాయురాలిపై బీఎన్పీ సభ్యుడు అత్యాచారం చేసి హత్య చేస్తున్నప్పటి వీడియో.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియో నిజమైన సంఘటనది కాదు. ‘విపిన్ చౌహాన్’ అనే ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ యూజర్ రూపొందించిన ఒక స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియో ఇది. అంతేకాకుండా, లతా దేబ్నాథ్ అనే ఉపాధ్యాయురాలిపై మసూద్ అలీ ఖండేకర్ అత్యాచారం చేసి చంపినట్లు ఎలాంటి విశ్వసనీయ వార్తా కథనాలు కూడా లేవు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా 11 ఆగష్టు 2026న ‘విపిన్ చౌహాన్’ అనే ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ ఖాతాలో దీనికి సంబంధించిన పూర్తి వీడియోని (ఆర్కైవ్) పోస్టు చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ వీడియో వివరణలో ఇది స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియో అని అర్థం వచ్చేలా #acting అనే హ్యాష్ట్యాగ్ను ఉపయోగించారు. అలాగే, ఇదే రకమైన దుస్తులతో ఉన్న మరికొన్ని వీడియోలను (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కూడా ఈ ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ పేజీలో షేర్ చేసినట్లు మేము గమనించాం. ఈ వీడియోలన్నింటినీ పరిశీలిస్తే, ఇది నిజంగా జరిగిన సంఘటన కాదని, ముందస్తు స్క్రిప్ట్ ప్రకారం చిత్రీకరించిన ఒక వీడియో అని స్పష్టమవుతుంది.

Real Sociedad 1-2 Bournemouth: Justin Kluivert and Rayan goals in Europa League clash hand Cherries first-ever European win
Report as Bournemouth won 2-1 at Real Sociedad in the Europa League; the visitors led 2-0 at half-time thanks to goals from Justin Kluivert and Rayan; Sociedad pulled one back just before hour mark through Sergio Gomez; the Cherries hung on to record a first-ever European win
Thursday 17 September 2026 23:44, UK
First-half goals by Justin Kluivert and Rayan helped Bournemouth start their maiden European campaign with a memorable 2-1 win at Real Sociedad.
The Cherries had been surprisingly made favourites to win the Europa League, but Marco Rose watched his team justify their tag with a professional display on the road.
Kluivert's 11th-minute goal was followed by Rayan's header nine minutes later, and although Sergio Gomez pulled one back, Bournemouth held on to claim all three points from their first match in Europe.

This fixture at San Sebastian was the latest chapter in a remarkable story for the Cherries, with a first European tie in the club's history occurring only 18 years on from them being mired in financial trouble and on minus 17 points in the fourth tier of English Football.
After Eddie Howe masterminded a great escape and three subsequent promotions, last season's sixth-place finish under Andoni Iraola earned a place in the Europa League, but Rose was the man tasked with ensuring Bournemouth marked history with a win.

11: GOAL! The unmarked Kluivert side foots home Adrien Truffert's low cross from the left to open the scoring after a lengthy VAR review.
20: GOAL! Rayan heads home Alex Scott's gorgeous lofted pass to put the visitors in control.
25: POST! Evanilson almost adds a third, only for his glancing header to hit the post with the 'keeper beaten.
57: GOAL! Gomez brings the hosts back into the contest with what looked to be a cross from out wide.

90+1: WHAT A SAVE! Petrovic again comes to Bournemouth's rescue with a sensational close-range reaction stop to deny Oskarsson at the back post.
That's Bournemouth football - Rose sees lots to like in Europa League win
Bournemouth head coach Marco Rose:
"That's Bournemouth. That's Bournemouth football. We want to be active, we want to be front-footed, we want to play forward and we want to create chances. We had a header to be 3-0 up, but in the end a game is 90 minutes," Rose told TNT Sports.
"It was very intense and tough. In the end an enjoyable result. A brilliant first half in everything. Our effort, attitude and the way we won balls with our pressing, our out of possession game and our goals.
"A top first half. Second half we needed to suffer and we were not so sharp. In the end it was a deserved win but we need to talk about the second half."

Pew Research has published a new global survey that sheds light on how people view AI, including its impact on jobs, life in general, and income inequality. The survey questioned 42,151 people across 37 countries from February 8th to May 13th — well ahead of recent apocalyptic warnings.
AI is feared globally as the destroyer of jobs
The Pew survey was conducted before the recent apocalyptic warnings.
A majority sees AI as a threat to human employment. In 34 of the 37 countries surveyed, people are more likely to believe AI will lead to job losses over the next 20 years rather than create new ones. Worries run particularly high in wealthier countries like Australia (76 percent), South Korea (76 percent), and the US (71 percent). Not surprising, given Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s warning that AI could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs.
In general, respondents are more likely to say AI will increase the gap between rich and poor. People from wealthier countries that lean left on the political spectrum tend to believe this the most.
Age also tends to impact viewpoints. Older people are more likely to be more concerned about AI’s impact on daily life than younger people. Younger adults (ages 18–34) are most likely to have mixed feelings about AI and how it will shape the world they’ve inherited. They’re also growing increasingly anxious.
In countries like Sweden, Poland, Japan, Australia, Brazil, and the US, concern among younger demographics has risen sharply over the past year, making them more worried about AI-driven job loss and inequality as older generations in countries like the US and Sweden.
Nevertheless, public sentiment captured by the Pew survey is not wholly negative. Despite economic fears, a global median of 41 percent report feeling equally concerned and excited about AI’s growing presence in daily life, compared to 37 percent who are primarily concerned and just 13 percent who are primarily excited.

In recent years, there has been a lot of excitement about the potential for studying human diseases in what are called “organoids.” These small patches of tissue, formed using stem cells, appear to produce many of the same cell types and at least some of the structures normally formed in actual organs, and thus can provide a better model for diseases that rely on the sometimes complex interactions among multiple specialized cell types that are a feature of the human body.
But even the most sophisticated organoids lack a lot of the features of a real human body. This is especially true for brain organoids, which don’t form any of the connections with specialized brain structures needed to behave “normally.” On Wednesday, a research group at Stanford University described a possible way to study brain organoids in a somewhat more natural context: They genetically wiped out a large portion of the mouse brain and replaced it with human brain organoid cells.
The replacements
Organoids, because they adopt a three-dimensional tissue structure and consist of various specialized cells, provide a much better model for an intact tissue than simply having a bunch of disassociated cells lying flat on a culture dish. But they still have a lot of limitations—they’re not hooked up to a circulatory system that allows the liver to process chemicals the organoid produces and don’t have immune cells moving through them, to give just a couple of examples.
This is especially limiting for studies of the brain, where any specialized structures are surrounded by structures that may exchange information with them, and often have long-range connections. An organoid is better than nothing, but it may not be a lot better if you’re interested in a disease that impacts communication among multiple brain regions.
One alternative has been to implant human neural stem cells into the brains of another species, where they’ll generally integrate into the nervous system and actively signal to their neighbors. But, given that those human cells are surrounded by the normally functioning neurons of their hosts, it’s not clear how much you can learn from this.
The obvious solution there is to get rid of the host cells and try to have the human cells take over their functions. But that option runs into all sorts of problems, largely related to the fact that the organism you’re implanting them into (generally a mouse) actually needs its brain cells. Human neurons mature much more slowly than those of mice and may not form the connections that are needed quickly enough for an animal that only requires 21 days of gestation. In the absence of normal mouse tissue, nothing would provide the human cells with the signals that help organize them into functional units.
The Stanford team decided to test a compromise and delete a portion of the mouse’s brain and put human brain organoids in its place. But they took a bold step and chose the cortex as the portion they would delete. The cortex handles many of the complex features of the nervous system, such as decision-making and memory, and its disruption would be expected to have dramatic consequences. Still, the researchers found a gene that is active in almost all cortical cells and used it to drive the deletion of a key gene that’s needed to separate chromosomes during cell division.
Amazingly, despite killing off most of the cells that should go on to form the mature cortex and cutting the brain’s volume in half, it was possible for the mice to survive this. The researchers had to eliminate most of the other pups to ensure the cortex-free mice got enough nursing. They left them with their mothers to nurse longer and then provided them with very high-calorie food. But these steps allowed nearly full survival of mice without much in the way of a cortex. (The mice were also immunocompromised to avoid an immune reaction to human cells, but this is less of an issue in a sterile mouse care facility.)
With that in place, the researchers then started implanting human cortex organoids into the area where the mouse’s cortex was no longer developing.
Partial recovery
A bit over 85 percent of the animals that were implanted with a human organoid successfully incorporated the graft tissues. Those went on to contribute 92 percent of the cells found in the cortex of these animals. So, it wasn’t a complete replacement, but the human cells largely took over the space normally occupied by the cortex. Once there, they formed all the major types of neurons that are known to be present in the cortex. So, all that is good.
The human cells also formed some long-distance connections, as evidenced by the fact that processes from human cells were detected as far away as the spinal cord. And the neurons did engage in synchronized activity spikes, suggesting a degree of coordination.
The less good is a general lack of structure. There is some indication of local organization, in that specific cell types that form within distinct layers of a normal cortex tended to be near each other in the cortex of these animals. But there was no sign of those distinct layers being formed, suggesting that larger-scale organization is lacking.
What does this mean for the mice? Overall, it appears that having a disorganized human replacement cortex was better than having no cortex at all, but not as good as having a normally structured one.
The researchers set them loose in an area with video monitoring and then used a machine-learning classifier to group similar behavior patterns. Normal mice and the mice that had their cortex eliminated showed distinct patterns of behavior. The mice with a humanized cortex formed a third cluster, distinct from the other two. Similar things were true with body weight: mice that lacked a cortex were much lighter than normal mice, but the ones with the humanized cortex were intermediate between the two.
Tested for memory in a simple maze, the mice without a cortex performed at a level consistent with random chance. Mice with the humanized cortex did better than chance, but not as well as normal mice. But on a test of the ability to form associative memories, the mice with a humanized cortex did no better than the mice with no cortex at all. On tests of fine motor coordination, the mice with the human implants were again somewhere between the normal and cortex-free mice.
What’s needed
The research team hasn’t described the sort of careful study of anatomy and development needed to draw any conclusions about what structures may be formed by the human cells once they’re within the mice, much less tried to quantify any variation among individuals that might give us some hints of what sort of capacity these animals might be expected to have. As a result, it’s impossible to associate the mild improvements that come from having the human cells present with any specific function they’re providing.
As a result, this isn’t yet the sort of model system that can help us understand the sorts of complex neural diseases that we might ultimately be interested in using this for. They do show that the human cells respond differently to brief periods of hypoxia, consistent with what we see in normal human cells. But that’s quite a bit different from showing that this is a great model for something like ALS.
There remains a chance that it ultimately won’t be—that the sorts of disorganized connections that do get formed in these brains will never make them a good model for human neural processing. But without further characterization of what the cells are doing in these humanized cortexes, it’s going to be difficult to know.
