Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda
- Published
Teenage brothers Olly and Seb Fisher are closing in on their dream of international recognition - but it won't come from their homeland of Scotland.
Instead, the Partick Thistle duo are in line to play for Uganda.
They believe they would become the first white players ever to represent the African nation, thanks to their mother Kate being born there.
"My gran and grandad lived out here for, I think, four or five years," Olly, 18, tells BBC Sport Scotland. "My grandfather came out here to teach in a school then my mum was born here. So, it's a bit of a strange one."
The siblings became aware of interest from Uganda about six months ago, following a chance conversation some time before between their father and a football consultant at a game in Nigeria.
And, at the start of August, they were invited to attend under-20 and under-17s training camps.
They spent last week in Jinja in the country's eastern region and will stay on for one more week, with the pair saying they're "shocked" and "honoured" at the call-ups.
"I couldn't believe it," 16-year-old striker Seb said. "It's one of those things you look at and you're shocked. You can't believe it. Most other people couldn't as well."
Goalkeeper Olly had a similar reaction. "A real mixture of emotions," he said. "I was quite shocked. I didn't really think that this was a possibility but I was honoured to be asked to represent Uganda. I thought it was a real big opportunity."
Mum Kate is "ecstatic" and "thinks it'd be a great experience for us", adds Seb.
'The other boys have been brand new'
There is another Scottish link with Uganda, with former Hearts and Ghana midfielder Laryea Kingston currently coach of Uganda's under-20s.
And he is the one who believes the Fisher brothers are on the verge of making history.
"Coach Kingston was saying we'd be the first white boys to play for Uganda, which would be history in the making," Seb explained. "It is very special."
And Olly added: "It's never been done before, so definitely it is very special."
The pair feel like they're making connections with the African nation, having been reared on stories about Uganda from their grandparents.
And even though they have been training in oppressively warm conditions, they are embracing the opportunity.
"Everyone has been brilliant, welcoming, really great," Seb said. "The other boys have been brand new with us. Some of the boys actually come from the same area where my mum was born. So, they were all talking about that."
The boys will return to Scotland soon, combining training and playing with Thistle with university and school, but are planning to rejoin their new international team-mates in the near future.
Olly hopes to be part of his squad if they qualify for the Under-20's Africa Cup of Nations early next year, and Seb could be in the Under-17 squad for November's World Cup in Qatar.
"That's what you want as a footballer, being in an international environment," Seb said. "It makes you a better player and hopefully it does for the two of us, and I think it will, and benefit us very much going back to Scotland playing at Thistle."

When will Africa get its next Ballon d'Or winner?
- Published
Africa has only ever had one Ballon d'Or winner, and the wait for someone to emulate George Weah is likely to be extended further after this year's nominations were revealed.
Morocco captain Achraf Hakimi and Senegal forward Sadio Mane are the continent's two names on the 30-strong list.
Both players have previously recorded top-six Ballon d'Or finishes but, after a year in which Spain lifted the Fifa World Cup and Kylian Mbappe netted 10 goals to become the tournament's all-time top scorer, the chances of the Paris St-Germain right-back or the Al-Nassr winger lifting the coveted trophy appear slim.
And it is not the first time that Africa has failed to make a big impact.
Part of the reason for the historic lack of success is down to the fact the award, which was first handed out by France Football magazine in 1956, was not open to players representing non-European nations until 1995.
That was the year that Liberian striker Weah scooped the prize after his impressive form for PSG and AC Milan.
- How is the Ballon d'Or winner decided? 
  - Published2 days ago
- Favourite Kane makes Ballon d'Or shortlist 
  - Published2 days ago
Yet, for all the stars the continent has produced, the only other time an African player registered a top-three finish came in 2022, when Mane was second behind France striker Karim Benzema.
Of course, Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo have dominated proceedings for most of this century, scooping 13 of the 15 available Ballons d'Or between 2008 and 2023.
Journalists from the top 100 nations in the Fifa rankings will vote for the prize, with the recipient of the 2026 trophy announced at a ceremony in London on 26 October.
The "symbolic choice of venue" for the 70th anniversary of the award is in tribute to the inaugural winner, England winger Sir Stanley Matthews.
But how do the historic Ballon d'Or numbers stack up for Africa?
Weah claims the crown
The high point of Africa's Ballon d'Or history clearly came in the very first year the continent's stars became eligible, with Weah topping the vote in 1995 ahead of Germany's Jurgen Klinsmann and Finland's Jari Litmanen.
Five more Africans made that year's 50-player list.
But only once since, in 2007, has the continent had as many as six nominations. On that occasion Didier Drogba was the highest-ranked finisher, with the Ivorian coming fourth.
The pool has narrowed since then, with 30 players in contention since 2008 and just 23 in the running when the Ballon d'Or was combined with the Fifa's world player of the year award between 2010 and 2015.
One other stand-out year for Africa came in 2019, when three men finished in the top 10. Mane came fourth, Egypt's Mohamed Salah was fifth, and Riyad Mahrez of Algeria tenth.
Which African nation has the most Ballon d'Or nominations?
In total, Africa has received 76 nominations for the Ballon d'Or since 1995.
That makes up just 6.62% of the overall hopefuls.
Cameroon legend Samuel Eto'o has the most nominations, having been in the running nine times in a row from 2003 to 2011. His best finish came in 2009 when he was fifth.
Drogba follows with eight nominations, with Salah on six.
Five-time nominee Mane has the greatest longevity of any African, with the 34-year-old's first and most recent appearances on the list coming 10 years apart.
Nigeria has had the most individual players listed for the award, with eight in total. Victor Osimhen's eighth-place finish in 2023 is the best performance by a Super Eagles player.
Room for improvement
Thirty-nine African countries are still awaiting their first nominee, although Chad is surprisingly not among them after striker Japhet N'Doram was part of the 1995 list alongside Weah.
DR Congo and South Africa, ranked 43rd and 54th in the world respectively, are the highest-ranked nations still waiting to make the cut, while no player representing a club side on the continent has ever been nominated.
There have been nine years since 1995 when only one African was among the nominees.
The most recent of those instances was 2024, when Nigeria's Ademola Lookman finished 14th after scoring a hat-trick in the Europa League final for Atalanta.
African contenders have failed to pick up any votes on four occasions after being shortlisted: 1998 (Sunday Oliseh), 2000 (Geremi and Patrick Mboma), 2001 (Samuel Kuffour) and 2003 (Eto'o and Hatem Trabelsi).

Similar story for Africa's women
Since the women's Ballon d'Or was first awarded in 2018, only four African players have been nominated.
Nigeria forward Asisat Oshoala was the first, making the 20- and 30-name shortlists in 2022 and 2023 respectively.
Zambia skipper Barbra Banda has been nominated in every year since, joined by Tabitha Chawinga of Malawi in 2024 and then her sister Temwa Chawinga in 2025 and 2026.
It means no more than two players from Africa have ever been listed for the prize in any one year.
The continent has had a total of 10 nominations from the 195 players nominated overall.

Carney's new love-in with EU has everything to do with Trump
- Published
"Wouldn't it be lovely if Canada was the 28th state of the European Union rather than the 51st state of the United States?" asked Finland's President Alexander Stubb this summer.
The question was rather tongue-in-cheek. US President Donald Trump, who is currently locked in an escalating tariff tussle with Ottawa, has, on a number of occasions, declared his ambition to make Canada the 51st American state - causing deep offence amongst many Canadians.
Finland is one of the EU's 27 member states and a close ally of Canada as a fellow Arctic nation. Teasing tones aside, President Stubb put his finger squarely on the pulse of deepening EU-Canadian relations. "Canada is more Europe-minded than most Europeans!" is a smiling retort you often hear in Brussels at the moment.
On Sunday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters Canada was seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU.
And in a speech on Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she wanted to work "on opening the door" for Canada to be the EU's "associate member" - which would involve closer ties on various sectors including manufacturing and energy.
The catalyst for this very public, ardent new love-in is Donald Trump. Just the other day, the US president posted a map of North America on his Truth Social site, including Canada and Greenland - a territory that's part of EU country Denmark - all overlaid with the US flag.
- Carney's new love-in with EU has everything to do with Trump 
  - Published17 hours ago
- Carney eyes 'unique alliance' with EU as trade war with US intensifies 
  - Published3 days ago
- Iceland summons US ambassador over Trump's stars and stripes map 
  - Published8 September
Trade negotiations between the US and Canada broke down late last month. European countries, which have been hit by their own Trump tariffs, have privately watched the spat play out with a mixture of interest and, for many, admiration.
While the EU, led by the European Commission, simply accepted new blanket Trump tariffs without fighting back, Carney has prominently stood up to the US president, swiftly imposing counter-tariffs on the United States.
When it comes to courting the EU, Canada appears to some to be even keener than one of the bloc's closest neighbours.
"Canada right now seems more interested than the UK to get as close to Brussels as possible, as a non member state" says Mark Leonard, director of the European Council of Foreign Relations think tank. "It's remarkable."
Canada, but not the UK, successfully joined the European Union's Security Action for Europe (SAFE) defence fund earlier this year. The UK remained on the sidelines following a row over costs and political tensions. A summit designed to reset and improve EU-UK relations has just been delayed - again - over cross-Channel differences.
By contrast this week, Carney is invited as a special guest to the European Commission President's annual State of the Union address in Strasbourg, France on Wednesday. Carney will hold a speech in the European Parliament there on Thursday, a day after President von der Leyen outlines the EU's political and policy priorities.
Officials on both sides insist this is more than just "blah blah politics", as one EU diplomat put it to me. He was speaking on condition of anonymity so as to be able to discuss the subject freely. Carney and von der Leyen are both expected to mention plans to forge closer ties. "As close as you can get without (Canada) actually becoming an EU member," the diplomat told me.
'Trump effect' prompts efforts to diversify - but are they achievable?
The unofficial aim for both Brussels and Canada, I'm told, is to reduce reliance on Washington in several key areas:
- Digital and tech developments, in which the US and China dominate
- Energy: Canada is rich in liquified natural gas (LNG) the EU needs since it cut back its energy dependency on Russia
- Raw materials and critical minerals: Canada has them in abundance
- Trade and defence procurement: Canada has been on a "buy European" spree of late, purchasing German attack submarines, for example, and airborne early-warning planes from Sweden's Saab. Its view appears to be: why reward the US by buying American equipment after being slapped with trade tariffs amounting to 50% in some sectors?
A Nanos opinion poll from April suggests more than four in five Canadians favour strengthening ties with the EU.
Close to three in five support Canada actually joining the bloc, though Article 49 of the EU Constitution would appear to make that impossible. Without wanting to seem facetious, the European Union is not (yet) the Eurovision Song Contest, in which indisputably non-European Israel and Australia have - controversially - been allowed to compete.
Back to trade: ties between Canada and the EU are far from novel. The EU is already Canada's second-largest trading partner - albeit far behind the US, which buys about 70% of Canadian exports.
The far-reaching Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) trade deal was agreed just under a decade ago and has been provisionally implemented, eliminating 99% of tariffs on Canadian goods exports.
Privately, European officials admit this renewed high-level courtship between Ottawa and Brussels has everything to do with the actions of Trump's second term in office.
The US president is by now infamous amongst US allies for what they view as his unpredictability and his penchant to use trade or security ties as leverage.
There's a growing sense in Europe - which has, since World War Two, looked to the US as its closest ally abroad - and in Canada, whose economy has been intertwined with the US for decades, that neither can any longer fully rely on Washington. They believe it's time to diversify.
"The Canadian government is committed to trade diversification, doubling non-US trades in the next 10 years, and doing more with the European Union will be very key to achieving that target," Mark Camilleri, president of the Canada EU Trade and Investment Association (CEUTIA) told the BBC.
An even tighter Canadian-EU alliance, covering far more sectors than trade alone, would continue a recent trend of both parties to form new association agreements around the world. In Canada's case, this includes a sectoral deal with China, which raised international eyebrows earlier this year.
EU insiders put all of this down to the "Trump effect".
- Carney gambles on the world's biggest investors betting on Canada 
  - Published2 days ago
- The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts 
  - Published31 August
- What tariffs will really cost Canadians and Americans 
  - Published9 September
But decoupling from the US altogether would seem unrealistic - for both Canada and the EU.
The US is the EU's largest overall trading partner, if you take goods and services together.
Canada and the US have the largest bilateral trading relationship in the world, valued at nearly US$900bn (£668bn) last year. This dwarfs the $130bn of total EU-Canada bilateral trade during the same timeframe.
The vast majority of Canadian exports head to the US.
So, Ottawa could sign new trade agreements, but replacing customers and supply chains built around America's massive market would be a tall order.
This week, I hear, Carney and von der Leyen will vociferously defend a global system of rules-based trade.
"This is not about trying to keep the past alive. We need to forge a new rules-based future in trade and beyond. With or without Washington," diplomats tell me.
There's an EU-Canada summit scheduled for the end of next month. After that, working groups are expected to start the less-than-sexy task of tackling the legal and technical details in the different areas in which the EU and Canada now hope to establish closer ties.
So are EU and Canada really becoming BFFs?
A huge turning point for Europe in its attitude towards Washington came early this year when Trump refused to rule out taking Greenland from fellow Nato power, Denmark, by force.
Around that time, Carney - who's also the former governor of the Bank of England - gave a speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, calling on middle-sized countries to stick together against economic coercion by global super-powers. Europe sat up and took notice.
Why then, you might ask, haven't Europe's leaders been more outspoken in their support for the Canadian prime minister during the current escalation in trade tensions with the US? Carney has been defiant, declaring that Canada was "at war" with the US over trade.
He swiftly imposed counter-tariffs on the US in the name of "sovereignty".
Paolo Gentiloni, a former EU economy commissioner and former Italian premier, commented on social media: "Here is a speech I would like to hear in Europe."
Yet - in public - Europe's leaders have remained cautiously quiet.
Though not, it seems, out of any lack of support for Mark Carney.
A number of Europe's leaders, like Finland's president - but also French President Emmanuel Macron and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, herself once a true Trump fan - are involved in behind-the-scene chats with Carney about deepening relations, I'm told.
But - and it's a big but - no leading European politician wants to stick his or her neck out for Carney in public right now and risk having voters at home blame them for possibly incurring the wrath of - and fresh punitive tariffs from - the US president.
Over the coming months, every large country in the EU holds key elections. Germany's took place just over a week ago. France chooses a new president in April and early May. Italy, Spain and Poland have yet to set a date for their parliamentary elections.
When it comes to applauding Carney right now, Europe's leaders are hiding behind the EU institutions.
Under EU rules, the European Commission deals with trade on behalf of the member states. The EU Commission and EU parliament presidents invited Carney to Strasbourg this week.
But some officials I speak to in Brussels warn that Carney should also wake up and smell the European coffee.
Brussels may feel warmly towards Canada, and believe Ottawa shares many of the same values and priorities, but there are still loud EU voices, like France, that prefer to prevent non-member countries from getting too favourable a deal.
That's despite pressure on the EU to show more flexibility when it comes to accommodating allies, considering the turbulent times we live in.
It's a conundrum the UK faces too.
Carney flies to Liverpool later this week, after leaving the European Parliament, for his first face-to-face meeting with new UK prime minister, Andy Burnham.
As well as discussing UK-Canada ties, who knows - might the two men end up debating ways to best woo the EU, too?

This Olympic river has 500 crocodiles in it - but that's not the main concern
- Published
The annual rowing regatta for schools in the Australian state of Queensland usually passes off without too much attention.
Each year more than 600 of the state's most promising teenage rowers battle it out on the crocodile-inhabited Fitzroy River, in the city of Rockhampton.
"We've never had any media wanting to attend here," Anthea O'Loughlin, head of Rowing Queensland, tells the BBC.
But this year is different. In six years' time, the 2032 Brisbane Olympics and Paralympics are set to stage rowing and canoe sprint events in this very stretch of water, which has just passed a technical assessment and been endorsed as safe and fair for athletes.
While sightings of saltwater crocodiles on the river – which number around 500 and can grow to four metres (13ft) long – are not uncommon, state government files going back more than 40 years record no attacks by the reptiles on humans.
And while influential figures at last month's World Rowing congress in Amsterdam made occasional references to "safety", the presence of the reptiles was not their chief concern.
"Fairness" is what's been raised with British Rowing's chief executive Tom Solesbury – a reference to the tidal river's natural bends and currents, which many in the rowing community say make it unsuitable for elite competition.
Drew Ginn, who has won three Olympic gold medals for Australia in rowing, told BBC Radio he had concerns over potential flooding and "fairness and integrity" at the venue.
"Personally, I'm not fearful of the Australian animals but I've never had a crocodile near me," he said.
"I'm sure I'd row faster, I'm sure all the athletes would row faster. That's on the list of concerns, I don't think it's the highest priority in concerns but it was certainly cited very early on."
The German rowing body's president Moritz Petri said athletes had also questioned the sustainability of holding the event some 600km (373 miles) from Brisbane.
But the "so-called impediments" got short shrift from the most senior politician in Queensland, state premier David Crisafulli, who reached for less diplomatic language.
"Let's be honest, let's scratch beneath the surface and call it for what it is," he said days after the Amsterdam meeting.
"It is a group of interstate and overseas elites who are trying to bully their way because they don't want to go to regional Queensland and that's not right."
Rowing chiefs contacted by the BBC before Thursday's decision declined to comment directly on Crisafulli's "elites" remarks.
But both Petri and Simon Wickham, chief executive of Rowing New Zealand, said their concerns had nothing to do with regional or urban preference but with competitors getting fair racing.
Petri added it was about what's best for their athletes who will train four years for the event, "dreaming night [after] night of becoming an Olympic champion".
Whether it was crocs or currents that tipped the balance, ultimately it was the sport's governing body World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee (IOC) that had the final say on the river's suitability.
On Thursday they approved it after a technical assessment by an engineering firm and the Games' infrastructure authority – which looked at the riverbed, competition course, river flows, water levels and likely weather conditions during the Games.
"Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games," World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland said.
There was also now "confidence" in the river for canoe sprint athletes, said Thomas Konietzko, president of that sport's governing body, Paddle Worldwide.
The state premier was delighted. "The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours," an upbeat Crisafulli told parliament. "It's official. Signed, sealed and delivered."
In backing Rockhampton, the state government ignored a 2025 report it commissioned itself, which found the location unsuitable and concluded the best option would be to use a course built in Sydney for the 2000 Olympics.
The Fitzroy now needs to pass a final assessment of its design, value for money and long-term community legacy. As the decision rests with the state government, it's unlikely to fall at this hurdle.
But a wider debate will continue over whether Rockhampton is the right place to invest heavily in rowing facilities – and whether it can accommodate the 2032 influx of visitors.
The city is surrounded by cattle producers and normally experiences its peak number of guests every three years during Beef Week.
So what about the crocodiles?
They're not mentioned anywhere in the latest update from the IOC and World Rowing and they weren't considered in the technical assessment.
The safety management plan for this weekend's school regatta does however mention the word "crocodile" 28 times.
"The Fitzroy River is within recognised crocodile country," it says.
"Event planning must therefore assume that a crocodile sighting is possible… No natural waterway in crocodile country can be guaranteed to be crocodile-free."
Procedures this weekend include suspending racing and competitors returning to the bank if a croc is spotted. The official signal for a sighting is the call of "crocodile, crocodile, crocodile".
Asked specifically about crocodiles, New Zealand's Wickham told the BBC the primary concern was ensuring the "fairest possible course" for rowers. "We would obviously expect any course chosen to be safe for rowers," he added.
The company owned by Australia's richest person Gina Rinehart, Hancock Prospecting, which supported Rockhampton's bid and has pumped millions into sports including rowing, pointed to "fake media" concerns about risks posed by flooding and crocodiles in the Fitzroy.
"The people of Rocky for many years have sent their own children to train in this river, and for competitions, without a single crocodile incident," a spokesperson said in a statement.
Brisbane 2032's chief executive has said organisers are making contingency plans "as we would for any venue".
The 2000 Olympics venue in Sydney is ready and waiting as a backup – though that would be unconscionable for Queenslanders.
For the school-age rowers at this weekend's regatta, none of this debate really matters as they take to the water.
Among them are potentially some contenders for the 2032 Games.
"For our students, the Fitzroy is first and foremost their home water," says Phillip Moulds, headmaster of The Rockhampton Grammar School.
"The Fitzroy has also been the starting point for many… some of whom have gone on to compete at the highest levels of the sport nationally and internationally."

Half a year after Iranian drone strikes knocked out multiple Amazon data centers, the US tech company has acknowledged the permanent loss of some customer data that was hosted in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates.
Amazon Web Services was “unable to restore access to the resources and data” hosted in some of the war-damaged data centers, according to an AWS dashboard update posted on September 15. The development was first reported by Reuters and suggests that the Iranian strikes inflicted catastrophic damage on the data centers.
Customer data was irretrievably lost in one of three AWS availability zones in the United Arab Emirates region, specifically the mec1-az2 availability zone. Each availability zone is serviced by one or more Amazon data centers.
The company is still working on “recovering regional resources” and restoring resources hosted in the other two availability zones in the United Arab Emirates. The AWS update described ongoing work to replace “affected infrastructure” and promised to update customers on a restoration of services in the coming months.
But the destruction was apparently even more widespread for the data centers in the Bahrain region, because Amazon said it was unable to restore access to resources and data across all three availability zones there.
“The damage to our infrastructure spanned multiple availability zones and exceeded what our regional and multi-AZ services are designed to withstand,” the AWS update said.
The company had already suspended customer billing in the affected AWS regions in Bahrain and the UAE and has spent the past six months attempting to restore normal operations.
The Iranian drones first struck the Amazon data centers on March 1 in the opening days of the ongoing war that began with US-Israeli attacks on Iran on February 28.
AWS immediately urged customers to migrate resources to other cloud regions and use remote backups to restore any “inaccessible resources.” The cloud service also reportedly issued $150 million in customer credits following the initial Iranian strikes in March.
A follow-up Iranian strike focused on Amazon’s data centers in Bahrain on April 1. The latest AWS update acknowledged this “disruption” of a second availability zone in the Bahrain region in April but described most affected customers as having already followed the company’s recommendations to migrate their cloud computing workloads elsewhere.
On July 24, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched yet another strike using missiles that specifically targeted a remaining Amazon data center structure in Bahrain. That damage was independently confirmed by satellite imagery.
“We remain committed to supporting our customers in Bahrain in the long term and will share a further update in early 2027,” the latest AWS update said.
Meanwhile, the US-Israeli war with Iran has since spiraled into a broader regional conflict and growing global energy crisis because of attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. One of the few silver linings has been the surging interest worldwide in renewable power generation, such as solar rooftop panels.

In June 2026, numerous Chinese news media outlets reported on updated international guidelines advising researchers not to independently respond to extraterrestrial signals. English-language news outlets also reported on these updated guidelines, which came from an international scientific organization. It was not possible to find any evidence of the Chinese government sending a nationwide alert telling people not to communicate with aliens, nor of the existence of a U.N. "alien hotline."
In September 2026, a rumor circulated online that the Chinese government broadcast a warning to the country's population of roughly 1.4 billion people, instructing them not to communicate with aliens and to instead contact the United Nations if extraterrestrial life reaches out to them.
For example, one Instagram user posted a video making the claim (archived), during which the user said the alleged warning was distributed through several channels:
Broadcast was made as if it were a giant emergency. They did it through the radio, they did it like the way that you get Amber Alerts on your phone, they did a television broadcast and they had messengers going into rural communities to tell people this and give them this information.
The supposed announcement said, "If you are contacted by aliens, do not attempt to communicate with them. Call this phone number, which will send you to the United Nations desk of the alien communications specialist, and they will take care of it for you." The Instagram user later referred to the supposed number as an "alien hotline" and said similar messages circulated in Japan and South Korea.
The claim spread spread elsewhere on Instagram as well as on Reddit and Facebook. Readers also contacted Snopes to ask whether it was true.
In short, it was not possible to find any evidence the Chinese government issued the nationwide warning described in the posts, and a spokesperson for China's embassy in Washington, D.C., said no Chinese government agency issued such a warning. The real guidance behind the rumor also did not instruct ordinary people to call a U.N. "alien communications specialist" if extraterrestrials contacted them. As such, we have rated the claim as false.
Warning did appear in Chinese media
There is a real story behind the rumor. On June 1, 2026, the International Academy of Astronautics, a Paris-based nongovernmental scientific organization, published updated guidelines for people and organizations involved in the search for extraterrestrial intelligence, or SETI. The document says possible signals should be independently verified and that researchers should not send a reply before international consultation.
These guidelines did receive attention in China. For instance, on June 7, IT Home, a Chinese technology news website, published an article titled (translated using Google Translate) "Do not respond to aliens without authorization! The International Academy of Astronautics updates eight guidelines." China Science Daily, Shanghai-based digital newspaper The Paper and national television broadcaster CCTV News also reported on the updated declaration.
The article on The Paper's website appeared in its "Government Affairs" section, which could make it seem like an official government message.
English-language news media outlets similarly reported on the IAA's updated guidelines.
Graphic may explain how rumor spread
A blue graphic with yellow text in Chinese circulated alongside the rumor in some social media posts. Jingchu Network (荆楚网) — which is part of CnHubei, a news website in Hubei province — posted the graphic on its Douyin account (shown below). The message, translated using Google Translate, reads:
Do not reply to extraterrestrials on your own initiative; the International Academy of Astronautics recommends immediately notifying the United Nations upon the discovery of extraterrestrial life.
(Jingchu Network Douyin account)
The Douyin post cites Red Star News as its source and explains that the message concerned the IAA's guidelines. On June 7, Red Star News published an article about the IAA update.
Jingchu Network is a state-backed news outlet. According to its website, it is supervised by the Hubei Provincial Party Committee Propaganda Department and the Hubei Provincial Cyberspace Administration. "It is the only national key provincial news website in Hubei Province approved by the State Council Information Office," the website reads.
The graphic later circulated on English-language social media platforms, where users described it as an announcement posted in China. This may have contributed to claims that the Chinese government itself issued the warning.
Government website also links to the story
The story also indirectly appeared on at least one official Chinese government website.
On June 10, Fushun Municipal Science and Technology Bureau — a government department of the city of Fushun, in Liaoning province — listed (as shown below) a webpage titled, "Do not respond to aliens without authorization! Why did the International Academy of Astronautics call for a halt?" in the "Science and Technology Work Updates" section of its website.
(fskjj.fushun.gov.cn)
However, that webpage originated from outside the department's website. It was not presenting the message as a new government policy or warning.
Liu Chang, a spokesperson for China's embassy in Washington, D.C. said via email that the Chinese government issued no such warning:
Based on publicly available information to my knowledge, no Chinese government agency issued such a warning, distributed it through national alert channels, or instructed the public to contact the U.N. about extraterrestrial contact.
The claim may stem from confusion over a revised SETI protocol issued by the International Academy of Astronautics and reported by Chinese media. It was not a Chinese government notice.
Snopes also contacted the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs for comment. We will update this article if we receive a response.
Guidance is for researchers, not ordinary people
The IAA document explicitly says it was written for people and organizations taking part in scientific SETI research. It does not tell ordinary people what to do if an alien personally contacts them.
The declaration says that after a confirmed detection, researchers should take part in international consultations over whether a response should be sent. Until those talks are finished, "no reply should be sent." It also says those discussions should include the United Nations and other international bodies.
Chinese Science Daily interviewed Zhang Tongjie, a Beijing Normal University professor who took part in discussions about the revised declaration. He reportedly said the cautious approach was based on uncertainty about whether an extraterrestrial civilization would be friendly, hostile or neutral. He was also quoted as saying the declaration was not legally binding.
There is no UN 'alien hotline'
Social media posts also claimed Chinese citizens were given a phone number for a U.N. "alien communications specialist," but no such a number is in the IAA declaration. The document directs questions about its principles to the IAA itself.
Searching Google for a United Nations "alien communications specialist" returned no results (archived) suggesting that such a role exists.
Though the declaration says consultations about whether to respond to confirmed extraterrestrial intelligence should involve the United Nations and other international bodies, it also says the specific procedures for such consultations still need to be established in a separate agreement or arrangement.
The idea of an official U.N. representative for alien contact has appeared before. In 2010, a report in British newspaper The Times claimed astrophysicist Mazlan Othman, then-director of the U.N. Office for Outer Space Affairs, was appointed as Earth's contact person for extraterrestrials. Othman denied this and said no specific U.N. response role had been decided, while further action would be up to member states.
Therefore, the IAA declaration's reference to international consultation through the United Nations does not mean there is a U.N. "alien hotline."
Snopes has contacted the U.N. and, specifically, its Office for Outer Space Affairs to ask whether such a hotline exists. We will update this article if we receive any responses.
Bottom line
All in all, there is a kernel of truth behind the story. In June 2026, Chinese news media outlets did publish messages saying people should not "respond to aliens" without authorization, and an official municipal government website did link to a webpage on the topic.
However, that information came from guidelines for SETI researchers issued by the International Academy of Astronautics. The guidelines say a possible extraterrestrial signal should first be verified and that no response should be sent before international consultation.
Finally, it was not possible to find any evidence that China sent a nationwide emergency alert or gave people a phone number for a U.N. "alien communications specialist."

Here is a story that on the face of it seems so wildly unlikely it can only be true. Indeed, the very concept of a romantic documentary sounds almost oxymoronic, an indication of how much nonfiction films have become synonymous with grim histories full of suffering and injustice. Let’s hope this sweet work, directed by Orlando von Einsiedel (who’s made his share of hardcore, suffering-intensive docs including Oscar-winning short The White Helmets) launches a new trend in nonfiction film-making for stuff that makes you happy-cry.
The basic meet-cute happened in 1975, when PK (played by Chirag Lobo in the film’s extensive re-enactments) met Lotta (Mina Dale) in Delhi. He was a poor street artist, a Dalit, the lowest possible caste, once called Untouchables. The real PK Mahanandia appears on screen to explain how he had left his rural village for Delhi in order to get away from all that caste hierarchy. When he met Lotta he pretty much knew he’d met the woman of his dreams because he’d been carrying a horoscope his father had commissioned for him when he was a baby that prophesised he’d fall in love with a woman whose family owned a jungle. Lotta, a backpacker from Sweden, hailed from a clan back home that owned a forest, so that was good enough for PK to believe he’d met his fate. After a chaste holiday romance bloomed between these two crazy kids, she went back to Sweden and he decided to bicycle the 6,000 miles all the way there from India to prove his love.
As we hear the now elderly young lovers describe what they were thinking at the time, we watch Lobo and Dale act out the journey, with poor PK getting into a few scrapes that set him back a few steps as he plods his way westward. Some of the most touching interludes are the interactions he has with strangers along the way that seem incredibly naturalistic and semi-improvised. Cynics might quibble that one can’t help wondering what darker parts of the story have been left out, and note that the actors chosen to play the lovers are a few notches more conventionally beautiful than the actual people – but every love story has its soft focus, flaw-concealing fudges so we’ll let it slide here.

SC awards ₹12 lakh to Haryana woman denied Indian Oil Corporation job in 1988
Haryana woman was denied helper’s job at an LPG bottling plant in 1988 because the company considered the work of carrying gas cylinders unsuitable for women
The Supreme Court on Thursday directed Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) to pay ₹12 lakh in compensation to a Haryana woman who was denied a helper’s job at an LPG bottling plant in 1988 because the company considered the work of carrying gas cylinders unsuitable for women.
“It is an affront to womanhood and that too by a Government of India undertaking,” a bench of justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi said, pulling up the government entity for “disrespecting” women.
As the woman had attained the age of 63, well beyond the age of superannuation, the court noted that she had litigated for decades and directed IOC to pay a lump sum of ₹12 lakh in compensation.
“Day in and day out, when men are not at home, it is the women who lift gas cylinders in the house and change it. And you denied her appointment just because she is a lady. This is disrespect to womanhood,” the bench said.
The woman petitioner, Sumitra, was a resident of Karnal in Haryana and belonged to the Scheduled Caste community. She had sought employment as a helper when the LPG bottling plant opened in Karnal in 1988. She was one of the 49 persons shortlisted for the job. Although educationally qualified and meeting all the requirements, she did not figure among the 43 selected candidates. Later, she was told that she had been refused employment because she was a woman.
The IOC, in its response before the top court, said, “As the nature of the job and atmosphere and odd working hours in the company of the males was such that petitioner being lady was not considered fit for the job.”
Sumitra had first approached the trial court, where she won a decree in 1990 directing IOC to absorb her in any post other than that of a labourer. This judgment was challenged by the IOC before the Punjab & Haryana high court, which overturned the decision in October 2025. It was this order that Sumitra challenged in the top court.
The court noted the long litigation that the woman had to endure, in addition to the discrimination at the hands of IOC. The petition, filed through advocate Surya Nath Pandey, stated that gender was the only ground for denying her employment.
The bench observed, “In India, every day we say a woman is a goddess, respect her. This is a fit case for compensation.”
At one point during the hearing, the IOC lawyer was even willing to agree to mediation. However, the court was not interested in keeping the matter pending after going through the facts of the case and noting the considerable delay of over three decades since the litigation began.

LONDON — English health authorities on Thursday agreed to provide a breast cancer drug from AstraZeneca through the National Health Service, ending a years-long dispute that stoked questions about how committed the pharma company was to the U.K.
Notably, the move — one that will extend the drug, called Enhertu, to an estimated 1,000 people in England — is in part a result of a U.S.-U.K. drug pricing deal reached late last year. Under the pact, a U.K. health agency agreed to raise the thresholds for what would be considered a cost-effective drug and worth paying for on the NHS.
Now, women with metastatic breast cancer whose tumors have low levels of the protein HER2 will be eligible to receive Enhertu, a type of next-generation chemotherapy known as an antibody-drug conjugate. AstraZeneca noted that Scotland has covered the drug since 2023, and it’s paid for in 26 other European countries. (Patients with HER2-positive cancers have been able to get Enhertu in England.)

The story uses screenshots and not the actual viral video in view of its sensitive nature.
A 12-second long video is going viral on social media where a woman is seen bathing in river water while wearing a bikini.
The video was posted on September 15 by X user Barkha Trehan, who describes herself as ‘Activist | Voice Of Men | President, Purush Aayog’. She wrote, “Location : Haridwar. Madam: My Body My Choice. Your take ??” The video garnered over 1 million views. (Archive)
In her X bio, Trehan identifies herself as a “men’s rights activist” and the “president of Purush Aayog”. She also claims to be a TEDx speaker and a “Hindu entrepreneur”; she apparently also “directed a documentary titled The Curse of Manhood”.
Media outlet News 18 Hindi published a report with screenshots from the video pointing out that it had angered social media users. (Archive)
This same video was posted by content creator Piyali Banerjee, where she questioned the “basic decency” and “knowledge of clothing” of the woman.
Other social media users also shared the same video with similar captions, questing the woman for wearing a bikini in Haridwar, with misogynistic comments about her character.
The video is also viral on Instagram.
Fact Check
To verify its authenticity, we ran a reverse image search on a few keyframes from the viral clip. This search led us to a reel posted on Instagram on August 18. The 21-second long reel was uploaded by an account named ‘ishika_pandit’. It showed the same woman bathing at the same spot, but wearing completely different clothes.
This video matched the background of the viral clip with the steel railing on the river and the foundations of a bridge clearly visible in the background. The woman’s hand gestures also mirror the viral video, and the same two men are visible in both videos.
Based on these similarities, it can be concluded that the video uploaded on August 18 is the original footage. The woman in the original video is seen wearing a yellow suit, and not a bikini. Thus, the viral clip is a doctored version of the original video, manipulating the attire of the woman.
Some social media users highlighted the possibility of the viral clip being an AI-generated deepfake, claiming that the woman’s clothes had been purposely changed from a suit to a bikini. (Archive)

The Chinese president, Xi Jinping, has received a red-carpet welcome in India for a summit of Brics developing nations, as regional rivals Beijing and Delhi make a public display of thawing relations while quietly competing to lead at a time of shaky US global dominance.
As Xi stepped off the plane, he was walked past an honour guard of Indian soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses.
The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, and Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, had already been welcomed by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, who is hosting one of the group’s most closely watched gatherings since its inception.
The summit marks Xi’s first visit to India in seven years and is seen as the biggest step towards reconciliation after a deadly 2020 military clash along the disputed Himalayan border, in which 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers were killed.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming recently, with flights and high-level contacts gradually being restored. China was “willing” to work with India to properly manage differences and be “good neighbours and friends”, China’s foreign ministry said on Friday.
Leaders and diplomats have been convening in India for the annual gathering of the Brics grouping, named after five of its earliest members – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – that was conceived as a counterweight to western dominance.
This summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising US-China tensions, test the bloc’s ability to find common ground.
Since its inception in 2009, Brics has expanded as a forum for major emerging economies to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The group now rivals the US-dominated G7 forum of advanced economies, accounting for half of the global population.
But its growth has also created new fractures and disunity – Iran was bombing Saudi Arabia and the UAE earlier this year, and Brics foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May.
Reuters reported on Saturday that India’s summit would result in a generic joint declaration that would show unity by condemning unilateral war, but was unlikely to name any single country.
Jiang Shixue, vice-president of the expert committee of the China thinktank Council for BRICs cooperation (China), said the 11 members “cannot speak with one voice on many issues”.
“The only solution is to continuously strengthen political consensus,” he told the South China Morning Post.
Beijing and Delhi have differing views on the role of the group.
China has sought to expand Brics power as a counterweight to the US under Donald Trump’s leadership, which has launched global tariff and trade wars and retreated from multilateral institutions such as the UN, which afforded it international credibility.
India has taken a more cautious approach, seeing Brics as a bridge between the west and the developing world.
Chietigj Bajpaee, a senior research fellow for South Asia in the Asia-Pacific programme at Chatham House, said this week that Delhi had found it hard to maintain its policy of “strategic hedging” during such a disruptive US presidency.
“India’s position can appear out of sync in a forum whose membership includes countries with more overtly anti-western agendas, including China, Russia and Iran. And two other Brics countries, South Africa and Brazil, have suffered high-profile diplomatic disputes with the US,” he wrote.
“The challenge for Delhi is that it wishes to promote this worldview in a way that is non-western but not explicitly anti-western.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

Just over a year ago, Dylan Borland—a former Air Force geospatial intelligence specialist—told a House Oversight task force that he'd watched a roughly 100-foot triangular craft lift silently off the flight line at Langley Air Force Base in 2012. But there were some questions he couldn’t answer.
Nearly half a dozen times during the hearing, he told members of Congress he could only answer their questions, such as whether a private company he worked for was reverse engineering nonhuman technology, inside a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility, or SCIF. He said he was concerned whether he was “legally even allowed to answer” some questions and at one point cited a fear of being charged under the Espionage Act.
A year later, on September 14, the Defense Department announced it had lowered that risk, though it falls short of what some in the unidentified anomalous phenomena research community say is needed to achieve broad transparency.
The Pentagon said on Monday that it had issued a "targeted legal waiver" allowing all current and former “service members, civilian personnel, and contractors" holding UAP-related national defense information to disclose it to the White House–directed effort that has been dumping UFO files on war.gov since May.
The waiver, which hasn’t been made public, "supersedes civil and administrative enforcement provisions" of NDAs and special access program agreements, "strictly for communications directed to the PURSUE team," a reference to the White House program. Basically, if you signed a secrecy agreement and know something about UFOs, you can now tell PURSUE without being sued or losing your clearance, though the same protections don’t extend to speaking with Congress, the press, or the public. The release announcing the waiver says nothing about criminal law, and only covers agreements "previously executed within the United States."
President Donald Trump telegraphed the move over the summer when he reportedly directed the Defense Department and the intelligence community to waive UAP-related NDAs. It was reinforced on July 31 when Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence Aaron Lukas sent a memo to 18 intelligence chiefs declaring that any NDAs “prohibiting disclosure to the President, or designees like PURSUE, are no longer in force.” The memo cited a “Presidential Direction” it never quotes and gave the intelligence community 30 days to set up its own procedures. That deadline passed in August. The White House directed a request for comment to the Defense Department. An agency spokesperson said it had no additional comment outside the press release and referred further questions to the White House.
Borland, the kind of person all of this was written for, is unmoved.
“Bad-faith actors are talking about, ‘Oh, this allows whistleblowers to go and talk to the public.’ No, it doesn't. It changes nothing,” he tells WIRED. “It's one more place to go.
“Those of us who already became whistleblowers, we already were told that our NDAs were waived. We were legally allowed to talk to AARO,” he says, referring to the Pentagon's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, created in 2022 to investigate UAP reports and serve as the official channel for whistleblowers. He adds that the new directive essentially “just repeated what we've been told for three, four years.”
A provision Congress passed in December 2022 already states that an authorized UAP disclosure—meaning one made through AARO—"shall not be subject to a nondisclosure agreement," complies with classification rules, and "is not a violation" of the relevant section of the Espionage Act. The channel was AARO and Borland used it.
But AARO has little credibility with the people it was built to hear from, especially after its former director publicly questioned the credibility of whistleblowers, and its March 2024 historical report found no evidence the government had ever recovered alien technology. Borland told Congress that he met with AARO in March 2023, but that he withheld sources and methods because he considered the agency's public assessments up until then, "a misrepresentation of the truth." That August, after a former intelligence officer testified about an alleged decades-long crash-retrieval program, Borland filed a complaint with the intelligence community's inspector general over what he says he knew and the retaliation he says he’d faced.
Since then, he wrote in his statement to Congress, he has "been prevented from resuming my prior employment" and remains “blacklisted from certain agencies within the Intelligence Community.”
Other UAP whistleblowers have faced similar issues after coming forward, from break-ins at their homes to leaked personal details.
The new waiver also only covers those who have worked with the Pentagon, leaving a CIA-sized hole in it.
“I'm glad that they're waiving NDAs for everybody who was on the [Defense Department] side,” Borland says. “It doesn't change the [Intelligence Community] side.”
He pointed to the need to offer similar protections to the alphabet soup of intelligence agencies beyond just the CIA, including the National Security Agency, FBI, and others, as well as science agencies like NASA.
Marik von Rennenkampff, a former State Department analyst and Obama-era Pentagon appointee now at the Sol Foundation, a UAP research nonprofit, agrees with that sentiment because of where whistleblowers say the secrets about nonhuman technology are kept. He points to a specific unit in the CIA that’s “allegedly—allegedly, allegedly, allegedly, I can't stress that enough—the quarterback for this alleged legacy effort.”
“What has been announced publicly does not cover the core of the alleged legacy program yet,” von Rennenkampff tells WIRED.
There's a second gap that no memo can close. Many of the people alleged to hold this information work for private contractors, and the government can't waive an NDA it isn't party to. Only the 2022 statute addresses those types of agreements, and only for disclosures made through the official AARO channel.
Despite these shortcomings, UAP researchers and whistleblowers point to, von Rennenkampff argues this week’s announcement is still important.
“After 80 years of government denial, obfuscation, and ridicule on this topic, there's now true political capital invested in this,” he says. Unlike AARO, PURSUE is a “presidentially directed initiative” that is reporting ultimately to political appointees in the White House, “versus career bureaucrats.”
“It shows that the Trump administration is taking extraordinary claims about retrievals of a craft of nonhuman origins seriously,” he says. There’s a phrase in the release that von Rennenkampff says is another curious detail, particularly given how “wordsmithed to hell” government statements about UAP generally are. The Pentagon wrote that “individuals with direct knowledge of UAP-related programs” have historically feared legal liability for speaking.
“It doesn't say people with partial knowledge, half knowledge, alleging knowledge,” he says. “It says people with direct knowledge.”
Borland's hope is that PURSUE answers to someone with the power to act on what it hears. He points to White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller—who Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently confirmed is working on the UAP portfolio—as someone who would signal the White House is doing more than paying lip service to the topic.
Beyond that, Borland has an offer.
“There's enough smoke, and there's enough people behind the scenes,” he says, referring to himself and other whistleblowers. “If Stephen Miller and Trump wanted to actually know some stuff, they could call us into the White House right now, and I can throw down, and so can the rest of them.”
