Regarding your editorial (The Guardian view on child marriage: girls should not be wives, 26 August), every year, 12 million girls are married under the age of 18, while more than 70 million more are estimated to be at risk of child marriage between 2025 and 2030. Yet, as international development budgets face unprecedented contractions, traditional field programming alone cannot keep pace.
At current funding levels, international funding for ending child marriage amounts to less than $1 per girl at risk per year – a level of investment that cannot match the scale or urgency of the problem
Ending child marriage requires dismantling the patriarchal norms that perpetuate it. Over eight years of participatory research across Bangladesh, India and Nepal – engaging 350 grassroots partners – our team validated a cost-effective alternative: narrative edutainment. Field-testing a film-driven intervention yielded a striking 49.4 percentage point shift in community attitudes, proving visual storytelling can transform entrenched behaviours where policy alone stalls.
Through our film project, we are establishing a scalable model combining cinema, school toolkits, community screenings and policy briefings to reach 100 million people across south Asia, with a clear blueprint for expansion into sub-Saharan Africa.
Child marriage inflicts a staggering $175bn economic cost worldwide yearly. In an era of scarce global funding, investing in scalable-impact film assets is an urgent necessity. This vital tool can break the cycle of poverty and protect millions of young girls.
Ravi Baral
Activist film-maker and co-founder, Far Too Young Inc

In May 2014, Macklemore performed in a costume that featured several antisemitic tropes: a very large hooked nose, a fake black beard and a black, bowl-cut wig reminiscent of a kippah — a Jewish skullcap. His outfit also resembled the suits some Orthodox Jewish men wear. After experts and Jewish people online pointed out the tropes, Macklemore said in a lengthy post on his website that he did not realize his choice of costume evoked antisemitic imagery and apologized, linking to the Anti-Defamation League's website. The ADL reportedly welcomed Macklemore's apology and took him "at his word that he did not have any ill intent."
Following the removal of musician Macklemore as an opening act on singer-songwriter Ed Sheeran's tour in September 2026, a rumor spread online claiming Macklemore once performed in an Jewish caricature costume featuring antisemitic tropes. The cancellation of Macklemore's performances came after he advocated for Palestinian freedom during a concert.
The claim appeared across social media platforms, including Instagram, Facebook and X. Actor Josh Malina, who is Jewish, wrote on X, "Nah. Don't defend this guy" (archived):
Malina also shared photographs of a man, presumably Macklemore, in an obviously fake black beard and wig in a bowl cut, as well as an exaggeratedly large hooked nose. The man also wore black trousers and a black jacket, reminiscent of suits some Orthodox Jewish men wear. In one of the images, the man made a gesture reminiscent of a Nazi salute.
Meanwhile, several Snopes readers emailed us and searched the website seeking to confirm whether Macklemore had once performed in such a costume.
The claim is true and the photos are authentic. On May 16, 2014, Macklemore, whose real name is Benjamin Hammond Haggerty, performed in this costume at the opening night of an exhibition titled "Spectacle: The Music Video," at the Museum of Pop Culture in Seattle. (The museum was then known as the EMP Museum.)
While Macklemore was photographed with his arm up while wearing the costume, it's unclear whether he intentionally made a gesture resembling a Nazi salute, as posts suggested.
Macklemore posted on his website three days later, explaining his costume choice and apologizing.
We reached out to Macklemore for comment on the fact that the photos of his costume resurfaced. We also contacted the Anti-Defamation League, an organization dedicated to fighting antisemitism and extremism, and Malina. We await their responses.
The costume's antisemitic references
Many photos of Macklemore's performance and costume that day appeared on the reputable image repository Getty Images, including two of the photographs Malina posted.
We also found a video of the performance posted on May 21, 2014.
The costume harkens back to some of the most virulent antisemitic tropes in history. One example is appeared in 1893 on the cover of a notorious antisemitic newpaper in France known as La Libre Parole Illustrée, the illustrated supplement of La Libre Parole:
(Albert Esnault, La Libre Parole Illustrée, via Wikimedia Commons)
The newspaper bears the tagline "La France aux França
The 19th-century image shows a hand-drawn black-and-white caricature of a man with a torn coat and pockets full of money. The man is gripping the planet with claws growing out his fingers and toes as coins fall out and bills gather in his hands and between his toes. He is wearing a hat reminiscent of the Jewish skullcap — a kippah — and a black beard. He has a large hooked nose and is smiling. The caption reads "leur patrie" ("their fatherland" in French).
The caricature plays on racist stereotypes that Jews do not belong to any country and are loyal only to the global Jewish community (this was before the foundation of Israel in 1948). It also reinforces the prejudicial stereotype that Jews are greedy, appearing poor but secretly rich.
A more recent caricature known as the "Happy Merchant" appeared in the U.S. far-right antisemitic newspaper WAR (White Aryan Resistance) in 1992. The image, attributed to cartoonist Nick Bougas, shows a man with black hair and beard with a hooked nose, a humped back and a seemingly evil smile. He is wearing a kippah and rubbing his hands, as if he were plotting:
(A. Wyatt Mann (Nick Bougas), in WAR newspaper.)
Macklemore apologizes
In his explanation for his choice of costume, Macklemore said he loved to wear costumes and the costume store "usually" sold large noses. He said he chose black hair because it was "the furthest color from my natural hair," adding he wanted to be unrecognizable.
He said some people told him he looked like The Beatles' Ringo Starr, while others said he resembled former U.S. President Abraham Lincoln.
"I wasn't attempting to mimic any culture, nor resemble one," the singer wrote. "A 'Jewish stereotype' never crossed my mind."
Macklemore ended his post with an apology. "I truly apologize to anybody that I may have offended," he said. "I hope this better explains the situation and my point of view."
He added a post-scriptum linking to the website of the ADL, which offers educational material about such tropes.
In response, the ADL reportedly accepted Macklemore's apology, according to The Guardian.
"We welcome Macklemore's apology for wearing a costume that, regardless of his motives, reminded many people of an antisemitic caricature," The Guardian quoted ADL director Abe Foxman as saying. "We take him at his word that he did not have any ill intent and unreservedly accept his apology."
For further reading, Snopes verified in 2023 that Macklemore had posted about the "unfolding genocide" in Gaza. In the same post, the singer called Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel that resulted in the death of 1,200 people an "abomination."

New Delhi: India will take all necessary steps to safeguard its energy security and economic interests, the government said on Thursday, stressing that it had apprised Washington of the likely impact the proposed US law targeting Russian energy-importing countries could have on bilateral ties and the global oil market.
The development comes as crude oil prices topped the $100 a barrel level amid the prolonged West Asia conflict, adding to concerns for India, which imports about 90% of its crude oil, more than a third of it from Russia.
The US House of Representatives late Wednesday passed a bipartisan sanctions bill targeting Russia over the Ukraine war, giving President Donald Trump the power to slap up to 100% tariffs on countries such as India and China for their energy imports from Russia. The US Senate had already passed the bill. It is expected to be soon signed by Trump to become a law.
"India has noted the passage of the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act in the US Congress and it is monitoring further developments on this matter," the ministry of external affairs said in a statement. “This issue has been discussed at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors. Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side.”
Determined to take "all necessary measures" to protect its interests, the government said it will work closely with domestic trade and industry bodies to deal with the implications.
"As stated on several earlier occasions, India remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people. It will continue to do so through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics," the ministry said.
Indian trade and foreign affairs analysts warn that Trump could use the new law to put pressure on India to give in to his demands in the trade deal that both sides are currently negotiating. India will look to further diversify its energy sources, they said.
The analysts don't expect the US to slap heavy tariffs on China, as Beijing has leverage over Washington in critical mineral supplies, among other things.
Commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal will travel to the US later this month to attend the G20 trade ministerial in Milwaukee, where he may meet US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, commerce secretary Rajesh Agarwal had said this week.
The latest US move, aimed at forcing out Russian supplies from the global market, could disrupt the oil market and further push up global prices, inflating costs for net importers and developing countries such as India, analysts said. This could potentially stoke inflationary pressure and balance of payment issues in these countries, even as India is on a relatively strong footing.
Currently, India's exports to the US face different duty rates—about 55%, including engineering goods, are subject to the usual most-favoured nation (MFN) duties and a punitive tariff of 10% for alleged use of forced labour. Another 35-40% of goods—such as smartphones, pharmaceuticals and certain farm products—are exempted from the levy, while exports of steel and aluminium face a 50% tariff.
In the financial year 2026, India had exported goods worth $87 billion to the US, its biggest market.
An Indian commerce ministry spokesperson declined to comment on the matter. Queries emailed to the offices of the US Trade Representative, US commerce secretary and the American Embassy in New Delhi on Thursday afternoon were not immediately answered.
Russia has emerged as a key oil supplier to India over the past four years after Moscow started offering discounts, making its oil not just viable but also attractive for Indian refiners, after accounting for logistics costs. However, the discounts have now drastically narrowed.
India's total crude oil imports account for a quarter of its import bill. Its crude import bill for April-July jumped to $63.37 billion, up 56% from a year earlier.
Economic impact
Biswajit Dhar, economist and former professor at Jawaharlal Nehru University, said the US move could have significant economic impact for oil importing nations. "The US action is set to push up inflation and exert further pressure on the balance of payments in net oil importing countries," he said.
Estimates by Bank of Baroda show that a persistent $1 rise in crude prices can raise the country’s annual import bill by around ₹18,000 crore.
Dhar said it would be even harder for New Delhi to negotiate the trade deal with the US now, given that Trump would most likely use his new-found leverage.
Inflationary pressure has been building in India due to the volatility in the energy market since the start of the West Asia war on 28 February. In August, India's retail inflation rose to a 20-month high of 4.82%, driven by higher fuel and food prices, exceeding the central bank's medium-term target of 4% for a third consecutive month. Wholesale inflation, too, inched up to 9.92% in August from 9.78% in July.
India's current account deficit, while still within the comfort zone, rose to 0.5% of GDP in the June quarter from 0.4% a year earlier.
The new law will give Trump sweeping powers on tariffs: he can go up to 100% and also refrain from levying any duty if he so wishes, experts said.
"US Congress approval places such tariffs on stronger legal ground than earlier measures imposed mainly through presidential powers," said Ajay Srivastava, founder of Global Trade Research Initiative. "After the Act is signed, the US Trade Representative will identify the targeted countries and recommend tariff rates. These countries would normally have 180 days to reduce Russian energy imports or negotiate with Washington. However, the president can shorten this period," he added.
"With the passage of this bill in the US, even if India cuts Russian oil imports, it would not help India. The high US tariffs would continue. In order to avoid these tariffs, India will have to completely stop sourcing energy from Russia and that would be very detrimental for our energy security," said Kirit Parikh, former member (energy) of the erstwhile Planning Commission. "I feel India should not buckle down under US pressure and continue to source oil from all available sources, including Russia."
Jayant Dasgupta, former Indian Ambassador to the World Trade Organization, said he expected the US to go soft on China. "India, meanwhile, may be forced to buy more energy products from the US," he said.

Rockstar has officially announced the GTA 6 music album, including a physical vinyl release, but instead of getting excited, I got frustrated reading about it. What bugs me about Rockstar’s latest announcement is that the album has a physical CD and vinyl, but the game doesn’t come on a disc. Instead, GTA 6 physical copies have a code in the box, and frankly, that’s baffling.
I grew up collecting GTA games on PC, whether it was San Andreas or Vice City, and I always appreciated how Rockstar included physical goodies like a map, exclusive posters, and whatnot. Likewise, I was looking forward to what goodies GTA 6 would have, but that ship never sailed. And now, with Rockstar revealing the GTA 6 albums with a disc, they’re playing in my face.
GTA 5 Had 7 Discs, While GTA 6 Has None Outside the Music Album
When I bought GTA 5 on PC back in 2015, I couldn’t believe how many discs Rockstar packed into the box, along with a manual and a double-sided poster of Los Santos and Blaine County. Since it was 7 dual-layer installation discs, it felt like opening a new book, only much better because it was Grand Theft Auto.
PC discs haven’t been a thing in quite a while, so naturally, I moved to PlayStation to grow my physical collection. I was looking forward to the GTA 6 physical release on PS5 since the first GTA 6 trailer dropped in 2023. However, Rockstar decided to go the all-digital route with GTA 6, and I couldn’t, for the life of me, understand why.
I initially thought Rockstar might have delayed GTA 6’s physical release to avoid spoilers, as that did happen with Red Dead Redemption 2 months before its release, but a prominent leaker single-handedly debunked that theory. CyberLeek posted multiple GTA 6 leaks on social media platforms, even though the game is skipping a physical release.
And now, looking at the GTA 6 music album editions, all of which include a physical CD or a vinyl disc, I wonder what went wrong. Did Rockstar make this decision to please shareholders, or because Sony is killing physical PS5 discs starting in January 2028, and they just wanted to be ahead of the game? They do have a marketing deal with Sony, so maybe I don’t have the full picture just yet.
Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick previously said that GTA 6 discs don’t make sense for consumers, but their argument falls apart with the official physical vinyl release on November 19, 2026. A PS5 disc is generally cheaper to produce than a vinyl disc, so this decision really makes me wonder. I doubt Rockstar would even include a map in the GTA 6 “physical” release,
I Would Easily Spend More to Own GTA 6 on a Disc
This is a hot take, but I definitely would’ve spent more on a true GTA 6 physical edition with a disc; that’s not an album or a vinyl release. I’m already paying $80 for GTA 6, So, paying an extra $10–15 for a physical disc edition doesn’t seem unreasonable to me, especially given the circumstances.
Honestly, I would’ve even paid more if Rockstar had made the disc exclusive to the GTA 6 Ultimate Edition. Regardless, Rockstar has already locked five features with the GTA 6 Ultimate Edition, so including a physical disc would have made the $100 price tag feel even more worthwhile.
Rockstar not offering a physical disc for what is probably the biggest game ever made is pretty wild to me. They have already made a fortune, with GTA 5 selling over 230 million copies worldwide, as revealed by Take-Two in an earnings call. GTA 6 pre-orders are soaring too, so would it really have been that hard to give physical fans a disc, just like it’s doing with the GTA 6 album vinyl?
No physical disc not only limits options, but also sets a dangerous precedent for future physical releases, which is unfortunately what Sony is doing too. Even with all the backlash surrounding Marvel’s Wolverine, PlayStation’s newest release, it still comes with a physical disc containing the full game. I have to give Insomniac credit for at least doing that.
There are still 2 months left, so I’m holding out hope for an eventual GTA 6 physical disc, even though the chances are slim. Truthfully, if Rockstar doesn’t give GTA 6 a proper physical disc release, then maybe it should’ve kept the album strictly digital, too.

Lisa says new EP Press Play is 'like a movie' as she traces her journey from Thailand to global stardom
The Blackpink star describes her upcoming solo EP as a cinematic project with its own characters.
Lisa's upcoming solo EP Press Play is "like a movie" with each song having its own character. The Blackpink star – born Lalisa Manobal – charts her story from her Thai beginnings all the way to where she stands today.
Speaking on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon, she said: “This EP is about my journey from my roots to where I am right now today.
“There’s a lot of Thai elements in the songs as well, in the EP. And every single song has their own character, their own vibe and we combine it together. It’s like a movie. So you just press play.”
So far, fans have heard the opening track SaWaDiKa, which translates to Hello in her native language.
Press Play is set for release on Oct 23.
As well as forging a successful music career, she's also dabbled in acting with her debut in the third season of The White Lotus, however, Lisa insisted that she’ll never leave Blackpink behind entirely.
She told Variety: “If I’m 50, I still want to do Blackpink. We just finished our tour earlier this year, but we talk a lot about this and have discussions about doing a little break – like I did almost two years ago – but we’re always going to be together.”
As well as a new EP, Lisa is releasing the documentary Always Lalisa.
The film features interviews with Lisa's nearest and dearest, and also shows a more vulnerable side of the singer.
Asked why she decided to agree to the documentary when she did, she replied: “I feel like it’s about time. I’m more confident now, so I want to share my story to fans who have a big dream like me.
“I hope that this could inspire them.”
Always Lalisa will screen in Singapore cinemas from Oct 12 to 17.

British mum kidnapped in Malawi rescued after police shootout
Nusrat Osman, 47, has been reunited with her family following a police operation in the southern city of Blantyre
A British mother of two who was abducted in the southern African nation of Malawi last week has been rescued, police say.
Inspector General Richard Luhanga, the head of the Malawi police, said Nusrat Osman, 47, was safe and had been reunited with her family following a police operation in the southern city of Blantyre on Thursday that left her four suspected kidnappers dead.
The Malawi Police Service said officers exchanged gunfire with the suspects, who were armed with an AK-47 rifle and a Girsan Regard MC pistol.
"The criminals got shot and were rushed to the hospital where they succumbed to the injuries," police said in the statement.
During the operation, Deputy Inspector General of Police Noel Kayira also sustained gunshot wounds and is being treated in hospital in a stable condition.
Osman's brother, Shobi Jiwa, had earlier confirmed to Malawi news outlet Nation Online that she had been rescued in an operation in which the police officer was shot and wounded.
Osman, who works for a local auditing firm, was abducted about 12.30pm local time last Friday, September 11, in a neighbourhood of the southern city of Blantyre.
She and her family moved to Malawi from Leicester after her husband set up a business in the country.
Malawi police had said they were looking for four men who had used a grey car to kidnap her.
The motive was not clear, police said, and the suspects had not contacted Osman's family or authorities.
Authorities had offered a reward of about £12,600 for information leading to Osman’s rescue and the arrest and conviction of the kidnappers.
Local politician Atupele Muluzi described the case as “deeply disturbing”, adding that it was one of an increasing number of similar incidents in the country.
“Kidnappings and abductions are becoming increasingly frequent in Malawi, a country where such incidents were previously largely unheard of,” he wrote in a post on Facebook.
At the time, the UK Foreign Office said it was aware of reports that a British national had been abducted in Malawi and was in touch with local authorities about the situation.

Buttigieg: Democrats Need to Get Serious About Amending the Constitution
The former transportation secretary spoke with The Atlantic’s editor in chief about what comes next for Democrats should they win big in November.
In a conversation at The Atlantic Festival with The Atlantic’s editor in chief, Jeffrey Goldberg, former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg warned fellow members of the Democratic Party to resist the urge to revert to “the previous status quo” if they regain power in the midterms.
It would be a mistake, Buttigieg argued, for Democrats to try to reverse “the damage” of the past two years of the Trump presidency by trying to restore the country to how it looked in 2022 or “whenever we think that America was great.” He said that Democrats instead need to build for the idea that “the next quarter century between here and 2050, which is kind of a make-or-break quarter century for the whole American project, is subject to very different conditions and problems than the ones that we inherited.”
Buttigieg—whom many analysts see as a potential 2028 presidential contender—offered examples of what that vision might look like. He called for banning gerrymandering and passing a constitutional amendment to address the deluge of money in politics. “This idea that it is somehow beyond our power to use what is probably the single most elegant feature of the Constitution, which is its capacity to be amended—right?—is a complete failure of ambition and imagination,” Buttigieg said.
When asked by Goldberg about the Democratic Socialists of America, Buttigieg responded that he thinks “there’s a temptation to imagine that being bold is the same thing as being kind of maximally ideological.” Sometimes it is the case, Buttigieg said, that the leftmost idea is the boldest. But other, more ideologically moderate projects may require “radical reform to our institutions,” he noted.
“I know the commentariat wants to get it all fixed on some left-to-center-to-right spectrum,” Buttigieg continued. “To me, what’s more interesting is: Do we have the right package of base hits and big swings, and are we going after both of them, at the same time, all the time?”
The following is an edited transcript of the conversation:
Jeffrey Goldberg: I want to get to the state of our civilization, but there’s this thing—and we’ve talked about this already—there’s this thing that’s been bothering me more than most things bothering me in the last few days. The fact that a Putin-aligned oligarch, extremely dubious past—as opposed to the oligarchs with a wholesome past—
(Laughter)
Extremely dubious past, funded openly—or not openly, it was discovered, but there’s no secret—funded a two-day celebration for the president of the United States’ son. And we were talking a little bit about how that seems fairly normal in our new reality, but if you actually step back a few years ago, in a Bush presidency, Obama presidency, and told somebody, Oh, yeah, the president of the United States’ kid’s wedding is being underwritten by a Russian oligarch, no one would believe that we’ve entered that level of dystopic reality. So my question is: How screwed are we?
Pete Buttigieg: Well, if I thought we were altogether screwed, I wouldn’t be doing this.
Goldberg: What would you be doing? Moving to Canada?
(Laughter)
Buttigieg: I guess.
Goldberg: I just want to know; he’s got access to different forms of transportation.
Buttigieg: Is that what giving up looks like now? Moving to Canada? No, I think it’s symptomatic of this bigger pattern we’ve been in where we stare down something that is completely unacceptable and then just move on. And in some ways, the big thing, the spectacular corruption, actually is harder to face. It’s like if you’re in Washington, D.C., and you walk up to the Washington Monument and you stick your hand on it and you look up—which, by the way, is a fascinating experience if you ever get the chance, because you can walk right up to it—but once you do that, you cannot make out the shape or even the size of the Washington Monument, right? Because it’s right there.
And when we have monumental corruption or monumental systemic breakdowns, I think it can have the same effect. Part of what I’m trying to do, as I travel the country, is insist that we’ve got to deal with a whole set of things that we’ve just been talking about being wrong for a long time. I’m not just talking about the near term, the recent shocking, spectacular forms of corruption, like what you mentioned about the wedding or the sentences that are coming out of our mouth, right? Half a billion dollars of crypto money from a foreign prince going to the first family, or the jumbo jet—I mean, we all know this list of things, right?
Goldberg: Or renaming a cultural center named after a martyred president for yourself.
Buttigieg: For example, and then shutting it down because—
Goldberg: Because you ran out of money.
Buttigieg: You couldn’t get your way. I mean, even that, right? He becomes chairman of the premier cultural institution in the country, and within two years it’s shutting down, right? But my point is there’s something broader, bigger, and longer in the making than even Trump and Trumpism itself. Like, if I said the system is broken, that’ll be the least memorable thing I said all day, right? “The system is broken” is a cliché. Everybody says it. Certainly every politician says it because it’s true. The weird thing is, we say the system is broken, and then we act as if it wasn’t. We go right back to normal and—
Goldberg: The system is broken. What’s for lunch?
Buttigieg: Yeah, right? Like, if you’re getting ready for a flight and the captain comes on and mentions in passing that the airplane is broken—
(Laughter)
You’re not going to stay on the plane, right?
Goldberg: So that’s one of the things you worked on as secretary of transportation, right?
(Laughter)
Was that a bigger problem than we know about? Because that would be really useful.
Buttigieg: No, but that’s the point, right? When lots of planes were crashing in the ’60s and ’70s and ’80s, we did something about it and developed this incredible, civilizational achievement of aviation safety, because we didn’t think it was acceptable to have that happen. And here we are in this political system where everybody knows that the role of money in politics, the unrepresentative nature of Congress, what the Supreme Court has turned into, is a huge problem. And eight years ago, when I was talking about things like Supreme Court reform—pretty lonely position—everybody was looking at me funny. Part of why I was doing that was not only because I believe in Supreme Court reform, but because I believe in elevating our ambition as a country when it comes to reforming things that are obviously broken.
And look, at a political level, most of the time, most of what people like me should be talking about is the fact that diesel is at the highest price ever recorded, and the fact that interest rates are higher because of the policies of this administration, and the fact that most of us are paying higher health-insurance premiums because of what the Republicans are doing. But the reality is, those kitchen-table issues have become intractable, because you’ve got this political system kicking the legs out from under the kitchen table. And when people see that day after day after day, then when they see some cases of spectacular corruption by the first family, it’s just all part of that wash of low expectations that we’ve come to have for our politics and our system.
Goldberg: Is the system broken, or are people broken?
Buttigieg: The system is more broken than people.
Goldberg: But when I say people, I mean specific people, like the members of Congress.
Buttigieg: Okay, well, some of them. But here’s the thing.
Goldberg: I don’t mean our audience. They’re not broken. They look great.
Buttigieg: It would be an extraordinary run of bad luck if all of the people that we have elected to Congress over the last few years just randomly turned out to be terrible people, right? That would be just statistically—
Goldberg: You say that like that’s science fiction, but I don’t know, I mean, but it doesn’t sound that incredible to me either.
Buttigieg: Either something about the system makes people worse, or something about the system is actively selecting worse people, right? It’s not just bad luck, right? And I say this having dealt with the United States Congress quite a bit, and you can see how even people who start out good are incentivized to become less so over time. You sit in a committee hearing and it’s basically a content farm now. You go in hoping to have some legislative progress, and they look at you and tell you you’re right, and then explain why it’s never going to happen. So we can keep wondering why the people who our system produces and pushes into leadership are deeply flawed, or we can do something to create a system where it’s better than that.
Goldberg: I’m focusing on Congress because Congress has abdicated its oversight responsibility to a large degree. The judiciary is—put aside the Supreme Court for a second; you do have federal judges checking executive power. But Congress, in its current form, ain’t. So what do you do?
Buttigieg: Get a better Congress.
(Applause)
Goldberg: If you were king.
Buttigieg: Let me explain what I mean. Yeah, obviously, in the near term, what I mean is elect better people to Congress, which is why I’ve been to most U.S. states at least once in the last year and a half, trying to campaign for people who I think would make better representatives in Congress than the ones that we’ve got. So there’s that. But what I really mean is: Design a better Congress. For example, one way to make sure that you get better and not worse people in a job is to have a very competitive hiring process. We have 435 seats in the House. Roughly 40 of them are competitive, which means nine out of 10 congressional races are races where you pretty much know who’s going to win before the first vote is even cast. In a 50/50 country, right? Which means it is not an authentic, competitive process.
Goldberg: It is the most cost-effective job-protection system ever devised.
Buttigieg: Yeah. So we ought to ban gerrymandering nationally. We ought to ban gerrymandering.
(Applause)
And the last reason to have any hesitation about doing that fell when they gutted the Voting Rights Act in the Callais decision, because there was, up until then, an argument that, Look, because these states are badly gerrymandered anyway, the only way we’re getting minority representation is to protect minority districts. Now the Supreme Court has basically established a de facto right to partisan gerrymandering. We can have a law that changes that, right? The role of money in politics, obviously part of the problem here. These are not things that are completely beyond our power to deal with.
Goldberg: Well, the Supreme Court has basically said it’s beyond your power, on the role of money in politics.
Buttigieg: Right. So we should have a constitutional amendment on that.
Goldberg: And is that realistic?
Buttigieg: We’ve had 27.
(Laughter)
Goldberg: Not lately, though.
Buttigieg: We had a—
Goldberg: Stopped doing it.
Buttigieg: We had a constitutional amendment so that you couldn’t have a drink. And then, like, 10 years later, we thought that was dumb. And we changed it with another constitutional amendment. So this idea that it is somehow beyond our power to use what is probably the single most elegant feature of the Constitution, which is its capacity to be amended, is a complete failure of ambition and imagination.
(Applause)
There are some other things we can do in the meantime. I was in Montana helping gather signatures for an effort called the Montana Plan, which is using, because of what the Supreme Court has said, instead of setting it up as a regulation on speech—since the Supreme Court has said that, you know, money is speech and corporations are people—you go to the fact that corporations only exist as a function of state law, and corporations actually in state law don’t have rights; they have powers, and those powers are enumerated.
And so in the law that makes corporations exist, you just have a feature in there that basically says, You don’t get to be a corporation if you are using your Treasury dollars to manipulate elections. That’s one example of something that is designed to have an effect while we don’t yet have a constitutional amendment. Think of it this way: Citizens United came down, I believe, in 2010. So if the counter to a constitutional-amendment process is That could take 15 years, well, if we’d started in 2010, we’d be there, right? This is a level of ambition I think we need to have, or else every time we’re trying to make sure that more people can get health insurance or the minimum wage, which hasn’t been raised, I think, since 2009 or 2007, actually goes up—or any other outcome which a majority of Americans already agree—we’re going to keep getting frustrated.
Goldberg: I want to ask you something about an even deeper structure. You know, James Madison had a lot of fears, which is why he designed the system we have. James Madison feared that the rise of the daily newspaper would sink democracy, because the once-a-day addition of new information into the human brain was too much for people. You couldn’t go from emotion to reason before new information came the next day. We’re beyond that now.
(Laughter)
We’re well beyond that. And so the question is—it’s a cognitive question. One of the tricks of the Trump administration is to do so much so quickly that you reach overload. The other part of this is, in the social-media environment in which we have, is it irrational or a sign of poor character for a member of Congress to say, You know what, I’m not going out on a limb, because I’m going to get 10,000 death threats a day on social media, and I exist in that content farm, in another form of that content farm. So what do you do to reintroduce the possibility, the space for reason, logic, contemplation?
Buttigieg: I’ve come to realize that we have different levels within us of thinking, of consciousness. And part of the problem with social media is that it speaks to the lizard brain, right? Kind of the least contemplative of our levels of thinking. And there’s no question that the system of rewards and punishments that is kind of dominant in the digital world is not healthy for politics. But that is not the only realm where we can practice politics. So one thing that we can do more of is engage in actual spaces—real, physical spaces where people are actually in a room. And politics is often at its best when the public square is physical. I think about it in terms of how I travel, just when I’m walking around town or going through an airport. And 99.9 percent of people who come up to me are very positive. And that includes some people who say, I don’t agree with you politically, but it’s nice to see you. They’re just kind of excited to see somebody they recognize.
Goldberg: Having a human interaction.
Buttigieg: Yeah. And it’s not because obviously I have 99 percent support. I know this is a divided country. What that tells me is most people in an actual 3-D interaction aren’t assholes, right?
(Laughter)
Very different from how it is online. So I think one very simple thing is to try to cultivate and create more spaces and environments where those interactions happen. That’s in-person convenings, that’s the public square, that’s third spaces, that’s building social capital around existing physical spaces that bring people together, like schools.
It’s also something that is part of why I believe in ideas like national service, creating more opportunities for service. Because when I was in the military, that was definitely an environment where I was side by side with people that I had wildly different political values from, and we quickly learned to trust each other with our lives. And part of that had to do with the extreme pressure of being in a war zone. But part of that just had to do with the fact that this group of people was thrown together and tasked with doing something hard. You know, not everybody needs to be in the military for that to be available to more people. It’s why I think a voluntary but ultimately universal opportunity for service would do a lot of good. It would just rewire our brains in a healthier fashion.
Goldberg: The answer to Is Donald Trump a symptom or a cause? is both. Yeah, obviously. The question is what percentage is symptom and what percentage is cause? Is it possible to disaggregate that?
Buttigieg: I think of it in terms of the broad symptoms and then the cause of some acute problems. So the symptom stuff—this is what I’m getting at with my systems and reform talk: that if the economic and political and social systems in this country were working, we wouldn’t be here. You don’t get a guy like Trump just out of nowhere, right? So, that’s the evidence.
Goldberg: Let’s pause on that. What system in particular, or what aspect of the system would have—I don’t mean the cultural system, rise of reality TV and social media—but what part of the system would have stopped this?
Buttigieg: The part I think is worst is the part where in a supposedly representative system of government, people reach consensus, or at least overwhelming majority, that certain things should happen, and then they don’t. That is lethal to people’s confidence in their political system, and it leads, sooner or later, to a pattern where they say, You know what? I’m just going to vote to burn the house down because none of this is working. By the way, just a quick political digression here—it is really interesting that most of those big kind of two-to-one things are actually things that are Democratic positions in Washington. So if I think about, like I mentioned earlier, raising the minimum wage—raising the minimum wage at least to $12 is something a majority of Republicans believe we should do. Background checks on guns: 70, 80, 90 percent. Eighty percent of Republicans, gun owners, think we ought to at least do that. Tax fairness, where the wealthiest people are paying at least as much in their taxes as a percentage as a firefighter—overwhelming majority.
And what I’ve realized is we’re actually—Democrats are still getting used to being on the right side of the American public on a lot of issues. Because when I came of age, right—like now, everybody’s pretty much with us on taxes and health care—you know, when I came of age, we were on defense about things like the death tax and welfare reform and all of that. And my first time ever on the ballot was 2010, when Obamacare was the toxic issue that killed the Democrats, right? Now it is the winning issue for Democrats. So some of this is new, and I think Democrats aren’t used to that. But my bigger point is you have all these things where there’s actually two-to-one agreement among the American people on what to do. By the way, even immigration—this is true—the broad framework of a grand bargain on immigration that’s been there the whole time, and then nothing like that happens in Washington. That breeds a kind of cynicism that I think leads you to a guy like Trump.
But then back to the cause part. Even a guy like that didn’t have to do things like this. Like, you could imagine some disagreeable populist leader who is presented with the possibility that AI may threaten the continued existence of the human species and does not decide to call that a hoax. It really matters that we happen to have a president who does. Or if you think about what’s happening, if you’re imagining the calculations that are going on in Beijing right now, or Moscow, obviously they are preparing to take advantage of some specific issues that are attached to having a specifically unstable person running the United States of America. And that’s not just some, you know, world historical force. That’s the particular misfortune we have of being led by this particular man at this particular moment.
(Applause)
Goldberg: Right. They’re clapping for instability.
(Laughter)
I want to come back to the global picture in a second, but stay on this interesting subject of the Democrats. There’s been a switch, you’re right. Mainstream Democratic positions are, generally speaking, the more popular positions. How are the Democrats going to mess up in the next two months so that they don’t take Congress back?
(Laughter)
Buttigieg: Look, I feel really good about the tailwind that we have in the next two months. I was just in Tucson, Arizona, where I think JoAnna Mendoza, who’s a Marine drill instructor and a mom, is going to defeat the Republican congressman there. Then we were in southern New Mexico, where we have Gabe Vasquez, extraordinary frontline Democrat. I think he’s going to earn reelection. Just last night, I was up in Tarrytown with Cait Conley, West Pointer, [who] I think is going to defeat Mike Lawler. We have great candidates running great campaigns. What could go wrong? Two things. Well, lots of things could go wrong between now and the election. I’m mostly trying to make sure—obviously I spend all day, pretty much, when I’m campaigning, trying to make sure things go right at the election.
What about after the election? Two things I think would be a terrible mistake. One is to revert to the status quo, the previous status quo. I really think that’s going to be a strong temptation to say, Okay, we’re in; we’re going to reverse the damage. You hear the phrase reverse the damage, right? Which is understandable because the damage has been horrific. But the implication of reverse the damage, if that’s going to be our mantra, is, Okay, we’re going to put all these things back just the way they were, and we’re going to give you the world the way it looked in 2022 or 2012 or 1994, or whenever we think America was great. And that’s not going to work. So we’ve got to make sure we resist the temptation to be restoring some previous status quo and build for the new reality that we’re in, with the next quarter century between here in 2050, which is kind of a make-or-break quarter century for the whole American project, is subject to very different conditions and problems than the ones that we inherited. The other thing that I think we need to do is keep it simple in terms of a legislative agenda. So I’ve been thinking a lot about these.
For example, one thing that the chattering class will get into right away as soon as there’s hopefully a Democratic victory, is what’s going to be H.R. 1? What’s going to be the big, telltale, Christmas-tree, signature bill that you put all your hopes and dreams in that signifies the priorities of the party and of the new Congress, right? To me, I would like to see, like an H.R. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5—like 10 or 12 dozen things. Stand-alone bills, clean bills, not this ponderous 2,000-page thing that tries to take care of every single thing, but a set of things that are needed, popular, and wise, and will make a difference to people, especially in being able to afford everyday life.
So, what does that look like? Restoring the child-tax-credit extension. That puts money back in the pockets of lower-income families trying to raise kids. Obviously, getting us out of a war in Iran that has everybody paying more for gas and diesel. Restoring the help on health care. By the way, also, on the tax side—so usually the revenue part’s unpopular, so you have to tuck that in with the spending part that’s popular. Right now, fixing the tax code so that wealthy tax cheats couldn’t get away with it or even truing up the rates to be a little more normal for wealthy individuals or for corporations—those things are popular on their own. Even if you didn’t staple it to how you’re going to spend the money, just the tax side alone is popular because it’s the right thing to do, and because everybody can tell there’s something wrong with the way things are going.
So to me, a rapid fire of clean bills to do these things that everybody—raise the minimum wage, right—these things that everybody knows we ought to do, that’s how we move forward. How do we go wrong? We get tangled up, get in our own way, make it super complicated, and people don’t feel like we’re doing what we actually, hopefully will have gotten elected on, which is making everyday life better, and in particular, making everyday life more affordable.
Goldberg: Talk about the DSA temptation.
Buttigieg: I mean, look, I think there’s a temptation to imagine that being bold is the same thing as being kind of maximally ideological. To me, sometimes that might be true; sometimes the boldest idea maybe is the leftmost idea. Sometimes I think we’ve reached a point where actually, what I would consider to be kind of ideologically moderate projects—like everything I mentioned, is kind of moderate by definition because two-thirds of Americans want to do it—requires some radical reform to our institutions. And so there are big swings we need to be taking with some of the ones I talked about on reform in the Supreme Court and money and politics and gerrymandering, but also big policy swings, right?
I mean, eight years ago, the whole Democratic primary fight in the debates that I was in was about was universal health care going to become mandatory or was universal health care just going to be optional? And not much has changed since then, right? So we also just need to have a higher level of ambition. To me that’s the most interesting thing. I know the commentariat wants to get it all fixed on some left-to-center-to-right spectrum. To me, what’s more interesting is do we have the right package of base hits and big swings, and are we going after both of them at the same time all the time?
Goldberg: In the few minutes we have left, talk about the fact that we’re already in World War III and don’t even know it, and while we’re in World War III, the president of the United States is making enemies out of our allies.
Buttigieg: Yeah.
Goldberg: Discuss.
(Laughter)
Buttigieg: Another essay question.
Goldberg: Yeah, you have four minutes—I mean, because this is the Alice in Wonderland cut. We’re trying to have a rational conversation about all the things that you could do to make the lives of Americans somewhat better, you know? And, we have a president right now who seems to want to go to war against Canada, which is a South Park episode.
I mean, the question is like, we’re having this conversation, but we’re living in a reality that is South Park.
Buttigieg: First of all, every time we see one of these things, we have to remember it doesn’t have to be this way. It doesn’t have to be this way. And politically, what I’m trying to do is connect these things that are happening around the world to issues at home. Because foreign policy always codes as this kind of high-minded, kind of elite concern. But the reality is, foreign policy and what’s going on in the world hits us at home in a million different ways. Like my neighbors in Michigan, you know, a year ago, nobody filling up the pump necessarily had to know or care what was going on in the Strait of Hormuz. It’s not your problem. Now you’ve got gas closer to $5 than $4 in Michigan. Diesel’s through the roof. This is a direct relationship right between what’s going on in the world and what’s going on at home.
I was talking with union members in the hospitality industry in Las Vegas, cocktail servers getting fewer hours. Las Vegas has one of the highest unemployment rates in Nevada; generally, in the U.S. Why? Well, one of the reasons is, pissing off Canada meant that Canadians who normally come to southern Nevada, especially in the wintertime, decided to take their money elsewhere, right? So there are these very direct effects on working Americans that happen when you have an absurd foreign policy, like we do. And the result is that it leaves us worse off in the near term economically at home, as well as, of course, the bigger, longer-term picture, which is, we don’t know exactly how and when we’ll need our allies next, but we know that we’ll need our allies. And having alienated them, it’s realistically going to take a generation to have the right level of credibility.
Goldberg: This is the question. I mean, let’s assume for a minute that, you know, there’s a Democratic president in the beginning of 2029. How much of what’s happened overseas is reversible and how much is just—I guess the biggest question is, are we, right now, undergoing a midlife crisis, a nervous breakdown, or are we facing a terminal illness? And if you’re sitting in Canada, Paris, London, South Korea, Japan, you’re asking yourself, I don’t know anymore about these people.
Buttigieg: Yeah, no, that’s definitely what’s happening. I’ve talked to leaders who—one, who just looked at me and said, “Look, the first time you guys did this, it was,”—this is of a U.S. ally,—“it was a blip. I thought of it as a blip. Now it’s a pattern and our country has to prepare.” And obviously, this scenario where you have a Democratic president next, everybody’s going to be saying, Okay, that’s great, you’re saying all the right things now. But, you know. what’s going to happen in four years? Which is exactly why reversible is not the word on my mind. I’m trying to purge my vocabulary of just about anything with the prefix re in it.
But, again, this doesn’t have to be 100 percent negative, because we’re entering into a world where the old patterns and institutions are not coming back. And a lot of those institutions were pretty rickety to begin with. The UN Security Council was set up at a time when the vast majority of people in China were impoverished rural peasants, right? Now, a middle-class city dweller in China arguably has a more technologically sophisticated everyday life than a middle-class city dweller in America. We’re in a very different world in terms of technology, in terms of competition, in terms of the security balance. And so we’re going to need to revamp—there I go, re again. We’re going to need to—I think reimagine is okay.
Goldberg: What about refried beans? How do you feel?
(Laughter)
Buttigieg: Ambivalent.
Goldberg: Just going out for fried beans from now on.
Buttigieg: But I think there’s an opportunity, so it comes back to what I was saying earlier. You know, interpersonally, my experience is you can build trust in a hurry if you are working together on something hard and important. That’s true for people. That’s true for countries. So in addition to the generational project of earning trust and credibility by just consistently doing the right thing and being a dependable friend and ally and a sober voice in the world, there’s also no shortage of very difficult things that we need to be, starting with the response to AI—no shortage of very difficult things where we need to be working with friends, allies, partners, and, in some cases, the whole world. And I think we can quickly earn trust, in the same way that the entire pattern of the U.S. being the most respected and indispensable partner—that was kind of the pattern of the second half of the 20th century—really was built up in a matter of just a few years of doing the right thing when it was really hard. I actually see in that an opportunity, precisely because of how bad it is. I see an opportunity to build something that is going to serve us well for the balance of this century.
Goldberg: We’ll find out.
Pete, we can do this all day, but we can’t, unfortunately. So, thank you very much for coming.

In December 1892, Lizzie Borden was arrested on suspicion of killing her father and stepmother with a hatchet in their Fall River, Massachusetts, home.
Nearly 10 months after her arrest, Borden was acquitted of the crimes, in part because prosecutors lacked physical evidence linking her to the killings. No one else was charged in connection with the murders, and more than a century later, the case remains unsolved.
The crime has inspired countless adaptations, including Netflix's "Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story," the fourth installment of Ryan Murphy and Ian Brennan's anthology series, which premieres September 17.
While the story continues to draw audiences, the Borden home has become an attraction in its own right. Last listed for sale in 2021 for $2 million, the property now offers ghost tours and operates as a bed-and-breakfast, with rooms starting at $259 a night.
Take a look inside the site of one of America's earliest true-crime stories.
The Borden family house is in Fall River, Massachusetts.
Fall River is about 52 miles south of Boston, near the border between Massachusetts and Rhode Island.
Andrew Borden was a well-to-do businessman.
According to the Lizzie Borden House's bed-and-breakfast website, although Andrew Borden was born into a prominent New England family, he grew up middle-class.
He began his career as a carpenter and cabinetmaker, later amassing a considerable fortune through a mix of real estate investments, mill ownership, and banking. At the time of his death, his net worth was reportedly over $300,000, equivalent to roughly $10 million today, according to the website.
Andrew carefully selected their Massachusetts home.
The house was built in 1845 and purchased by Andrew Borden in the 1870s, local news outlet WJAR reported.
Borden chose the home in part for its practical location — a short walk from his Main Street businesses in a bustling part of town —according to the Borden bed-and-breakfast's website.
Over a century later, the Borden home has become a popular tourist attraction.
Donald Woods and Leann Wilbur operated the Lizzie Borden Bed & Breakfast Museum for more than 15 years before selling it in 2021.
Lance Zaal, founder of US Ghost Adventures, bought the property for $1.8 million and has continued operating it as an inn and museum, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The home looks as though it were pulled straight from the pages of a history book.
While some of the home's furnishings have been replaced over the years with replicas, its original doors and hardware remain intact.
Period details are scattered throughout the home, including sewing machines, lanterns, and mannequins dressed in floor-length, era-appropriate gowns.
The home is spread out over three levels.
Altogether, the home occupies a little over 3,600 square feet.
The spacious home can be booked in its entirety and accommodates groups of up to 20 people.
Floor plans of the home shared with Business Insider show it has 8 bedrooms and 3.5 bathrooms.
The second and third floors are almost exclusively devoted to living quarters.
All of the bedrooms have floral wallpaper, ornate dressers, and large wooden headboards.
For an additional $30, guests can also arrange to have an axe placed on the beds.
Most of the bedrooms are on the second floor, and some are on the third.
The primary bedroom includes an en suite bathroom with a tub, according to The Seyboth Team, the brokerage that handled the property's most recent sale.
You can stay in one of the home's rooms for $249 a night.
Though the home operates as a bed-and-breakfast, it also remains a museum and tour site. Guests staying more than one night must vacate the property between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m.
This is the John V. Morse Suite.
This room is where Abby Borden was found after her murder. Eerily, a photograph of Lizzie Borden hangs in the bedroom.
According to the bed-and-breakfast's website, guests have reported paranormal experiences in rooms throughout the home.
This was Andrew and Abby's bedroom.
It's the only suite in the entire home that has its own bathroom.
The kitchen is located on the first floor.
The home has an old-fashioned wood-burning stove that certainly looks like a throwback to the 1800s.
It also has modern appliances like a coffee maker and a dishwasher.
Despite modern appliances, the room still feels historical.
The first floor has several rooms dedicated to entertaining.
At first glance, this unassuming sitting room appears rather ordinary. But it conceals a dark history: Andrew Borden was killed here while sitting on the large black couch.
There's a less eerie space for entertaining.
For couples drawn to the home's spooky history, the Borden house hosts several weddings each year. This room would make an intimate setting for a cocktail hour.
The home also has a separate gift shop.
The gift shop sells items including a Lizzie Borden coloring book, a collector's miniature hatchet, and a mug modeled after Lizzie's mug shot.

Trump seen with image of apparent Kennedy Centre demolition
The US president has threatened to tear down the famed arts venue because he has been blocked from renaming it after himself
A photo of Donald Trump examining a depiction of Washington’s Kennedy Centre apparently being demolished sparked widespread attention on Thursday after the US president threatened to tear down the revered arts venue because he has been blocked from renaming it after himself.
In the image captured by Agence France-Presse photographer Brendan Smialowski late on Wednesday at Joint Base Andrews, the Republican leader was seen through the windows of Air Force One holding a placard with visible text in red declaring: “Kennedy Center DEMOLIS …”

The United States on Thursday (local time) approved visas for Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and other members of Tehran’s core delegation to attend the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York next week, despite the ongoing military conflict, the Associated Press reported.
The US State Department said the decision was consistent with Washington’s responsibilities as the host country of the United Nations. “Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level Week,” a State Department spokesperson told AP.
However, the Iranian delegation will be significantly smaller than in previous years and will face tighter travel restrictions, the State Department added.
Against this backdrop, Pezeshkian's planned appearance at the UNGA presents an unusual diplomatic picture.
The US and Iran are at war with each other, yet the Iranian leadership will be allowed to enter the United States to participate in the world's largest annual diplomatic gathering.
Why has US approved Iranian delegation's visas?
The main reason for this is that the US is the host country of the United Nations.
The UN headquarters is located in New York, for which the United States has obligations under the 1947 Agreement between the United Nations and the United States regarding the organization's headquarters.
The agreement establishes arrangements to ensure that representatives of UN member states and other authorized participants can reach and participate in UN proceedings.
Section 11 of the agreement states that US federal, state, and local authorities shall not impose impediments to the transit of representatives of member states and other specified categories of people to or from the UN headquarters district.
The agreement also contains a specific provision concerning visas. Section 11(3) provides that visas, where required for people covered by the provision, are to be granted “free of charge and as promptly as possible”.
However, the US has historically maintained that its obligations under the Headquarters Agreement do not completely eliminate its ability to protect national security or regulate entry into parts of the country outside the UN headquarters district.
It only establishes obligations connected to access to the UN headquarters and participation in UN business.
That is also why restrictions on the Iranian delegation's movements can coexist with the decision to issue visas.
What about US denying visas to Palestinian president?
Earlier this week, the US denied visas to Palestinian Authority and Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) officials, including Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, ahead of the UNGA, according to a State Department statement issued on Wednesday.
The department said that the restrictions were linked to what it described as the Palestinian leadership's failure to undertake reforms and actions that undermine prospects for peace.

US-based semiconductor equipment and materials-engineering company Applied Materials has announced a $5 Bn (₹47,980.8 Cr) investment commitment as part of its Applied Materials India Vision 2035. Prabhu Raja, president of the semiconductor products group at Applied Materials, made the commitment while addressing the SEMICON India 2026 at Yashobhoomi, New Delhi, today. This investment will be used over the next decade to accelerate and integrate India's semiconductor ecosystem into the global value chain, with a three pillar approach — to deepen its research and development (R&D) in India, to accelerate the semiconductor ecosystem in India and to foster talent in India. “Today, we are committing to a new 140-acre advanced semiconductor research park, bringing together cleanroom capabilities, engineering expertise, and collaborative R&D with customers and suppliers on one side. Second, accelerate the ecosystem in India. Inventions done here must scale globally,” Raja said. He further added that the company aims to grow its India-based supply chain capacity 10X by 2035, creating opportunities for Indian suppliers and bringing global suppliers here. Industry Expansion Targets Under Semicon 2.0 Meanwhile, Prime Minister Narendra Modi highlighted commercial production launches of two new semiconductor plants at Mohali and Surat today at the SEMICON India conference. In late August, the Union Cabinet approved the second phase of the Indian Semiconductor Mission, Semicon 2.0, with an outlay of ₹1.28 Lakh Cr, which will focus on six areas — chip design; semiconductor equipment and materials; fabrication plants (fabs); assembly, testing, marking and packaging (ATMP)/ outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) units; research and development; and talent development. Setting targets for the second phase, Modi said that the government expects least 200 chip-design startups and companies to participate in India, up from 105 that participated in the first phase, and 1 Lakh factory-floor and clean-room workers to be trained, alongside the existing chip-design talent goal with new 3D packaging unit coming up in Odisha. Semicon 2.0 is eyeing to attract more chipmakers to set up facilities in India, including silicon fabs, compound semiconductor fabs, discrete component fabs and display fabs. The government has received investment commitments of over ₹1 Lakh Cr ($11-12 Bn) since launch of Semicon 2.0 and has created 1 Lakh jobs, union minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said. PM also called for building a stronger domestic semiconductor supply chain by backing fabless chip companies, developing homegrown intellectual property and integrating silicon photonics into AI infrastructure. He urged players across semiconductor equipment, chemicals, gases and materials to tap the opportunities created by the 12 approved projects and the country’s growing chip demand.

On November 3, when voters across the US go to the polls, almost 200 election deniers will be on the ballot. Many of them have repeatedly undermined the very process they are participating in, and they will be looking to win some of the most powerful elected positions in the country—positions that would help determine how voting goes in future elections.
Following the primaries, there will be 197 election deniers on the ballot for congressional and statewide races in the midterms across 43 states, according to new data shared exclusively with WIRED by States United Action, a nonpartisan nonprofit that supports state officials in protecting elections.
These numbers include a sitting US congressman who voted against certifying the 2020 election results; a former state representative who integrated QAnon conspiracy theories into election denialism; and local election officials who have actively sought to undermine election results by pushing baseless conspiracy theories about noncitizen voting.
But for election experts and officials, one of the biggest concerns ahead of the midterms is the possibility that these election deniers could obtain oversight of the 2028 presidential election process. The data shows there are already 27 election deniers in 20 states who hold a statewide office with election oversight, like secretary of state or attorney general—positions that allow the holder to set voting rules or prosecute those they believe are cheating at the ballots. In November, 33 election deniers will seek to secure similar positions in states across the country.
“All Americans should be concerned if people who are trying to undermine trust in elections and trying to interfere in the election process are taking positions of responsibility over elections,” Wendy Weiser, vice president for democracy at the nonprofit Brennan Center for Justice, tells WIRED. “We've seen in recent years an increasing number of election deniers taking some positions of public trust. As the numbers increase, it just increases the risk to our election system. This really is an attempt to corrode the system from within.”
The huge roster of election deniers on the ballot in November has also been emboldened by a groundswell of local groups and individuals who have been working for years to promote baseless claims about mail-in voting, noncitizen voter fraud, and rigged voting machines.
And from the top, President Donald Trump has increasingly pushed election-denial conspiracy theories, according to data gathered by States United Action. The group’s data shows that 60 percent of Trump’s statements referencing elections since the 2024 election include an explicit claim of fraud, rigging, or theft. That percentage has risen to 84 percent in the second quarter of 2026.
"The election-denial movement is more powerful than ever, and it's a direct threat to our freedom to vote,” Joanna Lydgate, CEO of States United Action, tells WIRED. “Election deniers are embedded at every level of government, pushing conspiracy theories from positions of real power.”
WIRED is keeping a close eye on many of these impactful races featuring election deniers. Here are five of the midterm races featuring election deniers that WIRED and States United Action are tracking:
The Michigan Senate Race
In the wake of the 2020 election, former US representative Mike Rogers slammed Trump’s efforts to persuade Georgia’s secretary of state to change the election results as “more gangster than presidential.” He was also unequivocal in his assessment of Trump’s role in the attack on the Capitol on January 6, 2021: “You’re damn right you had responsibility for this,” Rogers said at the time.
But now, seeking a return to Congress as the Republican nominee for Senate in Michigan, Rogers appears to see election denialism as a winning campaign strategy. “I am thankful for President Trump’s commitment to transparency. The news coming out of the White House tonight is deeply troubling—especially that of a voter fraud scheme right here in Michigan,” Rogers wrote on X moments after Trump delivered a conspiracy-filled speech about election fraud, including a long-debunked claim about fraud in Michigan.
Polls show Rogers in a dead heat with Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed.
The Wisconsin Governor Race
In December 2020, as a member of Congress, Tom Tiffany signed up for a Texas lawsuit seeking to invalidate President Joe Biden’s victory. Tiffany also voted against certifying the results in Pennsylvania and Arizona on January 6, 2021, after the attack on the Capitol and has suggested he would have overturned Wisconsin’s results too. This year, Tiffany has warmly welcomed the FBI’s baseless investigation into the state’s elections.
As governor, Tiffany would have the power to appoint some of the state’s top election officials on the Wisconsin Elections Commission, giving him the ability to install election deniers to oversee voting for the 2028 presidential election.
Initial polls show Tiffany slightly trailing his Democrat opponent, David Crowley.
The Ohio Governor Race
Billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy has long questioned the 2020 electron results and has baselessly claimed that it was stolen by “big tech.” Ramaswamy has also called the January 6 attack on the Capitol an “inside job” and “entrapment.” He has provided no evidence to back up any of these claims.
As part of his campaign for governor, Ramaswamy has supported voter-suppression measures that enshrine restrictive voter ID law into the state’s constitution. If Ramaswamy becomes Ohio governor, he would be in a position to have much more power over forcing such measures through and could deeply impact the 2028 presidential election.
Polling suggests the race is extremely tight.
The Nevada Secretary of State Race
Former Nevada state representative Jim Marchant says being called an election denier is a “badge of honor.” Marchant was among the most ardent boosters of election denial in the wake of the 2020 election, going so far as to help arrange a QAnon coalition of candidates for the 2022 midterms.
November’s race will be a rerun of the 2022 race, when Marchant lost to current secretary of state Cisco Aguilar. While he won the GOP primary in June, Marchant lacks support from much of the Republican establishment and has struggled to raise money. (Filings from July show Marchant had just $13.86 in his campaign war chest, compared to over $1 million for his opponent.)
Marchant has radical plans to overhaul Nevada’s voting system if he wins, including deregistering every single voter in the state, moving to paper ballots, and requiring all votes to be counted by hand. As secretary of state, Marchant would be able to change election procedures and advise county election officials, and he would help certify statewide results for the 2028 presidential election.
No public polling is available for the race.
The Colorado Secretary of State Race
In Colorado, the Republican candidate for secretary of state is avowed election denier James Wiley. Wiley says the 2020 election was stolen and that, if victorious, his first act would be to delete Colorado’s voter lists and force every citizen to reregister. (This is illegal on both a federal and state level.) He also wants to do away with all voting machines but at the same time place all public records on the blockchain, according to his campaign website.
Wiley, who calls himself “the red flame of liberty” due to his red hair, has admitted using the ELLY tool to back up his claims that up to 25 percent of registered voters in Colorado have issues with their voter registration. The ELLY tool was developed by the creators of EagleAI, a tool created by a former doctor which was used ahead of the 2024 election by conservative activists to challenge voter roll registrations, often based on inaccurate data.
His opponent, Amanda Gonzalez, is the current Jefferson County clerk and previously ran Common Cause Colorado, a nonpartisan, good-government advocacy group.
No public polling is available for the race.
