Once famous for its ties to business schools, McKinsey is casting a wider net to meet its needs.
For decades, an MBA was one of the clearest routes into elite consulting. As AI changes the work firms do for clients, the consulting industry is looking for people who can build technology as well as devise the corporate strategy around it.
"Our recruiting changed dramatically in the last few years. We recruit from places we haven't recruited before," Ben Ellencweig, who leads McKinsey's AI arm, QuantumBlack, told Business Insider. "Today many, many of our colleagues are coming from non-MBA backgrounds, and then technology too is kind of the next wave."
That includes mathematicians, computer-science PhDs, startup founders without degrees, and people with experience at technology companies.
The shift is playing out beyond McKinsey. Job postings from Deloitte, PwC, EY, KPMG, McKinsey, BCG, and Bain fell by about 24% in the year ending May 2026 compared to the year before, according to labor-market intelligence firm Draup. At the same time, AI jobs grew from 1.4% to 5% of their total openings.
The number of forward-deployed-engineer openings across the seven firms rose from none to 1,404 in that same period, according to the analysis. Such roles require engineers who can deploy and run production AI systems inside organizations, and also do the client-facing work traditionally associated with consulting.
According to McKinsey's current job postings, most of those roles require at least four or five years of computer-related engineering experience.
Ellencweig said McKinsey is looking to fill these roles with "curious people" who are excited to work with clients and solve problems through technology, but who also bring deep technical skills. The firm is recruiting from different geographies, schools, and "outside-of-school, non-school backgrounds," he said.
In an email to Business Insider, the firm added that it is recruiting through "less traditional pathways," such as coding programs and bootcamps.
QuantumBlack itself has grown from 47 data scientists working with a Formula 1 team to "well above 5,000" AI professionals over the past decade, Ellencweig said. Those workers include data scientists, data engineers, designers, product managers, and product owners.
McKinsey rival EY has recently spoken about its own push to widen its talent pool. Ginnie Carlier, EY Americas' chief talent and culture officer, told BI earlier this year that the Big Four firm was once exclusively made up of accountants, but now it also hires engineers, creatives, and technologists.
Ellencweig said McKinsey is reinventing itself around technology, including how it hires and how it develops current employees.
"I view our entire workforce, the entire McKinsey, including our consultant cohort, becoming very technology savvy," McKinsey's Ellencweig said.

- The claim that the Flight 93 National Memorial changed the time of its 2026 9/11 observance to accommodate a visit from U.S. President Donald Trump or Vice President JD Vance but neither showed up is unproven.
- Though event pages for past Flight 93 National Memorial ceremonies showed the 2026 event started around an hour and 15 minutes earlier than in previous years, the 2026 program (archived) also was longer than previous years. Moreover, we found no evidence that Trump or Vance were supposed to attend the event at the memorial but failed to show.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We have reached out to the National Park Service regarding the reason for an earlier start time in 2026 and the White House to find out whether Trump and/or Vance were supposed to attend, and are waiting for responses.
After the U.S. commemorated the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, a claim (archived) circulated online that the Flight 93 National Memorial changed the time of its 9/11 observance to accommodate a visit from U.S. President Donald Trump or Vice President JD Vance but neither showed up.
United Airlines Flight 93 was one of four planes hijacked on 9/11. It was the only one that did not hit a building, instead crashing in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers attempted to retake control of the plane from the hijackers.
In sharing the claim about Trump and Vance, one X user wrote: "The 9/11 Flight 93 Memorial reportedly changed the time of their ceremony to accommodate a visit from Trump or Vance, but neither of them showed up. Trump traveled to a golf tournament instead."
The 9/11 Flight 93 Memorial reportedly changed the time of their ceremony to accommodate a visit from Trump or Vance, but neither of them showed up.
Trump traveled to a golf tournament instead. pic.twitter.com/SVhVbLaY6s
— Headquarters (@HQNewsNow) September 14, 2026
The claim also circulated on Facebook (archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim.
The claim is unproven. Though event pages for 9/11 observances at the Flight 93 National Memorial from 2020 to 2026 showed the 2026 event started around an hour and 15 minutes earlier than previous ceremonies, the program (archived) also was longer than in previous years.
We found no evidence that Trump or Vance were supposed to attend the event at the memorial but did not show. Trump attended a commemoration ceremony at the Pentagon with military leaders on Sept. 11, 2026, while Vance attended a commemoration event in New York City at the site of the former Twin Towers. Trump travelled to Dublin, Ireland, in the evening for a two-day visit that included attending the Irish Open at his Doonbeg golf club on Sept. 13.
We contacted the National Park Service, which manages the Flight 93 National Memorial, to ask why the 2026 observance started earlier than in previous years. We also asked the White House press office whether Trump or Vance were supposed to attend the Flight 93 National Memorial observance and await replies to our queries.
In the meantime, because the NPS had not confirmed why the 2026 event had a different start time than previous years, we leave this claim unrated.
Longer 2026 event also memorialized other 9/11 flights
According to event programs for the 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 events, previous 9/11 observances at the Flight 93 National Memorial started at either 9:45 or 9:50 a.m., which could be in order to coincide with the exact time Flight 93 crashed near Shanksville, at 10:03 a.m. Sept. 11, 2001. The 2026 event started at 8:30 a.m.
The event programs from 2021 to 2024 generally started with welcome remarks, the Pledge of Allegiance or national anthem, followed by a reading of the names of the 40 passengers and crew on board Flight 93 who died when the plane crashed.
The event programs then listed bells of remembrance, a moment of reflection and conclusion and a wreath-laying. Some events also featured speakers such as former President George W. Bush and then-Vice President Kamala Harris in 2021 and then-first lady Jill Biden in 2022. Trump attended a smaller, live-streamed ceremony during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
The 2026 program appeared longer than in previous years, and included remembrances for the three other hijacked flights on 9/11 that struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon. The 2026 program added musical selections and also included bell tollings and wreath-layings for American Airlines Flight 11, which hit the North Tower on 8:46 a.m., United Airlines Flight 175, which hit the South Tower at 9:03 a.m., and American Airlines Flight 77, which hit the Pentagon at 9:37 a.m.
If the 2026 event intended to honor the other three flights at the times they crashed, it would have needed to start earlier than the previous 9:45 or 9:50 a.m. start times.
For further reading, Snopes has investigated a series of other rumors about where Trump was or what he was doing on or around Sept. 11, 2001.

Anthropic says Claude 'leads' 26 percent of its AI R&D work
The company shared the stat alongside three measurements that help communicate the pace of AI development.
Anthropic — well, specifically CEO Dario Amodei — has a lot to say about AI safety in the aftermath of OpenAI's disclosure that its AI agents hacked Hugging Face, and it's already revealed some interesting details about how it works in the process. For example, in a new blog detailing measurement standards it thinks could help AI companies communicate the pace of AI development, Anthropic shared that its AI chatbot Claude "leads" 26 percent of its AI R&D work.
Now by "leads," the company means that the AI "can complete most of [a] task end-to-end from a high-level prompt, while [a] human supervises," but it's still a surprising metric. It also claims that AI now does at least "large chunks of work under close human direction" on more than 90 percent of its research, which includes the 26 percent Claude leads. That suggests Claude is touching the majority of the work Anthropic employees do, even if the company says the chatbot is "not operating fully autonomously for any measured subset of AI R&D work."
Anthropic came up with these stats through the first of its three proposed measurements, which is focused on "AI-led AI R&D." Using an index of how much of its AI research and development is performed by Claude and an automation rating scale developed by Epoch AI, Anthropic was able to create a chart that plots the "automation level" of Claude since August 2025, a process it believes any frontier AI model maker could reproduce with its own data and the validation of a third party.
The company also proposed ways to measure the oversight of AI agents (how much agent activity is monitored, how long it takes to be reviewed and how often agent behavior is flagged) and to track how much compute is being devoted to AI R&D as other ways to see if frontier development is being appropriately paced. The hope is that more transparency could make it easier to respond to potentially out-of-control AI development or at least give the public a clearer view.
So far though, the problem isn't really getting companies to agree on the idea of slowing down AI development. OpenAI has already paid lip service to the idea, and Anthropic has committed to allowing third-party evaluators to review its development practices. Amodei's stance on AI safety even got Elon Musk to agree on X. Whether the AI industry faces anything other than self-regulation is far more uncertain — President Donald Trump has largely downplayed the risks of AI.

Paediatric heart surgeries that can cost families anywhere between ₹5 lakh and ₹20 lakh each at private hospitals, were provided free of cost to children at the Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS) in Hyderabad. As part of its fifth paediatric cardiac surgery camp, NIMS performed 19 complex heart surgeries on a cashless basis on children aged between two months and 13 years. The week-long camp concluded on Saturday (September 12, 2026)
The surgeries were carried out by the NIMS Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery in collaboration with Healing Little Hearts, with a specialist team led by paediatric cardiac surgeon Ramana Dhanapuneni from the UK. The NIMS team was headed by M. Amaresh Rao, Head of Cardiothoracic Surgery.
From screening to surgery
The camp’s impact extended well beyond the 19 operations. Around 1,000 children were screened as part of the programme. Of these, few were found to require minimally invasive intervention rather than open-heart surgery. The surgical team, meanwhile, selected a mix of complex congenital heart cases for the camp, prioritising children who required specialised cardiac surgery. More than 100 children who require surgery are still waiting, with dates already allotted for their procedures, said Dr. Amaresh.
“Congenital heart disease is common and the cost of paediatric cardiac surgery in private hospitals can be prohibitive for many families, ranging from ₹5 lakh to ₹20 lakh. Hope for the poor is public sector hospitals like NIMS,” said Dr. Ramana.
80 surgeries through five camps
The latest camp is the fifth such programme conducted through the collaboration between Dr. Dhanapuneni’s team and NIMS. The partnership began in 2023, when two camps were conducted. One camp was held in 2024 and another in 2025.
NIMS Director Rahul Devraj said the five camps had resulted in about 80 surgeries so far. “NIMS would like Dr. Ramana and his team to visit twice a year, assuring continued institutional support to the visiting specialists and the cardiac department,” he said.
Around 7,000 children in Telangana with critical congenital heart diseases
Dr. Amaresh said there are around 7,000 children in Telangana with critical congenital heart diseases, while NIMS currently performs around 400 paediatric cardiac surgeries annually. The department needs to reach 1,000 surgeries a year, he said.
ECMO support under Aarogyasri
Another significant development pertaining to the camp was the availability of ECMO services at NIMS under the Aarogyasri scheme for the first time. “No patient needed it during this camp,” Dr. Amaresh clarified. However, he said the significance was that ECMO would now be available to eligible patients free of cost for as long as it is medically required, subject to the scheme’s provisions.

Meta has removed several Instagram and Facebook accounts and content related to the Jantar Mantar protest that Alt News had flagged as AI-manipulated visuals.
On September 2, a Meta spokesperson confirmed to Alt News that following a review, all the accounts and content were found to be violative of the platform’s policies and had been removed.
These posts included several AI-generated and AI-manipulated photographs and videos of women protesting at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar during the Cockroach Janta Party-led students’ protest in July. Alt News flagged Instagram and Facebook accounts and posts to Meta, in which real visuals women had been altered using AI, purportedly in an attempt to outrage their modesty.
In these posts, women’s clothes, bodies and poses had been altered in such a way that they looked starkly different from the original videos or photographs. Alt News’ investigation found that many such visuals were either entirely AI-generated or altered using AI. In some cases, techniques such as face swaps or body swaps were used.
Targeting Women CJP Protesters
Women protesters who participated in the CJP protests in Delhi were particularly targeted on social media. For several days, women faced online harassment and trolling, doxxing, rape threats and the public disclosure of personal information. These AI-visuals formed part of this larger pattern of attacks against female protesters.
These fake visuals were shared on Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, among other platforms, claiming that they were real footage from the Jantar Mantar protest. Users then mistook the AI characters for real women partaking in the protests which was followed by objectionable and misogynistic comments targeting their identities, physical appearance, clothes and character. A few of those comments are displayed below:
Alt News identified several Instagram accounts which circulated such malicious content, including @kauronfire, @sirfseerat, @tia_kaurr, @hey.siya_2.0, @kavya_homevibes, @annika0022, @divyankaha and @its_anushkaa69.
Right-wing Users Share AI Image
During the protest, several right-wing users, including RSS supporters Acharya Ankur Arya and Vikram Pratap Singh, shared an AI-generated image claiming that it was a real photograph from the Jantar Mantar protest.
The purported image showed a young woman wearing a crop top and jeans. Users who shared the post made objectionable comments about the woman’s clothing and character. Alt News fact-checked this viral image and found that it was entirely AI-generated.
However, in some cases that surfaced on social media during the final days of the protest, besides entirely AI-generated images, real photographs of women were being altered, making it difficult to determine its authencity.
Visuals Of A Woman In White Saree
An user, @divyankaha, shared a photo and video on their Instagram account and YouTube channel respectively. These showed a woman wearing a white saree and navy blue blouse, linking her to the Jantar Mantar protest. (Archive link-1, Archive link-2)
Alt News found the original video of the post uploaded on an Instagram page @khoji_reporter24news.
Comparing the viral clip with the original video, we found that the body and clothing of the woman were entirely different, thus confirming that the image had been altered using AI. The background and original footage of the viral video remained the same, but the appearance of the woman had been completely manipulated. After Alt News flagged this to Meta, they removed @divyankaha‘s account.
We found several such posts and videos on @divyankaha‘s page. In another post, a woman wearing a white saree is seen sitting on the road wit posters infront of her. Alt News found this photo was also an AI-deepfake. (Archive link)
Several different versions of the viral post, with a woman in a white saree, were also found circulating widely on social media. All of these were AI-deepfakes.
Visuals Of A Woman Standing With A Poster
Another photograph went viral showing different women near the stage at the Jantar Mantar protest, holding posters that read “Resign De De Bhai PUNE SE Aai hu..and Hum jeet gaye”.
In the different iterations of this photo being shared, the woman as well as the design of the poster kept changing. These photos were shared by right-wing handles and those opposing the CJP protest, with objectionable comments and captions. (Archive Link-1, Link-2, Link-3, Link-4)
We found that this photo had been altered using AI. The original photoe was posted on July 22 by an Instagram account named @nanddhini.
A comparison of the original and viral photos clearly showed the difference in the woman’s face and body. The design of the poster also appears to have changed across different viral versions. Thus, the face and body of the woman in the original photo were swapped using an AI editing tool.
Similarly, several AI-generated and manipulated photos and videos were shared on the Facebook and Instagram accounts of @sirfseerat. These posts either altered real visuals related to the Jantar Mantar protest or created entirely new AI visuals. Some of these posts, displayed below, were later deleted.
Woman Speaking To Journalist
An Instagram AI-digital creator page named @kauronfire shared a video on July 23 in which a journalist can be seen interviewing a woman participating in the protest. (Archive)
We found the original video posted on journalist Muskan Bhagat’s Instagram account. (Archive)

We found the original video on the Instagram account of content creator Himani Chawla, who can be seen wearing a blue suit in the video. This video is actually from Indore, Madhya Pradesh, where Chawla and her companions were serving sharbat to passersby. Thus, the video had absolutely no connection with the Jantar Mantar protest. These accounts misused AI, not only as a means to spread misinformation, but also to depict women in an objectionable manner, exposing them to online, and even real life harassment and abuse — all of which amount to punishable offences under the IT Act and the IT Rules of India.
On August 25, after receiving confirmation from Meta regarding the action taken, Alt News rechecked those accounts and posts, and some accounts and posts appeared to be available. On September 2, Meta responded and confirmed that all the accounts and content shared by Alt News had now been removed from the platform. However, Meta did not respond to the questions regarding the accounts and content that had reappeared. The article will be updated if Meta responds.

It has been hard not to despair while watching the ruinous floods swallow parts of Nepal, and harder, still knowing that the agony compounds each passing day for dozens of Indian families whose members remain unaccounted for.
Social media is awash with desperate pleas, photos and details of the young and old, men and women, from Mumbai to Kolkata, posted by families searching for traces of life. The disaster unfolded when a melting glacier slammed into the valley below, unleashing a deadly cascade of rock and ice down the Bhote Kashi River, which flows from Tibet into Nepal.
Among the 275 Indians missing at the time of writing are workers of a hydropower project and people undertaking the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet. Another 128 people of Indian origin, including a large group of Sadhguru’s Isha Foundation spiritual group, are also missing; 149 Indian people have been rescued as of Monday.
For Gauri Joshi, whose five relatives remained unaccounted for over the weekend, the last few days have been a blur of calling their numbers in vain, watching news of rescue operations and trying to reach Indian officials – over and over again. What she has pieced together so far is that her relatives, part of a pilgrim tour group from Maharashtra, cleared immigration at the Gyirong border between Nepal and Tibet and boarded buses shortly before the flood waters destroyed the crossing.
“Chances appear very bleak now. But maybe a miracle will happen,” Joshi said.
The tragedy has reignited the question of how vulnerable the Himalayas are to climate change, and what its implications are for India. To understand the risks of glacier collapse and thawing permafrost leading to sudden floods and debris flows, I spoke to Dr Ashim Sattar, a professor at Indian Institute of Technology Bhubaneswar and an expert on glacial lake outburst floods. The conversation has been edited and condensed.
What are the climate- or glacier-related risks emerging across the Himalayas?
“There are different forms of cryosphere and how they pose a hazard. In a layperson’s terms, the cryosphere is where water exists in solid form, for example a glacier. When it melts, it forms glacial lakes. If they have an outburst, they can cause damage downstream.
Another cryospheric component is glacier ice. This is what we’ve seen in Nepal, where a glacier detachment happened. The frontal part of the glacier detached from the main glacier and eventually led to a debris flow.
The third component is permafrost. They exist widely in the Himalayas, but there has not been much monitoring because it’s very difficult. Everything – these lakes, glaciers and permafrost – are all hazards. Unless they’re triggered, they would not cause damage.
With climate change, these grounds will go above zero degrees and will start to degrade. These would need very little … to mobilise debris. We might expect a higher frequency of debris flows in the future. We won’t know how they are getting conditioned, unless we have some monitoring stations and scientific investigation.
And given the Himalayas are very vast, monitoring every part of it becomes tricky. It can be the mountain ranges within India, or maybe outside India, eventually, which drains into the Indian subcontinent. That needs to be well studied.”
How big are the downstream risks for India?
“Right now, this is a gap in scientific studies; nothing [is] quantified yet. There is direct evidence of climate impacts, even in the Indian part of the Himalayas. The number of glacial lakes is increasing, the size of glacial lakes is increasing, the volume of glacial lakes is increasing, and glaciers are retreating. The risk exists because it might happen any time.”
Which parts of India are the most vulnerable?
“Everyone in the Himalayas, every Himalayan state has hazards. We can’t deny it. If you look at the eastern side, they have a lot of glacial lakes. They have already reached their maximum extent. Most full-grown lakes are about to reach their limits, like maximum extent. In the western Himalayas or even the central Himalayas, there’s a lot of scope for the lakes because they have not reached their full extent. As the glaciers would retreat, they would keep on growing.
We are still unsure when the status is going to change for any of these states. That’s a very, very difficult question, and I don’t think anyone [can] answer it at this moment without any scientific investigation.”
How would you describe India’s early warning systems and disaster preparedness?
“The National Disaster Management Authority is taking proactive steps now with the glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) Risk Mitigation Programme to install early-warning systems.
Maybe an early warning system should be community-based. It should be for the people and by the people. It’s not always the scientist or the policymakers who can actually make this work at its full potential. We need to have local knowledge, involve the communities to make them more effective.”
How long will it take to have these systems in place?
“I have no idea because each of these organisations are working at their own pace. They have their own style of working. I’m sure it is going to happen soon. I can just comment on the areas where I know, and I’ve been in touch.”
Is prevention possible, or can it only minimise the damage?
“Prevention is possible, but it is very expensive: computationally, financially and manpower-wise. Minimising is also possible. It would require a lot of intervention in the high mountains, which is very difficult in those terrains.
We know that the mountains are changing and the hazard levels are increasing, so the only way forward is to minimise the exposure to the risk below. That means how much of the hazard is going to interact with the downstream. If something is in the path, we remove them.”

Photographer Aashim Tyagi (@aashim), who once documented Art Deco architecture in Gujarat’s Balasinor, suggests a prehistoric side quest: “I was intrigued by the town’s reputation as the ‘Jurassic Park of India’ and a little digging led me to a dinosaur museum in neighbouring Raiyoli. YouTube star Ms Rachel has said she is matching rapper Macklemore’s $1m donation to organizations supporting Palestinians, calling on other public figures to follow suit.
Macklemore, who was fired as the opening act on Ed Sheeran’s tour after saying “Free Palestine” on stage at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium, pledged to donate the entirety of his earnings from Sheeran’s tour to several organizations focused on the Palestinian people.
Ms Rachel, whose full name is Rachel Accurso, wrote on Instagram: “Over 20,000 precious Palestinian children have been killed, and children continue to be killed every day.”
Accurso said her donation would go to the Palestine Children’s Relief Fund.
“We have a moral obligation to use our privilege and platforms to protect children and human rights,” she wrote.
Accurso, a children’s entertainer with over 21 million YouTube subscribers, has been vocal about the hardships Gaza’s young people face amid the war with Israel. She encouraged “every wealthy white celebrity” to match her donation.
Accurso is the latest public figure to back Macklemore, after he was dropped from Sheeran’s Loop tour for remarks he made at a 4 September concert about the plight of the Palestinian people.
“Free Palestine! I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them,” he said during a two-minute speech.
Macklemore’s words prompted a flurry of criticism from Israel-aligned groups. The singer Pink also called on Macklemore to be removed from the tour, and referenced a 2014 incident where he wore a costume decried for bearing resemblance to Jewish caricature. Macklemore apologized for the costume at the time.
Pink expanded on her position in an Instagram post, saying she was not speaking on behalf of the Israeli government, but rather wanted to advocate for Jewish concertgoers who may have been alarmed by the rapper’s remarks.
Macklemore directly addressed Jewish audience members at a second tour date on 5 September, saying: “Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you. My message is for peace, love; for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect and equality.”
Sheeran has maintained the decision to fire Macklemore was led by stadium owners, including Gillette Stadium and New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft.
Sheeran wrote on Tuesday on Instagram: “I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have them, and it doesn’t mean I don’t care. Nor does it mean I don’t support causes in my own, personal way.”
Kraft and Sheeran are both donating $2m each to Palestinian relief funds, Kraft said Wednesday, although it is unclear which organizations their funds will support.
Four supporting acts, among them American singer Finneas and Danish pop band Lukas Graham, have quit the tour in solidarity with Macklemore.

Netflix has unveiled the first look of its upcoming family drama series Unaccustomed Earth, starring Freida Pinto and Siddharth in the lead roles. The series is inspired by Jhumpa Lahiri’s acclaimed short story collection of the same name and is set to premiere on December 17, 2026.
Netflix unveils first look of Freida Pinto and Siddharth starrer Unaccustomed Earth, to release on December 17
Adapted by Madhuri Shekar, who also serves as the showrunner and writer, Unaccustomed Earth follows an Indian American community as its members navigate relationships, family expectations, loss and questions of belonging across generations.
Freida Pinto plays Parul Chaudhury
Freida Pinto plays Parul Chaudhury, a wife and mother whose life takes an unexpected turn after she is diagnosed with cancer. The character has previously made significant personal sacrifices, including giving up her college first love to respect her father’s wishes.
Following her diagnosis, Parul moves with her family from India to Cambridge, Massachusetts, a place where she had previously felt a strong sense of belonging. The move prompts her to reconsider the life choices she has made and pursue possibilities she had left behind.
Her decisions subsequently have an impact not only on her family but also on the wider immigrant community around her.
Siddharth plays Amit, with the series also featuring Indraneil Sengupta as Jai, Parveen Kaur as Nina, Sarayu Blue as Ruma, Justin Bartha as Adam, Adi Roy as Kaushik, Iyla Sundarsingh Mckaig as Hema and Jayant Kripalani as Pranab.
View this post on Instagram
Adapted from Jhumpa Lahiri’s short story collection
Unaccustomed Earth takes inspiration from Lahiri’s collection, which explores the experiences of Indian American families and their relationships with identity, culture, family and home.
The Netflix series is set across Cambridge and Boston, Massachusetts, and centres on multiple generations within the community. The story brings together themes of love, personal choices, family ties and the experience of living between cultures.
The series has Madhuri Shekar as showrunner and writer, with John Wells, Jhumpa Lahiri, Nisha Ganatra, Erica Saleh, Erin Jontow and Celia Costas also serving as executive producers. Ritesh Batra is set to direct and executive produce the first two episodes.
The additional cast includes Ishita Bansal as Divya, Meera Simham as Swati, Ravi Kapoor as Vishal, Swayam Bhatia as Sudha and Palomi Ghosh as Anjali.
Unaccustomed Earth is produced by Warner Bros. Television and will stream exclusively on Netflix from December 17, 2026.

Americans want answers on Social Security this midterm season
A looming 22 percent benefit cut is driving midterm voters to demand solutions — because lawmakers elected this cycle will still be in office when trust funds deplete in late 2032, voters say candidates cannot ignore the crisis
A vast majority of voters in key Senate battleground states favor candidates who present explicit plans to reform Social Security over those who pledge to leave the program untouched, according to research conducted by the Peterson Foundation.
The nationwide survey of 2,500 registered voters, conducted between August 20 and August 27, found that more than 80 percent of respondents preferred a representative with a strategy to prevent automatic benefit reductions. In contrast, 17 percent favored candidates promising not to touch the system.
The urgency stems from a tight financial deadline. A report from the Social Security Board of Trustees projected that the trust fund used to top off payroll taxes would run dry in the late months of 2032. If Congress does not intervene before then, the shortfall will force an immediate 22 percent pay cut for all beneficiaries.
Because senators elected this cycle will be in office when the depletion occurs, analysts emphasize that the upcoming elections carry increased weight.
“The voters who will determine the balance of the U. S. Senate are calling on candidates to strengthen the future of Social Security,” Michael Peterson, chief executive of the Peterson Foundation, said. “Senators elected this fall will be in office in 2032 when Social Security recipients will face immediate 22% cuts, so all candidates should be putting forth solutions in this campaign to prevent this catastrophic result.”
An analysis by the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget noted that 63 million Americans — including 54 million retirees and 9 million dependents and survivors — would be affected by the cuts. The average national loss would equal approximately $500 per recipient per month.
In five critical battleground states, the financial burden varies, according to the CRFB analysis.
Texas faces the largest overall hit, where 4.3 million Social Security recipients would see an average monthly reduction of $489.
Ohio follows with 2.2 million residents losing an average of $487 each month, while Michigan has 2 million beneficiaries facing an average monthly loss of $523.
In North Carolina, 2 million people would experience an average monthly decline of $501, and in Georgia, 1.7 million voters face an average monthly drop of $487.
The Peterson Foundation survey showed that 91 percent of respondents supported structural reforms once informed of the 2032 automatic cut projections. Additionally, 85 percent indicated that persistent inflation made resolving the funding shortfall urgent.
Survey results showed clear backing for a range of policy changes to keep the program solvent.
Most respondents, 72 percent, favored adding a 1 percent payroll tax on income over $184,500. Two-thirds supported capping annual benefits at $100,000 per retired couple, while 65 percent backed benefit cuts for the top 20 percent of earners. An equal 65 percent favored a combination of gradual benefit changes and tax increases.
“The good news indicated by this survey is that voters want this problem addressed, and there is strong bipartisan support for many available solutions that would sustain this essential program,” Peterson said.
Voters drew a firm line against using national debt to cover the gap. Just 29 percent favored federal borrowing to address the shortfall, while 68 percent explicitly opposed adding to the $40 trillion national deficit.

Asian governments are rushing preparations for the most severe El Niño weather event on record, with hundreds of millions of people bracing for multiple crises at once as extreme heat, heavy rain and food shortages hit the region.
Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific – and developing alongside the human-driven climate crisis – El Niño is virtually guaranteed to grow to a very strong intensity towards the end of this year and into 2027.
The World Food Programme has warned that about 50 million people will probably be pushed into acute hunger due to the exceptionally intense weather system, while UN secretary-general António Guterres said this month that El Niño was “being supersized before our eyes”.
Here are the steps countries in Asia are taking to prepare for El Niño:
‘Climate risk maps’ in China
In Hong Kong, authorities have already been forced to revise workplace policies, after the city experienced its hottest day on record on 9 August. During times of extreme heat, companies are expected to reschedule work, provide cooling equipment and rest breaks for their employees.
Employers in the international financial hub could even face prosecution if they fail to provide staff with support at times of sweltering heat.
In mainland China a 100-day campaign has been launched to prepare for extreme weather and help safeguard harvests against the opposing extremes of drought and intense rainfall.
Beijing has plans to upgrade early warning monitoring systems, and in July, it launched a national plan encouraging cities to draw up ‘climate risk maps’ to help identify areas most vulnerable to flooding and severe heat.
Taiwan, meanwhile, is treating the predicted extreme weather as an emergency situation, and preparing using methods similar to what it would do to train for a terrorist attack or earthquake. In early September, the island nation held a mass exercise simulating three consecutive days of temperatures above 40C. Hundreds of people took part in the field exercises, which simulated power and water disruption, rail problems, air conditioner failure and mass heatstroke.
The government has also been testing its “Cool Map” online platform, which helps to direct vulnerable people to airconditioned and cool spaces.
Sri Lanka plans to process salterwater
El Niño is already wreaking havoc across south Asia; in parts of India there has been a shortfall of monsoon rainfall of almost 50% in September, with knock-on effects on key crops such as rice, pulses, cotton and maize. Concerns are mounting that there could be a diminished harvest in the coming months, likely driving up food prices – already crippling for poor and lower middle class families.
The Indian government has taken a hyper-vigilant approach to establish what the agriculture minister, Shivraj Singh Chouhan, described as a “protective shield for farmers”.
In more than 350 vulnerable districts authorities are boosting water conservation infrastructure and water harvesting, and are encouraging farmers to plant low-water, short duration crops – such as pulses and millets.
But the most intense impact of El Niño in the area is in Sri Lanka, where the absence of rainfall and high temperatures have become so severe that the country is experiencing its worst drought in a decade. More than 160,000 people are now facing a drinking water shortage as several key reservoirs run dry.
Officials have been forced to close the tourist areas of the Yala national park, home to leopards, elephants, crocodiles and spotted deer, and have been bringing in tankers of water to fill the ponds to make sure the animals do not die. In Mullaithivu lagoon, in the north-east of Sri Lanka, thousands of fish were found dead due to the lack of fresh water.
The country’s disaster management centre is preparing for a situation in which freshwater supplies could vanish. “If water sources dry up, there will be no alternative means of obtaining water,” an official said. Colombo would then be forced to process salt water from the sea, although relying on the country’s one desalination plant is not considered workable.
Tackling an agriculture crisis in south-east Asia
In south-east Asia, El Niño is compounded by a series of ongoing crises. The Iran war has already disrupted global energy and supply chains and inflated fertiliser costs, disproportionately hitting the region. At the same time, severe haze from seasonal fires across Malaysia and Indonesia has choked cities and is damaging plants and trees.
During the 2023–2024 El Niño, south-east Asian governments successfully cushioned agricultural impacts by adjusting planting calendars and managing water, but those strategies will be insufficient to deal with the scale of the crisis, experts warn. Regional rice yields are already projected to fall by 8 to 10%.
“We can’t just assume that this El Niño is going to be the same as the last because there are so many challenges that have been stacking on top of each other,” says Elyssa Kaur Ludher, a climate and food security expert based in Singapore.
The Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia are particularly vulnerable to food price changes, says Kaur Ludher, a visiting fellow with the Climate Change for Southeast Asia Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.
“In Singapore, most of our income is not spent on food. It’s under 10%. But for Indonesians, it can be up to 50% or even more as a proportion of income spent on food. So any price rise affects them disproportionately.”
With the potential for price rises to leave people desperate and angry, Kaur Ludher has argued for food security to be reframed as a national security issue. In Indonesia and the Philippines in particular, she said, social stability depends a lot on food prices. “Rice is a lifeline to this region,” she says.
To prepare, south-east Asian governments and farmer cooperatives are promoting regenerative agriculture and shifting toward biofertilisers.
“We have come to a stage where climate change is putting so much pressure on us – on our existing, already crumbling or structurally unsound, systems,” say Kaur Ludher. “Nature will force us to have a reckoning.”
South Korea overhauls its heatwave alert system
South Korea saw the driest July on record in the country’s south-east. Weeks later came a freak reversal, as a weakening storm system dragged in a deluge that dumped some of the heaviest rainfall ever recorded at a Korean weather station. The heat was so intense that farmers described spoilt potatoes as being “boiled” in the ground.
The country’s weather agency has overhauled its heatwave alert system for the first time in 18 years, adding a top tier that triggers official guidance to stop non-emergency outdoor work once feels-like temperatures hit 38C. Nationwide, phones have buzzed for weeks with government alerts urging people to stay indoors during the hottest hours.
Officials are watching out for a rough autumn, with seas around the Korean peninsula remaining unusually warm for the season and forecasters expecting the north-west Pacific to produce far more powerful storms than usual this year, since a strengthening El Niño is weakening the high pressure that has so far kept them away.
Japan prepares for ‘cruelly’ hot days and typhoons
Japan is also bracing for the arrival of so-called super-typhoons, which experts attribute to a combination of El Niño and human-induced global heating.
El Niño was once associated with slightly cooler summers in Japan. But rising sea surface temperatures mean it is having the opposite effect, blanketing many parts of the country in record-breaking heat and humidity in 2023-4, the last time the weather pattern materialised.
Japan recorded its first official “cruelly hot day” – or kokushobi – in July, just after the start of the current El Niño event. The Japanese term, introduced in April to underscore the threat to health posed by rising temperatures, refers to days when the mercury exceeds 40C.
Now, as the summer heat dissipates, the country is bracing for the arrival of potentially destructive typhoons.
The public is encouraged to take measures to protect themselves and their homes, such as heeding official evacuation warnings and stocking up on food and water. People living in apartments are urged to secure or bring inside flower pots and furniture – anything that could become a dangerous flying object during a storm.
This month the infrastructure ministry said it had identified several high-risk underpasses on national highways that would be closed preemptively during heavy rain. Underpasses – which allow cars to travel beneath other roads or railway lines – became a focus of concern last month after two trapped motorists drowned during record-breaking rain in Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo.

Sixteen years ago, David Fincher wowed audiences with the dorm-room origin story of Facebook with "The Social Network."
The movie would go on to earn eight Oscar nominations and three wins and make stars out of Jesse Eisenberg as its creator, Mark Zuckerberg, and Andrew Garfield as Zuck's former friend and collaborator, Eduardo Saverin.
Now, Aaron Sorkin, who won an Oscar for penning "The Social Network" script, is taking on the writing and directing duties for the movie's follow-up, "The Social Reckoning."
In this movie, things have changed dramatically for Zuckerberg (now played by Jeremy Strong), as Facebook has grown into one of the most influential companies on the planet. But the company has some dark secrets.
Oscar winner Mikey Madison plays Facebook engineer Frances Haugen, who has put her trust in Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz, played by Jeremy Allen White, to expose the company's internal research and decision-making.
Sorkin based the script on The Wall Street Journal's expansive investigative series, The Facebook Files, which delved into the social network's impact on youth mental health, misinformation, and the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack.
Sony will release the movie on October 9. Here's everything to know.
Aaron Sorkin has wanted to do a "Social Network" follow-up for years.
Sorkin is no stranger to exploring power and the people who wield it. When he wasn't creating shows like "The West Wing" and "The Newsroom," he wrote the scripts for movies like "The American President" and "Steve Jobs."
But he's never been able to let go of Zuckerberg and Facebook. In a 2020 interview for the "Happy Sad Confused" podcast, he noted that what fascinated him about a continuation to "The Social Network" was exploring "the dark side of Facebook."
That interest intensified a year later when The Wall Street Journal released The Facebook Files.
By the spring of 2025, Sony announced that Sorkin was attached to write and direct a follow-up movie.
"There isn't a life that Facebook's algorithm hasn't touched, and that influence has reshaped everything," Sorkin told a room full of movie theater owners at their annual convention, CinemaCon, back in April. "It's time to say more."
Sorkin said he spent 3 days trying to convince Jesse Eisenberg to play Mark Zuckerberg again.
When Sorkin took on "The Social Reckoning," one of the first people he sent the script to was Jesse Eisenberg, whose performance as Mark Zuckerberg in "The Social Network" earned him an Oscar nomination.
"I felt like it belonged to him, and he was certainly battle-tested," Sorkin told Vanity Fair about hoping Eisenberg would reprise the role.
Sorkin told the magazine he spent three days trying to convince Eisenberg, but ultimately, the actor declined.
"He simply did not want to be conflated with Mark Zuckerberg anymore, that he has his problems with the guy," Sorkin told Vanity Fair. "He doesn't like kids coming up to him in airports with business cards that say 'I'm CEO, bitch' for him to sign."
Eisenberg told the BBC in February 2025 that he no longer wanted to be "associated with someone like that," referring to Zuckerberg.
This opened the door for Jeremy Strong to take on the role.
Jeremy Strong will play Mark Zuckerberg instead.
Strong has a track record of taking on challenging roles. He crafted the complex nepo baby Kendall Roy from "Succession" into one of the most memorable characters in modern television. He's since wowed audiences with his performances as Donald Trump's cutthroat lawyer, Roy Cohn, in "The Apprentice," and Bruce Springsteen's loyal producer, Jon Landau, in "Springsteen: Deliver Me from Nowhere."
Playing an adult Zuckerberg will be his biggest transformation yet.
Since founding Facebook, Zuckerberg rebranded it as Meta in 2021, focusing on virtual reality and augmented reality technologies.
Soon after Haugen testified at the Senate hearing, Zuckerberg announced on an earnings call that Meta was hiring 40,000 people to work in safety and security because, he said, "we care about getting this right." Facebook has long said it endorses establishing rules for online platforms.
Strong took an obsessively Method approach to emulating the CEO.
Strong's Method acting preparation to play characters has risen to Daniel Day-Lewis levels of mythology, and that won't change with "Reckoning."
In an August 2026 GQ profile, Strong, who spoke in a Polish accent for most of the interview as he was also prepping for another movie at the time, revealed that his goal was to play the real Zuckerberg, not copy Eisenberg's portrayal in "The Social Network." To accomplish that, he said he listened to every podcast, read every interview, and watched Zuckerberg speak at every tech summit the CEO has ever done. He even created a Facebook account so he could read all of Zuckerberg's posts.
But Strong also wanted to get across to Zuckerberg himself how committed he was to the role. So Strong reached out to him.
"I sent him an email," Strong told GQ. "Just to say that I take this responsibility very seriously, and the veracity of it seriously, and I'm approaching it with respect."
Strong said Zuckerberg responded to him, but did not divulge what Zuck said.
Strong was also dedicated to sounding like Zuckerberg, talking in his voice throughout the production of the movie, even when he was off set.
"I've talked to Mark Zuckerberg many times — I had a whole friendship with Mark Zuckerberg, and Mark Zuckerberg has no idea," Strong's friend, Bradley Cooper, told GQ of the actor's dedication.
Mikey Madison plays Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen.
This marks Madison's first role since she won the best actress Oscar for "Anora."
The Facebook Files is based on the thousands of pages of internal documents leaked by Haugen, who was a product manager at Facebook. Once Haugen's identity was revealed as the whistleblower, she did a "60 Minutes" interview and testified at a Senate hearing that Facebook knew it could be harmful to young people.
Madison said she told Sorkin she was worried about taking the role because she looks nothing like Haugen.
If your first reaction to Madison's casting was to note that she and Haugen don't look remotely similar, you're not alone.
The Oscar winner felt the same way, and voiced it to her director.
"I met Aaron, and I was like, 'I love this script. This is an amazing character. But I don't look like this person at all,'" Madison said in a Vogue cover story that ran online in September.
Though Madison said she was prepared to do a complete transformation to look more like the blonde-haired, blue-eyed Haugen, Sorkin didn't want that. He told her instead to just focus on the script.
However, Madison told Vogue she did play with her look a little. She took fewer trips to the gym to give the character a "softer physicality" and dyed her hair jet black.
Jeremy Allen White plays Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz.
White is best known for playing Carmen "Carmy" Berzatto on the hit series "The Bear," which earned him two Emmy wins. White has portrayed a real person before: he played Bruce Springsteen in the 2025 biopic, "Springsteen: Deliver Me from Nowhere."
Horwitz is a former technology reporter at The Wall Street Journal who was behind The Facebook Files.
The first 'Social Reckoning' trailer was released in June.
Sony released the first teaser trailer of the movie on June 10.
Meta did not respond for comment about the trailer.

Banks closed today: Check if your state has a holiday on September 18
According to the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) bank holiday calendar, banks will remain closed only in Meghalaya on September 18.
Banks will remain closed tomorrow, Friday, September 18, in Meghalaya on account of Unitarian Anniversary Day. If you are planning to visit a bank branch tomorrow, check the holiday schedule for your state before heading out.
According to the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) bank holiday calendar, banks will remain closed only in Meghalaya on September 18.
All public and private sector banks, including State Bank of India, Punjab National Bank, Bank of Baroda, Canara Bank, Axis Bank, HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank, will remain open in other states.
Also Read | Banks to remain closed for 4 days from today; Check state-wise list of holidays
Why is Unitarian Anniversary Day celebrated?
Unitarian Anniversary Day is observed every year on September 18 in the Khasi-Jaintia Hills region of Meghalaya. The day marks the beginning of the local Unitarian faith movement, founded by Hajom Kissor Singh.
Singh held the first Unitarian church prayer meeting at his home in Jawai on September 18, 1887. The faith is known locally as Ka Niam Unitarian. It emphasises traditional Khasi culture, social responsibility and human values, along with belief in one God. The Unitarian community continues to hold special prayer meetings on the occasion.
In 2026, the Meghalaya government has declared September 18 a local holiday to mark Unitarian Anniversary Day. The holiday applies to East Khasi Hills, East Jaintia Hills, South West Khasi Hills and Ri-Bhoi.
Banks will remain open in several states, including Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Odisha, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Goa, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and Telangana.

The U.S. FDA is holding a public hearing on Monday to gather feedback on the potential therapeutic use of psychedelic drugs, the latest step in a months-long push by President Donald Trump's administration to speed up development of the treatments for serious mental illnesses.
The hearing is part of a broader push launched in April, when Trump ordered the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to focus on qualifying psychedelic drug programs for its priority-voucher program.
The order also directed the FDA to work with the Drug Enforcement Administration on a pathway for some patients to obtain investigational treatments under a law, which allows certain seriously ill patients to seek experimental therapies, and to increase collaboration with the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Since then, the FDA has issued priority vouchers to three companies developing psychedelic-based treatments, one for psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression, another for psilocybin for major depressive disorder and a third for methylone for post-traumatic stress disorder.
The hearing focuses on practical issues that could shape how psychedelic therapies are tested and delivered, including provider training and credentials, patient screening and monitoring, access and reimbursement, clinic capacity and the collection of long-term safety data.
The FDA said it was not seeking views on individual drug applications, the scheduling of controlled substances or the legalisation of psychedelics.
Doctors, veterans, pharmacists and therapists during the hearing urged the regulator to establish clear safety and access standards for psychedelic-assisted therapies.
Experts said any approved psychedelic treatment must include trained staff in the room during sessions, along with proper screening, follow-up care and community support.
Robert Barrow, CEO of Definium Therapeutics, which is developing an LSD-based therapy, told Reuters that the hearing offers "a nice opportunity for that continuing public dialogue" among regulators, clinicians and patients.
He said regulators and industry should treat psychedelics "like it's normal drug development, normal science, normal medicine," rather than as an unusually novel category requiring special treatment.
Just days before the hearing, senior FDA officials, including Michael Davis, head of the agency's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, published a paper in the New England Journal of Medicine outlining a framework for developing and approving psychedelic drugs and saying the agency was "meeting this moment" on hard-to-treat conditions such as major depressive disorder and PTSD.
The American Psychiatric Association said it "appreciates the FDA's public hearing and coordination with federal partners on the potential therapeutic use of psychedelics."
"The FDA's determination of safety and effectiveness... must remain the foundation for any future clinical use."
Jefferies analysts said the framework suggested the FDA was willing to consider flexible trial designs to address challenges including "functional unblinding," when a drug's noticeable psychoactive effects reveal to participants which treatment they received.
The administration's support has stirred fresh investor interest in the sector, with industry executives telling Reuters it could improve coordination between the FDA and the Drug Enforcement Administration and help reduce regulatory delays, even as researchers noted that approved treatments were still likely years away.
Continued alignment among regulators, clinicians and developers on a safe, supervised rollout should benefit AtaiBeckley, Compass Pathways, Definium Therapeutics, Helus Pharma and GH Research, analysts said.
Helus CEO Michael Halstead said "the science continues to advance, and continued thoughtful engagement among regulators, researchers and clinicians is critical to advancing these promising new treatments."

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian visited New Delhi on 11 September 2026 to attend the 18th BRICS Summit. During his visit, he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi and participated in several engagements on the sidelines of the summit. On 11 September 2026, Iran’s Ambassador to India, Dr Mohammad Fathali, hosted an event in New Delhi where Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met religious leaders, intellectuals and other dignitaries, including Jain monk Acharya Lokesh Muni and Jagadguru Swami Satishacharya Maharaj.
In this context, a video of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian bowing down is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows him touching the feet of Jagadguru Ramanandacharya Swami Satishacharya to seek his blessings. Several news outlets, including Times Now Navbharat and ABP News, also reported that Pezeshkian touched the feet of Swami Satishacharya during the event. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian touching Swami Satishacharya’s feet for blessings.
Fact: The video does not show Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian touching Swami Satishacharya’s feet to seek his blessings. Pezeshkian bent down to pick up something that had fallen to the ground, while Satishacharya also bent down at the same time. The Iranian Embassy and people present at the event confirmed that the video does not show Pezeshkian seeking blessings from Satishacharya. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords and found reports published by News18 Hindi and Moneycontrol, citing sources from the Iranian Embassy, which reported that Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian bent down to pick up a piece of paper. According to News18 Hindi, the Iranian Ambassador and diplomats organised a special reception and interaction programme at The Oberoi Hotel in New Delhi, attended by Jagadguru Satishacharya Maharaj, along with several prominent Indian interfaith leaders, intellectuals and businesspeople. During the event, Pezeshkian bent down to pick up a letter that had fallen to the floor, rather than touching anyone’s feet. Moneycontrol also reported, citing Iranian Embassy sources, that the letter had been handed to Pezeshkian by another leader and accidentally fell from his hand, prompting him to bend down and pick it up.
We then conducted a reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video, which led us to social media posts by INN News (archived) and Ismat TV (archived). An INN News post featuring Sahil Naqvi, who was present at the event, addressed the viral video, claiming that Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had bowed to touch the feet of a Hindu priest in India. According to the post, Pezeshkian had bent down to pick up a pen that had fallen to the floor, while the priest also bent down at the same time, creating the impression that the President was touching his feet. The post described the viral portrayal as misleading and said the footage was being presented out of context.
Ismat TV shared a video from another angle, showing both Pezeshkian and Swami Satishacharya bending down to pick up the pen. According to the account, Pezeshkian first attempted to pick it up, followed by Satishacharya. The post said that the incident was a gesture of respect and courtesy and did not show Pezeshkian bowing to anyone.
We then contacted Ismat TV and spoke to Hussain Mehdi, a photographer employed by the organisation. Speaking to Factly, he said that the channel’s staff were present at the event and that the claim that Pezeshkian touched Satishacharya’s feet is false. He also shared another video shot from a different angle, showing both Pezeshkian and Satishacharya bending down to pick up a paper.
We found a Facebook post by Acharya Lokesh Muni, who shared pictures of himself at the event standing next to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. In the post, he said that he had invited Pezeshkian to host a first-of-its-kind peace summit in Iran, which the Iranian President accepted. He added that religious leaders and peace-loving groups from around the world would gather to promote peace through dialogue and discussion.
We contacted him, and speaking to Factly, he stated that the claim that the Iranian President touched the feet of a Hindu religious leader is false. He said that while he was showing Pezeshkian his magazine, Aahwaan, which is published by the World Peace Centre, an organisation he founded, the magazine fell from his hands. According to him, the video shows the Iranian President bending down to pick up the magazine for him as a courtesy, which was later circulated widely on the internet with a misleading claim.
We also contacted Maulana Taqi Haider Naqvi through the Iran Culture House, New Delhi, via WhatsApp. Naqvi, who was present at the event, also rebutted the claim that Pezeshkian touched Satishacharya’s feet. He also forwarded an Iranian Embassy statement regarding the matter, which reads, “The President bent down to pick up a letter that one of the leaders had given him and that had fallen to the ground.”
To sum up, this viral video shows Iranian President Pezeshkian bending down to pick up something, not to touch a Hindu religious leader’s feet.

St Leger win has removed Osborne's fear of failure
- Published
St Leger-winning jockey Saffie Osborne says the "fear of failure" has left her after she became the first woman to win a British Classic.
The 24-year-old said that despite wanting to achieve "so much more", her victory at Doncaster on Saturday means she will always be able to look back and think her career was "worth it".
Osborne said the sport can be "very lonely" - she estimates she drives 65,000 miles a year, often alone - and she has suffered some serious falls, breaking numerous bones.
But she told BBC Sport that winning one of British Flat racing's five Classics had been a dream since she was five. She has now fulfilled it.
While racing is a sport where men and women compete against one another, opportunities have not been equal.
Only six female jockeys have had rides in British Classics in 250 years, totalling 12 rides, according to the National Horseracing Museum.
They are Gay Kelleway (The Oaks, 1986; The Oaks, 1987), Alex Greaves (The Derby, 1996; 1,000 Guineas, 1996), Hayley Turner (The Derby, 2012) Josephine Gordon (1,000 Guineas, 2017), Hollie Doyle (The Oaks, 2021; St Leger, 2021; The Oaks, 2022) and Saffie Osborne (2,000 Guineas, 2024; 1,000 Guineas, 2026; St Leger, 2026).
"It has been a male-dominated sport for an extremely long time, and I suppose it's becoming less and less of a conversation, which is quite nice," she said.
"When people talk about the firsts of what women have done, I think to have my own one is quite special.
"I think it's also quite poignant because there's so few left of first things for women to do in this sport."
On Saturday's groundbreaking win, she added: "That sort of fear of failure has sort of disappeared. However much more I want to achieve, and I want to achieve so much more, it's kind of like I can always look back on my career and know that it was all worth it.
"I got to achieve what I always dreamed of achieving."
Osborne's ride on Highwayman in the St Leger was her first for trainer Joseph O'Brien, and only came about because of an injury to regular jockey Dylan Browne McMonagle.
She acknowledged that the success of a jockey is dependent on "being chosen", but is adamant that her gender isn't a factor in the opportunities she gets.
"I don't feel like in my position now that I'm ever looked at any differently because I'm a woman," she said.
"Any jockey, when you're starting out, it takes years to gain respect and be looked at as a person that people would want to use. And I don't think my gender at this point would have had anything to do with it.
"Hopefully Saturday will open more doors. But when it comes to me as a female jockey, I don't think I'm viewed any differently within the industry."
Osborne also said she is treated as "one of the lads" in the weighing room, and has never experienced sexism and misogyny unlike other female jockeys, including Bryony Frost.
Jockey Robbie Dunne was banned from racing for 18 months, with three months suspended, for bullying fellow rider Frost in 2021, which was later cut to 10 months on appeal.
Having ridden 60 winners since the start of May, Osborne is currently sitting eighth in the Flat Jockeys Championship, and is open about dreaming of being champion jockey in the future.
She would be the first female jockey to achieve that.
"You wouldn't be a jockey if you didn't want to be champion jockey one day. I think this is the first year that maybe I truly believe that I could one day," she said.
"It's been a phenomenal year that's been topped off by Saturday. But I'm very lucky. I have a very good agent [Tony Hind] and agents are so important in this sport. He's got an amazing book of jockeys, the likes of Ryan Moore, William Buick, Billy Loughnane. And I'm very lucky to be on his team.
"He makes champion jockeys, he's had a lot of them. And yeah, I would love to be the next one on the list."

Meet PitchFly, WIRED’s latest editorial recruit.
He has 165,112 neurons, and they’re all trained to generate story ideas. A sampling of his early output: “The Hidden Weather Problem Inside Surveillance”; “The Engineers Who Think Elon Musk Needs Less Computer Security”; and my personal favorite, “Everyone Wants Cooking. Nobody Has Solved Donald Trump.”
PitchFly uses a detailed map of the brain of a male drosophila—the common fruit fly. Developed by researchers from Google and a number of academic institutions, the map, known as a connectome, captures the way that 166,000 neurons and 125 million connecting synapses fire in response to stimuli. In essence, you can use it to simulate how a fly would respond to lots of stuff—it’s a very simple version of artificial intelligence based on charting real biological intelligence.
Because the researchers open-sourced it, you can easily use AI to import the connectome into a project with a little prompting. For PitchFly, I vibe coded a project in which the tiny digital drosophila brain generates story ideas. (I’m not sure why the fly has a little hat on, but I like its style.) This involved scraping together hundreds of the most popular story headlines from the site from the past year and feeding them into the connectome. I had Codex do the hard work, and it decided that the most efficient approach was to turn the headlines into words and phrases, then transform them into a representation that a neural network could understand. The connectome was fed the best-performing stories and told to generate its own ideas based on that.
In other words, this isn’t a fly-based language model—although someone apparently created one of those. The fly brain has no idea what any of the words mean, or if any of it makes sense. It’s just remixing the patterns it has seen in pleasing new ways. A cynic might suggest this is exactly how some journalists generate their own pitches, but I think that’s a bit unfair—and judging by its lunatic ideas, PitchFly won’t be replacing me anytime soon:
- The Tiny Shift in Agentic AI Is Rewriting the Rules of Food and Drink
- What Security News Is Quietly Doing to Donald Trump
- The Race to Reinvent Privacy Before Artificial Intelligence Breaks
- Is China About to Make Digital Syndication Obsolete?
In the future, perhaps I could have the program continue to learn by reading new WIRED headlines. For now, though, this seems like a decent proof of concept, not to mention evidence at last that the average WIRED writer is intellectually superior to a fruit fly.
After the connectome’s release in early September, dozens of other weird and wonderful projects powered by fruit-fly intelligence sprang up.
An X user called Lyra Bubbles, for instance, demo’d a project that involved training the virtual fly brain to play the VR game Beat Saber. Alex Wormuth, a software engineer at Coinbase, created StonkFly, which uses the fly’s tiny brain to decide how to trade stocks. (It’s losing money, but it’s doing surprisingly well, all things considered.)
“The fly brings lighthearted, humorous relief” at a time when everyone is worried about the existential risks of AI, Wormuth told me in a DM. He says he found playing with the fruit fly connectome philosophically fascinating, too. “It sparks questions about ethics of this and whether there is any consciousness [in the replication of fly’s brain],” he says.
Others trained the connectome to play Doom, Minecraft, and Pong. Some fly brains apparently learned to solve Rubik’s cubes. And someone also put the fly brain in charge of driving virtual cars—it turns out flies are terrible at parallel parking. (Then again, so am I, so I won’t pass judgment.)
I haven’t verified that all these projects actually use the connectome—they may just be fun animations. And some of them—like one that simply involves training the fly to take a well-earned break—seem like spoofs. But there are some serious science projects out there, too, including visualizations for exploring the connectome and tools for manipulating neural circuitry.
Mapping different animal brains may help neuroscientists decipher the biological foundations of intelligence. It isn’t possible—yet—to map all 86 billion neurons in a human brain, but peering into the brains of smaller creatures can provide useful insights. Neuroscientists can also test theories about how damage affects neuronal wiring—and how such damage might someday be repaired—by messing with the fly’s connectome.
As far as AI is concerned, all this fruit-fly frivolity also shows how easy it is now to train and deploy your own model. The best use for the giant LLMs run by big AI companies may be building specialized AI models for specific tasks (something I’ve written about previously). Sometimes even a tiny brain can do quite well.

Why Democrats Might Choose to Impeach Cabinet Members
The power to impeach secretaries and other executive-branch officers is not well known, but it’s an effective accountability measure.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
If Democrats win control of the House in November, they will face a dilemma: Should they attempt a record third impeachment of Donald Trump?
The president and his allies have warned that this would be a Democratic majority’s first move. “I’m going to be impeached. They’re going to impeach me,” Trump said last month at a rally in South Carolina. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has been noncommittal. “We haven’t ruled anything in, and we haven’t ruled anything out in terms of impeachment,” the would-be speaker told ABC’s This Week on Sunday. But Representative Jamie Raskin, the lead manager of Trump’s second impeachment, seemed more open. Earlier this month, on Meet the Press, he said that Trump had “undoubtedly” committed impeachable offenses. “We understand it’s not a panacea. It is a tool in the toolbox,” he said. “We will not hesitate to use it if we need to use it.”
Realistically, House Democrats may have a hard time resisting impeachment. Their voters are in a punchy mood. A new CBS News / YouGov poll found that opposition to Trump is the top motivation for Democratic voters in the midterms, and the political consultant Sarah Longwell recently wrote in The Atlantic that the most important priority for Democratic voters is not left-versus-right ideology but a willingness to fight Trump tooth and nail. Jeffries has already faced criticism for being too passive a leader, as well as for meeting with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, and he may struggle to ignore a groundswell of support for impeachment.
As a constitutional matter, the case for impeaching the president is solid. Trump has usurped congressional powers, started an unauthorized war or two, defied courts, and used his position for outrageous personal and family enrichment. In 2019, my colleague Yoni Appelbaum made the intellectual case for impeachment as a useful democratic process.
The political case for impeaching Trump is shakier. Regardless of the results in November, Democrats are unlikely to get enough votes in the Senate to convict and remove him, meaning that a third impeachment would hit the same dead end as the first two. An impeachment can still be effective as a way of damaging a president, but Trump is already deeply unpopular and will never face voters again, so the upside is limited, and an impeachment might give him a way to rally his remaining base around him—which would only strengthen his power and resolve.
But what if House Democrats impeached Trump’s Cabinet members instead? The power to impeach secretaries and other executive-branch officers is explicit in the Constitution but perhaps not well known, because it’s been used only twice in history. One reason such proceedings are rare is that a president usually fires a Cabinet member or forces them to resign before they can be impeached, but Trump has shown serious reluctance to fire aides because of public pressure. The congressional scholar Norm Ornstein has argued that if Trump won’t rein them in, Democrats should. On Tuesday, outgoing Representative Thomas Massie, a Republican, brought new attention to the possibility by moving to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. GOP leadership promptly shut down all voting until after the election.
In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached for corruption, but he resigned the same day and the Senate subsequently acquitted him; a number of senators doubted they had jurisdiction post-resignation. (This historical example resurfaced during Trump’s second impeachment trial, which occurred after he’d left office.) In 2024, House Republicans impeached Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas on vague grounds, but the Senate voted to dismiss the charges as unconstitutional without a trial.
A Democratic House could plausibly launch impeachment inquiries into several administration officials, many of which would dovetail with investigations that representatives say they already have planned. In some cases, Democratic representatives have already filed articles of impeachment against Cabinet members, including Hegseth, Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and Secretary of Education Linda McMahon, but those have gone nowhere in the GOP-led chamber. A new Democratic majority could change that.
The conduct of a few particular individuals makes them likely targets for impeachment efforts. Kennedy has done serious damage to American public health, undermining vaccinations and weakening the CDC. At least one Republican senator has accused him of lying about vaccination rules during his confirmation hearings, when he also falsely characterized a trip he took to Samoa. Hegseth has waged an unauthorized war against Iran, for which he seems to have no realistic game plan; mishandled classified information; possibly violated the Hatch Act by appearing at a fundraiser for a political candidate; and left the armed forces bereft of leadership by firing a slew of qualified generals and admirals.
Attorney General Todd Blanche has been instrumental in turning the Justice Department into a partisan tool for persecuting Trump’s political adversaries, and a federal judge rebuked him for his role in Trump’s attempt to set up a $1.8 billion slush fund for political allies. Multiple sources shared with my colleague Sarah Fitzpatrick serious worries about FBI Director Kash Patel’s leadership, including claims of emotional volatility, heavy drinking, and absence from the job. (Patel denied the allegations and sued Fitzpatrick and The Atlantic for defamation, demanding $250 million.) Russell Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget, has led a concerted effort to take congressional powers for the White House.
As a policy matter, impeachment of some of these officers could be more effective than ordinary investigations would be in halting the egregious actions taken by their offices and departments. It might also have a couple political benefits over impeaching Trump. First, such an effort could escape the Trump vortex: By moving the focus to officials who don’t command the same personal loyalty as Trump, impeachment might allow more emphasis on actual administration actions and policy, instead of on presidential personality. Second, conviction might still be a remote possibility, but GOP senators who are fed up with the White House might be more willing to vote to convict officers than they would be to risk taking on Trump himself.
The real question is whether controversial Cabinet secretaries will stick around to see whether Democrats try to target them. A midterm election, especially one that goes poorly for the president’s party, is typically a moment for some secretaries to exit. But Hegseth seems entrenched, continuing to push out rivals; Blanche just won confirmation; and Kennedy and Vought are ideologues pursuing treasured agendas. If neither they nor Trump are willing to change course, then a Congress that has done little for the past two years will have a chance to do something novel: act.

The Dead Silence of AI Therapy
By Steven Barrie-Anthony
Therapy can involve a lot of words, but it’s often the pauses that matter most. If you transcribed a session, the pauses would look like nothing: beats of silence, extra breaths, slowing down. But these can represent the crux of the practice: entry points into feeling. My job as a psychoanalyst is to listen as much to silence as to words, to be present with the patient while they’re quiet—to stay with them as they allow their feelings to emerge.
I was trained across diverse theories and techniques, but in my clinical work I have found that the cornerstone of the process is feeling. The patient’s emotional experience is the destination and the terrain. But I also feel; I am moved. And the work I do with my patients relies on our relationship and our capacity for mutual feeling. In many ways, the history of my field from Freud on has been a growing acknowledgement of the reality of this relationship—moving from the therapist as sealed off and standing apart, toward approaches that view the real human relationship between patient and therapist as the territory where healing happens.
