About 70% of the year-to-year variation in winter air pollution across northern India may be explained by the frequency of western disturbances, possibly providing warning of unusually polluted winter months in advance, researchers said.
Western disturbances are storm systems that travel eastwards from the Mediterranean region towards South Asia by strengthening vertical ventilation and bringing precipitation that helps clear accumulated pollution, including PM2.5, from the air.
The team said winters with more frequent western disturbances tend to experience lower air pollution levels, while winters with fewer of these storms are more susceptible to persistent severe pollution.
"Currently, many of the most disruptive air-pollution measures are taken only after severe pollution is already developing," lead author Yuanyu Xie, an associate research scholar at Princeton University's School of Public and International Affairs, U.S., said.
"If scientists can anticipate the overall severity of the coming winter months ahead of time, governments, businesses, and communities will have more time to prepare," Ms. Xie said.
They also found that the frequency of western disturbances is linked to ocean temperature patterns already evident during the preceding autumn.
The team said the overall severity of winter pollution in north India may thus be predicted about a season in advance. Air pollution levels across northern India, including Delhi-NCR, spike during the winter season, increasing residents' health risks.
A combination of vehicle emissions, stubble burning in the neighbouring states of Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh and weather patterns that trap pollutants close to the ground is attributed to the seasonal spike in pollution.
Emergency measures, including pausing construction, restricting industries and limiting traffic, are implemented on severe pollution days, but may be a challenge if put in place on short notice.
The researchers said seasonal forecasts could indicate whether the coming winter is likely to have relatively severe or mild pollution levels overall, rather than predicting pollution levels for a particular day months in advance, thereby offering a more practical approach.
The information could provide a lead time, allowing authorities to strengthen enforcement before the pollution season begins, coordinate responses across jurisdictions, and give businesses more time to prepare for potential restrictions, they said.
"Emission controls will remain of paramount importance," co-author Denise Mauzerall, a professor of public and international affairs and civil and environmental engineering at Princeton University, said.
"However, we show that forecasts of winter pollution based on observations from the previous autumn can allow additional pollution controls to be arranged in advance of extreme pollution periods. This could provide time to plan and implement cost-effective controls that mitigate peak pollution concentrations in winter in northern India," Ms. Mauzerall said.
The authors wrote, "Nearly 70% of the inter-annual variations in winter PM2.5 pollution across northern India are explained by western disturbances (WDs) — prevailing extratropical storms originating from the Mediterranean region — through PM2.5 removal via enhanced ventilation and precipitation."

A US federal court in Los Angeles sentenced a former Syrian government official who ran one of the country’s most infamous prisons to 60 years in prison on Thursday – the most significant punishment handed to an official of ousted president Bashar al-Assad’s regime by a foreign court and to a defendant present in person.
Samir Ousman al-Sheikh was the head of the Adra prison, on the outskirts of Damascus, between 2005 and 2008, when he oversaw an underground “punishment wing”, known as “Wing 13”, in which prisoners and regime opponents were interrogated and tortured as he watched through surveillance cameras. A federal jury convicted al-Sheikh last March of having tortured prisoners and then lying about it in US immigration forms.
“The conduct was heinous, unimaginably cruel and almost unspeakably violent and brutal,” said Hernan D Vera, a US district judge, before delivering the sentence.
Al-Sheikh’s legal team and the justice department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Following al-Sheikh’s conviction, Bill Essayli, first assistant US attorney, had said in a statement that the case showed the US “is not a refuge for criminals – especially criminals who engage in the brutality of the kind this defendant inflicted on his victims”.
Al-Sheikh, 73, who also served as governor of Syria’s Deir Ez-Zour province in 2011, at a time of violent regime crackdowns against protesters, moved to the United States in 2020, obtained a green card and applied for US citizenship. He was arrested in July 2024 at Los Angeles international airport on immigration fraud charges and prosecutors later added four-torture related charges.
He is the first al-Assad regime official to go to trial in the US and the highest ranking regime official to be tried anywhere in the world in person. Al-Assad was ousted by a lightning rebel offensive in December 2024 which toppled the regime in just 11 days.
Since then, Syria’s new government has held a number of in absentia trials for former regime officials in connection to crimes committed during the country’s years-long civil war, which killed about half a million people and displaced half the country’s prewar population of 23 million. In August, a court sentenced al-Assad and his brother Maher to death for crimes against humanity and war crimes, but the two men have been in Moscow since the regime’s collapse.
Other factions in Syria’s civil war have also been accused of abuse of detainees, including insurgent groups and the US-backed, Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces.
During al-Sheikh’s nine-day trial, several victims and witnesses testified. They described guards folding prisoners into car tires, restraining and beating them. Some they said, were cuffed by their wrists to pipes on the ceiling, beaten with cables, and left suspended for extended periods of time.
Others testified that they were placed on a device known as a “magic carpet,” which consisted of two large wooden panels with hinges in the middle onto which guards strapped prisoners, forcing the panels together to cause excruciating pain. One victim recalled al-Sheikh himself stomping on the device. Another testified he was subjected to the “magic carpet” as punishment for writing a letter of support to a political prisoner and also forced to wear a red jumpsuit assigned to prisoners designated for execution, leading him to believe he was going to die.
“[Al-Sheikh] chose to serve the ruthless, repressive Assad regime in Syria throughout his professional life, including for four years as the warden of Syria’s largest prison,” prosecutors wrote in a sentencing memo. “[He] knew that what he was doing was wrong. Nonetheless he ordered and participated in the torture of his victims because he had the power to do so and because he thought he would never be held accountable.”
Several victims and witnesses also submitted written and video testimonies to the court ahead of the sentencing, in which they spoke of being haunted and traumatized by their experiences two decades later.
“I still hear the screams of others begging for mercy,” said one of the men, Nidal Shikhani.
“Even though 20 years have passed, I still live in the prison of my memory,” said another, Sultan Abdul Malek. “I suffer from sudden panic attacks and constant anxiety.”
His brother, Khaled Abdul Malek, who was taken to “Wing 13” twice during his four years at Adra prison, spoke of the physical and psychological scars he was left with, including chronic back pain and mobility problems.
“My son Battal asks if he could ride my back and with a heart wrung with pain, I am forced to tell him I [am] no longer strong enough to carry him,” he said.
Several witnesses also submitted testimony on al-Sheikh’s behalf, speaking about his age and frailty as they asked the court for leniency. More than 50 people sent letters of support to the court, describing him as “a person of integrity, compassion, and generosity to his family and community”, his attorneys wrote.
Prosecutors had asked the court for a minimum sentence of 80 years; al-Sheikh’s attorneys had called for a five-year sentence, citing his poor health and noting that he was willing to be deported to Syria.
“Whatever moral weight this case carries in the broader arc of history – however much the world, or the victims, or the public might wish the sentence to ‘send a message’ – that desire cannot be the foundation of a just sentence,” the defense team wrote in a memo to the court.
“This case sends a message both to the new government of Syria and to other victims that justice is possible,” said Ela Matthews, an attorney at the Center for Justice and Accountability, which represented several victims. “The transitional justice process that is happening in Syria needs to continue to evolve and bring individuals like this to account, but in the US this sends a message that the rule of law is still functioning and that these types of cases are possible.”

Alice Augusta Ball lived a very short life. In 24 years, she had remarkable achievements, and was predictably forgotten for a while, until the world was shaken up to her brilliance. Her work on distilling chaulmoogra oil for use as effective treatment for leprosy brought hope to a number of patients globally.
An African American woman born into middle class in the late 1800s, Alice Ball benefitted from an early exposure to chemical processes as her family was involved in photography. She went on to shine in science at school, and could hope to move on to university, a rare opportunity for a woman and a person of her race at that time. She lived up to her potential and at the University of Washington, racked up her skills in chemistry and pharmacy. She finished two degrees – a bachelor’s in pharmaceutical chemistry and a bachelor’s in pharmacy – thus arming herself for a career –short lived, but so sparkling, people are still talking about her, though subsequent innovations have transformed care for leprosy.
With a full scholarship, another rarity for the times, Alice moved to the College of Hawai‘i, and became the first woman and the first African American to earn a master’s degree in chemistry. We mention it because it is an achievement, but also because it was an achievement that attracted the kind of attention a career flourishes on. It is said that Harry T. Hollmann, a public health officer, thought her thesis research on extracting active compounds from the kava (awa) root might have implications for his passion – finding cures for leprosy.
Leprosy or Hansen’s disease is caused by Mycobacterium leprae, and was discovered by Norwegian physician Gerhard Armauer Hansen in the 1870s. While it is prevalent in people living in tropical regions, leprosy which affects the nervous system, also has the moniker of being the world’s oldest disease. Evidence of leprosy has been found in skeletons from back in 2000 BCE. Those affected develop visible skin lesions and extremities including fingers and toes malformed and misshapen fingers. Sometimes amputations were also performed on limbs that could not be salvaged. As a result of the disfiguration, the stigma surrounding the disease was so high, those with leprosy had to be sequestered in camps and asylums outside the community.
Alice did accept Hollman’s invitation and what she managed to achieve was to revolutionise the field of leprosy care in the very near future. Described as the Ball Method, Alice devised a method that would “convert the oil’s fatty acids into water-soluble ethyl esters that could be injected into patients. Until then Chaulmoogra oil was promising as treatment for leprosy, but it was thick, not soluble in water, besides difficult to inject and swallow. Soon the world adopted the Ball Method and the landmark contribution changed life for the better for people who were battling leprosy across the world, without hope until then. Alice was in her early 20s at the time of this achievement.
Records of the time say, since the new formulation dispersed in the bloodstream instead of pooling under the skin, patients for the first time celebrated as earlier, there was none of the severe local reactions and oozing oil that the injections caused. Used on patients at Kalihi Hospital in Hawai‘i, researchers managed to show that patients administered the new formulation, became ‘bacteriologically negative, their lesions resolved, and many were discharged from isolation to rejoin their families, without fear of infecting them.’ This injectable preparation remained the best available treatment worldwide until sulfone antibiotics, Dapsone, in combination with other drugs, replaced it in the 1940s, facilitating a future unimaginable until then, for those who were diagnosed with leprosy and condemned to social isolation.
However, Alice’s contribution never made it to the headlines thanks to a set of factors – her gender, age and race were primary. She died young, it is speculated that it could be a result of a laboratory accident, a senior male colleague, her department head Arthur L. Dean appropriated and published her work without sharing any credit, in fact, promoting it as the ‘Dean method’, accounts of that period list.
It went unchallenged until decades later, when researcher Harry Hollmann revisited the archives and credited Ball. Finally, the historical records were righted, and Alice Ball’s name was affixed to the method she had painstakingly developed. By 24, despite the disdvantaged circumstances she worked in, Alice Ball had changed the world, it is a matter of speculation how much she would have achieved had she lived longer, but a safe bet to say she would have left a deeper impact. For the punch she packed in her short life, and the revolution she managed in that life, it’s time we say her name, say “Alice Augusta Ball.”

'I've turned the page' - Camara on Chelsea deal collapse

Monaco midfielder Lamine Camara says he has "turned the page" and is focusing on the Ligue 1 season after his £47.1m move to Chelsea collapsed.
The 22-year-old had completed a medical but the deal fell through shortly before the transfer window closed.
Two bids had already been rejected, but Monaco lowered their asking price in a turbulent end to the window when it looked likely that Folarin Balogun's move to Everton was in doubt.
When Balogun's transfer appeared to be back on track, Monaco appeared to change their decision to sell Camara, but in the end both players stayed with the Ligue 1 side.
"There was a possibility I could leave," Camara said, speaking before Monaco's game against Strasbourg on Saturday.
"It didn't go through at the last minute and that's part of football. I've turned the page and am focusing on the season."
Sources in France had stated Monaco needed to make a major sale this summer and preferred to sell Balogun. A source at the Ligue 1 club had previously indicated it would take a "substantial fee" to secure Camara's departure.

Who Will Foot The UPI MDR Bill? UPI transformed digital payments by making them virtually free. From October 15, this equation will change as high-value transactions will begin attracting MDR. While the new regime opens a new revenue pool for fintechs, it could reshape user behaviour. So, who will now bear the cost? UPI Ends Free Ride: The new framework imposes a 0.4% MDR on P2M UPI payments above ₹2,000, capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 and more. Merchants receiving up to ₹1 Lakh a month via QR codes remain exempt, but sellers crossing the threshold repeatedly will enter the MDR category. This could expose small businesses to payment acceptance costs, particularly during the festive season when higher-value transactions are the norm. The Merchant-Side Test: For many sellers, the financial effect will depend on ticket size and transaction mix. A business selling low-value goods may see little immediate impact, while retailers and D2C brands could face a meaningful recurring cost. More importantly, merchants will now have to weigh MDR alongside gateway fees, logistics and marketplace commissions when calculating margins. The Convenience Question: While the government has prohibited merchants from passing on the costs to consumers, the order does not guarantee that the cost will disappear. Businesses, under margin pressure, may absorb MDR through broad price increases rather than displaying a separate payment fee at checkout. On top of this, many fear that higher-value buyers could move back to cash if UPI loses its frictionless appeal. Sustainability Vs Scale: Nevertheless, fintech startups see MDR as essential for funding technology upgrades and wider payment infrastructure without relying on subsidies. The revenue could also make UPI more viable for smaller payment players competing against dominant apps. But the success of the policy will rest on maintaining a delicate balance between protecting small merchants and ensuring costs are not pushed onto consumers. So, can UPI finally become financially viable without losing the low-cost advantage that made it indispensable? In a world where AI is capturing every conversation, a series of experts is trying to figure out what it actually means for the world of entertainment.
“I think the word ‘AI’ is doing too much right now,” says Mira Line, Google’s vice president of technology and society. ”One of the things that we’re doing, especially with the industry, is figuring out, well, what does AI mean in the industry? How do you break it down?”
Lane made her comments alongside several entertainment and tech personalities during the “Entertainment and Media in the Age of AI” panel, one of several AI-focused conversations happening at Variety’s Entertainment and Tech Summit presented by EY. Moderated by Variety business editor Todd Spangler, the conversation saw executives from Netflix (Girish Balakrishnan, the streamer’s senior director, creative innovation), Lionsgate (Kathleen Grace, its chief AI officer), Hasbro (Bertie Thomson, head of its AI-focused studio Sixth Wall), Teads (Annaka Vasquez, senior vice president of sales) and Adobe (Meagan Keane, Pro Video’s head of business strategy) come together to walk through AI’s place in entertainment and the use cases for versions of the technology — once people figure out how to talk about it.
Popular on Variety
That comes down to building relationships with creators about how it can be used, including where it fits within the production landscape. Balakrishnan highlighted Netflix’s public framework for how the company uses AI within its production pipeline (on a generative level, for roughly 300 programs), a model he said “builds trust with the creative community” and gives those members ”a pathway to navigate to drive use cases that are meaningful to the creative process.”
The industry is already landing on other frameworks surrounding AI’s place in the industry, such as the Kathleen Kennedy and American Film Institute-led “Human Generative Workflows” paper published last month. Lane helped develop the paper, which she said breaks down the use cses in ways that can help AI-backed productions reach a still-elusive goal: being copyrightable.
“We did a whole exercise around tooling and looking at everything from de-noising techniques to fully synthetic characters,” she said. “Let’s start thinking about the vocabulary and breaking it down so it’s not just AI as one big monolithic.”
Adobe has tried to help distinguish that in its own tools, Keane said, delineating between “assistive,” “corrective“ and “generative” functions. That allows users who’ve found those use cases to prosper, she said. “People don’t even really realize that they’re AI anymore because so much of the conversation has shifted to generative,” she said.
Some of that trust built between companies and those working in the AI space has offered up another elusive item in the field: intellectual property, including renowned brands and high-profile characters.
“[Companies] are very careful about how we use those creative assets to maintain the integrity of the brand,” Vasquez said about Teads’ work with ad sales. “We have AI models to build the creative, but for those world’s largest brands, there’s a lot of scrutiny around that. So what I’m looking forward to, and the brands that we partner [with] look forward to, is what are the guardrails in place?”
Hasbro, through its Sixth Wall work, has worked to implement proprietary guardrails for the ElevenLabs-backed AI replicas of characters it licenses, such as those of Cobra Commander and Optimus Prime. While companies can license those characters for interactive experiences — one hypothetical Thomson offered was a Waymo with the voice of Prime — those can’t be manipulated in the way many unauthorized clips of Hasbro characters have been.
“If you think about the existence of lots of unauthorized characters out there… they’re not necessarily safe for our brand,” Thomson said. “Whereas working on the authorized AI version of the character means that, for these actors, it has a protective value for them too, and also for us as IP owners.”
Still, each company is still working through public misconceptions surrounding AI, whether the idea models are preparing for humanity’s imminent destruction or the notion that full-fledged blockbusters can be create with a quick prompting of ChatGPT.
“They don’t understand that, when you’re making really premium movies, TV shows, really engaging stories the way that Lionsgate and others on the stage do, the technology you have to use there is more complex than just prompting. It’s a whole process,” Lane said. “There’s a lot of consideration that goes into everything we make, and in my role, I’m here [saying] here are the tools you could use to make your thing better, bigger, more, and get to the end of the production faster. You choose what’s best for the story, and then, great, you chose the thing that’s best for your story, and it’s better. It’s not necessarily what people think of in pop culture. It’s not like ChatGPT. We just can’t throw something onto that.”
In the end, each leader said they wanted the technology to help creatives tell better — and more — stories, not feel like they have to adopt the technology for the sake of staying ahead.
“Filmmakers aren’t asking, ‘Do I want to use AI or not?’ They’re looking to solve meaningful creative problems that they’re faced with on their shows,” Balakrishnan said, citing several Netflix programs that made use of generative AI. “I think those are the opportunities that creators are looking for, and that’s where AI comes specific as an option to be able to solve real creators.”
It can also, in Grace’s view, help studios find and distribute new stories from creators who’ve utilized AI tools to help bring their visions to life. She cited the worlds of “John Wick” and “The Hunger Games” as examples of work the company has done to sell well-liked IP, and that it wants to have “all kinds of filmmakers we work with.”
“Just look at the range of our slate from this year: ‘Housemaid,’ ‘Michael,’ ‘Sunrise [on the Reaping]’,” she said. “Those are all very different filmmakers and different stories. To me, it’s just more creative people, and in some ways, easier to find them because the tools are democratized. Is it going to be an exciting challenge to bring in more talented people who have access to tools? Yes, but I’m interested to see what happens.”

OpenAI asks California court to dismiss lawsuits over Tumbler Ridge shooting
Tech giant argues British Columbia is best place for legal battle over mass shooting responsibility
OpenAI wants a U.S. judge to dismiss more than three dozen lawsuits filed in California by survivors and families of victims of the Tumbler Ridge school shooting who claim the tech giant and its chief executive officer could have prevented the tragedy.
In motions to dismiss some of the 37 U.S. district court actions, lawyers for OpenAI claim any legal action related to the deaths and injuries should take place in British Columbia.
The company says it will ultimately defend itself against what it calls "baseless accusations" but insists both private and public interests would be best served by putting the case in front of a B.C. judge.
"California is not the most appropriate forum for claims by British Columbians attacked by a British Columbian in British Columbia," the motion to dismiss reads.
"British Columbia plainly is an available and adequate alternative forum, so the key questions ... are where the parties can access evidence and which forum has the greater interest. The answer to both is British Columbia."
On Feb. 10, 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar killed eight people — including six children — before taking her own life.
Questions about the shooter's interactions with the health care system and police arose in the wake of the tragedy — turning to OpenAI after news reports about Van Rootselaar's use of ChatGPT.
The first lawsuits filed against OpenAI and CEO Altman were filed last spring in California, where the company is headquartered, with another wave of claims following earlier this month.
The claims alleged "ChatGPT played a role in the mass shooting and OpenAI could have, and should have, prevented it."
The victims claim the company flagged the shooter's ChatGPT account for "gun violence and planning" eight months before the attack, but "after a contentious internal debate, made the conscious decision not to warn authorities."
They claim to be suing both Altman and his company "for designing a dangerous product, ignoring the warnings of their own safety team, refusing to notify authorities when they knew the shooter was planning a mass attack, inviting them back onto the platform after deactivating their account, and choosing profit over the lives of the children of Tumbler Ridge."
'Forum non conveniens'
OpenAI has filed identical motions to dismiss a number of the suits over the past two weeks, citing a legal concept called "forum non conveniens" to argue that British Columbia is the logical place to bring any legal action related to the Tumbler Ridge shooting.
The company says most of the evidence in the case is in British Columbia as are most of the people likely to serve as witnesses.
OpenAI also says B.C has a "uniquely strong sovereign interest in having these actions resolved at home."
The motion to dismiss claims the court actions will require an examination of the role of "Canadian law enforcement, firearms regulations and British Columbia institutions in the events that preceded the shooting."
OpenAI says the actions would overlap "with Canada’s ongoing examination of its own institutions and policy choices."
"The jury may need to determine, among other questions, whether Canadian law enforcement acted reasonably in returning guns to the home of a mentally unstable teenager who had recently committed arson in an attempt to kill her family and had repeatedly been involuntarily hospitalized under British Columbia’s mental health legislation," the court document reads.
"The standard of care may turn on Canadian and British Columbia statutes and community practices — which differ from those in California."
Claims are 'not viable'
Wherever the lawsuits eventually take place, OpenAI says it intends to fight the allegations.
"[The] legal claims — blaming OpenAI for a horrific mass shooting by a deeply troubled teenager after systemic failures by the law enforcement, mental-health care, and educational institutions in her community — are not viable" the motion to dismiss says.
"Nor are the claims against Samuel Altman, who was not personally involved in the June 2025 review of the shooter’s ChatGPT account or the decision at that time not to refer her account to Canadian law enforcement."
In the wake of revelations about the shooter's ChatGPT history, Altman apologized to the Tumbler Ridge community and said the company has updated its protocols.
The B.C. government is also planning legal action against OpenAI, and has since demolished the site of Tumbler Ridge Secondary School.

Zara Larsson criticises White House for using her song in deportation video
- Published
Swedish pop star Zara Larsson has condemned the White House for using one of her most recognisable songs in a social media reel.
The clip used Larsson's Midnight Sun in a video appearing to show immigration enforcement raids. The song has since been removed from the post, but the video is still visible on the White House's TikTok feed.
The video is captioned "never ending deportations", riffing on Larsson's lyrics "never-ending midnight sun".
In a three-minute reaction video posted on social media, Larsson described the clip as "dehumanising", joining a growing list of singers, including Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande, who have told the Trump administration to not use their music.
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.
The reel splices together multiple videos of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, as well as other US law enforcement personnel, handcuffing men and putting them into vehicles.
Larsson reposted part of the original clip, which then cuts to a selfie video of her using her fingers to hold an 'L' shape against her forehead.
In the reaction video that has already clocked up more than 4.2 million views on TikTok, she tells her followers the White House video is "so dehumanising".
Larsson continues: "These people in this video – they're real people."
"The vast majority of these people who are undocumented are regular people with jobs and they're just trying to have a better future".
"It's so crazy how everything is so memefied and so 'ha-ha-ha'," she says, accusing the White House of using her song to sow "division", despite the lyrics reflecting a connection between people and nature, according to Larsson.
Earlier this year, Larsson condemned a video of President Donald Trump dancing at various events overlayed with her hit Lush Life.
White House social media accounts have been forced to remove various songs from their feed following interventions from artists.
Taylor Swift's seasonal track August disappeared from a reel shared by the Trump administration in August, while one of Olivia Rodrigo's songs vanished from a video after the singer condemned its use for what she called "hateful propaganda".
Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande have also warned the Trump administration in separate incidents to not use their music in social media content after the White House posted videos featuring their songs.

With greater clarity around the monetisation of UPI payments following’ the introduction of a new Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) framework, Walmart-backed fintech PhonePe is set to revive its initial public offering (IPO) plans, which were put on hold earlier this year. Sources told Inc42 that the fintech startup is now targeting a public listing between February-March 2027. “They have an almost 45% share of merchant payments. With greater clarity on the MDR regime, PhonePe is now looking to revise its IPO plans and could target a listing between February and March 2027,” the sources said. PhonePe will look to file its updated IPO papers by the end of this year, seeking a valuation of $10 Bn, sources in the know told Inc42 on the condition of anonymity. Inc42 has sent questions to PhonePe to confirm the development. The story will be updated based on their response. Notably, the MDR framework was introduced by the Central government yesterday, bringing charges back on select UPI merchant transactions beginning October 15. The move marks a shift from the broad zero-MDR regime in place from 2020. The charges will apply only to select transactions, with merchant UPI payments above ₹2,000 attracting a 0.4% MDR. However, person-to-person (P2P) transactions up to ₹2,000 will continue to remain free. Small merchants receiving up to ₹1 Lakh a month through UPI QR payments will also be exempt. A lower MDR of 0.02%, capped at ₹300, will apply to capital market payments, including transactions involving stockbrokers, securities dealers, mutual funds and investment platforms. The revised framework gives PhonePe, which has long been the UPI market leader, a greater clarity on monetising the service following years of no revenue. After filing for an confidential IPO in September 2025, PhonePe had filed its updated DRHP in March post receiving the SEBI’s approval for its OFS-only IPO. Existing investors including Walmart, Tiger Global and Microsoft were expected to sell shares. The IPO was earlier expected to value PhonePe at $9 Bn-$10.5 Bn, with the offering size estimated to be in the range of $900 Mn-$1.5 Bn. In its updated DRHP, PhonePe noted that UPI payments carried an MDR until 2020, allowing payment apps, aggregators and banks to earn revenue from transactions. The government later scrapped the MDR on UPI and RuPay payments to boost digital payment adoption. PhonePe’s DRHP also cited calls from the Payments Council of India to review the zero-MDR regime for large merchants and RuPay debit card transactions. The startup said a “carefully structured MDR regime” could support investments in infrastructure, innovation and merchant acquisition, while cautioning that changes to the MDR framework could affect its financial performance. PhonePe CEO Sameer Nigam has now welcomed the new framework, saying that the revenue generated from high-value merchant transactions could be reinvested in the UPI ecosystem. Speaking to ANI earlier in the day, Nigam said around 70-80 Cr UPI transactions take place every day and that about 96% would remain free under the new framework. He said the 0.4% MDR would help the payments industry recover some operational costs and invest in merchant digitisation, marketing, innovation and new use cases. “Now that a limited MDR has been introduced, we hope it will contribute to the further growth of the UPI ecosystem,” Nigam said. On the financial front, PhonePe’s net loss widened 62% to ₹2,792 Cr in FY26 from ₹1,727.4 Cr in the previous fiscal, as higher employee costs, marketing expenses, ESOP costs and one-time write-offs offset growth in revenue. Operating revenue rose 11.5% to ₹7,920.5 Cr from ₹7,105 Cr in FY25. Including other income of ₹467.4 Cr, total revenue grew 10% YoY to ₹8,387.9 Cr.

"I'm Russian, and I support my country," Ovechkin said Thursday from Arlington, Va. "I'm for peace and love, and I hope in the world it doesn't matter who you are, I hope everybody understands everybody wants peace, and everybody hope everything's going to be OK in the world."
Ovechkin said he did not hesitate to participate in the ad.
"They asked me to do that. I say yes," he said. "So, it's as simple as that."
Ovechkin previously voiced support for the Russian president in 2017 when he started a social movement called the "Putin Team."
At the time, he told reporters from the AP and The Washington Post, "I just support my country."
'No more war,' Ovie pleaded in 2022
When Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Ovechkin said, "Please, no more war," when asked about the situation. Asked then about his relationship with Putin, Ovechkin said: "He's my president, but I'm not in politics. I'm an athlete."
Russia's parliamentary election this week features United Russia, plus nine others that all support Putin's policies. The only party that opposed the war in Ukraine has been barred from the ballot.
Ovechkin, who turned 41 on Thursday, confirmed he plans to live in Russia when he retires from the NHL.
"I'm going to stay there. I'm going to live there, my kids are going to live there, family. So, I'm for peace and love, and I hope everything's going to be OK," Ovechkin said. "My home is Russia. DC is my second home. I have lots of friends.
“I grew up here as a person and I love DC. This is my second home. So I hope everything's going to be OK, and how I said — peace and love for everybody."
There was speculation last season would be Ovechkin's last, but he chose to stay with the Capitals for at least another year, and he remains noncommittal about what the future might hold after 2026-27.
"I'm focusing right now on training camp," Ovechkin said. "I have to make the team."

Uncontrolled AI could lead to 'silicon species' rivalling humans, warns Microsoft
- Published
The head of Microsoft AI has warned that without adequate safeguards, the development of AI could lead to the emergence of a new "silicon species" wich competes with humans.
Mustafa Suleyman said rival firm Anthropic is treating AI like it is human, an approach he called "misguided" which could create technology that humanity cannot control.
Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, the chief executive said it was "right" for people to be concerned about AI, but there were "very practical things that we can do" to control it.
The comments are the latest in a series of stark warnings from the AI industry about the technology's possible dangers. Anthropic has been approached for comment.
- A backlash over data centres is another threat to the AI juggernaut 
  - Published1 day ago
- OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms 
  - Published22 hours ago
Speaking to the Today programme on Thursday, Suleyman warned against firms continuing to create AI systems capable of setting their own objectives, earning money and owning assets.
That would mean "essentially seeding a new silicon species", he said, which could "no doubt compete with us for resources, no matter how much it cares about humanity and loves us".
Suleyman's comments to the BBC follow an essay he published earlier this week, external, in which he questioned Anthropic's approach to training its AI model Claude, despite praising boss Dario Amodei and his team as "intellectually honest people".
In it, he criticised Anthropic for teaching its AI to have human-like qualities, a practice known as anthropomorphising, which he said made it seem as though Claude had its own desires, values and sense of self.
He also warned tech firms risk creating something "impossible" to control by treating the technology like a human.
"AIs are not conscious," he wrote.
"They do not feel, experience, or suffer. They do not have innate preferences or underlying motivations.
"They are sequence completion engines, internally hollow, designed to follow instructions, and accomplish goals set by humans."
The Microsoft boss said greater transparency was needed around how AI systems are trained and evaluated.
This, he said, included independent scrutiny of AI behaviour and stronger tools to monitor and control the technology.
"We must not sleepwalk our way into a decision we later come to bitterly regret," he wrote.
Dame Wendy Hall, professor of Computer Science at the University of Southampton, described the comments as "the sort of conversation we need to be having internationally", contrasting it with the "histrionics" from some AI companies which she said only served to "scare everyone".
'Humanist' superintelligence
The question of how much autonomy AI systems should have is increasingly dividing the industry.
Speaking to the BBC about an upcoming AI summit, Suleyman called for "alignment" to create technology that must be "subordinate" to humanity.
Alignment is a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.
"I think that the good news here is that everybody who is human is going to have a very strong interest in making sure that the systems that we all create and... are used around the world in every nation are safe and controllable and subordinate to humanity," he said.
"Everybody must be aligned."
Microsoft founded its own superintelligence team in October 2025 and the company, much like its rival Anthropic, is also pursuing efforts in advanced AI development.
Suleyman's comments reflects Microsoft's initial draft of its Humanist AI Code of Conduct, external, a "training manual" published on Monday for how the company is developing its AI, which sets out the idea of "humanist superintelligence".
This, the code states, is "very advanced AI that always works for people, stays within limits, and remains under human control".
The company's vision of a "humanist" AI highlights the central challenge facing the technology - how to make it more powerful, without losing sight of the values it is meant to serve.
Additional reporting by Henry Moore

A video is going viral on social media (here, here, and here) claiming that Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he would eliminate poverty from the country in one stroke. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Prime Minister Narendra Modi saying that he will eradicate poverty from the country at once.
Fact: The viral video is presented out of context to make it appear that Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he would eradicate poverty from India in a single stroke. In the original video, PM Modi was referring to Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s earlier statement about eradicating poverty and questioning the claim, rather than making the claim himself. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to an extended version of the same video uploaded on Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s official YouTube channel on 14 April 2024, titled “PM Modi addresses a public meeting in Hoshangabad, Madhya Pradesh”. According to the video description, PM Modi addressed a public meeting in Hoshangabad ahead of the 2024 Lok Sabha elections and paid tribute to Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar on his birth anniversary. At the 28:05 timestamp, PM Modi can be heard referring to a statement by Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, saying that Gandhi had claimed he would eradicate poverty from the country in a single stroke.
PM Modi said, “Modi’s guarantee begins where expectations from others end. That is why a desperate Congress is making announcements that even its own leaders fail to comprehend. The Congress ‘Prince’ made a declaration that would make you laugh too: he claimed he would eradicate poverty from the country in a single stroke. The entire nation is astonished to hear this. People ask where this ‘royal magician’ has been hiding all these years. Fifty years ago, his grandmother had announced the eradication of poverty. Before 2014, they ran the government via remote control for a decade. And now, they claim to have found a magic mantra that can do the job in one stroke. Where did they get this ‘one-stroke’ mantra? Tell me, isn’t this a mockery of the poor? Isn’t this an insult to the poor? You tell me, can poverty really be eliminated in a single stroke? What are they saying? Who would trust them? It is because they make such claims that they become a laughingstock across the country; the nation does not take them seriously.”
We also found that the Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP) official YouTube channel uploaded the same video on the same day, featuring a longer version of the viral clip.
The full transcript of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s speech at the Hoshangabad rally was also available on his official website. The transcript confirms that PM Modi was referring to Rahul Gandhi’s claim about eradicating poverty in a single stroke, rather than making the claim himself, as the viral video suggests.
A few days before PM Modi’s rally, Rahul Gandhi said at a rally in Anupgarh, Rajasthan, “The Congress government will give one lakh rupees annually to one woman in every family. One lakh rupees, or 8,500 rupees every month, will be deposited into your bank account every year, and in one fell swoop, we will eradicate poverty from India.”
To sum up, PM Modi did not say he would eradicate poverty in one stroke; he was referring to Rahul Gandhi’s earlier statement.

Pennsylvania’s Measles Outbreak Is Enormous
The two latest deaths suggest that the true number of infections is much larger than reported.
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here.
Following America’s recent measles deaths, anti-vaccine activists have cast doubt on the virus as the culprit. They’ve pointed to a victim’s underlying health conditions or, as they did last year in Texas, blamed hospital error. But the two latest measles deaths in Pennsylvania—bringing the state’s total to four since mid-August—have made the United States’ measles crisis undeniable.
Last month, the Pennsylvania Department of Health announced two measles-associated deaths; both cases were later revealed to be infants too young to have been vaccinated. In response, Robert F. Kennedy Jr.—who was an anti-vaccine activist for decades before becoming health secretary—wrote on X that the deaths might have been “altogether fabricated.” (He later acknowledged a coroner’s conclusion that one of the deaths had been caused by measles.) Then, last weekend, an unvaccinated 40-year-old woman died in Jefferson County; immediately, people on Reddit and X insisted that her death wasn’t really caused by measles, because she’d had asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, both of which can make breathing difficult. Yesterday, state officials revealed that an unvaccinated 18-year-old died from a rare inflammatory condition of the brain and spinal cord that can be triggered by measles. Some commenters online deemed that death suspicious too.
What the armchair epidemiologists miss is that vulnerability to the infection doesn’t make a death less real. The two infants both tested positive for measles. The Lancaster County coroner’s office determined that one infant died of a ruptured spleen; however, when I spoke with that child’s parents, they told me that the mother had been extremely ill with the disease when she gave birth, the baby was not breathing when he was born, and they believed measles had killed their son. The other infant was born with a rare neurological condition, but the coroner found that measles was ultimately the cause of death. Greg Furlong, the Jefferson County coroner who investigated the 40-year-old woman’s death, told me that although the woman had conditions that made her vulnerable to measles, and was on supplemental oxygen, she was active before she contracted the virus. She cooked for her family and cleaned the house. Measles killed her in about a week. “If she wouldn’t have got the measles, would she still be alive today? I say yes,” Furlong, a Republican who is also the mayor of Summerville, said.
Four deaths in roughly four weeks suggest that the state is in the midst of an enormous outbreak. The Pennsylvania health department lists total cases at 693, with 99 in the past week. But considering that measles kills about one to three of every 1,000 children it infects, the actual number is likely much larger. Milder cases are going unreported. Many who fall ill, particularly in the Amish community, aren’t getting tested; the Amish parents of the infant who died with a ruptured spleen told me that their 13 living children had all caught the virus, but they never got swabbed.
These deaths are occurring after three unvaccinated people, including two young girls, died of measles in Texas and New Mexico last year. Those were the first measles deaths in the country in a decade. The last time the United States experienced four measles deaths in a calendar year was in 1992, at the tail end of a years-long outbreak that killed more than 100 Americans. That resurgence led to a recommendation that children receive two doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine, and prompted a nationwide push to increase vaccination rates. It worked, and measles was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000. But overall kindergarten vaccination rates started declining during the coronavirus pandemic, and some areas, including Lancaster County, have fallen well below the 95 percent needed to maintain herd immunity.
Now, in the face of a new increase in measles deaths, Kennedy appears more interested in scoring political points than boosting national vaccination rates. He has accused Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, of “the weaponization of infectious disease fears for political gain”; Shapiro, in turn, charged Kennedy with “playing games with public health” after the CDC declined to update its measles statistics to include the deaths in his state. Kennedy’s stated reason for the omission is that the agency is “applying a consistent national standard.” But the delay marks a shift in policy: Last year, the CDC counted both Texas girls’ deaths and the death of the adult in New Mexico after the states announced them. (In a post on X, Kennedy wrote that the National Center for Health Statistics will determine if measles is the true cause of the deaths in Pennsylvania after examining death records; a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to questions about that investigation. In a statement, Pennsylvania’s health department said that its investigation had determined that all four deaths met the criteria for measles-associated fatalities.)
Tomorrow, Kennedy is scheduled to be the keynote speaker at the annual conference for Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine organization that he founded before becoming health secretary. Children’s Health Defense has a long history of ginning up fears about the vaccine for measles, mumps, and rubella while downplaying the seriousness of the diseases. Kennedy does, too. In July 2021, Kennedy told attendees at an Amish country fair in Pennsylvania, “The cure for measles is chicken soup and vitamin A.” In fact, no known cure for measles exists; vitamin A has shown some promise in people with severe vitamin A deficiency, which is exceedingly rare in the United States. Since becoming health secretary, he has stated publicly that vaccination is “the most effective way to prevent measles infection,” but as I’ve reported, he also undercut that message by telling the father of a girl who died in West Texas that “you don’t know what’s in the vaccine anymore.” Kennedy has been a stronger advocate for measles itself, which he’s falsely credited with boosting resistance to cancer and cardiac disease, than he has for the vaccine that prevents it.
As cases and deaths rise, the reality becomes harder to ignore: Measles, a disease the country seemingly overcame 30 years ago, is once again killing Americans.

Stellar performance and cooling. Great battery life. Excellent and fun cameras with a customizable camera app. Bright, responsive screens with a smaller Dynamic Island.
TIRED
Pricier than ever. No base model (yet). Living in the iPhone Duo's shadow.
There is no iPhone 18 this year. If you were hoping to upgrade your smartphone right now, Apple is only offering the new iPhone 18 Pro models (and a very expensive folding iPhone coming next month). Don't let that be a reason to spend extra money on a phone you might not need.
Apple hasn't confirmed the next base-model yet, but the iPhone 18 is expected in spring 2027 alongside a mid-tier iPhone 18e. If you've historically been more than satisfied with the base iPhone model, you should absolutely wait to upgrade. Don't let the hype machine sway you.
That said, if you're a Pro connoisseur, the iPhone 18 Pro ($1,199) and its bigger sibling, the 18 Pro Max ($1,299), are very good phones, despite the $100 price hike over last year’s Pro models. No, you don't need to upgrade if you're coming from an iPhone 17 Pro, 16 Pro, or even a 15 Pro—hold onto your devices for longer!—but Apple's flagships deliver where it matters, even if they feel eclipsed by the spectacle of the foldable iPhone Duo.
Minor Refresh
Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro models have significant upgrades, but let's be a little more measured here.
Battery life has been stellar on the Pro models over the last few years, and that remains true here. The Pro Max is the more notable of the two because it packs a denser battery. With average use (around 5 hours of screen-on time), I hovered around 50 percent by the end of the day, and easily made it through day two on a single charge. I spent a little less time with the smaller Pro, but so far it has also comfortably gotten me through a day with around 40 percent left by bedtime. Safe to say, most people will very much enjoy the battery life, but the update doesn't feel drastic.
Next, there's the processor: the A20 Pro chip. I hardly run into problems with Apple's flagship silicon, and that hasn't changed. The phones run every app fluidly, and my benchmark tests show a surprisingly sizable leap over the A19 Pro in the 17 series.
It runs Control—a AAA game from 2019 ported to iOS earlier this year—decently well. However, aggressive upscaling makes the graphics look grainy, and character movements can feel a little sluggish. (I maxed out the graphics settings.) It's certainly not perfect, but I still can't believe I'm playing such a demanding title on an iPhone.
More impressive is Apple's thermal management on these phones. The company has expanded the vapor chamber's surface area by three times—the phone's cooling technology that helps spread heat around—meaning the entire phone felt toasty after close to an hour of gameplay in Control, with no uncomfortable localized hot spots. This larger vapor chamber also lets you game longer before phone’s thermal throttling kicks in and slows everything down.
The iPhone 18 Pro models come with iOS 27 out of the box, which features the all-new Siri AI. Yes, Siri AI is infinitely more capable than any version of Siri that Apple has offered before. It still doesn't quite have the spark or versatility of other AI assistants, but you might be fine with that. If you throw Siri AI a question, there's a good chance it can actually give you a satisfactory answer now. Remember that Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features aren't exclusive to the latest models, though you do need an iPhone 15 Pro or newer to access them.
The Dynamic Island, the pill-shaped bar housing the selfie camera and Face ID sensors, is noticeably smaller this year. To take full advantage of it, you can now view three live activities—like a DoorDash order status or your Uber ETA—simultaneously inside the Island, up from two. I was navigating in Apple Maps, chatting on a phone call, and had a DoorDash order en route to my home, and it spaced out all of these activities neatly.
Speaking of the iPhone 18 Pro design, I do like the new burgundy color, though I miss brighter, more playful options like last year's Cosmic Orange. But the real headline feature is almost invisible—embedded into the main camera on the back of the iPhone.
Aperture Priority
Apple is debuting a variable aperture in the iPhone 18 Pro models. This is by no means the first time we've seen a smartphone with a variable aperture—Samsung and Huawei both launched phones with the capability years ago. While Samsung abandoned the tech, Huawei and Xiaomi still ship it on their flagships.
What is a variable aperture? Simply put, the aperture is the physical opening that lets light reach the camera sensor. A wider aperture lets in more light and has a lower “f-stop” number, while a narrower aperture restricts light. Most smartphones rely on fixed apertures—the iPhone 17 Pro's main camera, for example, is locked at f/1.78. A variable aperture gives the lens mechanical blades that physically expand or contract in a circular shape, adjusting how much light hits the sensor. Apple gives you four f-stops to select from: f/1.48, f/1.78, f/2.8, and f/4.
Open the aperture to f/1.48 on the iPhone 18 Pro and more light floods in, delivering cleaner low-light shots and faster Night Mode captures. This also creates a real optical bokeh—the soft blurred background effect phone makers have spent years simulating with computational Portrait modes. Step it down to f/4, this blur recedes, keeping more of the scene and background in crisp focus. All of this can be very confusing for people unfamiliar with these camera terms, which is why Apple defaults the aperture to “Auto.”
I love it. I shoot manual on my mirrorless camera, so I immediately took to the new customization features in the Camera app to show Shutter Speed and Lens Aperture as easy-to-access settings. Shooting at f/1.48 delivers a nice bokeh effect—especially in low light—so I stopped using Apple's Portrait mode altogether. (Some parts of the image may look less sharp than on an iPhone 17 Pro because the plane of focus is narrower.) Apple will point out that Portrait mode is still useful, as you can always add more bokeh post-capture.
Photograph: Julian Chokkattu
iPhone 18 Pro Max, main camera with a one-second shutter speed.
Move to f/4 for group shots when you want everyone in the frame to be in focus. (Or if you want a very fun starburst effect with light sources!) As you change between the four aperture settings, you can see the blades moving on the main camera—it's very cool. In auto mode, the camera largely sticks to f/1.78, or f/1.48 in low light. It chooses the other two apertures for specific, usually brighter, scenes.
I have also enjoyed the ability to adjust the camera’s shutter speed. Yes, you can already do this with a third-party camera app, but now it's baked in! With a one-second shutter, you can capture some fun shutter drag to accentuate motion in a photo. However, you'll definitely need to buy a neutral density filter for super-bright scenes to balance exposure. It's fun to play around with.
I compared several of the 18 Pro’s photos with shots from Google's Pixel 11 Pro, and I do have to note that the iPhone tends to over-brighten scenes that should be very dark. So much so that it can misrepresent the dark mood you might be chasing. The Pixel tended to preserve more of those shadows, though it delivered more lifted blacks that made the image appear more matte. The iPhone can also struggle with backlit scenes, more so than the Pixel.
Apple has added texture and grain control to its Photographic Styles, and this is a fun element to sink your teeth into and explore. Phone makers have realized that ultra-clean, sharp, “perfect” shots are perhaps not what most people want, and these stylings—like the new Camera Looks on Pixel phones—offer a new degree of “authenticity.”
The iPhone 18 Pro's camera system is fun without feeling overwhelming. You can pick and choose what degree of control you want, tweak Photographic Styles to your tastes, and add more depth after the fact, whether it's for videos or photos. Who knew people liked having more control? There aren't any sweeping improvements to the camera lenses or sensors, but this is a system that shutterbugs will love to experiment with, and that's what the Pro iPhone is all about.

Throughout the Trump era, Democrats have wrung their hands about how they can win over working-class voters.
These Democrats won over working-class voters. Here’s their advice for candidates.
A new report explains which topics they emphasize — and which they don’t.
Why not ask the Democrats who’ve actually done it?
That’s what Robin Johnson — a political consultant based in rural Illinois, and a part-time political science professor at Monmouth College — set out to do after Donald Trump first won the presidency, asking Democratic state legislators who won tough districts how they pulled it off.
But after Trump’s shocking second win in 2024 revived concern about Democrats’ working-class woes, the time seemed ripe to ask legislators about how they’ve managed to cope with the challenges of a new decade.
So, working with the center-left Progressive Policy Institute and co-authors Stuart Malec and Jolie Libert, Johnson interviewed 28 state legislators who won in heavily working-class areas in the seven main presidential battleground states.
They include Nevada state Assemblymember Max Carter, a retired union electrician; Michigan state Rep. Tullio Liberati, a construction small business owner; Arizona state Rep. Lorena Austin, a self-described “five-time college dropout” with sleeve tattoos; and Wisconsin state Rep. Karen DeSanto, a nonprofit executive and former professional circus clown.
The report, which Vox reviewed exclusively ahead of its publication, comes amid a factional debate within the party between rising left-wing and socialist candidates who have argued for more far-reaching policy proposals, and more moderate Democrats who have pushed for concessions to working-class cultural sensibilities. In the report, the authors said that lawmakers they focused on “could hardly be more different from the left-wing populists who’ve captivated the national media this summer.”
Generally, the legislators in the report focused on pocketbook issues, though in different ways — some embraced populist causes, while others positioned themselves as business-friendly. And they broadly agreed that cultural issues were Democrats’ biggest challenge in reaching the working class.
“It’s really interesting how common the themes and the challenges are from rural Georgia, right down to the border of Arizona, to Las Vegas, northern North Carolina, and then up in the ‘Blue Wall’ states,” Johnson told me.
I spoke to Johnson last week about his findings, and about what these state legislators’ experience has to tell us about the debate over the Democratic Party’s future. Our conversation, which has been condensed and edited, is below.
What’s changed in 10 years of interviewing legislators facing tough races
Walk me through where the idea for this project came from.
I’ve been working on this for 10 years. It started at a conversation at a little diner in Maquoketa, Iowa — a little “choke and puke,” as we call those places. I was with a former state senator from Iowa named Jeff Danielson, and it was right after Trump won. Most of the focus was on what happened at the congressional or presidential level, and we thought, why not take a look at state legislators competing in these tough districts?
I approached my friend and my congresswoman, Cheri Bustos, who I’ve known really well and helped on her campaigns, and said, would you be interested in working with us and sponsoring it? She said, absolutely, because her district, the 17th in Illinois, is rural working-class. And she was able to win these voters.
We talked to probably 75 current and former legislators for that first report. We did another one in 2021, focused on members of Congress and state legislators who win Trump districts. Then we did a third one last year, on Democrats in working-class districts in the heartland. Then she retired from Congress and I went to a PPI conference this past February, and PPI agreed to partner on this with a different focus, slightly — on the seven battleground states, on districts that are really close and have more working-class voters than the national average.
So, having done this several times before, what’s new in the latest version? What are people saying now that they weren’t, necessarily, in previous rounds of this?
In the past, when we focused on the Midwest, it was mostly all white, mostly men, some women. Now, we went to North Carolina and Georgia, and there were African American legislators, men and women. And we went to the West, and there were Latinos.
But what was interesting to me was: Nobody brought up their identity in these interviews. I had to bring it up to one woman from Nevada, mentioning, “Well, you’re Native American.” “Yeah, but I don’t really talk about that much,” was the response.
That was one big takeaway: Nobody talked about identity. Their focus was totally on their constituents, their working-class constituents.
What were some of the common themes you saw in the responses?
There’s no secret sauce. They’re deeply rooted in their communities, they know the people that live there, they know the language, they work hard.
But they focus on economic issues. If somebody asks them about cultural issues, they’ll respond, but they try to get back to economic issues, because that’s what they’re hearing about from voters, mostly.
These folks are from a variety of backgrounds. Some are true working-class, they don’t have college degrees. One guy near Detroit runs a construction company, didn’t get a degree. Another woman we focused on from Arizona had tattoos all over and took 14 years to get her BA. Some are the traditional route — attorneys, some small business people.
But it’s a lot of different backgrounds, and we want to contrast that with the consultants who tried to make the perfect Frankenstein candidate out of [former Maine Senate candidate Graham] Platner. These people are out there — you don’t need to create it. They’re out there.
Cultural issues
On how politics has changed over the years, there’s a particularly vivid quote in the report from state Assemblymember Elaine Marzola from Nevada.
She tells you: “My campaign’s biggest adjustment in 2024 was shifting away from leading with social and cultural issues and instead focusing more directly on affordability and economic concerns.” And she adds, “While I remain progressive on many social issues, voters across backgrounds increasingly want leaders focused on affordability, education, and public safety rather than endless culture war debates.”
How widespread was that sentiment?
It’s very widespread. Their focus is on the issues that matter, that they’re picking up from their constituents. A lot of times they reported that some of the people in their campaigns told them they should talk more about abortion or other social issues — mainly abortion — and they refused to do it.
A lot of them talked about a major problem in the party being these litmus tests that groups have, that you can vote with them on nine out of 10 issues, but on the tenth issue, if you’re not with them, you’re an enemy.
If you’re going to have a true big-tent party, you’ve got to have some room for disagreements on some of these issues that reflect the local voters that people have in their districts. Several in Georgia told me pointedly that their leadership understood and would give them passes on votes that they knew they couldn’t be with them on. But in other cases, I heard a lot of pointed comments about these groups demanding 100 percent allegiance, that it’s all or nothing.
In a lot of districts down South, I heard from a couple gentlemen; it’s the Bible Belt. People go to church regularly. African Americans, the older generations of African Americans, are more middle-of-the-road, if not conservative on some of these cultural issues. So there’s got to be room for people to vote their districts on some of these cultural issues.
But on the economic issues, they’re there. They’re unified with the rest of the party.
Economic issues
Well, it’s interesting on economic issues, because there’s unity on focusing on affordability and pocketbook issues in some form. But you also describe how some people take a more populist approach, and others have a more business-friendly approach. Is there tension there?
We asked people, how would they describe themselves? And most of them describe themselves as moderate. But the range of issues you have at the state level may differ some compared to the federal issues. A true populist approach at the state level may not have the same meaning as a populist at the federal level.
In fact, some of the folks with business backgrounds were pretty aggressive in some of their policy ideas. I think [Assemblymember] Joe Dalia from Nevada is one, he actually combined with [Rep.] Ro Khanna on a policy idea, the congressman from Silicon Valley who’s definitely a progressive. Dalia’s background is in business entrepreneurship.
Is all politics local?
The dynamics are a little different in state legislative races, even tough competitive ones, because there’s just so much less national money, national interest, group interest, virality, all of the dynamics that are so important to national politics. These are truly local races. So do you think these lessons can apply to national politics?
These state legislators are easy to overlook. They’re close enough to the people that they’re in, they can knock doors more than like a member of Congress. You can’t really knock doors in a congressional race — you can do some and have volunteers do it, but these people are out doing it individually.
But they still get hit on national issues. Some of them didn’t do much TV — Georgia’s got smaller districts — but they’re on TV in Wisconsin. And they’ve got to raise money and then have the party help them out. They’re used to getting hit on national issues because the Republicans try to tie them to some of the more far-left ideas.
They also feel that the deep roots they have in the community help overcome that because they’re better known, they’re battle-tested in that regard. A lot of times, especially with social media, you think you’re going to come up with some neat little line to put on social media that’s going to carry you to a victory, or some pithy slogan or whatever. It’s really not. For these folks anyway, it just comes down to doing the hard work.
But this is the bench that the Democrats need. You want to pick some people down the road that have proven ability to win these tough districts — here they are.

Rescuers dig 4 bodies from a Nepal hydropower tunnel as families demand answers
Rescuers in Nepal have recovered four bodies from a hydropower plant tunnel three weeks after a devastating flash flood
KATHMANDU, Nepal -- Rescuers in Nepal have recovered four bodies from the tunnel of a hydropower plant as search operations continued for those still missing three weeks after the devastating flash flood last month that killed hundreds and left thousands missing.
Families of the thousands missing, meanwhile, are seeking answers from authorities on their whereabouts.
Nepal's army said that four bodies were recovered Wednesday from the Chilime Hydropower plant, which was situated on the Trishuli River that flooded on Aug. 26.
Nepal's disaster management agency said five more bodies were located in a different location and equipment was being sent to recover them.
The number of bodies that have been recovered since the flooding has reached 1,403 while 6,150 people are still missing, according to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.
Families of the missing have been pressuring the government to speed up the rescue and recovery process from the tunnels.
They have held rallies and many have called on the government to declare the missing as dead because they want to receive death certificates, which would allow them to move forward with legal proceedings and religious rites and give them some emotional closure.
At the Tribhuvan University Teaching hospital in Kathmandu, the lobby walls have been pasted with photos of hundreds of missing people. Relatives go there seeking news of their loved ones.
Usha Khatri's husband Indra Bahadur was working as a cook with a group of pilgrims when the flood hit the Nepal-China border. Since then she has been searching for him in many of the towns where the river flows and where bodies have been recovered.
“The government has not done much for us. They have not met us or given any information or any assurances. I am by myself searching for my husband,” Khatri said.
There were 13 hydropower plants that were damaged by the flooding and many workers were either swept or trapped by the raging water or debris.
Finding the workers who were trapped has been a priority for the government and rescuers. But access to the tunnels has been hampered by thick mud, debris and damaged infrastructure, making it difficult for rescue teams to reach the areas.
Two Nepali workers were found alive by rescuers on Sept. 4, days after the flooding. A day later a Chinese worker was pulled out alive from a separate area.
The government estimates the country's reconstruction costs at around $4.78 billion.

Combining healthy dietary practices with regular physical activity is the most effective non-drug strategy for achieving sustained weight loss and improving key metabolic health indicators among adults with overweight or obesity, according to a major review by the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (NIN) here.
The findings, published in the international journal Obesity Pillars, are based on an umbrella review that analysed evidence from 112 systematic reviews and meta-analyses covering 2,332 randomised controlled trials and more than 5.07 lakh participant observations across over 50 countries.
The review, led by ICMR-NIN scientists Mahesh Kumar Mummadi and Samarasimha Reddy, compared the impact of dietary interventions, physical activity, lifestyle changes and combined approaches on weight management and cardiometabolic health.
Researchers found that all major non-pharmacological interventions produced statistically significant, though generally modest, reductions in body weight and Body Mass Index (BMI). However, the combination of diet and physical activity delivered the most sustained results, with participants losing an average of 3.68 kg beyond 12 months compared with control groups.
Low-calorie diets were found to be the most effective for short-term weight loss, resulting in an average reduction of 2.64 kg within the first three months. Physical activity alone led to smaller reductions in body weight, but its benefits increased over longer follow-up periods.
Lifestyle interventions such as behavioural counselling, goal-setting, self-monitoring and health education also showed positive outcomes, with their effectiveness improving over time. Beyond weight loss, the study highlighted significant improvements in metabolic health. The combination of diet and physical activity produced the greatest benefits in blood sugar control, reducing fasting blood glucose levels and insulin resistance after 12 months.
Physical activity emerged as the most effective strategy for lowering blood pressure, reducing systolic blood pressure by about 6.1 mmHg between six and 12 months. Intermittent fasting showed the largest short-term reduction in diastolic blood pressure and supported weight loss for up to a year, although these benefits were not sustained beyond 12 months.
ICMR-NIN director Bharati Kulkarni said the findings underscore the importance of an integrated approach to tackling obesity. “Healthy dietary practices, regular physical activity and behavioural support each have a role, but their combination can provide broader and more sustained benefits. This is particularly relevant for India, where scalable and sustainable approaches are needed to address the growing burden of overweight, obesity and related non-communicable diseases,” she said.
Mr.Mummadi noted that although the review drew evidence from more than 50 countries, most studies originated from high-income and upper-middle-income nations. India and other lower-middle-income countries remained under-represented, highlighting the need for more locally relevant research, said a press release on Saturday.

WASHINGTON — Normally, discussions about how congressional advisers study Medicare spending are quite dry. Not so at the House Ways and Means Committee on Wednesday.
In a party line vote, committee Republicans pushed forward a bill that seeks to change how the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission studies Medicare Advantage spending. In particular, this bill would direct the nonpartisan agency to study the topic of overpayments to Medicare Advantage plans in a manner that’s more favorable to insurers.
Medicare Advantage insurers have come under increased scrutiny in recent years in part for their cost to taxpayers. MedPAC this year estimated that Medicare will pay 14% more per enrollee, or $76 billion in total, to Medicare Advantage plans than it would if those same seniors were covered by traditional Medicare.

Cooking gas distributors are evaluating the likely impact of the flat ₹5 Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) that the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has proposed on transactions above ₹2,000 from October 15.
Commercial liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) cylinder sales coming under the purview of the levy is a given since the 19-kg refills priced nearly ₹3,000 each. But what is not clear to the distributors is whether they will end up attracting MDR on the domestic refills sales, to households, too.
Though the 14.2 kg cylinders come for less than ₹1,000 each, the common practice of permitting delivery personnel to collect payments from customers and remit the same to the agency subsequently may trigger the charge. “Delivery boys collect payments on their individual UPI account for the refills they supply through the day to the households. In the evening, they transfer the sum collected to the distributor. But from October 15, such bulk remittance are likely to attract the MDR,” Telangana LPG Distributors Association president Jagan Mohan Reddy said.
Stating the practice has become common with distributors not sharing QR code with each of the delivery personnel, he said the LPG distributors are studying the likely impact and plan to approach government soon seeking exemption from the MDR. Like the petroleum dealers, the cooking gas distributors are expected to flag the impact of the charge citing the fixed, thin margins on which they operate.
While announcing the MDR framework, the NPCI said for specific merchant categories such as railways, telecom services, insurance and fuel, among others, a flat MDR of ₹5 per transaction will be applicable for transaction above ₹2,000. The fixed fee instead of a 0.4% variable rate, for the specified sectors, will prevent cost escalations in critical public services, utility bill collection and thin-margin sectors like fuel retail. It ensures essential consumer services remain low-cost and digitally efficient, NPCI had said.
