- Social media users alleged in September 2026 that U.S. truckers planned to strike over high fuel costs beginning on Oct. 1, leading to food and supply chain shortages.
- There was no evidence to support this unfounded rumor.
- Searches indicated the claim largely spread because of a video one social media user originally posted on Sept. 15. Other users then reposted his clip without first looking for credible evidence.
- A spokesperson for the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association said they had no knowledge of an upcoming strike. We also emailed the International Brotherhood of Teamsters and the man from the video, and will update this article if we receive more information.
In mid-September 2026, social media users alleged U.S. truckers had announced a plan to strike beginning on Oct. 1 to protest record-high diesel fuel costs of more than $6 a gallon. The posts claimed the stoppage of transportation would lead to nationwide food and supply chain shortages.
There was no evidence to support this unfounded rumor. Queries of DuckDuckGo, Google and other search engines found no news media outlets or other authoritative sources reporting about truckers planning to strike. Reddit's r/Truckers subreddit, a forum with hundreds of thousands of weekly visitors, featured a post with commenters saying they had heard nothing of a strike.
We emailed the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association to ask about this rumor. The organization's website says it has over 150,000 members in the U.S. and Canada operating more than 240,000 trucks and truck fleets. A spokesperson responded, "Our awareness is consistent with yours in that it seems to be social media chatter at this point in time."
We also emailed the International Brotherhood of Teamsters to ask about the rumor. The labor union has a freight division it says is made up of tens of thousands of Teamsters. We will update this article if we receive a response.
Where the unfounded rumor spread
Searches of social media websites indicated a video, first posted on Facebook (archived) and Instagram (archived) on Sept. 15, was potentially the most-popular content promoting the rumor. Users have since reposted the same video across platforms, including Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived) and X (archived). Others also generally shared the rumor of a trucker strike.
In the video, which ends with a request for users to buy paid subscriptions, a man tells viewers about the purported strike and subsequent food shortages:
In the trucking world, they put out a deal to strike until the fuel prices drop. Shut down Oct. 1. Park it. Stand together. Make their voices heard. Truckers are done.
You know what that means if they do that? Food shortages. Food's not getting to grocery stores. Nothing's getting anywhere.
What have I been telling you? Make sure you've got enough f***ing food for a month to three months, even six months. S***'s gonna hit the fan. S*** is hitting the fan, currently. And with this deal, this is huge.
A lot of people don't understand if trucks aren't moving, you're not getting anything. Grocery stores aren't getting a f***ing thing. Nobody's getting a thing. Just FYI.
That should probably freak you out a little bit because that happened basically during COVID. Remember when you couldn't find anything in the f***ing stores. This'll be a lot worse, if it comes to fruition. Just FYI. 
Please like, share, follow. Share my s***. Subscribe for a buck. 
We messaged the man in the video on Facebook and Instagram to ask for evidence, and will update this story if we receive more information.
A TikTok user's video (archived) also promoted the rumor with the caption "50,000 Truckers Threaten Strike: What It Means For America." In the video, the user claims, without evidence, that 50,000 truckers "are reportedly said to" no longer drive as of Oct. 1.
The unfounded rumor potentially originated out of a previous strike claim (archived) appearing to pertain to the dates of Oct. 1-10, 2025.
For further reading, we previously reported the truth of a story regarding truckers banding together to save someone from jumping off an overpass.

USA midfielder sues doctors after on-pitch cardiac arrest
- Published
United States women's national team player Savannah DeMelo is suing a hospital and two doctors after she suffered a cardiac arrest on the pitch last year.
Midfielder DeMelo, who has seven senior caps for the USA, has filed a lawsuit against University of Louisville Health (UofL Health) for negligence.
The 28-year-old, who plays for Racing Louisville, collapsed in the first half of a National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) match on 14 September 2025.
According to documents, external seen by BBC Sport, the case was filed on Tuesday morning with Jefferson Circuit Court in Kentucky, where her club is based - a year and a day after her on-field collapse.
DeMelo's filing claims UofL Health and two doctors, Dr Sarabjeet Suri and Dr Jennifer Daily, "failed to act as a reasonably prudent and competent medical practice, and such negligence was a substantial factor in causing DeMelo to suffer severe physical injuries, including, but not limited to, her cardiac arrest".
Dr Daily, according to her online UofL biography, external, is Racing Louisville's chief medical officer. The lawsuit states DeMelo was under the care of Dr Daily from January 2024 to July 2026.
It states that in March 2025, Dr Daily referred DeMelo to Dr Suri for "evaluation and treatment" after she had been complaining of chest pain, dizziness and shortness of air; Dr Suri obtained a history, performed a physical examination and ordered diagnostic tests.
Nearly six months later, DeMelo suffered the cardiac arrest.
"She was subsequently diagnosed and treated for ventricular tachycardia [an abnormal heart rhythm]," the suit states.
DeMelo, who has spent her entire professional career with Racing Louisville, has not played since her collapse.
In a post to her Instagram page, external on Tuesday, De Melo - who was picked in the USA squad for the 2023 Women's World Cup and started their first two games - marked the anniversary of the incident.
"A year ago today, while playing soccer, I collapsed due to an undiagnosed cardiac arrhythmia, that caused me to go into cardiac arrest," she wrote.
"I respect and appreciate the privacy everyone has met me with while going through everything I have this year. I'll never be able to fully put into words how emotionally hard this year has been. There has been a lot of uncertainty and emotions intertwined with it all."

Why dealing with defeat is key for Lampard at Coventry
- Published
Managing a newly-promoted team in the Premier League is very demanding, as Frank Lampard is finding out at Coventry.
It's the highest level, not just for the technical ability of the players that your team faces but also the sheer physicality that these players possess, and it feels like the gap to the Championship is getting greater every season.
From my experience in the same situation, you have to be really smart in the way you approach each game and recognise the importance of preparation for each specific opponent, because your team has to be organised in possession, and definitely out of possession.
Teams in the Premier League counter-attack with greater efficiency so being solid behind your own attacking play is absolutely vital.
But the real advice I would give to managers in Frank's shoes is to manage yourself, and your own time, as well as your players.
By that I mean you have to try to stay fresh and positive, because invariably you are going to go on bad runs of defeats like Coventry are on, which can drag your mood down.
Find a way of getting everyone back on track
I can tell you now that, whoever you are playing, if you get beaten - and especially beaten heavily like Coventry were by Brighton on Sunday - then it resonates with you. It's the same for every manager.
For Frank, whether it is losing at home to Hull or Brighton, or against Arsenal and Manchester City, then it will hurt.
But it is how he deals with those defeats that will decide what happens next.
Being the leader of a group of young men, you cannot look washed out and empty on a Monday morning after a heavy loss.
Yes, inside you will be hurting and your pride will be taking a bashing but everyone at the club will be waiting for your reaction, and will act accordingly.
Walking into the training ground in a dark mood and with your head around your backside just does not work, irrespective of what you are feeling inside.
I've been in that situation many times myself as a manager and what you have to do is puff your chest out and find a way of getting everyone back on track and working even harder with a set focus on the next game.
That's what all good leaders do. It is draining at times, but that is why managing your time and prioritising the issues that you can resolve is so important.
When I took Stoke up to the Premier League in 2008, I was learning on my feet.
We did not make a great start and I had to roll my sleeves up and get on with what I'd got in my squad, and really focus on getting results.
But away from that I was always forward thinking and I was quick at recognising what was needed to improve our chances of staying up.
When the window opened again in January, we were already in discussions with Tottenham for Matty Etherington, to supply us with crosses and chances from the wing.
We needed more goals too, so I took James Beattie from Sheffield United. They were a Championship side but that didn't matter because he had a record of scoring goals in the top flight.
We have heard so much about recruiting the right players in the right positions, and it is true today as it was in my day. Both lads played a significant role in keeping us up.
Coventry haven't scored a goal yet, and people might look in from the outside and feel the forward areas are an issue for them because the usual thinking is that the centre-forward has to lead the scoring charts, or a wide player or the number 10.
But the emphasis is on everyone to chip in and I would also reinforce one of the points I made in this column last season, about the importance of defending properly too.
On average, clean sheets earn you more points than scoring a goal, which is something I always stressed to my players. Nailing down the importance of both ends of the pitch is the narrative, whatever kind of run of results you are on, because games are won and lost there.
Why I was confident Stoke would stay up
Coventry have made a poor start but what has happened in their first four games does not have to become the story of their whole season.
With Stoke, we got a win in our first home game - against Aston Villa - but that was our only victory in our first seven league matches after getting promoted.
The thing I remember most from that time is that Hull had come up with us and, after seven games, they had won at Newcastle, Arsenal and Tottenham and were in the top five in the table, while we were third or fourth from bottom.
I went out for dinner with my chairman, Peter Coates, and he said how Hull had made a wonderful start. I replied by telling him I bet you now that we finish above Hull... and we did.
The reason I thought that was because of the mindset of the team, and the fans.
I was confident my players were not going to go weak at the knees, and the togetherness we needed was already there in the squad, while the support was just off the scales, which helped us enormously at home.
Every defeat was taken on the chin, and accepted, but the lads were always ready to go, again and again.
Survival is success for every promoted team
It was Steve Coppell who said to me how you have to deal with the fact you are going to lose a lot of games - or at least not win a lot of them - when you take a team up into the Premier League.
It is a very unusual situation, to go from being in the Championship and winning regularly week after week, to dealing with defeat after defeat.
Steve told me to get ready for going on runs where we would not win for five or six games on the bounce, but then if we could win two or three games in the same period after that, we would fly up the table.
But getting your head around that is hard, and it is the same for the players who were part of that promotion - especially if you were dominant like Coventry were last season.
They were expected to challenge at the top of the Championship, but in my opinion over-achieved by finishing clear at the top.
It was different for Hull, who achieved a promotion under Sergej Jakirovic that no-one outside that club believed was possible.
They have started the season on fire, just like the Tigers did in 2008 when Phil Brown was in charge, and now they have to try to sustain it.
They are third at the moment but if they are 17th come the end of May, which is where they finished under Brownie, then that will be a successful season.
I will be taking a closer look at Hull's progress in this column in the weeks to come, as well as the other promoted team, Ipswich.
Gary O'Neil has a really tough gig at Portman Road but it is one he will relish. I gave Gary his senior debut with Portsmouth in the Championship in 1999 and he's a smart lad who was always football mad.
Ipswich are a great club and I hope both are successful this season. Gary has experience of the Premier League with Bournemouth and Wolves, and he is going to need it.
New season, nine new managers - which appointments make sense?
Including O'Neil, there are nine new managers starting with clubs in the Premier League. It's a bigger number than usual and I wanted to quickly run through all of them.
Enzo Maresca at Manchester City seemed like common sense to me, even before they started the season with four league wins out of four, because he has worked with Pep and the club before.
City had a large turnover of players with their ins and outs over the summer, but I'd expect them to be in the mix for all the trophies again this season.
Another place where lots of changes have taken place is Stamford Bridge. Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has experience of playing in England and will understand that no game in the Premier League is a shoe-in - as Saturday's draw with Hull showed us again.
Andoni Iraola did an amazing job at Bournemouth but he will need all of his managerial ability and acumen to succeed at Liverpool.
At Liverpool, teams will drop deep and rely on counter-attacking situations. At Bournemouth that did not happen very often.
So, Andoni has to prepare his coaching philosophy to overcome teams who will definitely play deeper and be much more defensive-minded against Liverpool than they were against Bournemouth.
In my opinion, given time he will a great success but as he prepares to take his new team back to face his old one at Vitality Stadium on Sunday, we are already seeing that Liverpool will need more changes to develop into the title-winning side that their fantastic supporters demand.
At Nottingham Forest, Oliver Glasner did a wonderful job at Palace and I am sure we will see more of the same at the City Ground.
At the moment I know less about Marco Rose, Matthias Jaissle, and Pierre Sage, at Bournemouth, Newcastle and Crystal Palace.
Unlike the other managers I have mentioned, they have no experience of the Premier League but they are all joining established top-flight sides which is a huge help.
Finally, there is Alvaro Arbeloa at Fulham. He had a fantastic playing record at Real Madrid and Liverpool and coached in the Real Madrid academy and their B team before taking charge of the first team for the second half of last season.
While he has not had much experience in the dugout, he has worked with many top managers and players.
Fulham will be a real test for him, as we've seen from the way they have started the season, so again they are a club I will be keeping a close eye on - but there are plenty of those!

US Rep. Darrell Issa (R-Calif.) has proposed a law that would require Internet service providers and other network operators to block foreign piracy websites. Issa’s bill would help copyright holders obtain judicial blocking orders to be served to ISPs, domain name resolution services, and virtual private networks.
Issa, who is retiring from the House at the end of this year, is the latest in a string of Republican and Democratic lawmakers to propose a site-blocking regime that’s been sought by the Motion Picture Association (MPA). He submitted the bill this week, after indicating in a June 30 hearing that he planned to introduce site-blocking legislation.
“While millions of listings for copyright-infringing content are removed every day under [the] notice-and-takedown process set forth in the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, right-holders have raised concerns with the speed,” Issa said at the hearing. Issa asked, “Can we do it at the speed of sound? Can we do it at the speed of light? More importantly, in a 45-minute or sometimes a fraction of that live sports broadcast, can we do it soon enough to make it no longer profitable for those who pop up and sell their clandestine wares?”
Issa argued that online piracy helps fund terrorist groups and other criminal networks. Advocacy groups opposing his bill say it would impose a broad censorship regime and disrupt small businesses falsely accused of piracy.
“Rather than attacking the problem at its source by bringing the people running overseas piracy websites to court, Congress and its entertainment industry allies have decided to build out a sweeping infrastructure for censorship,” said Meredith Rose, senior policy counsel at Public Knowledge. “Site-blocking orders force any service provider, from residential broadband providers to global DNS resolvers, to disrupt traffic from targeted websites simply accused of copyright infringement.”

College Is Coming Apart
Successive, overlapping crises reveal that American higher education makes no sense.
Sign up for Ordinary Extraordinary, Ian Bogost’s newsletter on making everyday life vivid.
Artificial intelligence arrived on campus as a crisis but has since become banal. Students can now do basically all their schoolwork automatically with AI—answering scientific problem sets, writing computer code, and drafting essays. Professors like me have no idea whether we are really teaching or just LARPing for students who are also pretending to occupy their role. Worse, some of us are offloading the drudgery of writing recommendation letters, grant proposals, and even scientific papers to AI.
But at the same time that AI fouled up the student-teacher relationship, the technology benefited other corners of campus. Researchers quickly discovered that AI is enormously useful for knowledge production, especially in the natural and applied sciences: in protein-structure prediction, materials design, and drug discovery, for example. Pressured, in part, by donors, boards, employers, and parents, college administrators have announced AI initiatives, invested in AI infrastructure, and established AI degree programs.
These two forces—students using AI to their detriment and colleges using it to their benefit—might seem to be in conflict. Students are supposed to do everything longhand to preserve the sanctity of learning, but they are also urged to meet the new professional demands created by AI. Faculty and administrators are policing the classroom for AI, largely in vain, while also using AI liberally in their own work. Campuses are defending themselves against AI as an interloper while concurrently retooling themselves for the AI future. Colleges are racing toward and away from AI simultaneously. It feels like artificial intelligence is wresting higher education apart.
That’s what I thought at first too. But I’ve come to the conclusion that something bigger, stranger, and more damaging has been taking place for a long time. AI has combined with two other recent campus crises—the coronavirus pandemic and the research-funding cuts of the second Trump administration—to amplify a deeper truth: American college is incompatible with itself. Americans speak of “college” as if it is one coherent thing. That’s wrong. Higher education is a bundle of unrelated things held together by custom, history, and accident. The college bundle was always a tenuous one. It has little reason to remain together, even as the institutions inside it are too entrenched to separate.
College in America makes two promises. On the one hand, college is a credentialing service: It awards a degree that affirms knowledge and sends a graduate into a career. On the other hand, college is a coming-of-age service. It forms identity through social exploration and intellectual development. It is the American ideal for how a young person figures out who they are. Partying, drinking, Greek life, sports, and other forms of college life always risked undermining the educational project—and vice versa. But the two categories coexisted well enough.
Now two things that got packaged together as “college” have begun to unbundle and disperse. The coming-of-age experience—friendships, independence, experimentation—has become less obviously dependent on the campus surrounding it, partly because college’s monopoly on exposure to a wider world weakened. Globalization and the internet bring much of that world to students long before they arrive on campus. Other aspects of college life have been moving off campus too. College football has gone national, abandoning regional affinities and local rivalries. Greek rush has become an outsourced industry. Campuses are hospital systems, major local employers, and real-estate-investment operations as much as, or more than, they are schools.
Optimizing college for professional preparation also began to pull the two purposes apart, and eroded the unrepeatable social experience that college is supposed to provide. The economy demanded more of students outside the classroom—internships, networking, publications, volunteering. In a brutal job-search environment, where entry-level gigs seem to demand nepotism, luck, and 10 rounds of interviews, today’s undergraduates may feel that their older professors do not fully understand the gap between the delivery of the credential and the career it promises.
Then COVID-19 revealed that the credentialing process could continue if campus life was reduced or even eliminated entirely. Considerable controversy and confusion accompanied this moment; some students tried to sue expensive universities on the grounds that a closed campus was not worth the full-freight price. But in the end, credentialing proved entirely possible with a compromised or absent version of campus life.
Now AI has separated the two purposes of college almost entirely. Writing an essay previously required doing something resembling the assigned academic work. Because AI makes it possible to complete coursework without much or any intellectual labor, AI has disconnected the output from the process (if students choose the shortcut). Suffering through a term paper no longer inherently affords opportunities to take a break to get a late-night coffee with your fellow students, to commiserate with hallmates over a difficult professor, or to reach an unexpected realization while drunk at a house party. Social and academic progress are no longer woven together. No particular quantity of shared time or deliberation is required to carry out one inside the other.
A combination of factors (among them shifting values, educational entrepreneurship, regulatory arbitrage, and the speed of technological change) has altered the meaning of a diploma. Yet schools have had no trouble continuing to award degrees to the students who spent their whole undergraduate careers on campuses that tout the same traditional look on quads and inside libraries, but that AI has hopelessly mangled beneath the surface.
Immediately after taking office, the second Trump administration embarked on a series of attacks against higher education. The attacks were politically motivated, but they were effective because they hit campuses where it hurt. Since World War II, the American research-university sector has become defined as an enormous, distributed, scientific-research industry. The Trump attacks undermined this project by disrupting the tens of billions of dollars of federal funding that pays for that research (which includes graduate education).
At the same moment that AI was widening the conflict between credentialing and coming of age, the Trump cuts exposed a different structural incompatibility, between education and research. The fact that big universities were driven by research was not a secret, but it was also not well understood by the American public, including parents and students. If you find out that a friend or neighbor is a university professor, you’d probably ask them, “What do you teach?” And if they squirm when asked, that’s because many faculty often do not see teaching as their primary job. Yes, a professor is expected to teach undergraduates and produce research, because a university’s mission entails education and scholarship. But national universities do not value or reward those activities equally.
Research brings grants, prestige, graduate students, rankings, and career advancement. At research universities, undergraduate teaching is seen, if not described, as a necessary act to keep the tuition dollars flowing and to maintain the appearance of undergraduate education as predominant—the thing that people think of first when they imagine what college is for.
University administrators often argue that the research and teaching missions bolster each other: A star researcher, the story goes, can bring the latest knowledge to the classroom. Basically every college tour on an American campus will include a schtick about how undergraduates can participate in faculty research. Universities have a strong incentive to make research and teaching appear to align. But in truth, those purposes sit more in tension than in unity.
A revealing term helps explain how tenuous this relationship really is. A researcher who gets a big grant can use part of those funds for a “teaching buyout,” paying their way out of the classroom. Success at one of the university’s missions literally purchases relief from the other. (There is no research buyout.)
Campuses such as mine, Washington University in St. Louis, take in $1 billion or more of research funding every year. That money pays for the work done in labs, but also for equipment, buildings, and staff. It forms the foundation for the metrics (grants won, and “research expenditures,” or money spent from those grants) that campuses use to compete against one another for faculty, graduate students, philanthropic gifts, and other forms of prestige. Threaten the flow of research money and you don’t merely endanger the labs; you destabilize the financial and organizational structure of the whole sector.
Every major college and university touts the liberal arts as the core of an undergraduate education, but the humanities in particular—fields of arts and letters such as literature and languages, which generally do not receive much, if any, federal research funding—enjoy mostly vestigial value that does not match the underlying economics of higher education very well. Universities are different from colleges in this regard. Small liberal-arts colleges focus almost exclusively on undergraduate education and are earnestly committed to the arts and letters. That’s one reason they are particularly well positioned to weather the Trump attacks. But these schools serve much smaller populations, and they are still tied to the broader American university system, from which they draw faculty and to which they send students on to grad school. And even at these schools, the humanities are particularly vulnerable to AI, because the intellectual labor that the technology can now eliminate—wrestling with the meaning of texts, figuring out how to express complex ideas—is the fundamental point of that type of education.
The AI crisis on campus, mated to the COVID-19 and federal-funding crises that flanked it, dismantled the pretense that everything happening on campus shared any kind of common project. AI might substantially improve scientific research while destroying the humanities. And AI might troublingly reduce the effort a student must exert to complete a degree while allowing a scientist to carry out experiments with reduced labor, uncontroversially.
Undergraduate education, credentialing, scientific research, professionalization, and coming of age still occupy the same campuses. But they are clearly no longer parts of the same enterprise. They have not been so for many years—probably many decades. Looking back at my own career, I can see clearly that every single term of it has taken place in the shadow of this family of mismatches. Teaching and research sometimes align, but not always. Becoming educated has little to do with becoming an adult, apart from taking place on the same campus. I used to understand a university as akin to a city—expansive, diverse, and necessarily host to multiple purposes. But now I wonder if even that generous account is a fantasy. I wonder if one organization can support all of these conflicting projects well—and if it ever did.
Now that these incompatibilities are harder to ignore, will the American collegiate project reinvent itself in a way that would resolve them? Perhaps, but also: I doubt it. Universities are purpose-built to resist change of almost any kind. College leaders have repeatedly adopted a “wait and see” or “keep our heads down” approach, treating disruption as mere interruption: The pandemic ended, AI will settle down, federal funding will resume, and all of this, whatever it is, will blow over. These are far more tolerable conclusions to reach than, say, the idea that credentialing has no business sharing a venue with coming of age, or that undergraduate education is at odds with the mission of a research institution.
Each recent crisis gave college an alibi. AI was an alien technology that corrupted an otherwise functional educational institution. The Trump funding cuts were an aberrant political attack on a healthy research enterprise. COVID-19 was an emergency that forced campuses to suspend campus life and education alike in the interest of public health. But surviving any one of these crises, let alone all of them together, changes nothing about the underlying circumstances that they exacerbated. The incompatible purposes of college carry on.
I see no reason to believe that the structural inconsistencies that have come to define higher education will resolve. The degree will become ever more a goal and less a process of self-discovery. The research and teaching missions will further retract from each other. College is at war with itself as much as it is with the public, or the government, or the private sector, or the technology industry.
As a degree or a ritual, college will continue to have value, and you or your kids may want to attend one for a credential or a coming-of-age experience (or both). The old names will persist, and the campus buildings will still stand. The coursework will continue whether humans or machines complete it (or assign it). The leaves will fall onto the quad in the autumn, and the caps will fly into the air in the spring. The appearance of college can endure, even as its spirit—a community organized for the education and formation of young people—comes undone.

Nandan Nilekani-led panel on NEET reforms to submit first report by month-end: Centre to SC
New Delhi, The Centre on Friday told the Supreme Court that the Nandan Nilekani-led high-powered panel constituted to suggest structural reforms in NEET has held exhaustive consultations and is likely to submit its first interim report by the end of this month.
Solicitor General Tushar Mehta told a bench of Justices P S Narasimha and Alok Aradhe that all the suggestions had been placed before the panel, which held consultations with the members of an earlier committee led by former ISRO chairman K Radhakrishnan.
The bench asked the joint secretary to the Department of Personnel and Training , who is assisting the Nilekani panel, to file an affidavit before the court on the steps taken so far.
It told Mehta that the most important thing in the matter is that the government should look into institutionalisation of the entire process to conduct the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test .
"You must know that permanency of the entire system is key. There should be a permanent setup, permanent staff, permanent verticals. Very less deputation should be there. Only then a permanent structure will come up," the bench told Mehta.
Justice Narasimha said he and Justice Aradhe would like to visit the newly-upgraded facility of the National Testing Agency to examine the system.
The education department has said that a new, upgraded system has been created.
"Permanency of the structure has been ensured. However, human resources are partially ensured at the moment," Mehta said.
On August 19, observing that there is a need to institutionalise the reforms in the NTA, the top court directed the Centre to inform it about the steps taken to implement the recommendations of the Radhakrishnan panel and the Nilekani committee.
The apex court was hearing a batch of petitions, including one filed by advocate Tanvi Dubey on behalf of the Federation of All India Medical Association .

Healthtech startup Practo has overhauled its top leadership, appointing former COO Jagnoor Singh as CEO, while cofounder and former CEO Shashank ND Singh has moved to the expanded role of MD and executive chairman. Singh’s appointment took effect on September 1. He will lead Practo’s overall strategy, growth, and operations across its global markets, the startup said in a statement. Meanwhile, Shashank will focus on Practo’s long-term vision, product and strategy, innovation agenda, capital strategy, inorganic growth, and corporate development initiatives. Singh joined Practo as COO in January 2025 and has since worked on its growth strategy, operational execution, and entry into new markets. Before joining Practo, he held senior positions at Bharti Airtel, Unacademy, and OYO. Practo has also expanded the responsibilities of three senior executives as part of the leadership reshuffle. Cofounder Siddhartha Nihalani has taken on the additional responsibility of COO – B2C and will oversee Practo’s consumer businesses. Rowel Coelho, previously its head of monetisation, has been appointed COO – B2B and will lead the soonicorn’s enterprise and corporate businesses. Meanwhile, cofounder Abhinav Lal has been named chief scientist. In the research-focused role, he will lead Practo’s exploration of AI applications in healthcare, build research partnerships, and develop an innovation hub focused on emerging technologies. Practo’s IPO Preparations The leadership changes come as Practo steps up its international expansion and prepares for a proposed public listing. Earlier this year, the startup appointed former Union health secretary CK Mishra as an independent director as part of efforts to strengthen its board. Inc42 previously reported that Practo was in advanced discussions to raise $100 Mn to $125 Mn in a pre-IPO funding round at a post-money valuation of around $700 Mn. The startup is reportedly targeting a public listing in 2027. Practo claimed that it is currently growing at 40% YoY and has remained profitable for the past two-and-a-half years. The startup turned EBITDA profitable in FY25, reporting an operating EBITDA of ₹15 Cr on revenue of ₹234 Cr. This marked a turnaround from FY24, when it posted an EBITDA loss of ₹17 Cr on revenue of ₹240 Cr. Founded in 2008 by Shashank and Lal, Practo operates a digital healthcare platform that allows patients to find doctors, book appointments, consult physicians online, order medicines, and schedule diagnostic tests. It also offers practice management software for doctors, clinics, and hospitals, and operates 40 co-branded dermatology clinics across India. Its platform connects patients with more than 7 Lakh doctors and healthcare providers across over 2,400 cities globally. Practo also operates Insta, a hospital information management system used by more than 500 clients across over 1,200 facilities. Besides India, Practo has expanded into the US and the UAE. It entered the UAE last year and launched a pilot in the US, where it claims to have onboarded more than 2 Lakh doctors and built an annual GMV run rate of over $75 Mn. It has raised a total funding of about $230 Mn to date from investors like Peak XV Partners, Sofina, Thrive Capital, and Capital G. The leadership reshuffle also comes months after Shashank launched preventive healthcare startup Cent alongside former Ola CMO Anshul Khandelwal and sales executive Arpit Garg. Cent raised $5 Mn in seed funding from OneFlow Holdings, Shashank’s family office, and South Park Commons.

But the head coach was especially forthright in the away dressing room at Elland Road on Monday.
It was a night the visitors suffered a chastening 4-1 defeat against Leeds United.
"There was all clarity in the room that the learning curve needs to be really fast," Jaissle said a few days on.
Even during the course of a previous five-game unbeaten run, there was a recognition within the club that this was "always going to be a work in progress" following a summer of huge change.
Newcastle have gone from having one of the most experienced starting line-ups in the Premier League last season to the second-youngest this time around.
Yet the manner of Newcastle's first loss of the campaign still came as a jolt.
It already feels like much will be learned from how Jaissle's team respond against in-form Hull City on Saturday.
"If you're tougher in the duels, if you're more aggressive, if you're more sharp and hungry to collect the second balls, then it will be automatically a huge step already," he said.
"That means that you're more dominant, that you have more possession, and then that leads also to the fact that you threaten the opposition much more.
"So they will be the elements where we will focus on and there will be a reaction."
A bruising night at Elland Road
Jaissle was parachuted into the hot seat just three weeks before the start of the season after predecessor Eddie Howe stepped down.
He is still adapting to the Premier League and injuries to, among others, Dan Burn, Joelinton, Anthony Elanga and William Osula have hardly helped in that regard.
That being said, no team have faced more shots (76) in the opening weeks of the season in the top flight, while at the other end Newcastle have been averaging little more than three efforts on target per game in the league.
The visitors struggled to gain a foothold against an aggressive Leeds side, even before influential midfielder Nico Gonzalez went off with a concussion in the 19th minute.
Vertical football is Jaissle's trademark, in an effort to "stress" the opposition, but too often Newcastle's main tactic appeared to be punting the ball forward for Yoane Wissa and Matias Fernandez-Pardo to chase hopefully at Elland Road.
Leeds' three towering centre-backs outnumbered the pair and Newcastle were also swarmed in midfield after Jaissle stuck with his preferred two-man pivot.
However exposed Jaissle's system was, though, that does not excuse those on the field failing to do the basics from the off against one of the most physical sides in the league.
Meek Newcastle lost 56% of their duels in the first half against Leeds and defenders Malick Thiaw and Sven Botman were bullied by Dominic Calvert-Lewin, who scored twice.
A warning had previously been sounded when Newcastle failed to match Bournemouth's intensity and found themselves 2-0 down after just 35 minutes earlier this month.
Jaissle's team showed admirable grit and spirit to come back and draw that game at St James' Park, but a similar response was never on the cards in West Yorkshire.
No wonder one or two Newcastle players threw out their palms apologetically as they trudged over to the away end at full-time.
'He's still in a phase of figuring things out'
Jaissle repeatedly stressed his "fundamentals" - being physical, intense and competitive in duels - were "non-negotiable" and how his players needed to take losing a duel personally.
He spent the bus journey home digging into the detail behind the defeat with his analysts.
However, just as Jaissle has not allowed himself to get too high following positive results, he has not tended to emotionally rip up the foundations after a setback, either, as former Red Bull Salzburg midfielder Zlatko Junuzovic explained.
"They analysed the situation and, where necessary, made one or two adjustments, but nothing drastic," he said of his approach to defeats during their time in Austria.
"I think he's still in a phase of figuring things out [at Newcastle], where he has to see for himself which players fit his system and which ones don't."
Jaissle, 38, may still be a relatively young manager but he has experience to fall back on in that regard.
It was a different level, a different sort of capitulation and a different squad, but Jaissle also suffered a bruising away defeat at a similar point of his reign at Al-Ahli after the Saudi Pro League side were hammered 5-1 by Al-Fateh in 2023.
Could that difficult night in Leeds prove a similarly valuable learning experience or will this campaign be characterised by further ups and downs?
"We don't search for excuses, even with a young squad," Jaissle said. "We need to learn fast."

US to allow Iran delegation to attend UN meetings in New York as war passes half-year mark
- Published
The US government has granted visas to Iranian officials so they can travel to the UN General Assembly in New York next week, as the war between the two countries grinds into its seventh month.
The BBC understands the core delegation permitted to attend includes Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
A spokesman for the US State Department confirmed the decision on Thursday, saying that the delegation will be placed under travel restrictions and will be banned from purchasing certain American products.
The move comes as the war shows no sign of ending. Since it began in February, it has driven up global energy prices, and expanded into neighbouring countries.
"Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level Week," a spokesman for the US State Department told the BBC.
"The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy. The delegation is smaller than last year."
Last year, diplomats attending from Iran were banned from shopping at wholesale stores like Costco. They also were required to seek permission from the US before purchasing luxury goods, including jewellery, alcohol and cars.
The 81st session of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) is currently underway. The General Debate - the centrepiece of the annual event - is due to begin on Tuesday.
Tuesday will include speeches from US President Donald Trump, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, and France President Emmanuel Macron.
Wednesday is expected to see speeches from the leaders of Ukraine, Syria and Iran.
Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country.
Since the war began, Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel.
The BBC recently learned that the US denied a visa to Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and the Palestinian delegation to attend UNGA.
The White House, which does not recognise the legitimacy of the Palestinian delegation, denied them visas for a second year in a row.

SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for the two-hour series premiere of NBC’s “The Traitors: New Blood,” now streaming on Peacock.
“The Traitors” castle isn’t just for the rich and famous anymore. Peacock’s Emmy-winning franchise has arrived on NBC, with “The Traitors: New Blood,” a new season composed entirely of civilian players in the game of murder, mayhem and more money than ever before.
In the show’s two-hour series premiere, host Alan Cumming welcomed 22 appropriately bloodthirsty competitors to his Scottish castle and immediately threw them into the deep end of the loch. Because of the show’s international popularity, the players walked into the castle knowing exactly where to go and what to investigate. Feeling right at home with the game is exactly what the creative team wanted.
“To have a sense of familiarity meant they felt comfortable in their surroundings and they played hard straight away,” executive producer Sam Rees-Jones tells Variety of the premiere.
At the first roundtable, with a sly tap on the shoulder, Cumming chose Tomica Adams (a pilot from Boston, MA) and Joe Vanella (a funeral director from Wantagh, New York) as his first Traitors of the season. But during their midnight confab in the turret, he informed them a third Traitor was incoming, and that they had to pick the person. In addition to their first murder (RIP faux college basketball coach and real lawyer Kim Daily), the Traitors chose two “accomplices” to audition to become their fellow chaos agent.
Katie Fites (a marketing manager from Jacksonville, Florida, and the youngest player at 23) and Xavier Scruggs (former MLB player turned analyst) got to work scheming and stirring the pot against each other to claw their way to the turret. But the ultimate test came in the second hour when they were directed to deceive the Faithfuls in plain sight by stealing a cleverly titled book on crime and punishment and delivering it to the Traitors. The premiere leaves audiences hanging on whether they manage to smuggle the book out without the Faithful seeing it..
What is for sure is that the blood of the Faithfuls has already been spilled. In addition to Daily’s murder, a tense first roundtable saw Mississippi realtor Kriste Lewis go for the jugular on San Diego construction manager Madeline Kostopulos over a throwaway comment she believed proved she was one of the cloaked killers. Caught in the crossfire was Kostopulos’ ally and resident eye candy, New York business executive Victor Vollbrechthausen, who took heat for immediately snagging a shield of protection in the first challenge. The pair nearly split the vote evenly.
Popular on Variety
Below, “The Traitors: New Blood” executive producers Rosie Franks, Mike Cotton and Rees-Jones go deep on slimming down their hit for broadcast, why they incentivized identifying Traitors for the first time and how including an all-civilian cast makes the game so much more personal.
Being on broadcast means these episodes run for about 41-42 minutes, along with the commercial breaks. That’s very different from the Peacock episodes, which often exceed an hour. How does the time constraint change the storytelling and the rhythm of the show?
Mike Cotton: I would say that was one of our biggest challenges. In truth, the game is the game. We call it a game, but there’s always a cycle. It’s a day in the castle. There’s always breakfast, someone gets murdered, there’s the mission, there’s a roundtable, and the Traitors meet in the turret. We haven’t changed that, in terms of how they played the game. But we had to look at different places where we could create cliffhangers, and so we put quite a lot of thought and work into that before we started shooting to make sure that the audiences still got what “The Traitors” was. We always say we’re like a murder mystery, but we treated it a bit like a drama. Where’s a good place for a cliffhanger? We actually put quite a lot of planning in our pre-production to work out those different points that could cliffhanger the episodes. One thing we didn’t want to do is cut it like it’s a drama. We didn’t want to make the episodes faster or fit everything into a short amount of time. We still wanted to breathe and be able to explore the characters, and I feel like we’ve achieved it.
You’re at a disadvantage this season where you don’t have the backstory of celebrities to help you prep. In the premiere, we see one of the competitors holding a card that asks their preference to play as a Traitor or Faithful. Is that something you’ve always done, or is that new reconnaissance this season?
Sam Rees-Jones: No, that was something new for the civilians. What we loved about this version was Alan inviting these players. He sent out these invitations, so it should feel like these players are actually being invited to this crazy experience in the Highlands of Scotland. And within that invitation was whether they wanted to be a Traitor or a Faithful.
Rosie Franks: Alan always asks them in the “gold chats” by the fire in the premiere what role they want to play in the game. But this just felt like a really nice throughline from the opening of the raven flying across America, dropping the invitations, and this is like their RSVP.
Rees-Jones: We pick Traitors only if they want to become a Traitor, because it’s a hard job. There’s a lot to do, so they should want to become a Traitor. But what we always say to everyone is that once you enter the game, you could be made a Traitor at any point. As you can see at the end of Episode 1, we picked our original two Traitors, and then we left it in their hands who they were going to pick as the third one and that was Katie and Xavier.
Cotton: You’re right, though. It’s more difficult working out who those initial Traitors should be when they’re a cast of regular people who we don’t have a history with on a reality show or on television. That then comes down to casting, and really digging into who these people are and the characters that they are. We don’t decide who the Traitors are until everyone’s arrived at the castle. So they’ve been on the train, and we’ve seen them interact. They’ve all sat down with Alan and had quite in-depth chats with him about whether they want to be a Traitor or not.
That uncertainty extends to the cast’s hunt for Traitors as well. The celebrities often have pre-existing relationships and feuds that can guide accusations. But in this premiere, the cast is largely at a loss on who to target at the first roundtable.
Franks: What’s so exciting is that they all come in with a completely clean slate. It’s a game about identity, and they can basically be whoever they want. But we’re watching them get to know each other, and we’re getting to know them at the same time. So it’s a level playing field for the viewers and the players, which is really exciting to watch. You feel very much like you’re part of the process.
One of the biggest differences between the celebrity and civilian editions is the impact of the money. Watching celebrities play challenges for money doesn’t quite have the same thrill because, depending on their personal wealth and situation, $250,000 may be life changing or it may be a drop in the bucket. But for the “New Blood” cast, it is different. Mark Zgoda makes a comment after the first challenge, where they add $50,000 to the prize pot: “That’s a full person’s salary already added to the pot.” This money will simply mean more for these players. How does that change the game play?
Rees-Jones: We love that moment, and I’m glad you mentioned it. That perfectly summarized all of their approaches to the game, to the challenges, to the missions, and yeah, the money means so much to them. As far as the game is concerned, what it means is that they all have to work together really hard to build that prize pot. But ultimately, that also means that betrayal cuts even deeper. Because the whole game is built around the Faithfuls and the Traitors coming together to put up that prize pot, which in one mission can be as much as the person’s yearly salary, then when treachery happens, it hurts even more. But to see the missions play out and to see them throw themselves into it, whatever their age or physical ability, was amazing. You see what it meant to them at the end of Episode 1 when they win a huge amount of money.
Alan also reveals in the premiere that, for the first time, each Traitor banished from the castle will earn a $15,000 bonus for the prize pot. Is that in addition to the possible $250,000 they can raise?
Rees-Jones: It’s in addition to the $250,000. We’ve talked about it for a while. Obviously, the most important thing is to get a Traitor out. But we felt there was something really interesting in that added incentive.
That could make the difference between speaking up or staying quiet at the roundtable if you know there is more money on the line.
Franks: Exactly!
In the premiere, as soon as they arrive in the castle, you let them roam free. But after several seasons of this show, this cast has been watching at home and they clearly know the place. A few even knew which book to pull to open the secret room in the library. Does that much familiarity with the castle pose any issues?
Cotton: I love that they knew the castle! The castle is a real place. It’s not like it’s a “Big Brother” house that’s reconstructed every year. So I think we all love the fact they felt at home immediately in there, and that they knew the game and they knew the rhythm of it. Every year is a different murder mystery, so we put a lot of plans in place to keep the players on their toes. But we never change the core game of Traitors versus Faithfuls. It will never change the overall rhythm of the game, but we always, every season, put in new twists and turns just to keep them guessing even if they think they know it and the castle.
Rees-Jones: I think it actually really helped this cast. To have a sense of familiarity meant they felt comfortable in their surroundings and they played hard straight away.
James and Oliver Phelps are here! Fred and George Weasley from the “Harry Potter” movies are seen being mischievous in the premiere. What can you tease about their role this season?
Rees-Jones: That is their role! They’re mischievous, mysterious castle creepers.
What a job title to have.
Rees-Jones: Yeah, it was just a fun tongue-in-cheek extension of the murder mystery world. You have Alan’s castle, and you would imagine in that world there would be people that are keepers of the castle. So there’s some fun to be had with little scenes that can be peppered throughout the season.
Cotton: One of the things I’m most excited about with the NBC version is that we have a chance to expand this world to a broader audience. In the U.K., the show has become a massive shared viewing experience, like a family hit. People gather with their children to watch the show. Although it’s about betrayal and murder, there’s also elements of “Harry Potter” and magical fantasy within the show as well. So I feel like who [James and Oliver] are, and that world they’re from, sort of ties in neatly with the world of “The Traitors” too.
In the first challenge, there is a decoy crate filled with salmon. Was this an acknowledgement that there is apparently not enough salmon in Scotland for your previous casts, who protested the lack of smoked salmon at breakfast before?
Franks: It’s always about the salmon!
It’s hard not to make that connection given how much your last celebrities talked about it!
Franks: Yes, we do like putting in little Easter eggs like that for the fans.
In previous seasons, the music in the show has been appropriately moody but generic. “New Blood” has covers of real songs, including Justin Timberlake’s “Cry Me a River” at a particularly sinister moment. Was this something new available to you on broadcast?
Franks: That was one of the things we were so excited about in terms of making the show feel familiar but also fresh, that we were going to be able to use some commercial music in this version. I don’t know how you felt watching it, but I feel like there’s tonally a shift in the way that it feels and I think the commercial music definitely helps with that.
You don’t often speak about why you chose the Traitors, but you did let them choose two accomplices to audition for the third Traitor slot. We don’t yet see who wins, but what did you think about their two choices, Katie and Xavier?
Cotton: I love that the Traitors chose Katie and Xavier, because they chose almost completely opposite people.
The height difference alone! You can barely get them both in the same camera frame.
Cotton: Right! They are so different that it was surprising and really thrilling for us when it happened.
Should we be worried that, physically, the book they have to steal is almost as big as Katie? Seems like it might be hard for her to sneak away with it!
Cotton:You’ll have to wait and see what happens!

Thousands of patients in India are diagnosed with melanoma, a type of skin cancer, each year. While melanoma is far less common here than in Western populations, it is far from rare and the way it presents in our patient population makes it uniquely difficult to detect early. Too many patients come to us when the disease is already advanced, precisely at a time when treatment options have never been more powerful or more personalised. This contrast between available therapies and the stage at which patients are diagnosed defines one of the most pressing challenges in melanoma care in India today.
Why melanoma gets missed
The warning signs most people associate with skin cancer come from research developed for fairer-skinned populations, where melanoma tends to appear on sun-exposed areas as an irregular or darkening mole. That picture does not reflect what clinicians see in India.
Melanoma here, most commonly presents on the soles of the feet or beneath the nails, sites that are rarely examined and even more rarely associated with cancer. This condition is called acral lentiginous melanoma, a subtype that accounts for 35 to 60% of cases in dark-skinned individuals. Such lesions are frequently mistaken for bruises, fungal infections, or diabetic ulcers, and by the time a biopsy is taken, the disease has often progressed.
Mucosal melanomas, a rare type of cancer that starts in the mucous membranes, are highly aggressive with a very low chance of recovery and produce few early warning signs. Most are diagnosed only after spread has occurred.
Any pigmented lesion that changes or persists, wherever it appears on the body, deserves investigation rather than reassurance.
A decade of transformation
When I began my oncology career, managing advanced melanoma meant offering patients limited and rarely durable options. That has fortunately changed significantly.
The foundational shift came from James Allison and Tasuku Honjo, whose discoveries on CTLA-4 and PD-1 earned them the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Their research established the principle of immune-checkpoint blockade: rather than attacking a tumour directly, we can sometimes release the biological brakes that stop the patient’s own immune system from doing so. The results can be extraordinary. Former U.S. President Jimmy Carter was diagnosed at 91 with melanoma that had spread to his liver and brain. Surgical resection of liver disease, stereotactic radiation for the brain, and immunotherapy with the checkpoint inhibitor pembrolizumab produced a durable remission, and he lived to 100.
Precision medicine has reshaped the approach in parallel. Some melanomas carry specific mutations, particularly in the BRAF pathway, that can be directly targeted with molecularly designed therapies. This is where next-generation sequencing, or NGS, becomes critical. In simple terms, it reads the genetic blueprint of a patient’s tumour and identifies the alterations that should guide treatment, turning what was once a single clinical decision into a detailed, individualised process.
The melanoma story is not over; it is only becoming more exciting. TIL therapy takes tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes, expands them in the laboratory, and reinfuses them in far greater numbers, a step toward truly personalised cellular treatment. In August 2026, intismeran, a personalised mRNA vaccine built from the patient’s own tumour sequence, was combined with pembrolizumab in high-risk melanoma patients after surgery. The results were striking: a significant reduction in recurrence compared with pembrolizumab alone, making it the first positive late-stage trial of a personalised mRNA cancer vaccine, though survival data remain pending.
What still needs to change
All of these advances deliver their best results when treatment begins early. The more sophisticated our therapies become, the more clearly we see that they work best before the disease has spread. In India, awareness and referral gaps continue to push diagnosis toward advanced stages.
Recalibrating public health messaging to reflect how melanoma actually presents in Indian patients is a start. Faster pathways from primary care to specialist centres matter equally. More fundamentally, India needs a national melanoma registry, stronger epidemiological and genomic data, more clinical trials in Indian patients, and deeper international collaboration. The advances of the past decade are genuinely extraordinary. Whether they reach the patients who need them comes down to one thing: a diagnosis early enough to act on.
(Prof. Jyoti Bajpai is director – medical precision immuno-oncology, Apollo Hospitals, Mumbai & Western Zone. drjyoti_ba@apollohospitals.com)

Shehzad Poonawalla set to join Prime Video's 'Rise and Fall' Season 2 after BJP exit
The politician's participation in the Prime Video show was confirmed after a trailer for the second season aired online on social media.
Former BJP spokesperson Shehzad Poonawalla is set to join reality TV show ‘Rise and Fall.’ The politician's participation in the Prime Video show was confirmed after a trailer for the second season aired online on social media.
Poonawalla's participation in the reality TV show also comes after his exit from the Bharatiya Janata Party.
The political commentator quit the BJP earlier this year in August. Speaking to reporters, the spokesperson said he submitted his resignation after “long and hard contemplation."
“Due to pressing emergency financial and personal circumstances, I will move into the private sector, but wherever possible and in whatever format possible, I will continue to support the vision and work of Prime Minister Modi and the BJP,” he said. “I am only leaving the Vyavastha (organisation) not the Vyakti (people) or Vichar (ideology),” Poonawalla added.
Tehseen Poonawaalla also took to X to congratulate the former BJP spokesperson on his "new chapter."
"Dearest Shehzad, here is wishing you all the best as you embark on your new journey in "Reality Television entertainment!". May you have all the "Rise" & may you never "Fall!". You genuinely were the best Spokesperson that I came across, much much better than me & may you RISE, RISE, RISE and do much better than me on Reality TV. (that's not difficult!)," Poonawaalla wrote on X.
Rise and Fall Season 2 to air Sept 26
The new season for Prime Video's Rise and Fall is set to air on September 26, 2026.
Produced by Banijay Asia, the series will stream daily at 12pm on Prime Video and the MX Player Android app.
Along with Poonawaalaa, actress Swara Bhasker, reality television veteran Priyanka Chahar Choudhary and television actor Karan Patel will also be joining the show.
The second season will be hosted by cricket legen Virender Sehway, replacing Asheneer Grover.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday (September 17, 2026) said that there is no more a culture of cut-money in West Bengal. He made the statement in a virtual address after releasing the fourth instalment of the Annapurna Yojana to women beneficiaries in the State.
“The money is directly transferred in the bank accounts of the women, without any intermediary. Now there is no cut-money in West Bengal,” Mr. Modi said during a virtual address.
Cut-money refers to commission charged by local politicians to help citizens avail benefits of the government schemes. The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leadership, including PM Modi, had promised to stop this corruption in the election campaign of the Assembly elections in the State which the party won.
Speaking about the BJP government in West Bengal, Mr. Modi said that the government believes in “speaking less and working more”.
The Prime Minister, who was addressing the event on his 76th birthday, also added that no eligible women will be deprived of the benefits of Annapurna Yojana in West Bengal. Mr. Modi released the fourth instalment of the cash transfer scheme of ₹3,000 to around 1.5 crore women beneficiaries in West Bengal.
“Within a few days of forming our government in Bengal, work began on the Annapurna Yojana. Today, many women receive financial assistance directly into their bank accounts.... Our government aims to ensure that not a single eligible woman is deprived of the benefits of Annapurna Yojana,” he said in the virtual address.
Mr. Modi said that the Annapurna Yojana is an important effort to strengthen the confidence of Bengal’s women and added that he believes that the women of the State should have both the power to make decisions and the courage to move forward.
Annapurna Yojana was promised by the BJP during the campaign for the West Bengal Assembly polls. The promise was to counter Trinamool Congress government’s Lakshmir Bhandar scheme where over 2.2 crore were getting ₹1500 per month.
After coming to power in May 2026, the BJP government started verification of beneficiaries, something which was criticised by the opposition as a diversion from what the BJP had promised. The Lakshmir Bhandar was a universal scheme, whereas Annapurna Bhandar has an eligibility criterion. There have been some protests with women claiming that they are being denied benefits of the scheme despite being eligible.
The Prime Minister said that the people of Bengal have been deprived of the benefits of many central schemes for a long time. “The BJP is taking forward all the stalled schemes after coming to power,” Mr. Modi said, adding that more than 50 lakh families will be identified and given pucca houses.
“We will all build a new Bengal together,” he added.

NEW DELHI: The Election Commission on Friday told the Supreme Court that over 37 lakh appeals against the deletion or inclusion of names in West Bengal electoral rolls under the Special Intensive Revision remain pending.The poll panel told the apex court in its response affidavit that tribunals appointed by the court have disposed of only about 1.02 lakh of the 38.20 lakh appeals filed so far.This comes after a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymala Bagchi and V Mohana sought the poll panel's response to a plea seeking disclosure of assembly constituency-wise data on claims and objections filed by voters whose names were deleted during the SIR exercise.A total of 38,20,683 appeals had been filed against orders relating to the SIR of electoral rolls. Of these, 1,02,231 appeals had been disposed of, leaving 37,18,452 pending, the poll panel said.The affidavit, however, did not provide a break-up of the appeals filed by electors whose names were deleted and those filed against the inclusion of names in the electoral rolls.Prasenjit Bose, who filed the affidavit, claimed that more than 58 lakh electors were excluded during the enumeration phase of the SIR exercise in West Bengal.
He added that while 9.64 lakh applications for inclusion (Forms 6 and 6A) and over 99,000 applications for deletion (Form 7) were received during the claims and objections phase, only around 1.82 lakh additions were reflected in the final electoral roll published on February 28.On August 25, the top court directed the Election Commission to submit data on the pendency and disposal of appeals before tribunals challenging exclusion or inclusion in electoral rolls.Observing that these appeals needed to be adjudicated in a time-bound manner, the bench had asked the poll panel to explain what steps were being taken to streamline the mechanism for disposing of pending appeals and how many additional tribunals were required.
The EC data submitted to the court showed that 34.13 lakh Form 6 applications had been filed between December 17, 2025, when the draft electoral roll was published, and August 7, 2026.Form 6 is the statutory application for inclusion of a name in the electoral roll.On April 24, the apex court asked the appellate tribunals to give out-of-turn hearings to those who made a case for urgent hearing against deletion from electoral rolls after the SIR.Approximately 700 judicial officers from West Bengal and neighbouring Odisha and Jharkhand were deployed to deal with around 60 lakh claims and objections.Later, the chief justice of the Calcutta high court, on the direction of the top court, set up 19 tribunals headed by former high court chief justices and judges to decide the appeals.

Manitoba adopts permanent daylight time after survey suggested overwhelming opposition to clock changes
More than 90% of 72,000 Manitobans who voted in online survey wanted to ditch twice-yearly changes: province
Manitobans no longer need to remember to spring forward or fall back one hour on their clocks.
Daylight time will be in place permanently, Premier Wab Kinew announced in a news release Thursday.
This change means clocks will not revert to standard time on Nov. 1.
Manitoba joins several other provinces and territories that have adopted or are moving toward a permanent time, including British Columbia, Yukon, the Northwest Territories, Alberta and Saskatchewan.
Just six months ago, Kinew said his government was too busy with more important matters to consider changes to the clocks.
He was asked about it in early March, shortly after B.C. announced it intended to remain on daylight time permanently.
He later softened his stance, suggesting it may be time to revisit the issue for Manitoba.
In April, Alberta announced plans to table legislation to cement a move to permanent daylight time. Days later, the Northwest Territories said it will also end time changes. Yukon has been on permanent time since 2020 and Saskatchewan since 1966.
In May, Manitoba launched a survey, asking the public to weigh in the issue. For those who did want to see the twice-annual changes halted, the survey asked if they preferred to stay on standard or daylight time.
In its news release at the time the survey launched, the province included a link to an analysis by Manitoba Health, which concluded that eliminating the time change would be better for population health.
On Thursday, the province said nearly 72,000 votes were submitted in its survey, with 92 per cent of respondents saying they wanted to see an end to seasonal time changes. Among respondents, 58 per cent preferred permanent daylight time and 34 per cent sided with standard time.
Permanent daylight time is good for health, business and families with young kids, whose routines, especially sleep cycles, can be disrupted for days with those one-hour time changes, Kinew said in Thursday's news release.
The province is working with organizations, businesses and industry partners to adapt to the change, he said.
Manitoba enacted the Official Time Act, bringing provincewide daylight time into official effect on May 12, 1963. However, some cities, like Brandon and Winnipeg, had been experimenting with daylight time off and on since as early as 1916.
Under the Official Time Act, daylight time began on the first Sunday in April and went until the last Sunday in October, when clocks fell back to standard time.
Daylight time was extended in 2007, starting the second Sunday in March and continuing until the first Sunday in November, to match U.S. changes.

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.
